In our northern countries, most years, the weather is very cold during Sukkot, and there is no greater discomfort than this. Many times, one could get sick from sleeping there. Besides this, since it is established that one who is distressed is exempt from the sukkah, as I will write in Siman 640. According to our Sukkot, in the vast majority of cases, it is inevitable to feel distressed when sleeping in the sukkah, as we can see evidently. There is a very small minority who do not feel distressed sleeping in the sukkah. Therefore, the custom is to be lenient in this matter. Nevertheless, it is not called unsuitable for sleeping, as I wrote in paragraph 11. There is nothing more unsuitable for sleeping than a sukkah that is seven by seven [handbreadths]. However, since one can sleep there with difficulty, it is valid. And one who is genuinely distressed in this manner is exempt. However, one who fears the word of God should strive to sleep in the sukkah.

Maimonides writes in Chapter Six, Law 6: Eating in the sukkah on the first night of Yom Tov is obligatory. Even if one eats an olive-sized portion of bread, he has fulfilled his obligation. From then on, it is optional: If one wishes to eat a meal, he eats it in the sukkah. If he wishes, he may eat only fruits or roasted grains outside the sukkah for the entire seven days, and he fulfills his obligation as with eating matzah on Passover. This is the end of his words. According to his view, there is no obligation at all to eat bread on Yom Tov, except for the first night. And also in Chapter Six of Yom Tov, he did not mention eating bread at all on Yom Tov, but rather the enjoyment of meat and wine. Only in the chapter on Shabbat, Chapter Thirty, did he mention three meals with bread, but not on Yom Tov. This is also the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh in Sukkah (27a), but not so in Berachot (49b). The Ran in Sukkah there writes that there is an obligation to eat foods made from grains, but not necessarily bread for hamotzi. And the Jerusalem Talmud implies clearly in Sukkah there like the opinion of Tosafot and the Rosh in Sukkah, see there. And we have already written this above, in Siman 639, Section 3, see there. And the halacha seems to follow the opinion of the Ran, of blessed memory. Nevertheless, if one forgets "Ya'aleh Veyavo" in the Grace After Meals on Yom Tov, he must repeat it, as I wrote in Siman 188, see there, because even in the shortened blessing for the three festivals, we mention Yom Tov. (Also, the Or Zaru'a the Great in the laws of Sukkah, Siman 301, ruled like Tosafot in Sukkah. And so it is in the glosses there.)

Our Master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 3, ruled in accordance with the words of the Rambam. And our Master, the Rema, wrote about this that one should not eat on the first night until it is definitely night. And one should eat before midnight. And one should not eat during the day (on the eve of Sukkot) from midday onward, so that one will eat in the sukkah with an appetite, similar to the eating of matzah. Thus far his words. And the reason: since we derive it from matzah, we require it to be similar to matzah. However, regarding what he wrote that one should not eat on the eve of Sukkot from midday, he was stricter than with matzah, for there the prohibition is only from the tenth hour and above, as I wrote in Siman 471. And perhaps because here one can eat bread, he was stricter (see Magen Avraham, subsection 12). Also, what he wrote about eating before midnight is merely a stringency, for regarding matzah itself, the Rambam ruled at the beginning of the sixth chapter of Chametz and Matzah that it can be eaten all night. But since there are those who hold that matzah can only be eaten until midnight, he was therefore also stringent with the sukkah. And furthermore, he should have considered the fact that during all the days of the festival, a kezayit (olive-sized portion) is considered a casual meal, and one can eat outside the sukkah. But on the first night, it is considered a fixed meal, and it is forbidden to eat it outside the sukkah, as we derive from Pesach. And this is explicitly implied in the Jerusalem Talmud (see Taz, subsection 11).

He further wrote at the end of Section 5 that regarding rain, the first night has a greater stringency than the rest of the festival. For during the rest of the festival, if it rains, one leaves the sukkah and goes out. And if he does not go out, he is considered like an ordinary person, as will be explained. But on the first night, one must eat an olive-sized portion in the sukkah even if it rains. He should make Kiddush in the sukkah in order to recite "Shehecheyanu" on the sukkah. Thus is his language. This is also the ruling of the Tur and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), and the Ran also wrote, and this is his language: Others say that therefore we learn the first night of the festival from the festival of Passover, to say that even if it rains, one is obligated to eat in the sukkah, even though he is exempt on the other days. Thus is his language, and the same is written by the Rosh in Berachot (Chapter 7, Siman 23). However, the Rashba [in his novellae] (in his novellot) rejected these words. And he also wrote in the name of his teacher that there is no difference between the first night and all other nights. He also wrote in the name of the great sage of France, who required sleeping on the first night, even if it rains, at least a temporary sleep. And he rejected this, see there. The same was written by the Sefer Mitzvot Katan (SeMaK).

The reason for their dispute: Those who exempt (from eating in the sukkah when it rains) hold that we require "teshvu" – "you shall dwell," similar to the way you live in your home, and no one lives in a house where rain falls. And if you argue that it is compared to the Festival of Matzot (Passover) – it means that one should eat in the sukkah when it is fitting to sit in the sukkah, and even the first night does not depart from the rule of "teshvu" – similar to the way you live in your home. However, those who obligate (eating in the sukkah even when it rains) hold that the first night is not included in "you shall dwell in booths for seven days," which requires "teshvu" – similar to the way you live in your home. This applies to the entire festival, but the first night is derived from the comparison of the fifteenth day of Sukkot to the fifteenth day of Passover (as stated in Sukkah 27a). This verse is written at the beginning of the section in "Emor": "On the fifteenth day of this seventh month is the Festival of Booths for the Lord..." and it does not say here "you shall dwell," which requires similar to the way you live in your home. And where does it say "you shall dwell"? At the end of the section: "You shall dwell in booths for seven days." Therefore, for the seven days, we require similar to the way you live in your home, but not for the first night, whose obligation is from the beginning of the section, and it is an independent commandment to fulfill the mitzvah of sukkah, eating and sleeping, just as one is obligated to fulfill the mitzvah of eating matzah on the first night of Passover. Even someone who is distressed is obligated, and so too in the sukkah. Therefore, a kezayit (olive-sized portion) is sufficient, just as with matzah. And a brief sleep is sufficient, which is like eating a kezayit, which is a brief eating. The Torah decreed to fulfill this without conditions, even if one is distressed, and even if it rains. And thus the custom follows those who prohibit (eating outside the sukkah). Therefore, even a sick person who is distressed, if he can go to the sukkah to hear Kiddush and eat a kezayit, is obligated to do so. However, for sleeping, we do not practice this in the rain, even briefly, because in any case we are lenient with sleeping, as explained. Additionally, perhaps the comparison to matzah is only for eating like matzah, and not for sleeping, which does not apply to matzah. (According to what I have written, all the objections to those who prohibit are resolved.)

Regarding the blessing of "Leishev Basukkah" (to sit in the sukkah) on the first night when it is raining, it would seem that one should not recite the blessing, as it would be a situation of doubt regarding the blessing. However, from our teacher, the Rema, it is clear that one should recite the blessing, as he wrote that one should sanctify in the sukkah so that the "Shehechiyanu" blessing can be recited on the sukkah – thus it is evident that the blessing on the sukkah is recited. It appears that he holds in accordance with the opinion that obligates it, and according to what we have explained based on their reasoning, there is a basis in the text. Nonetheless, in practice, it seems to me that the custom is not to recite the blessing of "Leishev Basukkah" when it is raining. 

There is a practical difference regarding the second night as well, meaning if it rains on the second night: if one needs to recite the blessing on the first night where the law is clear, then one must also eat an olive-sized portion in the sukkah on the second night when it rains, due to the doubt of the day, similar to matzah. But if on the first night one does not need to recite the blessing because it is a doubtful situation of the law, then one does not need to sit in the sukkah on the second night when it rains to eat an olive-sized portion, since we are knowledgeable of the calendar. And the custom is not to sit in the sukkah on the second night when it rains. (This is also written by the Magen Avraham in subsection 15. See also Taz subsection 17, examine and you will find clarity.) And one who wishes to be stringent even on the second night – should eat an olive-sized portion in the sukkah, either after the meal or in the middle of the meal, and should not sanctify in the sukkah.

All seven days, one should read and study within the sukkah. And if he requires many books for his study, he should bring them into the sukkah. And even though this may be burdensome for him, nevertheless, he cannot exempt himself from the sukkah because of this. This is also included in "You shall dwell" — similar to how you reside. However, if due to the depth of his learning it is difficult for him to concentrate in the sukkah, he may study in his house, since this type of learning is not possible for him in the sukkah. And the reasoning is clear: if they said that one who is physically distressed is exempt from the sukkah, all the more so for mental distress regarding Torah study, since one's mind needs to be settled. Regarding prayer, there is no obligation at all to pray in the sukkah, for in this matter "similar to how you reside" does not apply, as he does not pray regularly at home but rather in the synagogue. Therefore, if he wishes, he may pray in the sukkah, and if he wishes, he may pray in his house. However, it is proper to pray in the sukkah if he has a comfortable place there where he can pray.

When it rains, one should enter the house. Just as one leaves the sukkah due to rain, so too in hot climates one leaves because of heat and mosquitoes, and in cold places due to wind and cold. Sometimes at night the wind extinguishes the candle, necessitating one to leave for their home. The general principle is: anyone who experiences discomfort is exempt from the sukkah. And anyone who is exempt from the sukkah and does not leave does not receive a reward and is called a fool, as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Shabbat, that anyone who is exempt from something and does it is called a fool.

It seems to me that the reason is: even though there are things where a person can be stringent with themselves, nevertheless, it all depends on the situation. For example, with the sukkah, the Torah said "dwell" – similar to how one would live in their home, and therefore if it is not similar to living in one's home, it is not a sukkah at all. A person would not sit in their house if it rained or for other reasons. Therefore, this is not the sukkah that the Torah commanded, and there is no greater fool than this. How can one receive a reward for this? After all, they are not sitting in a sukkah as commanded by the Torah. All the more so, one should not enter the sukkah when they are exempt from it.

However, when one leaves the sukkah due to rain, they should not leave angrily or in frustration, but rather with great humility, like a servant who comes to pour a cup for their master, and wants to mix the wine with water, and their master pours the pitcher of water on their face. (And the “Makor Chaim” explained this that the water sweetens the red wine, which is an allusion to mercy sweetening judgment, and it is not allowed from the heavens. And it is said that this applies to the Land of Israel.)

What is the measure of rain that necessitates leaving the sukkah? Initially, the rain falls on the sukkah's covering (schach) but has not yet entered the sukkah itself. When is it permissible for one to leave the sukkah and go into the house? It is when enough drops fall into the sukkah onto the table, such that if they were to fall into a dish, it would spoil the dish. Even a dish of beans, which quickly spoils, is used as a measure. And even if there is no dish before him, we still use this measure, for the sages determined that with this amount, the commandment to "dwell" in the sukkah, similar to how one resides in their home, is no longer fulfilled. Someone who is not skilled in determining this measure should estimate for themselves: if they would leave their house because of such rain, they should also leave the sukkah. It has already been explained that this applies to the other days and nights of the festival. However, on the first night, it is an obligation to recite Kiddush and eat in the sukkah even when it is raining.

And know that there is a doubt regarding our built sukkahs, where we remove the roof and during rain we replace it. The usual practice is to replace it immediately when the rain begins to fall, because if it remains open until the rain starts dripping inside the sukkah, a lot of rain will collect on the schach (roof covering) and drip afterwards, nullifying the mitzvah of sukkah. However, if rain begins to fall at the start of the meal, in a way that one can finish the meal even if it remains open, is it permitted to replace the roof immediately so that the rain does not collect and nullify it later? Or perhaps the mitzvah of the moment takes precedence, and one should not replace it until after finishing the meal, to ensure eating in the sukkah now? And if later this would nullify the sukkah, he is exempt. This seems to be the appropriate ruling, but the common practice is not so. Perhaps, as our Sages said: "Desecrate one Sabbath so that he may keep many Sabbaths" regarding someone dangerously ill; here too, it is better to nullify this meal in the sukkah to ensure many meals in the sukkah later. However, on Hoshanah Rabbah, if it begins to rain during the meal, do not replace the roof; since there is no Torah requirement to eat in the sukkah anymore, do not nullify a Torah commandment for the sake of the Shemini Atzeret meal, which would prevent eating in the sukkah.

And similarly with sleep: One who was sleeping in the sukkah and rain began to fall – he goes to his house to sleep. And in this case, it is more lenient than eating, for with eating, one needs to estimate whether the food will be ruined, but with sleep, there is no need for such an estimation, for even a small amount of rain is distressing for someone sleeping there, and he may leave. Therefore, as soon as some drops fall on his bed, he leaves his sukkah and sleeps in his house. And also, one should not be stringent in this matter, as he would be considered a simpleton, unless he is not bothered at all by a few drops.

One who went in the middle of his meal to his house because of rain, and the rain stopped while he is still in the middle of the meal – in any case, he is not required to return to his sukkah and can finish his meal in his house. Similarly, if he was sleeping and it rained at night, and he went inside to sleep in the house, and the rain stopped: if he has not yet lain down on his bed in his house, he must return to the sukkah, just like one who has not yet lain down, who is obligated to sleep in the sukkah. But if he is lying on his bed, the sages did not trouble him to return to his sukkah for the rest of the night, even if he wakes up during the night. He remains in his house until dawn, meaning until daybreak, and he wakes up naturally, then he is obligated to go to the sukkah if he wants to sleep further. The reason for this, it seems to me, is that everything is included in "you shall dwell" (in the sukkah) – in the manner of living. It is not customary for a person, when eating outside his house, to interrupt his meal and go home to finish it. Nor is it customary for a person, when sleeping outside his house, to get up in the middle of the night to go home to sleep. Rather, he waits until the day breaks and he wakes up from his sleep. Similarly, one must conduct oneself in the sukkah.

There is a doubt as to whether this law also applies to our constructed sukkahs, where we open the roof and during rain we close it. If one started a meal and it began to rain, and he closed the roof, and then the rain stopped—does he need to open it again in the middle of the meal, just as he is not required to leave his home for his sukkah? Similarly, in the middle of the night while sleeping, if the rain stops—is he required to get out of bed and open the roof, just as he is not required to leave his home for his sukkah? Or perhaps, since there is no change of place, but merely a slight inconvenience in opening the roof, he is required to do so, even in the middle of a meal or sleep. And this seems to be the primary ruling: that he is required to open the roof. However, in the case of sleep, if it is difficult for him to rise, dress, and wash—this is akin to walking from his home to his sukkah, and he is exempt. But any God-fearing person will certainly rise joyfully to open the roof and fulfill the mitzvah. This is not similar to entering from his home, which is considered foolish, as there is no change of location.

According to the Talmudic law (Sukkah 46a), one must recite the blessing "to dwell in the sukkah" each time they enter it, because the commandment is to dwell in the sukkah, beyond just eating and sleeping. This is as it is written: "You shall dwell in booths," meaning you should remain there for seven days. Similar to the commandment of wearing tefillin, where one blesses each time they put them on. Therefore, even if one enters and exits their sukkah ten times a day, they are obligated to bless "to dwell in the sukkah" each time, because once they leave the sukkah, the previous blessing becomes void. However, this applies only if one leaves for a significant purpose and does not intend to return immediately. But if one only leaves to speak with a friend or to bring something to the sukkah, or similar cases, they do not need to bless again. This is also the ruling of the Rif and the Rosh there. Similarly, the Rambam rules in the sixth chapter, law twelve, as follows: Whenever one enters to dwell in the sukkah throughout the seven days, they bless before sitting: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to dwell in the sukkah." Thus far is his wording. The reason for requiring "before sitting" will be explained in Siman 643 with the help of Heaven.

Indeed, Rabbeinu Tam ruled that one only needs to recite the blessing "to dwell in the sukkah" at the time of the meal. And this is the language of the Tur: "And Rabbeinu Tam explained: Since the primary establishment that a person makes in the sukkah is eating, one blesses over the eating and exempts all other activities, even sleeping, which is more stringent than eating. For one can eat casually outside the sukkah, but one cannot sleep casually outside the sukkah. Even so, since eating is primary, it exempts the rest." So ends his language. Likewise, the Rosh and the Mordechai in his name wrote that since all activities are subsidiary to eating, like walking and sleeping, therefore, they are all exempted by the blessing over eating. And they wrote that the custom is according to Rabbeinu Tam. Therefore, Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 8: "The custom is not to bless over the sukkah except at the time of eating." So ends his language. And Rabbeinu Rema added: "And this is the custom." I do not know what he added to the words of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef. 

There are those who hold that according to Rabbeinu Tam, there is a stringency: if one sat in his sukkah all day and ate twice, he should bless over each meal (Bach, and Taz paragraph 20). And there are those who disagree (Levush and Magen Avraham paragraph 17), and this seems to me to be the main point. For the method of Rabbeinu Tam is not to be stringent over the previous method, but to be lenient. And since according to the previous method, one does not need to bless at the second meal, all the more so according to Rabbeinu Tam. And so is our custom, and certainly, in the case of doubt about blessings, we are lenient. And if one is uncertain whether he blessed "to dwell in the sukkah" or not, he should not bless, nor should he strive to bring himself to a state of obligation, so that he does not transgress with a blessing in vain (see Shaarei Teshuvah paragraph 18). 

And nowadays, some have the custom to bless every time they enter, according to the words of the Rif and the Rambam (according to the opinion of the Gra). But we only follow the words of our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch. And the measure of eating is when one eats something that requires a sukkah, that is, when one eats more than the size of an egg of bread or sweet foods of the mezonot type, then one needs to bless.

And know that it initially seemed clear to me that even according to the opinion of Rabbeinu Tam, this only applies to one's own sukkah. But if one enters to sit in his friend's sukkah, he should not eat there, and blessing for his own sukkah would not exempt another sukkah. If so, he must bless when entering his friend’s sukkah. This is not the custom. And perhaps this is the intention of Rabbeinu the Rema when he wrote: "And this is the custom." Meaning: even in his friend's sukkah. The reason is that we hold that the essence of the mitzvah is eating, and we only bless on the essence of the mitzvah. See what I will write in Siman 643. It is simple that if in the middle of the meal he went to another place and stayed there, and returned to the sukkah to eat, he must bless "to sit in the sukkah" again (Magen Avraham, end of Se'if Katan 17). And if he did not bless at the beginning of the meal, he should bless in the middle, and even after the meal, for at any rate, the sitting is also part of the mitzvah (there). And since he did not bless at the main part of it, he should bless at least at the secondary part, and it is still considered "before performing the mitzvah."

The sages taught in the Mishnah (Sukkah 28a): Women, slaves, and minors are exempt from the sukkah. For every positive commandment that is time-bound, women are exempt. Slaves are compared to women, and minors are exempt from all commandments. In other positive commandments, such as the shofar and the lulav, the Tanna did not need to inform us of this, since it is taught in Kiddushin (34a) that women are exempt from time-bound positive commandments, it follows automatically. However, regarding the sukkah, one might have thought that they are obligated, and not just on the first night, which we learn from the comparison of "the fifteenth" to "the fifteenth" from the Festival of Matzot, as I wrote in the previous section, and women are obligated in matzah, so one might say they are also obligated in the sukkah on the first night. But even for all seven days, since it is written "you shall dwell" as you dwell at home – and what is dwelling? A man with his wife and children – we would obligate them in the sukkah. However, in this matter, a specific halacha was given to Moses at Sinai (Sukkah 28a) that women are exempt. This is also hinted at in the verse, as it is written: "Every citizen in Israel shall dwell in sukkahs," and it does not say "every citizen." This comes to teach that only the principal citizens, meaning adult men, are obligated, not women and minors (Sukkah 28a).

However, our women—many of them sit in the sukkah and recite the blessing "to sit in the sukkah." And this is not a blessing in vain, for it is established for us to say regarding every positive commandment that is time-bound: they have permission to perform the mitzvah and bless over it. But a man should not recite the blessing "to sit in the sukkah" on behalf of a woman if he himself does not need the blessing (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). And a minor, although from the Torah he is exempt, nevertheless, due to the mitzvah of education, one must educate him to eat in the sukkah from the time he no longer needs his mother, which is around five or six years old, depending on each child's sharpness. And the responsibility of education lies on the father. If there is no father, the mother educates him. If he has neither father nor mother, the court educates him. Some say that education is only the father's responsibility, see what I wrote above in Siman 643. In any case, to initially feed him with one's hands outside the sukkah is not proper (ibid., subsection 3). I do not understand why people are not careful about this in our times. Perhaps it is because in our country, it is usually cold during Sukkot, and it is difficult for the minor to eat in the sukkah; this requires further examination. A tumtum (one with indeterminate sexual characteristics) and an androgynous (one with both male and female sexual characteristics) are obligated out of doubt, but they do not recite the blessing "to sit in the sukkah" because in cases of doubtful blessings, we are lenient. However, since women recite the blessing, as I have written, they can bless. And someone who is half-slave and half-free is obligated and recites the blessing, for the half that is free is certainly obligated. A minor who is obligated in education blesses.

The sick and those who attend to them are exempt from the sukkah. And it is not only a dangerously ill person, but even if it is not life-threatening, if the sukkah is difficult for him, and even if he has a headache or eye pain, which is a minor ailment and not a full illness, he and his attendants are exempt when the sukkah exacerbates this ailment. And some say that his attendants are only exempt when the sick person needs them. The reason that attendants are exempt: some say it is because one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah (Levush and the Gra). This does not seem correct to me: this reasoning applies if one is serving for free as it is for the sake of a mitzvah, but if one is being paid, they should be obligated. We do not find this distinction in the Talmud and the Poskim (decisors). Additionally, if the reason is because one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from another mitzvah, what is the reasoning of the first opinion that exempts them even when they are not actively engaged in the mitzvah?

And it seems to me: that this all falls under the general principle of "teshvu" – similar to the way you dwell. Just as a person who finds his residence detrimental to his health leaves his residence, so too with the sukkah. And just as those attending to a sick person leave their home and sit with the sick person, so too with the sukkah. And even if they are doing so for payment, they are no less exempt than fruit guards, as will be explained. The sukkah is no more important than a person's residence. Therefore, the first opinion holds: just as it is customary for attendants not to leave the sick person immediately after attending to him, but rather stay with him and converse with him as people do, and do not immediately return home – so too with the sukkah. And the other opinion holds: that in any case, once he has finished attending to the sick person – why should he not fulfill the mitzvah of sukkah? This is not included in the principle of "teshvu" – similar to the way you dwell.

Our teacher, the Rema (Rabbi Moses Isserles), wrote in paragraph 3 that one who lets blood is obligated in the sukkah. This is his language. And this ruling is from the glosses of the Rosh (chapter two). The reason given is: because he is not considered sick, but on the contrary, he is happy and increases in eating and drinking. Moreover, he shouldn't have let blood during the festival, but rather before or after it. This is his language. And the explanation is found in the Or Zaru'a HaGadol (Siman 299): it does not refer to a sick person who lets blood, but rather this was their custom to strengthen the body by letting blood. And at the time of letting blood – they were happy and increased in eating and drinking. Therefore, he is not considered sick to be exempt from the sukkah. Another proof that letting blood does not prevent one from the sukkah: if it did prevent him, he should not have let blood during the festival, since he does this willingly. But certainly, if someone lets blood due to some illness or ailment, and the sukkah is not comfortable for him – it is obvious that he is exempt from the sukkah. Therefore, one who has an upset stomach and takes a purgative drink, and finds it difficult to sit in the sukkah – is exempt from the sukkah. (And see Magen Avraham paragraph 4, who compared this to that, but it is not a comparison. He erred because he did not have the Or Zaru'a HaGadol. And the Taz paragraph 3 understood this correctly. See there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

One who is distressed is exempt from the sukkah. This means that if the sukkah causes him distress, and he would not have this distress if he were not in the sukkah, such as if he cannot sleep or eat in the sukkah due to flies or mosquitoes, or because of the wind blowing there, or because of a bad smell reaching there, he is exempt. Even if this does not cause him any illness, it is still included in the principle of "you shall dwell" in the sukkah as you reside in your home. It is not customary for a person to live in a dwelling that causes him distress, and he would leave it. Here too, he leaves his sukkah. However, on the first night, even if he is distressed, he is obligated to eat an olive-sized portion in the sukkah. As we have already explained in the previous section, paragraph 17, on the first night we do not require "you shall dwell" as you reside in your home. See there.

He is exempt only himself, and not his attendants, for attendants are only relevant in the case of a sick person, who necessarily requires them to assist him. But a healthy person—his attendants are not like him. For if it were not so, a wealthy woman who has many attendants would exempt all of them from the sukkah because she sits outside the sukkah and they are attending to her. And here, it is the same. This is not similar to the case of the fruit guards, where it is necessary to guard the fruit so that they are not stolen. But attendants for a healthy person are only for general comfort. And because of this, should they be exempt from the sukkah? This is astonishing.

And specifically, this applies when the discomfort arises from a different incident after the sukkah was made, and at the time when the sukkah was made, this discomfort was not present. However, it is forbidden to initially build the sukkah in a place where one will experience discomfort due to wind, odor, or in a location with flies and fleas. Furthermore, our master the Rema wrote in section 4 that if one constructs the sukkah in such a place, it is not considered a sukkah at all, and one does not fulfill their obligation with it. His words are: "And if one originally made it in a place where one would be distressed in eating, drinking, or sleeping; or if it is impossible to do any of these in the sukkah because one fears robbers or thieves while in the sukkah - one does not fulfill their obligation with that sukkah at all, even with matters that do not cause distress, as it is not considered like a dwelling where one can perform all their needs." Thus far his words.

And his words need explanation: If so, in hot climates where flies are found everywhere, and conversely in cold climates where the cold is severe and it is almost impossible to sleep there, should we exempt ourselves completely from the sukkah? However, the matter is as follows: The Torah said "you shall dwell" – in a manner similar to how you live, meaning the sukkah should be like one's house and residence. It is well known that a person who makes a residence for himself seeks out the most suitable place. If there is a suitable place and an unsuitable place, he will choose the suitable place. But if all places are unsuitable, he is compelled to make a residence however he can. Similarly, with a sukkah: if all places are unsuitable due to heat or cold, it is obvious that one is obligated to make a sukkah however he can. However, when he has the option to choose, such as if in one place there is wind, bad odor, or flies and fleas, and in another place they are not found, he is obligated to make it in the place where they are not found. And if he made it in a place where they are found, he has not fulfilled his obligation, for this is not similar to how one lives. Therefore, one should not make a sukkah in the public domain, for a person does not make his residence in the public domain. However, in an alleyway it seems permissible, for even though there is concern that thieves might steal the belongings, it is still considered a residence, as he can bring them into the house. And indeed, thieves are also found in courtyards. And what our master the Rema wrote, that in a place where one fears robbers or thieves he does not fulfill his obligation, this is when there is a concern that they might harm him physically, for such a place is certainly not fit for sleeping at all. But not because of theft of belongings.

He also wrote: If someone's candles in the sukkah went out on Shabbat, and he has a candle in his house – it is permitted to leave the sukkah to eat in the place where there is a candle. He does not need to go to his friend's sukkah where there is a candle, if it is a great burden. This is his exact wording. And it implies that if it is not a great burden, he should go to his friend's sukkah if possible, and his friend allows it. Therefore, if it is raining in his sukkah, and it is not raining in his friend's sukkah – he should go there if it is not far from his house, and it does not involve great effort (Ba'er Heitev, subsection 6, in the name of Shevut Yaakov).

Additionally, he wrote: If a wind comes to extinguish the candles in the sukkah, it is permitted to spread a sheet or garment from the side, but not under the s'chach (the covering of the sukkah). Thus are his words. And on Yom Tov, it is forbidden even under part of the s'chach, because of the prohibition of making a tent. And on Chol HaMoed, it is forbidden under all the s'chach, because it nullifies the s'chach. There are several specific laws regarding this matter: also regarding the tent, which are explained in Siman 315, and also regarding the nullification of the s'chach, which are explained in Siman 639. (And see Magen Avraham, section 1, that if one intends to protect, it is permitted, although there are differing opinions on this matter. And regarding the tent, when there is no space of a tefach (handbreadth) - it is certainly permitted, see there.)

He also wrote: One who cannot sleep in the sukkah because there is not enough space to stretch out his hands and feet is not considered distressed and is obligated to sleep there, even though he needs to bend his hands and feet. Thus is his language, and there is clear proof of this from the measurement of the sukkah, which is seven by seven, and it is impossible to sleep there with outstretched hands and feet. And one cannot say that this measurement is for eating, but for sleeping, a larger sukkah is required, because if so, it would have been explained in the oral law how large it should be. And there is someone who says that if initially a small sukkah like this was made, he is obligated to sleep there. But if initially a large sukkah was made, and afterwards, due to some reason, it became smaller, and he is forced to sleep with bent hands and feet, he is considered distressed and is exempt (Taz, subsection 5). And from this, he questioned our teacher, the Rema, see there. And I say that the words of our teacher, the Rema, are clear in their reasoning. For if you think that in such a case he is considered distressed and exempt, how could the Torah command to make such a sukkah? Rather, it is certain that for most people, this is not considered distress. And this is what our teacher, the Rema, wrote afterwards, and this is his language: A person cannot say I am distressed, except in a matter that people usually feel distressed about. Thus is his language, and his intention is regarding this matter of sleeping with bending, because since we see that the Torah commanded thus, presumably most people do not feel distressed by this. But for other matters, certainly there are things that for this one are considered distress and for that one are not considered distress. As we find in the Gemara (29a) with Rav Yosef, in whose sukkah the wind was blowing and dropping twigs from the s’chach on the food, and he said he is exempt from the sukkah because he is fastidious and cannot endure this, see there. And it is obvious that not everyone can say: I am fastidious, unless it is known that he is fastidious. And as we wrote above in siman 614 regarding rain on Yom Kippur, who is permitted to wear shoes, see there. However, with sleeping by bending, he cannot say I am fastidious and distressed, as I have written. (And the Taz in subsection 6 was pressed by this, and according to what I have written, it is clear and simple. See Magen Avraham, subsection 9, and examine and you will find light.)(And the Chacham Tzvi disagrees with the Mordechai and the Rema, as brought in Shaarei Teshuva, subsection 5. And his words are not compelling at all, see there.)

It is clear that one who is distressed is exempt from the sukkah—this is when leaving the sukkah will alleviate the distress. However, if the distress is unrelated to the sukkah, even though it might be that the distressed person needs solitude, and in the sukkah this is not possible, and thus it would be better for him not to be in the sukkah; nevertheless, since the sukkah is not the cause of his distress, he cannot exempt himself from the sukkah. Therefore, a mourner is obligated in the sukkah, because this distress is not due to the sukkah. And although it might be better for him to sit quietly in a corner of his house, he is still obligated to sit in the sukkah. And an onen (one whose close relative has died but has not yet been buried) appears to be exempt from the sukkah, just as he is exempt from all commandments. (And the language of the Gemara 35b regarding a mourner is that he needs to calm his mind. Rashi explained: It is an obligation upon him to calm his mind for the mitzvah. This implies that if he cannot calm his mind in any way, he is exempt. It seems this is what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 10 in the name of Tanya, that if the deceased was so beloved that he cannot remove him from his mind, he is exempt, see there. And the Rashba in his novellae there wrote in the name of his teacher that the explanation is: The sukkah calms his mind, and if so, even in the case of a beloved one, he is obligated, see there. Therefore, the ruling of the Tanya requires further examination.)

The Tur writes that the Rambam wrote that the groom throughout all seven days of feasting is exempt from the sukkah, as well as his groomsmen and all the members of the wedding party. And my master, my father the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that the groomsmen are not considered as those engaged in a mitzvah and are obligated in all the mitzvot, etc. And although the groom is exempt from all the mitzvot, he is obligated in the sukkah, for it is possible for him to rejoice in the sukkah. So far his words. And in the Gemara (Sukkah 25b), it is explained according to the Rambam, but it is stated there that some were stringent upon themselves, and this is also found in the Jerusalem Talmud. The Rambam holds that this is an act of piety. The Rosh rules according to those who are stringent. And our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in section 6, ruled according to the Rambam. The reason for the groom's exemption is that there is no joy except in the wedding canopy and the place of the meal, and it is impossible to do this in the sukkah, which is an open place, and he would be embarrassed to rejoice there. And the groomsmen are required to be with the groom. It seems to me that all this was in their times. But nowadays, due to our many sins, all joy has diminished, and it is not customary for the groom to rejoice so much. Also, the groomsmen are not always with the groom. Therefore, we cannot exempt from the mitzvah of sukkah. Moreover, since it is by compulsion that he marries before the festival, and among us, we do not make meals for all seven days of feasting as is known. Therefore, among us, we maintain to say according to the Rosh, and the groom and the groomsmen are all obligated in the sukkah. And in my humble opinion, it seems that this was the main reason of the Rosh, of blessed memory, and see in the next section.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote that the meal of a brit milah, as well as the meal eaten in the house of the woman who gave birth, must be held in the sukkah. This is his language. And certainly, this is correct, for it is not like the joy of a bride and groom. Even if it is a mitzvah meal, nevertheless, it can indeed be held in the sukkah. Furthermore, the mitzvah meal refers only to the brit milah itself, not to the meal in the house of the woman who gave birth. We have no knowledge of such a meal at all. Similarly, the night before the brit milah, which is called "Vach Nacht," should not be considered a mitzvah meal exempting one from the sukkah. This applies to all other types of meals as well (Magen Avraham, subsection 13). However, I have seen that because of the multitude of people who cannot all fit into the sukkah during a brit milah, the remainder eat inside the house. It appears that this is a complete allowance, since they do not have a sukkah, making them like travelers who are exempt from the sukkah. It cannot be said that they should wait until the first group finishes eating and then eat, for such an idea is not found, and if so, there would be no end to it. Nevertheless, one who fears the word of God should strive to eat in the sukkah. All this applies to types of food that establish a meal. But with other types of food, we are not concerned, since it is not a fixed meal but only a casual eating (see Shaarei Teshuvah, end of subsection 10).

We learned in the Mishnah (Sukkah 25a): Those who are on a mission for a mitzvah are exempt from the sukkah. Those traveling for the purpose of a mitzvah, such as to study Torah, to greet their teacher, or to redeem captives (Rashi), are exempt even during their rest periods (ibid.). And as we learned in the Baraita there (Sukkah 26a): Those traveling for a mitzvah are exempt both by day and by night. This means: Even though their travel is only by day (Tosafot). The reason is: If we require them to exert effort to find a sukkah, they will be prevented from traveling during the day. Therefore, if they can find a sukkah at night without exertion, they should stay in the sukkah at night (Magen Avraham, subsection 14). And if they cannot sleep well in the sukkah, and because of this, their travel during the day will be diminished, they are exempt (ibid.). The reason that those on a mission for a mitzvah are exempt is that we hold the principle that one who is engaged in a mitzvah is exempt from [another] mitzvah. Therefore, if the mitzvah of the sukkah does not interfere with the mitzvah they are performing, they are obligated in the sukkah. Hence, all those engaged in mitzvot should know this and consider whether the sukkah will interfere with this mitzvah or not.

It was also taught (there): Travelers during the day are exempt from the sukkah during the day, but are obligated at night. Travelers at night are exempt from the sukkah at night but are obligated during the day. Travelers both day and night are exempt from the sukkah both day and night. Rashi and Tosafot explained that all this is derived from "you shall dwell" — similar to the way you live. Just as a person does not refrain from leaving his house for business or other matters, so too he should not refrain from leaving the sukkah. The explanation is: When one travels during the day, he is exempt from the sukkah, even if he encounters a sukkah, he is not obligated to stop there to eat. Rather, he continues on his way and eats on the road when it is time to eat. However, at night, when he does not travel but sleeps, he is obligated to sleep in a sukkah if he encounters one on his way at night. He should stay there and is not permitted to leave and sleep outside the sukkah. Travelers at night are obligated to eat in a sukkah if they encounter one during the day. But if they do not encounter a sukkah, they are exempt. We do not tell them to build a sukkah, just as they do not build a house on the road, so too they do not build a sukkah on the road. There is an opinion that one is obligated to build a sukkah (Magen Avraham, section 15). These statements are puzzling: Certainly, if one needs to stay in a place for a long time, it is considered like his home and he must build a sukkah. But if he only stays for a day or two, how can we obligate him to build a sukkah? (And this is why one who guards grain is obligated, because he stays there for many days, as will be explained.)

And so it is explained from the words of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 8, who wrote regarding this law, and this is his language: "And specifically when they can find a sukkah. But if they do not find a sukkah, they can go on their way, even if they do not sit in it neither by day nor by night, as on other days of the year, for one does not abandon one's journey because of one's home. And even though he only travels by day, he is exempt even at night, for he is not to make a dwelling there. And those who go to villages to collect their debts, and they do not have a sukkah in those villages, should be stringent with themselves and return to their homes every night to eat in a sukkah. And although it is permissible to be lenient, in any case, the one who is stringent, a blessing shall come upon him." So ends his language; meaning: those who regularly go to the villages surrounding the city, sometimes even throughout the year, return to their homes every night, and therefore, they should do the same during Sukkot. And this is included in "you shall dwell" – similar to how you live [the rest of the year]. Nevertheless, by law, it is impossible to obligate them because, most of the time, they do not return home except after many days (see Bava Batra 29b regarding merchants, etc., see there). Therefore, he wrote in the language of stringency, that it is appropriate to be stringent, because sometimes they do return every night. However, in any case, we learn from his words that there is no obligation to make a sukkah, but if one finds a sukkah, he is obligated to sit there.

City guards by day are exempt [from the sukkah] by day and obligated by night. City guards by night are exempt by night and obligated by day. This is when they need to patrol around the city (Magen Avraham, subsection 16). But when they guard within the city, they must go to the sukkah to eat. However, at night, if they are guarding, it is impossible for them to go sleep in the sukkah, since they need to stay on guard. If they doze off a bit, they must necessarily doze off outside, as is evident.

Those who sit in a shop, even though most of the time they eat in the shop, nevertheless during Sukkot they should eat in the sukkah since they live in the city. And there is an opinion that even if they live outside the city, they are obligated to make a sukkah in the city (there). And this is according to what is held in Section 17, that one who is on the road for several days needs to make a sukkah. But according to what I wrote there, it is not so unless he stays there for an extended period. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that Rabbi Huna was traveling and was thirsty, and he did not want to drink until he entered a sukkah; see there. This is a pious practice and not a legal requirement.

Watchmen of gardens and orchards are exempt from the sukkah, both by day and by night. And even though they stay there for a long time, because it is not feasible for them to make a sukkah. For if they make one, the thief will know that the watchman has a fixed place and will come and steal from another place. Therefore, if one is a watchman of a grain pile, where this concern does not exist, and he stays there for a long time, he is obligated to make a sukkah. He should make it in a place from which he can watch over the grain pile. And even though he cannot bring all his utensils there, nevertheless, he dwells there as he does all year (there). Those who make wine with a non-Jew during Chol HaMoed Sukkot should not sit in the sukkah, because they need to ensure that the non-Jew does not touch the wine. But if it is a situation where no guarding is needed, they are obligated. And if the wine is placed in a courtyard, it can be guarded from the sukkah.

Even though it is a positive commandment to make a sukkah, nevertheless, we do not recite a blessing at the time of its construction, "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to make a sukkah," as we do for circumcision and the redemption of the firstborn. The reason seems straightforward: two blessings were not instituted for one commandment. Therefore, for circumcision and the redemption of the firstborn, this is their blessing. But for a sukkah, which has a different blessing, "to dwell in the sukkah," no additional blessing was instituted. This is also the reason for tzitzit, tefillin, shofar, and lulav, for which we do not recite a blessing on their making. However, in Menachot (42b), other reasons are given. One reason is that since a sukkah made by a thief is also valid, it means we are not commanded on the making of the sukkah. Another reason is that this is not the completion of the commandment, as the completion is in the dwelling, and therefore we need to bless "to dwell in the sukkah" at that time. (And this reason can be aligned with the reason we explained; consider this carefully and you will find it easy to understand.)

Indeed, in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berachot, Chapter Nine, and the first chapter of Sukkah (Halacha 2), it states: One who makes a sukkah for himself says: "Blessed... who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to make a sukkah." For another: "to make a sukkah for His name." When he enters to sit in it, he says: "Blessed... who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to sit in the sukkah." And it is puzzling: First, it says that a sukkah of Ganevach is valid, so how can he bless "to make a sukkah"? However, it appears to me that the Jerusalem Talmud follows its own reasoning: that in an old sukkah, one must renew something for the sake of the mitzvah of sukkah, as I wrote in Siman 636, and the same applies to a sukkah of Ganevach. And our Talmud, which does not require anything new, as I wrote there, therefore does not require a blessing at the time of making. And the Jerusalem Talmud, which requires some renewal for the sake of the mitzvah of sukkah, requires a blessing at the time of making. And we follow our Talmud.

However, the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" at the time of making [the mitzvah item] is required both in our Talmud, the Jerusalem Talmud there, and the Tosefta at the end of Berakhot; see there. And the reason it is not required at the time of making the shofar is because it is for many years. But the sukkah, most of it is made every year (Magen Avraham). Nevertheless, our custom is not to recite "Shehecheyanu" at the time of making [the sukkah], but rather we incorporate it into the Kiddush, where we recite "Shehecheyanu" for the holiday, and thereby fulfill the obligation of "Shehecheyanu" for the sukkah.

The Tosafot and the Rosh wrote that if one recited the Shehecheyanu blessing at the time of constructing the sukkah, he does not need to recite it again during the Kiddush. This is puzzling, for the Kiddush is due to the festival. It must be said that they hold that the Shehecheyanu of the festival is also fulfilled beforehand, since the sukkah is being made for the festival (Beit Yosef). And if one did not eat in the sukkah on the first night, even though he recited Shehecheyanu in his house during Kiddush, nonetheless, the next day when he eats in the sukkah, he must recite Shehecheyanu for the sukkah, if he did not recite it at the time of its construction. There is someone who disagrees with this (Bach in his responsa, Siman 132). However, the main ruling follows the first opinion. And if he did not eat in the sukkah on the first day either, when he makes Kiddush in the sukkah on the second night, he should recite the blessing for the sukkah and then Shehecheyanu, as on the first night. The details of this law will be explained in Siman 641: whether the blessing for the sukkah should precede Shehecheyanu or vice versa, see there. (And see Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 2.)

Evening: One enters the synagogue and prays the evening service, recites the Shema with its blessings, and says "U'feros," "Vayedaber Moshe," and prays "Ata Vechartanu... on this Festival of Sukkot, the time of our rejoicing." The Sephardim say: "this holy convocation day." If it falls on Shabbat, one also mentions Shabbat, and says "Vayechulu" and "Magen Avot." Even though on the first night of Passover we do not say "Magen Avot" when it falls on Shabbat, this is because it is a night of watching. But for Sukkot, this does not apply. And even though the first night is derived from "the fifteenth"-"the fifteenth" from the Festival of Matzot, as I wrote in Siman 639, in this matter it does not apply, as is obvious.

When the holiday falls on Shabbat, we do not recite "Ma'ariv" to avoid the risk of tilting the candle during the recitation, as one is not accustomed to the liturgical poem. On the second night, which is the conclusion of Shabbat, the poem from the first night should be recited, and the poem for the second night is deferred. In Poznań, they recite the poem of the second night. At the end of Sukkot, it is explicitly indicated that the poem for the second night is deferred (see Magen Avraham). Note that some mistakenly use a new fruit during the Kiddush of the second night. This is an error, as this practice is only for Rosh Hashanah, since it is considered one single sanctity, and not for other holidays (see Magen Avraham, previous section 600). Some maintain this custom (Eliyahu Rabbah), reasoning that if one already recited the "Shehecheyanu" blessing when making the Sukkah, then one is exempt from reciting it during Kiddush, and thus the first night is not worse than before the holiday. Nevertheless, this is not the prevailing custom.

The order of Kiddush: wine, Kiddush, Sukkah, and then Shehecheyanu (the blessing for a new occasion). Now, regarding the precedence of Sukkah over Shehecheyanu: it is established in the Gemara (Sukkah 56a) that Sukkah comes before Shehecheyanu, even according to the law of the Baraita (Sukkah 46a), which states that these two blessings should be recited when one enters to sit in the Sukkah, and not at the time of Kiddush. The reason is that although Shehecheyanu is more frequent compared to Sukkah, nevertheless, Sukkah, which is an obligation of the day, takes precedence over what is frequent (Gemara). Certainly, for us, since we arrange the blessings over the Kiddush cup, there is another reason to prioritize Sukkah before Shehecheyanu, as the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: because Shehecheyanu applies to both the sanctity of the day and the mitzvah of Sukkah. Meaning: one needs to recite "Shehecheyanu" for the festival and for the Sukkah, for us who do not recite it at the time of construction. Therefore, it follows that Shehecheyanu should be recited last, so it applies to both. And for this reason, some say that on the second night, Shehecheyanu comes before Sukkah, as I will write in Siman (Chapter) 661. According to this, on the first night as well, if the Sukkah was already made and standing, one would recite Shehecheyanu and then Sukkah (Bach and Magen Avraham). Because in that case, Shehecheyanu is not needed for the Sukkah, the first night is like the second night. However, regarding this very law of the second night – there is much to investigate, and it will be explained there with the help of Heaven.

According to the fundamental law of the Gemara, one who enters to sit in the sukkah recites the blessing "to sit in the sukkah." Therefore, even on the other days, one must recite the blessing "to sit in the sukkah" before the blessing "hamotzi." And even according to the opinion we follow, which is the view of Rabbeinu Tam, that the primary mitzvah is the eating, and therefore one only recites the blessing before the meal, as I wrote at the end of Siman 639, nevertheless, since this is before eating, one must recite the blessing immediately (Beit Yosef). This is also the opinion of Maharam, the teacher of the Rosh. However, the Rosh writes that the common practice is not to do so, but rather to recite the blessing on the sukkah after the blessing "hamotzi" and before tasting, to indicate that the obligation is only on the eating. This is not considered an interruption between "hamotzi" and eating since it is necessary for the meal, similar to how Kiddush is not considered an interruption. This applies on Chol HaMoed, but on Shabbat and Yom Tov, one recites the blessing after Kiddush. If one is permitted to make Kiddush in the house and eat in the sukkah, this has already been explained above in Siman 273.

However, Rambam wrote in Chapter 6, Law 12: Whenever one enters to sit in the sukkah for all seven days, he blesses before sitting: "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to sit in the sukkah"... It turns out that he sanctifies while standing, blesses "to sit in the sukkah," and sits, and afterward blesses on the time. And this was the custom of my teachers and the rabbis of Spain, to sanctify while standing on the first night of Sukkot, as we have explained. This is his language, as he holds that "you shall dwell in booths" means actual sitting, and since one must bless before performing the mitzvah, it follows that he sanctifies while standing and then sits after the blessing "to sit in the sukkah." The Rosh objected to this, saying that certainly "you shall dwell" does not mean actual sitting, for if one were to eat while standing, he would not be obligated to bless. Rather, "you shall dwell" means to remain, as in "and you remained in Kadesh many days," and therefore even on the first night, one sanctifies while sitting, and blesses "to sit in the sukkah" while sitting, and so on all days. This is also considered blessing before performing the mitzvah before eating. And this is the custom of the world according to the Rosh. However, Rambam also clearly did not interpret "sitting" literally, but rather meant that through actual sitting, it is evident that one is fulfilling the mitzvah. For as long as one is standing, it is as if he is prepared to leave, which is not the case when he sits, as this indicates permanence. Therefore, one must bless before this (Taz, Small Paragraph 2). And our custom is like the Rosh (see Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Dvar Shmuel, that on other days when there is Kiddush, one does not bless "to sit in the sukkah" during Kiddush, but rather at the time of "Hamotzi." His words are puzzling, and one should not do so. And so our ancestors and teachers blessed after Kiddush, and one should not change this).

In the morning, one should go early to the synagogue (Tur), unlike on Shabbat, because on Yom Tov one goes slightly later (Megillah 23a), as I have written in Siman 529 (see Beit Yosef). The prayers are conducted up to "Barchu" like on Shabbat, and afterwards the Shema with its blessings is recited, followed by the Yom Tov prayer, and the chazzan repeats it. Piyutim (liturgical poems) are recited, each place according to its custom. "El Na Le'Olam Te'areitz" is not said on the first day (Magen Avraham), as it is only said where the piyut includes "Chai V'kayam" (Levush). For this reason, "Le'Olam Te'areitz" and "Le'Olam Tokadesh" are said. On the first day of Sukkot, this does not appear in the piyut. (The reason the Kalir did not compose this on the first day is because on the second day he composed the piyut on the mitzvah of the sukkah, where "B'Sukat Chai V'kayam" is said. On the first day, he composed the piyut on the four species, and it was not possible to say this. Therefore, he omitted it.)

After the Shacharit prayer, we recite the Hallel. Since during Hallel we shake the four species, it is necessary to bless over them before Hallel. We bless "on the taking of the lulav" and "Shehecheyanu." On the second day, we do not say "Shehecheyanu." And even though with the shofar we say "Shehecheyanu" on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, the lulav is not comparable to the shofar, for the blessing on the shofar is only on Rosh Hashanah itself, and therefore, due to the doubt of the day, we bless. This is not the case with "Shehecheyanu" for the lulav, for one can fulfill the obligation even before Sukkot, as I wrote in Siman 641. Therefore, the first day is not considered less significant than the day before the festival. And know: the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" on the festivals, if one did not bless on the first day, one blesses throughout the entire duration of the festival, as it is stated at the end of the third chapter of Eruvin. See there.

Throughout all eight days of the festival, one completes the Hallel, as each day is a distinct festival in itself, since they differ in their sacrifices. One recites the blessing "to complete the Hallel," whether in a congregation or individually. However, we always recite the blessing "to read the Hallel," as explained in section 488: because one might skip a word, see there. Some recite it in segments, waiting for the prayer leader. Others recite up to "Hodu" without interruption. According to their custom, so they should do. It is forbidden to interrupt with conversation in the middle of Hallel, even between sections. Its rules are as those stated regarding the recitation of the Shema: that in the middle, one asks out of fear and responds out of respect, and between sections, one asks out of respect and greets anyone. If one interrupts in the middle and delays even long enough to complete it all, they do not return to the beginning but to the place where they interrupted. This law is explained in section 65, see there. Even if one spoke in the middle, they return to the place where they stopped.

In Hallel, hearing is like responding. And an expert can fulfill the obligation for someone who is not an expert, provided that he listens well, word for word. And regarding hearing, we hold that two voices cannot be discerned simultaneously, and therefore one should only listen to one person. But with Hallel, our sages of blessed memory said (Megillah 21a): Even if ten people read it together, it is heard, because it is beloved to him. This is explained in Siman 588, see there. With the help of Heaven, the laws of Sukkah are concluded.

It is a positive commandment to take on the first day of Sukkot four species: an etrog, a lulav, hadassim, and aravot. As it is written: "And you shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a beautiful tree, branches of palm trees, a bough of thick trees, and willows of the brook." And tradition has conveyed that "the fruit of a beautiful tree" refers to the etrog, "branches of palm trees" refers to the lulav, "a bough of thick trees" refers to the hadas, and "willows of the brook" refers to the aravot. These derivations are also expounded in the Gemara. What is a lulav? It is the way of the palm tree that the lulav – which is the branch at the beginning of its emergence from the palm tree – grows entirely as a single shaft like an arrow. After it grows a bit, it begins to open slightly as the leaves start to separate, yet they remain attached to each other. The more it grows, the more the leaves stretch out, remaining all together. However, if they remain for a long time on the tree, the leaves separate from one another and spread out like the branches of the tree, distant from each other. If they remain even longer, the leaves harden and become like wood. This is the growth process of the lulav.

Our Sages taught in the Mishnah at the beginning of "The Stolen Lulav" (Sukkah 29b): "If its leaves were spread apart – it is valid. If its leaves were detached – it is invalid." And Rashi explained: "Spread apart" means that they are attached to the spine, but at the top they are separated from each other, like the branches of a tree. It is valid even if they are not bound together at the top. But if they are completely detached from the spine, such that they are not connected to the spine at all, and each one is separate on its own, even if they are bound together – it is invalid. However, the Tosafot did not explain "detached" in this manner, as this is obvious, but rather they explained it as follows: Each leaf of the lulav is doubled, and "detached" means that each leaf is split into two, but they are still attached to the spine, and it is invalid. And the Rif and the Rambam in the eighth chapter explained that it means they are loosened from the spine, but still somewhat attached to it, like the leaves of a palm branch. According to all interpretations, it is invalid.

If its leaves separated, it is kosher – even if all the leaves separated. “And if they were split” means if most of the leaves were split, it is invalid. Similarly, according to the explanation of the Tosafot: if most of them were split, meaning that the majority of the leaves were divided into two parts, it is invalid. And how are they divided? Lengthwise along the lulav, along most of the length of each individual leaf (see Beit Yosef). It seems to me that even if all the leaves on one side of the spine were split, it is invalid. However, if the majority of one side is split, in a way that overall there is a majority that is not split, it is kosher. And the fact that separated leaves are kosher – this is specifically when they have not yet hardened like wood, and it is possible to bind them together. But if they have hardened like wood, such that it is impossible to bind them together to be attached to each other, it is invalid. Similarly, if it is not possible to attach them to the spine, it is invalid. Even though separated leaves are kosher, it is still a mitzvah of the best quality to take a lulav which does not have completely separated leaves. And if he took separated leaves, it is proper to bind them, so that it will be more beautiful.

If the spine itself is broken and bent—not only if most of its width is torn and broken, which is invalid, but even if a small part is torn, yet as a result it bends and cannot stand—it is also invalid for all seven days, as it certainly is not included in the category of "hadar" (beauty) at all. However, if it is not broken, but due to its softness it bends slightly, one can bind it and it is valid. There is an opinion that wants to validate it when broken similarly to the breaking of the spine in an animal (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). This is not analogous at all, for there the spinal cord holds them. Additionally, in any case, this is not considered "hadar," so what relevance does this have? (And so has written Eliyahu Rabbah and Sha'arei Teshuvah.)

It is stated in the Gemara (32a): If the twin leaf is split – it is invalid. Our rabbis have debated what is the twin leaf. The Rif and the Rambam explained that it does not refer to a specific leaf, but to all the leaves of the lulav. This is because the natural form of lulav leaves is such that each leaf is doubled, and from the back they are attached, and from the front, they appear as two. It turns out that each leaf is like a twin, like twins. Therefore, if most of the lulav leaves are split along most of their length – it is invalid. But if only a minority are split, even if the upper leaves are split – it is valid.

And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "Two upper middle leaves, where the spine splits, and the spine cracks until the leaves below them." Thus is his language. And behold, in our lulavim, we do not find two middle leaves, but rather one leaf. And the Rosh brought Rashi's explanation, and it does not say "two upper leaves," but rather "upper leaves," see there. And why did Rashi specifically require that the spine be split? It seems because the Gemara said that if it is cracked, it is kosher, as will be explained, and therefore, necessarily, if it is split – it is invalid regarding the spine. And know that in Bava Kama (96a) Rashi explained "tiyomet": the middle upper palm – that is the tiyomet. Thus is his language. And it appears that this is also his explanation in Sukkah, and his intention is that the middle upper one is two leaves like a tiyomet. For it cannot be said that his intention is as we explain regarding the one middle leaf, which is doubled into two. For if so, how does he say that the middle one is a tiyomet? Is it not so that all the leaves of the lulav are like this? Rather, certainly their lulavim were of this pattern, that in their middle there were two equal upper leaves. And some have taken that Rashi's explanation in Bava Kama is not like his explanation in Sukkah, and so it appears from the words of the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 96). But in my humble opinion, it is not so.

The Tosafot and the Rosh also bring in the name of the Geonim that there are two upper leaves. They further state that these leaves are attached to each other, and if they are separated – the lulav is invalid. The Tosafot and the Rosh write that if this is the case – we would not find even one kosher lulav in five hundred! This means: even if we find lulavim that have two middle leaves, we still would not find them attached to each other. Therefore, they wrote that the intention of the Geonim is: if they were attached and then separated – it is invalid. But if they were never attached at all – it is kosher. 

According to this, in our lulavim, where there is no such thing as two middle upper leaves being attached, and even if they are not attached – they are not found. And for us, there is only one middle leaf. If it is split even mostly – we do not find it invalid according to the Rif and Rambam, for they hold that it is only when most of the leaves of the lulav are split in this way; nor according to Rashi, for even if we say that for Rashi one of our leaves is equivalent to their two leaves – in any case, he requires that the split be specifically in the spine; nor according to the Geonim, for they specifically require two leaves that are separated from each other. (And in the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot he wrote: that top part of the lulav, where they are attached to each other, etc. And the Tosafot assume that his intention is like the Geonim. But the Rosh wrote that his intention is like the Rif, and so it seems, see there. And in the Aruch entry "Tayom" he also brought the explanation of the Rif, but later he wrote in the name of Rav Hai Gaon, and this is his wording: the "tayom" they mentioned – are two sides: two attached in their creation, and one that is two halves divided from above and connected from below in any amount. This is his wording, and it is not understood at all. And in the book "Tamim Dayim" by the Ra'avad, Siman 232, he also wrote like the Rif, see there. And in the Jerusalem Talmud it is explicitly explained like the Rif and the Rambam, for it says there: if its leaves are spread out – it becomes like the split of the "tayom." This implies that in all the leaves it is similar to the spreading of its leaves. So wrote the Ran, and more will be explained on this matter.)

Regarding the law: Our master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 3, only brought the explanation of the Rif and the Rambam. And our master, the Rema, wrote, and this is his language: "And some explain that if the upper middle leaf on the spine splits down to the spine, this is called 'split the twin leaf,' and it is invalid. And this is the custom. However, ideally, the preferred mitzvah is to take a lulav whose upper leaf has not split at all, because there are some who are stringent even if it is slightly split. And if that leaf is not double from its inception, it is invalid." Thus far his language.

And behold, his words are taken from the words of the Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 96) who wrote: "It appears that one should follow one of Rashi's interpretations, etc., that the middle leaf which is usually double like other leaves splits into two, this is 'split the twin leaf.' And it is not called split until it splits below the leaves." And the Or Zaru'a added to be lenient, that it requires the spine itself to be split as well down to the leaves below it, and this is 'split the twin leaf' according to Rashi's interpretation. And Rabbi Yitzchak of Or Zaru'a wrote regarding this: "I rely on Rashi's interpretation for practical halacha." And the language of the Smak also implies to permit according to Rashi's interpretation. And I have also seen one of the great ones who would permit lulavim that were split at the top of the middle leaf to the width of a finger and more. Thus far his language.

And it is necessary to say with his intention, that he referred to Rashi’s explanation in Bava Kama there, and he had a different version before him. And this is what he wrote, "until it is split below the leaves," meaning: until the very end of the leaves and a bit below it. And the Or Zaru'a added to be lenient, that it is specifically when the spine is split until the end of the lower leaves. And I do not know why he attributed this to the Or Zaru'a, for it is explicitly stated in Rashi on Sukkah like this, and the Or Zaru'a wrote that he relies on Rashi's explanation. And according to this, it is specifically when the spine is split. And this is what he concludes, that he saw great ones who permitted those that are cracked at their tops the width of a finger or more – the owner of Berko that even much more, as long as the spine is not split. And our teacher, the Rema, held in his intention that even until the spine it is invalid. And I do not know from where we say this, for he follows the path of the Or Zaru'a. And the Or Zaru'a explicitly says that it is specifically when the spine is split. And our teacher, the Rema, did not hold like this, and it requires investigation.

Regarding the main issue, I am astonished, since for the Rif, the Rambam, the Raavad, the Bahag, and the Geonim, there is no invalidation if the single twin split, just like in our case. And according to Rashi's explanation in Sukkah, there is no invalidation if the spine did not split. This is also the case in Rashi's explanation in Bava Kamma. And even if you hold according to the Terumat HaDeshen that if the entire spine split it is invalid, how could one explanation of Rashi override his own explanation in Sukkah and against all these authorities? Moreover, it is explicitly mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud, as I have written. And even the Ran, of blessed memory, who brought this interpretation, immediately rejected it, only writing that it is proper to be stringent, see there. And the Rashba in Bava Kamma brings from Tosafot, who explained like Rashi in our Sukkah. The Rashba, the Ran, and the Maggid Mishneh themselves agree with the Rif and Rambam that it applies to all leaves, see there. And if so, even if we find such an interpretation in Rashi, why should we invalidate them? After all, in all Torah laws, we follow the majority. And here, there isn't even a single opinion against it, as Rashi in Sukkah also permits. What did our master the Rema see to be stringent in this matter? It requires investigation. (In the glosses of the Sefer Mitzvot Katan, it is found this way, and so what? It requires investigation.)

Therefore, it seems clear to me in my humble opinion: Certainly, since it was stated by our teacher, the Rema, one should not take a lulav whose central spine is mostly split when another can be found. However, if there is no other lulav available, such as in a village or similar situation, one should recite the blessing over it even on the first day, without any concern or hesitation, as this is the essential ruling. Particularly among us, the lulavs that come from Italy—most of them are split, but if the split is less than half, there is no issue at all.

If a lulav had single leaves from its beginning and did not have twin leaves, or if all its leaves were doubled on one side and the other side was bare without leaves, it is invalid. However, if there are leaves on the other side, but they are not doubled, it appears that if the majority of the leaves are doubled, it is valid. If not, it is invalid, as in all these cases we follow the majority of the leaves. And our teacher the Rema, who wrote that if the top middle leaf is not doubled from the beginning, it is invalid - this is all according to his opinion, as it is considered the teiomess and is the main one. But according to our other rabbis, this is not the case. And even according to his opinion that if it is split it is invalid, I still do not know where he derived that it is also invalid in this case. For it is understandable that if it is split, one could say it is not beautiful and it is not a complete taking, since the split is noticeable. But if it only has a single leaf that is not doubled, how do we know it is invalid? This requires further examination.

If the leaves are not arranged one on top of the other as is the case with all lulavim, but rather one below the other: if the tip of the lower leaf reaches the base of the leaf above it, so that the entire spine of the lulav is covered with leaves – it is valid. However, if the tip of the lower leaf does not reach the base of the leaf above it, or if it does not have many leaves one on top of the other, but rather from each side emerges one leaf lower down near its base, and it rises to its tip – it is invalid, because it is not considered beautiful. The language of the Gemara (Sukkah 32a) is: a lulav that has its leaves growing in a single row – it is blemished and invalid. All the rules in this section are included in this.
