But if there are two leaves on each side – it is valid. (And this that we wrote that it does not have many leaves – this is the language of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, section 4. It is not specifically required, but because this is the usual way of the lulav. Pay attention and you will find it simple.)

A lulav whose majority of leaves have dried out is invalid because it is not beautiful (hadar). Similarly, if the spine has dried out, even though the leaves have not dried out, it is invalid. However, this scenario is almost non-existent, as surely the leaves dry out before the spine (Beit Yosef). What is considered dry? When its green appearance has disappeared, and its surface has turned white. Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 5: "Some say that it is not called dry unless it crumbles with a fingernail due to its dryness, and this is the custom in these regions where lulavim are not readily available." Thus far his words, and this is a significant leniency: for surely, once the greenness has gone, it is called dry. One must be very careful about this (Taz, subsection 5). Especially now in our times, when many lulavim are brought in, and also in our country, lulavim and hadassim are grown – one should not bless on a lulav that has turned white, and certainly not on the first day which is a Torah obligation. However, in Siman 649 it will be explained that according to the Rambam, a dry lulav is kosher.

And it appears to me that if through soaking in water it returns somewhat to its original vegetable state, as we have seen with our own eyes – it is not considered dry, and is therefore kosher. For indeed, in all matters it is thus: regarding dried blood, if soaking it returns it to its moist state – its status is like that of moist, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 188, regarding the blood of a menstruant woman, see there. And similarly, we learned at the beginning of the seventh chapter of Niddah: "The flow, and the spittle, and the saliva, and the creeping animal, and the carcass, and the semen – they impart impurity when moist, and do not impart impurity when dry. And if they can be soaked and return to their original state – they impart impurity, etc.," see there. And similarly, in all matters that have changed – we follow the current state, as it is taught in Ohalot, chapter 2, Mishnah 8, and in Menachot (54a). And if because of the issue of rejection, if before the festival it returned to its original state – this is not considered rejection at all. And even on the festival itself – we hold that there is no rejection concerning commandments, as will be explained in section 646 regarding the myrtle branch, see there.

We learned in the Mishnah: If the tip is cut off, it is invalid because it is not beautiful (Rashi). The Rosh, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch in paragraph 6 explain that this means if most of the upper leaves are cut off, it is invalid. Tosafot wrote that it refers to the two middle upper leaves; see there. This applies to a lulav that has two central leaves, based on the lulavs they had which had two upper leaves, unlike our lulavs as I wrote in paragraph 6. In our lulavs, if the twin leaf, which is the upper central one, is cut off, it is invalid. This is the opinion of the Magid Mishneh in chapter 8, law 3, who wrote: "The correct view is that if the tip of the upper leaf, where the lulav ends, is cut off, it is invalid." This is what Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote in paragraph 6: "If the upper central leaf on the spine is cut off, it is invalid." However, if there is no other lulav available, one can still recite the blessing on it. This is his language. 

And they questioned him: He should have written it in the language of "some say," since according to the first opinion, it is only invalid if most of the leaves are cut off (Taz, paragraph 6). Additionally, they questioned him: The author of this opinion, that if there is no other lulav, one can still recite the blessing on it, is the Mordechai, who only wrote this regarding the hadas (myrtle). But regarding the lulav, the Jerusalem Talmud clarifies that it is invalid because it is not beautiful (Magen Avraham, paragraph 6). For in the case of the hadas, the Gemara concludes (34b) that even if all three leaves are cut, it is still valid, but not for the lulav. Therefore, for the lulav, if the tip is cut off, it is invalid all seven days (there).

And it appears to me that his words are correct. For even though the Tur wrote "the majority of leaves," and this is based on the words of the Rosh, nevertheless, in the Rosh himself, it is not so, as he wrote (beginning of Siman 2): "It seems that the interpretation is regarding the two middle upper leaves…", and it is difficult: for it says in the Gemara that if the twin leaves are removed, it is invalid. And even if the tips are cut off, it is invalid, all the more so if they are completely removed. And it must be said that "cut off" refers to the tips of the majority of leaves being cut off. The language is strained, and it can be said that "removed" is needed to teach us, for it might be thought that it is more aesthetically pleasing than cut off. Up to here are his words, and if so, his words are like those of the Tosafot. And there is no one who disagrees with this, for in the Mishnah, Rif, and Rambam it is stated simply that if the tip is cut off. And indeed, the words of the Tur are perplexing, as he wrote not according to the conclusion of the Rosh. Therefore, he did not write the language "some say," because he held that all agree on this. And he also held that the Mordechai is also referring to a lulav, and according to the opinion of the Rambam that will be explained in Siman 649, which permits a dry lulav. And the Maggid Mishneh wrote there that the Geonim relied on this, that a dry lulav, and one whose tip is cut off, and all invalidations – one can fulfill the obligation with them in pressing circumstances, even on the first day. Up to here are his words. And it will be explained there. And if so, our master the Rema correctly said that if there is no other, one recites the blessing on it (Taz, Siman 7).

Cracked – it is kosher, and this refers to when the tips of the leaves are cracked (Rashi 32b). However, if two cracks are separated from each other such that they appear as two separate entities – it is invalid. This applies when most of the leaves have cracks separated from each other. Even if the upper twin leaf is intact and not split in a manner that would invalidate it according to those who hold that a split twin leaf invalidates – nonetheless, it is invalid. One should not ask: according to the Rif and the Rambam, when most of the leaves are split – it is invalid in any case. So why do we say that cracked is kosher? This is not a question, because when we say split, it specifically means when most of the length is split. However, cracked refers only to the tips, and therefore it is only invalid when separated.

If he has something like thorns on his spine, or if it is constricted and shriveled like an ill person, whose limbs are constricted and shriveled; or if they are contracted, which is also like a strong shriveling; or if he is bent forward, meaning he is strongly bent towards the spine, and his back becomes like a hunchback – he is disqualified. Similarly, if he is bent to the sides – he is disqualified, even if bent to one of the sides. But if he is bent backwards, meaning to the other side of the spine – he is fit, for this is his natural form.

If it is not naturally bent but rather its top is bent due to its softness, it is invalid. This applies specifically when the spine is bent. However, if the spine is straight but only the leaves at the top are bent, as is common with many lulavim, it is valid, whether they are bent in one direction or the other. The Rosh, of blessed memory, cherished those whose leaves were slightly bent, as this prevents the leaves from splitting, and the integrity of the middle leaf is maintained. Some say that this only applies if only the top leaves are slightly bent, but if all or most of the leaves are slightly bent, it is invalid (Levush and Magen Avraham). There are those who disagree with this (Taz, subsection 10). This specifically applies when only the tips of the leaves are bent. However, if all the leaves are bent downwards, it is invalid (ibid.). Some are also stringent even with those that are slightly bent.

There are places where they plant lulavim (date palm branches) and hadasim (myrtle branches) in vessels filled with soil inside the house, and they use these lulavim and hadasim for the mitzvah of the four species on Sukkot. There are those who are uncertain about this practice (Chayei Adam, Klal 151). In the Jerusalem Talmud, Orlah, Chapter 1 (end of Halacha 2), Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yannai states: A tree planted inside a house is subject to the laws of orlah (the prohibition of using the fruit of a tree during its first three years), but is exempt from tithes, as it is written: "You shall surely tithe... the produce of the field..." and a house is not considered a field. Thus, concerning orlah, even though it is written "when you plant any kind of fruit tree," nevertheless, a tree planted inside a house is still called a tree. Here with the four species, which are more than just trees, it is certainly not required, as it is written: "the fruit of beautiful trees, branches of palm trees," and we do not need it to be from your field (there). Similarly, it is taught in Menachot (84b) regarding bikkurim (first fruits): I only know about fields, but how do I know to include those grown on a roof, in a ruin, in a pot, or on a ship? The verse states: "the first fruits of all that is in your land," see there (see Mishneh LaMelech, Chapter 2 of the Laws of Bikkurim). If so, the custom of Israel is Torah, and they act correctly.

"The branch of a thick tree" – The Sages expounded (Sukkah 32b): that its branches cover its wood, meaning that it has many branches to the point that the wood is not visible, and this is the myrtle. And what is considered 'thick'? For example, when three leaves are positioned on one node (Gemara). This means: that three leaves emerge adjacent to each other in one circle, such that one is not lower than the other. This is what we call 'triplets'. However, if there are two leaves aligned opposite each other, and the third leaf is above them – this is not considered 'thick', but rather it is called in the Gemara 'a wild myrtle', meaning: it is not in its proper form. It is invalid even in a pressing situation, and it is invalid for all seven days."

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 3: "There is an opinion in the Gemara that it is valid with two leaves at the same level and one above them. Therefore, it is customary in these countries to initially use these myrtles that are brought, even though there are not three leaves on one stem. And there is someone who wrote that our myrtles are not called 'wild myrtle,' since they are two on top of two, and they are not like the wild myrtle mentioned in the Gemara. Therefore, it has become customary to be lenient as written by the Maharik and Maharai Isserlein in their responses." This is the end of his words, and we will explain his words with the help of Heaven.

In the Gemara there: What is the definition of "interwoven"? Rav Yehuda said: It is when three leaves grow from each node. Rav Kahana said: Even two leaves and one. Rav Acha the son of Rava sought out two and one because it was said by Rav Kahana. Mar the son of Amemar said to Rav Ashi: My father called such a myrtle a "wild myrtle". See there. The first opinion holds that in conclusion it is rejected and invalid. But in truth, a "wild myrtle" does not cease to be a myrtle, but there are better ones, similar to a foolish firstborn, who for redemption is considered a firstborn but not for inheritance. After all, it is still a firstborn, and the Torah calls it "firstborn". Here too, the term "interwoven" truly applies even to two. Evidence for this is from the breastplate and ephod, as it is written in the portion of Tetzaveh: "You shall make them twisted work," and Onkelos translated: "braided". And Rashi explained: The term for braiding and twisting is that which is intertwined with two, as it says in Yevamot (5b) "braid" means two. "Braiding" is also with two, as explained in the Rambam at the end of the ninth chapter of Shabbat, that "braiding" is a derivative of weaving, and one is liable as if weaving. In weaving, it is taught at the beginning of the thirteenth chapter of Shabbat: one who weaves two threads is liable. Braiding is also with two. Therefore, it is clear that when the Torah says "a branch of interwoven tree," it refers even to two. However, in the Gemara there: What is the definition of "interwoven"? Meaning: the choicest. And it says: When three grow. Rav Kahana said even two and one is considered the choicest. This was rejected, saying it is a "wild myrtle," meaning the three are more choice. Nevertheless, this is not invalid, because two are called "interwoven," as I have written. Some have written that ours are better than two and one, for there is never a distinction between two and three, for the reason we have explained. And what is called "wild myrtle" is because of the single third one over the two, as this single one removes it from the category of "interwoven," for interwoven is not less than two. Therefore, ours, which are two and two, are properly called "interwoven" and are completely valid.

If many leaves came out in one cluster and many of them fell off, leaving only three in one cluster, it is valid. Even if most of them fell off, such as if there were seven in one cluster and four fell off, leaving three, it is valid. This is the language of the Tur: "If most of the leaves of the measure of density fell off, it is invalid." The Geonim wrote that the entire length of the hadas (myrtle branch) must be "dense," and if not, it is invalid. Ba’al HaItur wrote: Even if it only has one instance of three leaves in one cluster, it is valid, and so wrote the Rambam. My lord, my father, the Rosh, ruled according to the words of the Raavad, that for the mitzvah, we require the entire measure to be dense, and for invalidation, most of it, even if the density is not at the top. Thus concludes his language.

Explanation of his words: If most of the clusters have fallen off, meaning two out of the three have fallen off, it is invalid. But if one of the three has fallen off, even along the entire length of the myrtle branch, it is valid (Bach). And how much is needed for the primary clustering? The Geonim said that it needs to be clustered along its entire length, and the Itur said that it is sufficient if it is clustered once. This is also the opinion of the Rambam according to the Tur, who wrote in the eighth chapter: If most of its leaves have fallen, if three leaves remain in one cluster, it is valid. This is his exact wording. The Tur holds that he means in one specific place. But the Maggid Mishneh wrote that his intention is for every cluster, see there. And the Rosh ruled according to the Raavad, that initially, the entire branch needs to be clustered, but after the fact, it is sufficient if most of it is clustered. But less than most of it is nothing. However, if most of it is clustered in any place, it is valid, even if there is no clustering at the top. According to this, if most of it has clustering, and part of it does not, whether there were never three leaves there at all or there were and they fell off, it is valid, even if this is at the top. And what is taught: if the top is cut, it is invalid – this is when the wood is cut. But it does not refer to the leaves as with the lulav, because the lulav does not have wood at the top. But with the myrtle, there is wood at the top.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, also followed the path of the Rosh and the Tur, though it was not clearly explained. For in Section 1, they wrote: A myrtle whose top was cut off is kosher. If most of its leaves fell off, if three leaves remain in one cluster, it is kosher. And in Section 4, they wrote: If many leaves sprouted in one cluster and fell off until only three remained in one cluster, it is kosher... And in Section 5, they wrote: For the mitzvah, it is required that the entire length of the myrtle be dense, and essentially for the majority, even if not at its top. Thus far is their language. Therefore, according to this, what they wrote in Section 1 that if its top was cut off it is kosher – this refers to when the wood was cut. And although in the Mishnah it is stated as invalid, the Rif and the Rosh wrote that the halacha does not follow this Mishnah, but rather Rabbi Tarfon who said there: Even if all three were cut off, it is kosher. And so ruled the Rambam and the Tur. However, the Raavad disagrees, and he holds that "cut off" according to Rabbi Tarfon refers to the leaves, and "cut off" in the Mishnah refers to the wood. This will be clarified further with the help of Heaven. And in the Shulchan Aruch, this dispute is explained in Section 10, see there.

And this is what they wrote: If three leaves remain in one cluster, it is valid – their intention is for each and every cluster. And regarding the measure of its density: ideally, the entire cluster, but for requirement, the majority of it. According to this, in practical halacha, this is the case: if the myrtle is dense in the majority of its measure, which will be explained in Siman 650, even if a minority of it is without density, and even if the minority is at its top – it is valid. And it seems that if in the majority it is dense, and in the minority all the leaves fell off – it is also valid. And although I did not find this explicitly stated, nevertheless it must be so: for what they wrote that it is valid if the majority is dense – it necessarily means that in the minority only one leaf remains, for if two remain – then the entire cluster is valid if two remain, as I wrote in Section 5, that specifically if the majority of the density is missing, it is invalid, which means if two fell off. But if one fell off – it is valid even for the whole cluster. And although this law is not explained in the Shulchan Aruch, nevertheless it is not disputed. Therefore, if there is a majority density – then in the minority it is valid, even if only one leaf remains in the cluster. And one leaf is considered as nothing, obviously.

If they have dried out – they are invalid. If they have wilted – they are valid. And what is the measure of dryness? When their appearance has turned white. However, as long as they are green, even if they can be crushed with a fingernail – they are valid. And why do we consider dryness in the lulav based on its ability to be crushed with a fingernail? Because with the lulav, the whitening precedes the crushing, as its primary color is white. This is not the case with the hadas, whose primary color is green, where the crushing precedes the whitening – therefore, we follow the whitening. However, this is according to the opinion of Rema. But according to the opinion of Beit Yosef – even with the lulav, we follow the whitening, as I wrote in the previous section.

And the law regarding dryness is like the law regarding shedding, that we follow the majority. If most of the leaves have dried out—it is invalid; if it is a minority—it is valid. Therefore, if in all the branches two have dried out, or even in most of them—it is invalid. But if one has dried out on each branch—it is valid. There is only one leniency regarding dryness that does not apply to shedding according to most authorities, and that is: if on the top branch, at the head of the stem, there remain three moist leaves, even if most of it has dried out—it is valid. This is not comparable to shedding, which in such a case would be invalid. Only according to the opinion of the Itur is it valid, as I wrote in paragraph 5, because they are not entirely absent. But if they are dry and present—everyone agrees it is valid. And this applies specifically to the top, because otherwise, it would not be considered aesthetically pleasing (hadar). When the top is moist—it is considered hadar in its entirety, even if the rest are dry, and this does not apply to other areas.

The opinion of the Rosh and the Tur is to be lenient entirely in this matter. That is, even if two of the upper leaves have dried up and only one moist leaf remains, it is still valid. Provided that this one leaf is at the top of the stem, meaning: of the three leaves that emerge, one comes from here, one from there, and the third appears to be combined with both, and in it lies the main aspect of beauty. However, the leniency that we granted when three moist leaves remain applies specifically when they are fully moist. But if they are withered, even though withered leaves are valid as I have written, nonetheless, in this specific case where only they remain, they are invalid in this manner, as the main aspect of beauty is lost. This is not comparable to a situation where all the leaves are withered. And the Rosh validates even in this specific case.

In the case of myrtle branches, sometimes small fruit-like growths, resembling grapes, develop on them. It is taught in the Mishnah (Sukkah 32b): "If its berries are more numerous than its leaves, it is invalid. But if they are reduced, it is valid. And one may not reduce them on Yom Tov." The disqualification due to having more berries than leaves specifically applies when the berries are black or red, as they are not of the same species as the myrtle and thus nullify the myrtle leaves. However, if the berries are green, it is valid, as they are considered the same species as the myrtle. One may not reduce them on Yom Tov because that would be considered making a utensil. If one did reduce them, even though it was prohibited, the myrtle is still valid. The Gemara (Sukkah 33b) states that if one has another myrtle branch and does not need this one for the lulav, one is permitted to pluck the berries one by one to eat them, since plucking them for eating does not indicate an intention to repair the myrtle. Only if one doesn't have another myrtle branch, thus forcing him to repair this one, it would be a "psik reisha" (an inevitable consequence). When he has another branch, it is not considered a repair at all, and therefore, this branch later becomes valid for the lulav.

And our Rabbi, the Rema, wrote in section 2 that the disqualification of a lulav whose berries are more numerous than its leaves is only invalid on the first day, but on the other days, it is valid. His words have been refuted, for anything that is disqualified due to lack of beauty (hadar) is invalid for all days, as I wrote in Siman 649. Therefore, one should not be lenient (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Additionally, since during Chol HaMoed one can reduce the number of berries, why should we validate it (Taz, subsection 6)? In my humble opinion, their arguments are correct, for certainly according to Rashi's explanation in the Gemara (there) that the reason is because it is not beautiful, it is certainly invalid on all days. However, the Yerushalmi explains the reason is because it is written "the branch of a tree"—that the branch should resemble the tree, meaning it should be green. But when it is black or red, it does not resemble the tree. This is a scriptural decree and not due to the reason of beauty. Therefore, it is obvious that on the other days it is valid, since they are rabbinic. Even on the second day of Yom Tov, when one cannot reduce the number of berries, it is also valid. However, during Chol HaMoed, it is certainly necessary to reduce the number of berries.

And know: it is explained in the Gemara there that if they turned black before Yom Tov, and he cut them on Yom Tov, even though when Yom Tov arrived they were disqualified from the mitzvah of lulav, nevertheless when he cut them they became valid, because a disqualification from the outset—even with sacrifices—is not considered a disqualification, and certainly not with mitzvot. And this is called a disqualification from the outset, since at the onset of Yom Tov it was not fit for the mitzvah. However, if they turned black on Yom Tov, there is a doubt in the Gemara there whether it is permissible to fulfill the obligation with them, because it is like something that was initially fit and then became disqualified, and then became fit again. For with sacrifices, such a case is considered a disqualification, and perhaps the same applies to mitzvot. And the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch did not mention anything about this. We must say that although there is someone in the Gemara who is uncertain about this, nevertheless, since Rav Pappa says there “This means there is no disqualification with mitzvot even with something that was fit and then became disqualified,” this is the ruling we follow, and this seems to be the main opinion (and so wrote the Taz there). However, there are some of the early authorities who hold that it is a doubt, and one does not fulfill the obligation with it (Ran there).

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef writes in paragraph 11: If one only has a myrtle (hadas) with more berries than leaves on Yom Tov, he should take it but not recite a blessing over it. This is his exact wording. It has been questioned what he is teaching us, as this is the case with all invalid species, as I wrote at the end of Siman 649 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 9). It seems to me that he means to teach us that one should not have a non-Jew take it for him, because for him, since he is not obligated in the commandments, it is not considered a remedy as it is for us when there is another [myrtle]. And according to this, it appears that one can tell a non-Jew to pick and eat them, and this is only a rabbinic prohibition even for us if we have another [myrtle]. According to this reasoning, telling a non-Jew would be a rabbinic prohibition upon a rabbinic prohibition, which is permitted in a situation of a mitzvah. And he teaches us that since for us it is considered a complete remedy, the rabbinic prohibition is not permitted in the place of a mitzvah. And we have already written that if its tip was cut off from the tree, it is valid, even if no new bud grew because the leaves cover its top. The same applies if the top of the tree dried out. There are those who invalidate it if the tip of the tree was cut off, and it is good to be stringent if another [myrtle] is available. But if another is not available, one recites a blessing over it, as the primary opinion follows the majority of poskim who validate it. There are those who say that if the tip dried out, even if another [myrtle] is not available, it is invalid (Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subparagraph 8, and this requires further study). Know that there are those who invalidate a grafted myrtle, just as a grafted etrog is invalid. None of the poskim mentioned this matter, for when it comes to an etrog, which is a fruit, there is indeed a difference in taste between a pure etrog and a grafted one. But with myrtle, where the commandment pertains to the tree and its leaves, what relevance does grafting have? This requires further study (see Sha'arei Teshuvah, subparagraph 8). Nevertheless, in practice, if it is known to be grafted, it is not advisable to take it for the mitzvah if there is another [myrtle]. But if there is no other, in my humble opinion, it is permitted.

The Rambam writes at the beginning of Chapter Seven: The "willows of the brook" mentioned in the Torah do not refer to everything that grows by the brook, but to a specific kind called "willows of the brook." Its leaf is long like a brook, its edge is smooth, and its stem is red. This is what is called "willow." Most of this species grows by brooks, hence it is called "willows of the brook." Even if it grows in the desert or mountains, it is valid. There is another species similar to the willow, but its leaf is round, its edge is serrated like a saw, and its stem is not red. This is called "poplar," and it is invalid. There is a type of willow whose leaf edge is not smooth and not like a saw but has very small grooves like the edge of a small sickle - and this is valid. All these details were transmitted through tradition from Moses, our teacher. Thus is his language.

And this which is written that "there is a type of willow... and it is not like a saw but rather small furrows..." – this is from what is taught (34a): If it resembles a sickle – it is valid; if it resembles a saw – it is invalid. And "saw" refers to a serrated blade. Rambam explains that the difference is that resembling a sickle means having small furrows, and resembling a saw means having large furrows. According to this, we do not have a clear measure for what is considered large and small. However, Rashi, the Rosh, and the Tur explain that there is a difference in the actual form of the furrows, meaning: resembling a saw is when the notch goes straight across, and it has two prongs, one on each side, similar to the notch of a knife. Resembling a sickle is when all the notches lean to one side, curved towards its handle (Rashi). And this is the language of the Tur: but there is a type of willow whose stem is red, and its leaf is elongated, and its edge is not completely smooth, but resembles a sickle with its notches curved and leaning to one side – and it is valid. Until here is his language. And I am astonished at our master the Rema for not bringing the words of the Tur, and in the Shulchan Aruch it is written like the Rambam.

In truth, among us, there are two types, and both have elongated leaves, and the stalks are red. However, one type has large leaves that are not smooth but resemble a sickle as per the explanation of Rashi and the Tur, and the stalk is very red. The other type has small and smooth leaves, and the stalk does not have a reddish hue. Indeed, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that even if it is green, it is valid because it will eventually turn red when the sun shines upon it. Some people are meticulous about the large ones because of their redness, and some are meticulous about the small ones because of their smoothness. Additionally, they are stronger, as the large ones shed their leaves frequently and dry out quickly. In practice, both types are valid.

And similarly, those that resemble a sickle, whether according to the interpretation of the Rambam or according to the interpretation of Rashi and the Tur, are valid. For in truth, the nicks are not the main factor regarding the willow branch. And I found a support for this in the Tosefta, Chapter Two: What is a valid willow? One whose stem is red and whose leaf is long. What is an invalid willow? One whose stem is white and whose leaf is round. So ends its wording. Clearly, it does not mention the criterion of smoothness at all, and this is also found in the Yerushalmi, see there. Therefore, even in our Gemara where smoothness is mentioned, it explains that only something that resembles a saw is invalid, and this is a serrated tool. And the serrated tool has large nicks and two prongs. Consequently, anything that does not have large nicks as seen by the eye, or does not have two nicks, does not resemble a saw and is valid. (And it seems to me that there are two types of sickles: a hand sickle and a harvest sickle, as it is taught at the beginning of the thirteenth chapter of Keilim. And the harvest sickle: we see its shape as explained by Rashi. And the Rambam interprets it as a hand sickle, and he does not explain its smoothness like Raavad in the name of the Beitzah, where it is clarified that it is a craftsman's tool. And indeed, among silversmiths and goldsmiths and clock repairers, there is a tool shaped like a sickle according to the Rambam. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And know that in the Gemara there it is stated: "Willow branches of the brook" – I would only know those that grow by the brook, how do I know those of the field and of the mountains? The verse states: "Willow branches of the brook" – in any case. And Rashi explains: those from water brooks are a mitzvah. However, those from the field are valid, as it is written: "willows" – in the plural form, see there. According to this, there is a greater mitzvah for willows that grow by water. Yet, none of the poskim mentioned this, and we have never heard of anyone being meticulous about this. And our Rabbis, the Tosafot (Sukkah 34a, s.v. "v'Rabbanan") were even stricter, that even after the fact one has not fulfilled the obligation, because since we derive the validity of those from the field and the mountains from the plural form "willows." This applies to those who hold that one willow branch is sufficient. But we, who maintain that two willow branches are required, need "willows" for the requirement of two willow branches, and there is no derivation for those from the field and the mountains, see there. The Rosh has already refuted these opinions, stating that the derivation is not from the plural form, but that the term "willows of the brook" means: from the species that typically grows by the brook. However, it does not matter where it grows. This is also evident from the language of the Rambam. Therefore, there is not even a higher level of observance in this, see there, and this is the common practice.

Nevertheless, it is difficult to establish a constant mitzvah against our Rabbis, the Ba'alei Tosafot, and also against Rashi, at least for the optimal mitzvah. Therefore, it seems to me, in my humble opinion, that we should be precise in this matter when it says: I only have "willows of the brook." From where do we know those that grow on the fields and on the mountains, etc.? What kind of contrast is there between those of the fields and the mountains and those of the brook, that we needed to include them? And if it is because a brook is merely a place of water, as it is written "streams of water," then why specify these? It should have said: From where do we know even those not in a brook? Additionally, in every place where it mentions fields, it mentions irrigated land, like at the beginning of Moed Katan and in several other places. It should have said: From where do we know those of the fields and those of irrigated land? And if you say that one does not fulfill the obligation with those of irrigated land, it should have explained such a new law. And we have not found anyone who says so.

Therefore, it appears to me that the explanation is as follows: The term "nachal" in the Holy Tongue has two meanings. The first is a river or stream, as in "streams of water," and the second is a valley, as in "a mighty valley," according to Rashi's explanation regarding the eglah arufah. This is also found in Niddah (8b), see there. Similarly: "And he camped in the valley of Gerar, and the servants of Isaac dug in the valley," which means a valley and a plain. This is what it means when it says: I only have the willows of the brook, meaning either those that grow near a river or stream, where there is a ready supply of water, or those that grow in a valley, even though there is no water there, which refers to a level land that proceeds evenly. How do we know to include those of a private owner? Meaning, this is the opposite of a river or stream, where there is no water, but the rain waters it. The same applies to an irrigated field, where a person waters it, as the main point is that there is no ready supply of water. Similarly: How do we know to include those of the mountains? This is the opposite of a valley, obviously. The text says "willows" – in any case. According to this, the plain meaning of "willows of the brook" includes those that grow in a valley or level land. This is the majority of our plains. And there is no need for inclusion except for those of the mountains, which is not common, as is known.

A willow branch (aravah) that has most of its leaves dried out, or if most of its leaves have fallen off, or if the top of the branch has been cut off, is invalid. And even though we permit a myrtle (hadas) with a cut top, this is because its dense leaves cover it and it retains its beauty, which is not the case with the willow. The Rambam permits even a willow with a cut top, as it is not more stringent than a myrtle. One may rely on the Rambam when there is no other option. If a date has grown on it, it is valid just like with the myrtle (Eliyah Rabbah). And just as if most of the leaves have fallen off, it is invalid, so too if they are detached, meaning they have become loose from the stem, even though they are still attached, it is invalid, similar to the leaves of a lulav that have become detached. Similarly, if the leaves are split and most of them are divided, it is invalid (Maggid Mishneh and Magen Avraham). However, if it is withered, or if only a few leaves have fallen off, it is valid after the fact. What is considered dried leaves? When they turn white, like with the myrtle. We do not follow the breaking of the leaf under the nail, as with the myrtle, but rather the change in appearance, when they turn white. Particularly with willows that have large leaves, which dry quickly within a day, it is impossible to follow the breaking of the leaf under the nail as they break quickly, but rather the change in appearance, when they turn white. And know that care must be taken when inserting the willows into the lulav that the leaves do not get detached for most of the required length.

"The fruit of a beautiful tree" – this refers to the etrog, for "the fruit of a tree" implies that the taste of its wood and its fruit is the same, and this is true for the etrog. Additionally, we expound: "the fruit of a beautiful tree" – one that remains on its tree from year to year, because the etrog can remain on the tree for two or three years. When new ones grow, the old ones are still present. Moreover, this has been received by tradition from Moses our teacher, who received it from Sinai. The reason the Torah specified all the species but left the etrog ambiguous is so that we would need to rely on the Oral Torah. This demonstrates to us that there is no commandment explicitly detailed in the Written Torah, and the Oral Torah explains it. As we explained in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 350 regarding "an eye for an eye," the Oral Torah breathes life into the Written Torah. See there in section 8.

A dry etrog is invalid. The Tur writes: The measure of dryness, as explained by the Raavad, is when all moisture is gone, and it does not emit any moisture. For moisture in fruit is like blood in living flesh; as long as it is moist, it will emit moisture, either from the pressure of a knife or from squeezing. But after it has dried, it will not emit moisture. However, its examination is difficult because it is impossible to squeeze or cut it. But since a puncture that does not cause a defect renders it valid, one can pass a needle or thread through it, and if there is moisture, it will show on the thread. This is the Raavad's opinion.

However, our ruling is that a puncture that goes through from side to side invalidates it, even without causing a defect. Therefore, one must be careful that the needle or thread does not pass even to the chambers of the seeds, and certainly not from side to side. For even to the chambers of the seeds invalidates it, as will be explained (Beit Yosef and Taz, subsection 1). Therefore, one should not thrust the needle strongly, so it does not reach the chambers of the seeds (Magen Avraham, subsection 1).

And our master, the Rema, wrote in section 1 that an etrog from the previous year is certainly dry and invalid. This is his exact wording. It is clearly implied that the needle test does not help, and even if it exudes moisture, it is still invalid. For in the Gemara (Sukkah 31b) it is implied that it is not considered "hadar" (beautiful), as it is taught: an old etrog is invalid. And "old" generally means from the previous year. The reason is explained there that it is not "hadar." Alternatively, one could say that our sages understood that all its moisture has dried up, and even if it appears to have moisture, it is meaningless. And so agreed the great authorities (Bach and Eliyah Rabbah). There are those who wish to say that if we see that its appearance remains intact, the thread test is effective (Taz, subsection 2). But this is not convincing, since our sages invalidated it, it remains invalid in any case (Eliyah Rabbah).

And there are those who bury the etrog in honey, as the honey preserves its moisture. Nevertheless, without inspection, it cannot be deemed kosher. It should be inspected: if it has moisture, it is kosher (Bach). There are those who invalidate it due to the reason of it being pickled (Taz, Section 17), and pickled is invalid as will be explained. The first opinion believes: since the honey preserves its moisture, as we see with all fruits, pickling does not apply regarding the mitzvah (and this is also implied in Eliyah Rabbah). However, in practice, it is difficult to rely on this. And I have also heard that when it is buried in wax and sealed all around with wax, it lasts a long time, but this too should not be relied upon in practice.

Even though a dry [etrog] is invalid, nevertheless, a withered one, which is called "zu veyalet," is valid, just like other species. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Sukkah 31a), which says: "And all withered ones are valid." According to this, what is found in the Rokeach and in the responsa of Mahari"l that a withered one is invalid is surprising. In the Mordechai, it is written that it is valid in pressing circumstances. Also, in this matter, Rabbi Yosef Karo in his great book at the end of Siman 649 wrote that it is a printing error and it should say "pickled," see there. It seems that those who invalidate a withered one mean that due to the withering, part of it has also dried out. This also appears to be the implication in the Hagahot Asheri, which begins with withered and ends with dry (Magen Avraham at the beginning of the Siman). However, in the Bahag, the baraita (Sukkah 36a) is quoted: "An etrog that is swollen, rotten, pickled, boiled, etc., is invalid." And in the Bahag it says "withered" and not "pickled." According to this, it must be said that the withered ones that are valid are only those other than the etrog. It is clear that this is the version of the Rokeach and the Mahari"l. According to this, it is obvious that a withered one is invalid, and this is how one should rule. (And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, see there.)

Rambam writes in Chapter Eight, Law 7: An etrog that has a perforation that goes all the way through, no matter the size, is invalid. If it does not go all the way through, if it is the size of an isar or larger, it is invalid. If it is missing any amount, it is invalid. This is his language, meaning: a perforation that involves a loss, and the loss is of the flesh of the etrog itself, even if it does not go all the way through, it is invalid. But a perforation that does not involve a loss, such as if a peg or something similar was stuck into it, making it like a perforation, but nonetheless, no part of the etrog itself is missing, there is a distinction: if it goes all the way through, it is invalid in any case, but if it does not go all the way through, it needs to be the size of an isar.

And what is considered "pierced through"? Some say specifically from one side to the other. And some say that certainly at the bottom, at its base, where all the seed chambers are – it needs to be pierced through from one side to the other. However, regarding the entire etrog, if it is pierced through to the seed chambers – it is considered "pierced through," for that is its definition. And be aware that within the etrog, up to the seed chambers, there are three peels: the first, the outermost, which is very thin, and it is like a membrane, and in it, there is no disqualification unless it is completely peeled off. Regarding this peel, the Rambam wrote in the eleventh chapter of Terumot concerning etrogim of terumah, that their peels, even though they are usually discarded, are still forbidden to non-priests, see there. For this is like the thin peel found on all fruits. The second is the thick peel, which constitutes the entire wall of the etrog up to the seed chambers. This is also called "peel," just as the entire thickness of the gizzard is called "skin," even though it is its main edible part. Similarly, with the etrog, the main part of the fruit is the seed chambers, and the flesh around them is called "peel." And it is within this that the measurement of the holes that has been explained applies. And the third: within the seed chambers, there is a very thin peel, like the membrane on the yolk of an egg, and it is between seed and seed (Taz, section 6). This peel has no significance. There is someone who wants to say that all the holes pertain to the outer peel. But this is not so, as we have explained (there).

And the Raavad disagrees with the Rambam, and this is his language: "This is an error. Rather, a perforation that is completely through—with a loss of any amount; if it is not completely through—with a loss of the size of an isar... until here his language," and he critiques the Rambam who invalidates a completely through perforation even without any loss at all. Rather, also for a completely through perforation, some loss is necessary. And it is clear that one should be stringent like the Rambam. And also Rashi, of blessed memory, and many of the decisors hold like the Rambam. Therefore, even though our teacher the Beit Yosef in his great book wrote that the invalidation of a perforation is rabbinic, see there, nonetheless, one should be stringent. And similarly, it is explained by our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 2, where he wrote the opinion of the Rambam without qualification and the opinion of the Raavad in the name of some say, see there. And the measure of the isar that we mentioned—there is no difference whether it is round, or square, or long and thin; if only its total area is the size of an isar—it is invalid (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). And we do not know how much the amount of an isar is. And in the Behag it is written that it is like a small dinar.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in paragraph 2 that it is customary to permit the perforations made in an etrog by thorns, even though they cause a defect, because this is the way they grow. However, if one sees that the skin and flesh are not intact within the perforation, it is invalid according to the first opinion, even though it is not completely pierced through. In a pressing situation, one may be lenient according to the latter opinion, to permit a defect that is not the size of an isar and is not completely pierced through. Thus far is his wording. The explanation of the matter: it is not because a perforation caused by a thorn is less significant, but the matter is as follows: in the Gemara (36a), an etrog is compared to a lung. Regarding a lung, we maintain that if there is a pit, if the skin is intact at the bottom of the pit, it is kosher, even though some flesh is missing, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 36. And here too with an etrog, sometimes a thorn from the tree penetrates it during its growth, and consequently some flesh inside is missing, yet if the skin at the bottom is intact, it is kosher. You can find this when the thorn is not sharp. Therefore, the skin is intact, only the flesh inside is slightly dissolved. However, if one sees that the skin is not intact at the bottom of the perforation, the ruling reverts to the two opinions mentioned. According to Maimonides (Rambam), it is invalid, even though it does not pierce through to the seed chambers. According to the Raavad, it is kosher if the defect is not the size of an isar. Therefore, although we follow the opinion of the Rambam, in a pressing situation, one may rely on the Raavad and permit it.

And there are those who say that if there is doubt whether the skin exists or not – it should be deemed permissible, because according to the Ra'avad it is permissible even if the skin is not present, as long as it is not the size of an issar and perforated (Taz, subsection 5). This also seems logical, since this disqualification is rabbinic, as I wrote in subsection 8. All the more so, according to the Ra'avad, it is completely permissible, and therefore one should be lenient in cases of doubt. For this reason, it seems to me that if there is doubt whether it is the size of an issar or not – one should be lenient as in all cases of rabbinic doubt. This is not a case of lacking knowledge, which is not considered a doubt, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 110, because an issar is not common in our times – this is a doubt hidden from everyone, and it is indeed a proper doubt, as I wrote there. However, this is all in a pressing situation, for if there is another who can obtain it easily – why should one take the doubtful one? And this is all on the first day, for on other days even if it is missing – it is permissible, as will be explained in the next section, with the help of Heaven. And there it will be further clarified.

An etrog whose internal flesh has liquefied, but its outer peel remains intact, and the seed chambers inside are intact, such as when this is discernible by touching, or when it is visible through the outer peel that they are intact, is valid. This is a matter of debate in the Gemara, and we lean towards leniency for the reason we have written, that this is a rabbinic matter. There are those who are stringent, and the Tur leans towards this view, and writes the reason: since it is a doubt regarding a Torah matter, see there. This is puzzling, as the Rosh explicitly writes that all these doubts are rabbinic. There is someone who explains that this is because the matter is related to a Torah law (Bach), but this is not understood at all. To me, it seems that the Tur holds that even though other punctures render it invalid rabbinically, nevertheless, when the entire core has liquefied, it is not considered an etrog at all, and is invalid according to Torah law.

If the entire length of the etrog is cracked, even if it is only cracked on one side from top to bottom, and the depth of the crack extends along the entire length to most of the thickness of the thick peel, which is the second peel we explained in section 7, it is invalid, even though no part of the flesh is missing. However, if a portion remains at the top and a portion at the bottom that is not cracked in depth, even if it is cracked on both sides along its entire length, if a portion remains on both sides at the top and the bottom, it is valid. This ruling is similar to the case of the trachea in animals, as explained in Yoreh De'ah, section 34. There is an opinion that if the crack reaches the tip, which is the upper part of the etrog, even the smallest amount renders it invalid. Others disagree, stating that only regarding a change in appearance is there a distinction between the tip and other areas, since it pertains to the aspect of beauty, and the tip is the main part for enhancement. But regarding punctures and cracks, where the reason is due to the requirement of a complete taking, there is no distinction between the tip and other areas. Nevertheless, some have ruled that a crack at the tip renders it invalid. (Taz, end of subsection 9, but Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 9, validates it. See Magen Avraham, subsection 17. In any case, one should be stringent, except in pressing circumstances. I am puzzled why the Alter Rebbe omitted this entirely.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 5 that there are those who are stringent and invalidate if most of it is cracked. And as long as most of its thick shell is not cracked, it is not called cracked. Thus are his words. And this is certainly correct, that a crack which does not penetrate the depth of most of the shell is of no consequence. And even when there is doubt whether it penetrated the depth or not, it also seems to me that it is valid, as this is a rabbinic doubt, as I wrote regarding peeling. However, regarding what he wrote that there are those who are stringent and invalidate if most of it is cracked, many have rejected his words. For in the Gemara it is compared to the windpipe, and regarding the windpipe, we specifically require the entirety and not the majority. Therefore, they ruled it valid (Turei Zahav there, and Magen Avraham sub-paragraph 6). And also the Levush omitted this.

And I am puzzled: Certainly, the words of our master, the Rema, are correct, and the same applies to the gullet. For in the case of the gullet, we require that something remains above and something remains below. But if only something remains above and not below, or vice versa, it is a trefa (unfit). And the same applies here. Now we must ask: What is the law when it is cracked from its top to most of its length, and much remains below but nothing remains above? One could say it is kosher, for the abundance in one place is not worse than having something above and something below. And one could say it is invalid, for having something on both sides is better than having much in one place. And this seems to be the main ruling. (In this, one could say it is worse than the gullet, for the gullet is very long, both above the place of slaughter and below it. Its opening is not so apparent, unlike the etrog. And one could also say that even in the case of the gullet, it would be a trefa in such a manner. Investigate and you will find clarity.)

And similarly, if it is cracked along the circumference of its width: even if it is cracked on both sides, opposite each other, and there remains something whole at the top between the two cracks on both sides, and something whole at the bottom between the two cracks on both sides – it is still valid, even though the depth of the cracks reaches most of the thickness of the thick peel. And know that all these disqualifications, namely a hole, a missing part, and a crack – are not because it is not beautiful, but because it is not whole and complete. And the Torah said "and you shall take," and the Sages expounded: a taking that is whole and complete (the Gra). Nevertheless, the disqualifications are only rabbinic according to what appears from the Rosh, as this is merely an allusion. And see Section 12 and Section 35.

If the outer thin peel is removed, which is the first peel mentioned in section 7: if the entire peel is removed, it is invalid, because once it is entirely peeled, it withers and is no longer beautiful. However, if any part of it remains unpeeled, it is valid, because that small remaining part will help it return to its wholeness. This is similar to the case of a flayed animal. Therefore, some say it is not valid unless a portion the size of a sela remains unpeeled. This should be taken into consideration, since the same applies in the case of a flayed animal. 

What are we discussing here? When the peeled area has the same appearance as the etrog. But if the peeled area looks different from the rest of the etrog, it is not valid unless the peeled area is a minority of the etrog and is not scattered in two or three places. Rather, it is all in one place and not on the top of the etrog, as will be explained (there). The reason is that in such a case, its beauty is diminished, and thus its invalidity is from the Torah.

There are two types of thin stems on an etrog: one is its "stem" (oketz), by which it hangs on the tree like all fruits, and it is the "tail" of the fruit at its bottom. In the language of the Mishnah, it is called "oketz" (Mishnah, Tractate Lulav 34b). Among our people, the masses call this "pitom," and it sits deep within the etrog, so that if it is entirely removed from its root, a cavity will remain. The second is on the other side, at the top of the etrog, like a flower on certain types of apples. Some etrogim do not have this at all, and some do. In the language of the Mishnah, it is called "pitom," and in our language, it is called "shoshanta," because it beautifies the etrog like the petal of a lily flower. It does not enter deep into the etrog, but rather sits on its top. Because these terms are interchangeable, we have explained that the oketz is the lower one that enters deep, and the shoshanta is the upper one. There are etrogim that do not have a shoshanta at all, such as the etrogim of Corsica – they do not have a shoshanta. Similarly, some etrogim from the Land of Israel have it, and some do not. The etrogim from Corfu, Genoa, and Morocco all have a shoshanta. Now we will explain their laws according to the opinions of our Rabbis, with the help of Heaven.

And this is the language of the Rambam in the eighth chapter: If its "dad" (small stem) is removed, which is the small head where its "rose" (blossom) is – it is invalid. If the "etz" (stem), which is attached to the tree from the base of the etrog, is removed and its place remains a cavity – it is invalid. Thus far his words. But if what is outside the cavity is removed – it is valid (Maggid Mishneh). And similarly, the "dad", if not the entire head is removed, but only the upper part which is slightly wider like a rose – it is valid (ibid.). And why is it invalid if the "dad" is removed, since it does not enter into the etrog? Because the flesh of the etrog spreads also onto its bottom, as can be seen. Therefore, when it is entirely removed – it is considered lacking from the essence of the etrog. This is not the case with the "oketz" (stem), as the flesh of the etrog does not spread onto it, like with all fruit stems. Furthermore, its adornment is the "shoshanta" (blossom), and when it is removed – its adornment is removed. But with the "oketz", there is no adornment. (This is what seems to me in my humble opinion, and with this, several nuances become clear. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And this is the wording of the Tur: If its pitom (the protrusion at the top) is removed, according to the explanation of Rabbi Yaakov ben Yakar, it is invalid. But if its stalk is removed, it is valid in any case. According to the explanation of Rabbi Yitzchak HaLevi, if its pitom is removed, it is valid in any case. And if its stalk is removed: if only the part outside the depression is removed, it is valid; but if it is removed from the root and the place is recognizable as missing, it is invalid. And Rabbeinu Chananel invalidates in both cases, and so wrote the Rif and the Rambam, of blessed memory. And my master, my father the Rosh, of blessed memory, wrote that we customarily invalidate in both cases. This is specifically when it had a pitom and it was removed. But there are etrogim that never had pitomim, and they are not invalidated because of this. And similarly, it is specifically when the stalk is removed and none of it remains at all on the etrog. But if any part of it remains, it is valid. Thus far his wording.

And behold, according to the explanation of Rabbi Yaakov ben Yakar, the disqualification depends only on the "shoshanta" (blossom), and not on the "oketz" (stem), which we call the pitom. The reasoning for this is that the stem is merely wood, even if it enters the etrog, and it has no connection at all to the etrog, like all stems of fruits. It is explicitly stated in the end of the first chapter of Okatzin that the stems of fruits have no connection to the fruit: they neither become impure nor impart impurity, except for the stems of figs and dried figs, which are considered food itself. There are those that become impure as a handle, as explained there. But they have no connection to the fruit. And it is so stated in the eleventh chapter of Terumot, Mishnah 4, that only the stems of figs and dried figs are considered terumah like the fruit itself, and it is explicitly explained that this does not apply to other stems. And concerning the etrog, it is proven explicitly that its stem is not like it, as it is taught in the Tosefta at the end of Terumot that the peels of watermelon and etrog, even though they do not contain edible parts, are forbidden to non-priests. And so wrote the Rambam in the eleventh chapter of Terumot, see there. It is thus explicit that only the peel is included with the etrog, and not the stem. But the shoshanta is essential for its beauty, as it is the main adornment, as I have written. Therefore, it is called "shoshanta" like a flower, "shoshan" (rose). Additionally, the flesh of the etrog is upon it, as I have written. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, in the tenth chapter of Terumot, it is explained that when its pitom (blossom) is removed, which is the shoshanta, the fruit is considered as cut, and it is equivalent to its outer peel, as I have written. The Rambam also writes this in the fifteenth chapter of Terumot, end of Halacha 8, and this is his language: "And similarly, if its pitom and outer peel are removed, it is considered as cut," see there. (And Rashi of blessed memory agreed to this in Beitzah 3b. According to this, the Mishnah is simple: if its pitom is removed, it is disqualified; and if its stem is removed, it is valid. And that which is taught: if its "bokanta" is removed, this is to explain the pitom of the Mishnah, because it is sharp and made like a pestle.)

And the opinion of Rabbi Yitzchak HaLevi is entirely the opposite: if the pitom (the blossom end) and the shoshanit (the floral disc) are removed, it is valid in all respects, and the disqualification applies only to the stem when what is inside the etrog is also removed. And one can say the reasoning is: since there are etrogim that do not have a shoshanit at all, how can it be disqualified by the removal of the shoshanit? And since when it does not have it, it does not invalidate, even when it has it and it is removed, it does not invalidate. And even though we find with the fats of the sacrifices that when they do not have it, it does not invalidate the eating of the meat, but when they have it, it does invalidate (Pesachim 77b), this applies when it is still present. But when it is absent, meaning it was lost, it does not invalidate. And here too it is the same: even though when it is present it invalidates, when it is absent it does not invalidate. And certainly when some etrogim never had it at all, and it is not part of the etrog itself, even though it spreads over it like a membrane, it is not more significant than its upper membrane, where if part of it is removed, we do not consider it. And the removal of the stem from the inside that invalidates, it is not because of the missing stem, but because of the hollow that remains in the etrog, and it appears clearly as lacking, and this is not a complete taking. (And in the Aruch it is written that Rabbi Gershom Meor HaGolah also explained this way. And according to this, the pitom and the stem mentioned in the Mishnah refer to the stem. But the stem is what is outside the cavity, and the pitom is what is inside the cavity. And this is what is explained in the Baraita: if the bokneto (the knob) is removed, meaning that part which is like a pestle in a mortar.)

And know: It seems to me that the dispute among these Rabbis is a dispute in the Jerusalem Talmud. For it says there: "If its pitom is removed" – there, they say "shoshanata." And Rabbi Yitzchak says: "pika." And "pika" is a round object hidden within another object, as in the twelfth chapter of Parah: "He shall not sprinkle either on the spindle or on the pika." And the Ra'av explains: "What is placed at the end of the spindle to make it heavier." And it is round, as it is stated in the twenty-first chapter of Keilim: "One who touches the pika," and the Ra'av explains: "Like a small circle, etc.," and they place it at the top of the distaff. And in Ohalot, chapter seven: "Until they round the top like a pika." And this can be observed with the senses, that the end of the stem embedded in the etrog is truly round, more than what is outside the etrog. According to this, there, they say like Rabbeinu Yaakov bar Yakar, and Rabbi Yitzchak says like Rabbeinu Yitzchak HaLevi. (And I found this in the Ran. And he added further that Rabbi Yitzchak Hakula of the Jerusalem Talmud is Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar of our Talmud, who explains "its cavity" as stated in Pesachim 113b. If so, our Talmud rules that if its shoshanata is removed – it is valid. And indeed, this is a clear proof. However, what we hold is that when the Jerusalem Talmud says "there they say" – this refers to Babylonia, and they interpret "its pitom" as shoshanata. This requires further study; investigate and you will find it light.)

The Rif, the Rambam, Rabbeinu Chananel, the Tosafot, and the Rosh all interpreted it in the same way: "Nitela pitmato" means its blossom end was removed, and "Nitela buchnato" means the tip of its stem was removed. If either of these are removed, the etrog is invalid. This is also the ruling of our Rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in sections 7 and 8, and this is their wording: "If its dad (small head) is removed, which is the small part where its blossom end is, it is invalid. Some are stringent if the blossom end, which we call the 'pitom,' is removed. It is good to be stringent where possible. However, regarding the law, it is only invalid if the dad is removed, which is the wood on which the pitom head rests. The head is called the 'shoshanta.' This is specifically if it was removed, but if it never had a dad, it is kosher. Most of the etrogim brought to these regions are like this. End of their wording, and it needs clarification."

And this is its explanation: The "pitma" mentioned in the Mishnah and the Poskim, which refers to the "shoshanata," is a somewhat long wood that extends from its top, resembling a nipple. At its top, it is slightly wider than the rest of its extension. It is the essence of the "shoshanata," as the name "shoshanata" refers to the upper lip, as it is written: "the lip of a lily flower." Therefore, some say that even if only the upper surrounding part is removed, and the entire nipple remains intact, it is invalid; as it says in the Gemara, "if its shoshanata is removed," they interpret it to mean that if only the upper flower is removed, it is invalid. But this is not correct; what the Gemara means by "shoshanata" is the lower part of the stem. This is like saying: the upper part and not the lower part. And because there is a sign of the "shoshanata" – it says that this is the "pitma" mentioned in the Mishnah, and not the lower part. However, it is never invalid until the entire nipple is removed up to the body of the etrog. And this is what they said, that it is good to be stringent even with just the top. However, regarding the law, it is not so. And some wrote that it must be with the "bukna" (Magen Avraham, Small Section 9). And I am astonished: for our eyes see that there is no "bukna" at all, but it ends evenly with the etrog. Only those that do not have a "shoshanata," sometimes it is noticeable like a slightly recessed place. And even then, there is no depth at all. (And there is a need to examine the Beit Yosef and the Magen Avraham, who relied on the Ran that it has a "bukna." But it is not so, see there. And be precise and you will find correctly.)

In section 8 they wrote: If the wood that is attached to the tree is removed from the base of the etrog, leaving a hole – it is invalid. However, if only part of the wood is removed, and some thickness remains, covering the width of the hole – it is valid. Thus far their words. This implies: But if only part of the hole is covered – it is invalid. And someone has written that joining by means of a needle is considered a valid joining, but this is not so (Sha'arei Teshuva, subsection 15, in the name of Shevut Yaakov). It is astonishing that anyone would permit this, for if so, would we permit two halves of an etrog that were joined together by means of a splinter or a needle? And be aware that someone has written that in a pressing situation, where there is no other etrog in the town – it is permissible if the entire stem is removed from the etrog, even on the first day (Be'er Hetev, subsection 14, in the name of Chacham Tzvi). It is difficult to rule this way against all these authorities, and it requires further investigation.

We are particular about selecting an etrog (citron) that has a pitom (stem). Nevertheless, if there is an etrog without a pitom that is beautiful, or if part of the top was removed and it is still beautiful, and there is another with a complete pitom that is not as beautiful — it is a greater mitzvah to take the beautiful one without the pitom than to take the one that is not as beautiful with the complete pitom (Taz, section 12).

A grafted etrog is completely invalid, even when there is no other etrog available. In ancient times, there was someone who wanted to permit it, but all the sages of Israel in Tzfat opposed him and completely forbade it (Responsa of Rabbi Moshe Alsheich, Siman 110, and Rabbi Moshe Padua in Responsa Rema Siman 126). Because when an etrog is grafted with a lemon or another species, it merges with the tree onto which it was grafted. As it is said: "A young tree that was intertwined with an old one is exempt from orlah because it is considered part of the old one" (Sotah 43b). They wrote that the grafted etrog has much acidity and a thin peel. An ungrafted etrog has little acidity and a thick peel (Alsheich). Some wrote that these are the signs: The grafted etrog is smooth, while the kosher ones have small bumps all over. In the grafted etrog, the stem protrudes, while in the kosher ones it is sunken. In the grafted etrog, the juice is abundant, and the peel is thin, while in the kosher ones, the juice is sparse, and the peel is thick (Rabbi Moshe Padua). Additionally, someone wrote another sign: In the grafted etrog, the seed lies across the etrog, while in the kosher one, it stands lengthwise (Magen Avraham at the end of this Siman in the name of A”Sh).

And the signs are not received from the ancients, but rather from what they saw in their own country. As he himself wrote, he brought from one place etrogim that were in doubt (R. Moses of Padua). And if the signs were received, they should have examined the signs. Furthermore, the etrogim of Corfu that are called "Carpiori etrogim" are completely smooth, and many have the stem protruding. And if we say they are indeed grafted, as many of the great rabbis of the generation have prohibited them for many years. And behold, also the etrogim of the Land of Israel and the etrogim of Morocco, many of them are also smooth. However, they wrote according to their country in Italy, where they had two types of etrogim: the etrogim of Genoa which were called "Genoese etrogim" by us, and the etrogim of Corsica, which is an island of Italy and now under French rule, called "Corsican etrogim." And indeed, they are all with protrusions, and the stem is submerged. But from other places, there is no proof. And we examined the signs internally, and it was not clarified to us. Therefore, it is difficult to establish the signs for practical halacha.

According to this, we do not have any permission regarding etrogim (citron fruits), except for those that Israelites testify they know the plantings from their beginnings, that they have no grafting at all. Like the etrogim of our holy land, where great rabbis of Israel, Torah scholars, and God-fearing individuals supervise the gardens to ensure there is no grafting. But regarding the etrogim of Corfu, there is no permission, even with their certifications, as it is well known that there are few Israelites there, and they are under their control, and they fear them. How could they know what is being done in their fields and vineyards, whether they graft or not? 

And perhaps you might say: they are not suspected of causing harm unless they have a personal benefit, as explained in Yoreh Deah, Siman 118? Indeed, they have great personal benefit here, as it is known that every grafted plant produces beautiful fruit, and any plant that is not grafted produces inferior fruit. This is true for all fruits. On the contrary, the perfection of the Corfu etrogim is their flaw, as they are indeed very beautiful, unlike any other, and this is due to their grafting. Therefore, every Israelite who has fear of God in his heart should only take etrogim from the Land of Israel. How can we not be ashamed and humiliated when in a mitzvah that we can fulfill with the fruit of our holy land, we choose to take from foreign lands? Woe to such shame, woe to such disgrace! Regarding this, it is said: "And they despised the pleasant land." Therefore, one must be very, very careful about this. (Also, the Levush, the Magen Avraham at the end of this Siman, and the Taz in the next Siman, disqualified them.)

If a blemish called "chazazis" appears on an etrog, which is like small blisters similar to boils and is tangible because its place is elevated from the surface of the etrog (Tur): if it is in one place – it only invalidates the etrog if it covers most of the etrog. But if it is in two or three places – even if it is on a minority of the etrog, it is also invalid. However, this is only if the places are distinct with some noticeable separation. But with a small separation, it is considered as one place (Taz, subparagraph 114). The reason why it is worse in two or three places is because the eye perceives it in several places, and it is not "hadar" (beautiful). When the separation is not large, the eye does not perceive it as multiple places, and it is considered as one place. (Therefore, the Talmud says "two or three," and isn't three certainly worse than two? Rather, it means that the separation should be noticeable. Pay close attention and you will understand.)

In the Jerusalem Talmud it says: If a scab covers most of one side. This means that we do not require a majority over the entire surface, but even if a majority is on one side – it is invalid. However, some explain that its intention is like our Talmud, that from one side means in one place. That is, when do we require a majority? Specifically in one place. But in two places, even without a majority – it is invalid. And our master the Beit Yosef wrote in Section 10: Some say that when it is invalid in two or three places, it is specifically when the blemish has spread over the majority, even though in the area of the spots it is a minority. But if it is a minority, such as all on one side of the etrog – it is valid. And some invalidate even if it is a minority on one side. So far his language, and this is according to the interpretation of "some explain." But according to the first interpretation, that a majority on one side is like a majority over the whole, we must say according to the first opinion: that if the blemish spreads over the majority of one side, even though in area it is not the majority of one side, but if it is a minority of one side – it is valid. And some invalidate even in its minority. And our master the Beit Yosef who wrote so, that one side is considered a minority – because it was obvious to him that the interpretation in the Jerusalem Talmud is like "some explain," and not like the first interpretation, as he wrote in his major work. But there are some of the earlier authorities who interpreted like the first interpretation, and we must be concerned about this (see Magen Avraham, Section 12). And even according to our master the Beit Yosef’s interpretation, if it only reaches a bit to the other side – it is called a majority, which is the majority of its circumference, even though it is not the majority of the whole etrog. (There, Section 13, and see the Gra, Section 20. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

If the scab covers half and half in one place – some deem it valid, for it is specifically when it covers the majority that it is invalid, but not when it is half and half, and it is possible to be precise. And some deem it invalid because we require the majority visible to the eyes, and it is not possible to be precise (see Beit Yosef). And this is the main ruling in practice. It is true that we learned: If the scab covers the majority – it is invalid, which implies that half is valid if we say it is possible to be precise, and we do not require the majority visible to the eyes. Nevertheless, in the latter part, we learned: If it covers a minority – it is valid, which clearly implies that half is invalid (Taz, subsection 16), and consequently, we are stringent. And so it should be instructed.

The Talmud (Sukkah 35b) states that a "chazazit" (blemish) only invalidates an etrog if it covers most of it, or if it appears in two or three places—this applies when it is not on the top of the etrog. The Gemara says: Rava said: If it is on the tip of the etrog, even the smallest amount invalidates it. Rashi explains: On the tip—on the thickness of its height, where it tapers and slopes down toward the top. This is because the eye focuses more on that area, and it is not beautiful. From this language, it seems that even on the thickness of its height itself, it is considered as if it is on the tip and slopes down toward the top. However, the Tur wrote: From its tip onward, this means from the place where it starts to slope until the pitom, etc. This clearly indicates that it is only at the sloped area, not on the thickness of the height itself. This is also explained by the language of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 9, who wrote: Its tip—this means from the place where it starts to shorten and become pointed toward its top. Based on this, it is possible to say that Rashi's intention is the same. When he wrote "on the thickness of its height," this is merely a marker for the place from which onward is called its tip, but not the thickness of the height itself. This is also explained by the language of the Rambam. Moreover, from the language of the Rambam, it is clear that he did not refer to the entire slope, as he wrote: If it is on the bulge, even the smallest amount invalidates it. And "the bulge" is only the part closest to the "rose" (the topmost point). The Maggid Mishneh brought that the Ri Ge'ut explained "its tip" as the pointed end and top of the etrog. It is clear that only the tip is invalidated by a small blemish. I am surprised that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch did not bring the opinion of the Rambam at all. (The Ran brought both interpretations. The Rosh wrote that according to Rashi, the entire slope is not called the tip. This requires further study.)

Just as a blemish (chazazit) disqualifies an etrog (citron) from its nose and upward, so too any change in appearance from its nose and upward – even the slightest amount – disqualifies it. However, this specifically refers to a change in appearance that disqualifies an etrog, which means black or white, and even this only if it is clearly visible to most people (Magen Avraham, small section 18). But a mere dot does not concern us, even from disqualifying appearances. Redness is not a disqualifying appearance, and all the more so any kind of green (as also written in Sha'arei Teshuvah, small section 21). And a golden appearance, which even in the case of menstrual blood is not considered red, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, section 188 – see there.
