Similarly, if the change in appearance is due to a thorn or leaf, which in our language is called "blattish" or "ritish," it is considered nothing. A change in appearance is only disqualifying if it is an inherent change. However, if the place becomes crooked and red due to thorns pricking it – it is valid (Magen Avraham, small section 19). And the same applies to any change in appearance caused by this.

There are those who say that the same applies to dryness—it invalidates the etrog if it is dry at its tip in any amount (Tur in the name of the Raavad). However, if it is cracked, it does not invalidate the etrog at its tip more than it would in any other part of the etrog (Magen Avraham, Subsection 17, in the name of the Rosh). And there are those who are concerned even about a crack, reasoning that it is not beautiful, and anything that affects the beauty invalidates the etrog at its tip in any amount. But in truth, a crack is not an issue of beauty but rather of complete taking (taking an unblemished etrog). Therefore, there is no distinction (there in the name of the Rema in Darkei Moshe). Similarly, when it is punctured or missing a part, there is no distinction between the tip and any other part of the etrog. See also Subsection 12.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in Section 13: A "chazazit" is like blisters. It has substance, its presence is noticeable by touch, as it is raised above the etrog. Therefore, those types of "chazazit" that are called "mol" are permissible, because they are not raised above the rest of the etrog. Some have written that they are permissible because they are considered part of the appearance of the etrog, as it is common for many to have them. Thus is his language: meaning, if so, even if they are raised above the rest of the etrog, it is permissible (there, Section 2). And I do not know what this "mol" is. Some have written that it is called "blat mol," and some have explained that it is called "plek," and in our language "pleyama," which is a lack of cleanliness. This occurs several times. And since it is not raised above the etrog, it is not considered a "chazazit." Indeed, in our etrogim, such "chazazit," like boils, are not found at all. This was found in the Genuva etrog and the Corsican etrog, but not in our etrogim. There is no distinction in this matter between the tip of the etrog and the rest of the etrog (Dagul Merivavah).

A fundamental principle to know is that whether the invalidation is due to a change in appearance or due to a scab, even if a scab appears on it in a manner that renders it invalid or if it is heavily speckled, if peeling it returns it to the appearance of an etrog, it is valid. However, this is specifically when peeling it does not cause any loss from the body of the etrog. But if there is a loss from the body of the etrog, it is invalid on the first day due to the defect. This is obvious, and we have seen many times that by attaching wax, the adhesion is removed. Similarly, when it is wiped with a soft item, sometimes it is removed and it becomes valid.

If water fell on it when detached, and as a result, worms entered it, or it became swollen or spoiled and emits a foul odor; or if it was pickled in vinegar for the amount of time it takes to place it on the fire and bring it to a boil, or pickled in water for twenty-four hours, or cooked, or speckled – it is invalid. The law regarding withered was explained in section 5, see there. "Speckled" means that the majority of it is speckled like spots, and not like scabs. Similarly, if it is black or white, which are among the invalid appearances: if it is in one place – it invalidates if it is in the majority. And if in two or three places – it has the same law as scabs, to invalidate even a minority, according to the laws explained regarding scabs.

The fact that a black etrog is invalid applies to etrogim that grow in regions where their appearance is green, like our etrogim. However, an etrog that grows in the land of Kush, where due to the intense heat everything tends to be black, even if they are slightly black, they are valid, for this is their natural way of creation and growth in those places, and this is not considered a deviation at all. However, this is only if they are slightly inclined to blackness. But if it is very black, like the people of Kush, it is invalid, as this does not fall under the category of "beautiful" (hadar) at all. And they are invalid for all seven days.

And the spherical like a ball - is invalid, for it does not have the shape of an etrog at all. Specifically, like a ball, but if it is round like a pot, meaning it is not like an etrog which is rounded in the middle and slopes downwards, and slopes upwards, but from its top to its bottom it is round, and it is long and not like a ball - it is valid. Some are concerned about this too (according to one version in Tosafot 36a, beginning with the words "etrog" which reads as a jug, see there). It is proper to be stringent initially (see Taz). Similarly, if it grew in a mold that was made for it while it was still small, and they placed it in there while it was still attached to the tree, and it grew inside it according to the mold's shape and form, until it changed from the shape of an etrog and became like a different kind of creature - it is invalid. But if the mold was in the shape of an etrog, even though it does not exactly resemble it, such as if it was made with some kind of boards like wooden panels - it is valid.

A twin etrog, that is, two etrogim that grew attached to each other – is kosher. One takes both of them together as one and recites the blessing over them. This is not considered "adding to the mitzvah" (bal tosif), because since they grew together, they are considered as one. On the contrary, if one separates them, it is considered as lacking (deficiency).

There is a doubt about if they were separated and became like two etrogim, and each one is separate from the other without any deficiency in their bodies, are they kosher? Or are they considered like half an etrog and therefore invalid? The Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG) invalidates twins, but the Rambam validates them, and so is ruled in the Shulchan Aruch. (In the Talmud there. And some say even twins are invalid, and they hold like the SeMaG, that perhaps the first Tanna does not dispute this. But for the Rambam, it is clear. See Beit Yosef.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 21: A green [etrog] that resembles the grasses of the field is invalid unless it returns to the appearance of an etrog when left to sit, in which case it is valid. Thus are their words. And among us, the etrogim of Corfu all come green and all return to the appearance of an etrog, and consequently, they are valid even while still green because they will return to the appearance of an etrog (Taz, Subsection 18). The invalidity of green is not due to lacking beauty but because the fruit is not fully ripened. Therefore, since it can return to the appearance of an etrog, it is considered to have fully ripened (there). And there are those who invalidate it until it entirely returns to the appearance of an etrog, but this is not so (there and Magen Avraham, Subsection 23). Nevertheless, the Maharil would invalidate it until part of it begins to return to the appearance of an etrog (there), for perhaps it has not yet fully ripened. But when it begins to return to the appearance of an etrog, it is a sign that the fruit has ripened, and over time it will completely return to its appearance. Certainly, initially, one should be concerned with his words, but when there is no other etrog, it seems that one can recite the blessing on it even on the first day, since it is known that the majority, if not all, will return to the appearance of an etrog.

An etrog of orlah is invalid because it is forbidden to eat, and the Torah says: "And you shall take for yourselves" – meaning it must be suitable for you in all manners of enjoyment (Rashi 31a). If you want to eat it, it must be possible to eat it. And orlah, since it is forbidden to eat, we do not call it "for you." And an etrog of doubtful orlah – it appears that in the Land of Israel it is forbidden, but outside the Land of Israel it is permitted according to the law of doubtful orlah, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, section 294.

An etrog of impure terumah is invalid because, as explained, it is not fit for consumption. However, an etrog of pure terumah should not be taken initially because the lulav is placed in water to prevent it from drying out, and it might come into contact with the etrog, causing it to become susceptible to impurity. It is forbidden to cause terumah to become impure, and even causing it indirectly is prohibited. If one took it, they have fulfilled their obligation since it is fit for consumption. Even a Levite or an Israelite fulfills their obligation, for although they themselves cannot eat it, it still fits the requirement of "you shall take for yourselves," as they can give it to a relative who is a Kohen (Rashi 35b). An etrog of untithed produce (tevel) is also invalid since it is not fit for consumption. An etrog of demai (produce of uncertain tithing status) is valid because if one wishes, they can renounce ownership of their possessions, become poor, and then it would be fit for them, as demai is permitted to the poor. An etrog of second tithe in Jerusalem should also not be taken initially due to the concern of susceptibility to impurity, similar to terumah. If it was taken, it is valid. However, outside of Jerusalem, since it cannot be eaten there, one does not fulfill their obligation. If one has vowed not to derive benefit from an etrog, its status is discussed in Yoreh De'ah, section 215; see there.

Regarding the size of the etrog, there is no upper limit. Even if it is very large, to the extent that it must be carried on the shoulder, it is still valid. However, there is a lower limit, which is that if it is less than the size of an egg, it is invalid. The reason is that most etrogim do not grow to be less than the size of an egg. If it does not reach the size of an egg, its fruit has not yet fully developed. The Torah states "fruit of a tree," implying it must be a fully developed fruit. Even if it would not grow any larger while remaining on the tree, it is still not considered an important fruit. But if it is the size of an egg, even though it is still unripe and its growth is not complete, since there are etrogim that, when fully grown, do not exceed the size of an egg, this too is considered a fully developed fruit, and one fulfills their obligation with it. However, it should not be as green as a leek.

We learn in Sukkah (41b): "The Sages taught: 'And you shall take'—this means that each individual must take it in hand. 'For yourselves'—from your own property, to exclude borrowed or stolen [lulav]. From here, they said: A person does not fulfill his obligation on the first day of the festival with his fellow's lulav." See there. And also with a shared [lulav], one does not fulfill his obligation, as Tosafot, the Rif, the Rambam, the Tur, and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in Siman 658. This is also explicitly stated in Bava Batra (137b), and Rashbam explains that it is written: "And you shall take for yourselves"—from your own property, meaning it must be entirely his, and not partially his. For even though we derive in the chapter "Reishit HaGez": "Your garments, your dough, your tithes"—to include a shared tallit, a shared dough, and shared produce, which are obligated in tzitzit, challah, and terumah, here too: if it were written "the fruit of the hadar tree for you"—even if shared. But since it is written "for yourselves"—it must be entirely his. And the reason it is not written "and you shall take for yourself"—is to indicate that each individual must take. This is his language. And I am perplexed: For regarding mezuzah, we say there that even though it is written "your house," nevertheless, since it is written "that your days may be multiplied" in plural form—we infer that even a shared [house] is included, see there. And is "for yourselves" worse than "your days"? The main points are not understood, as will be explained with Divine assistance.

For the essence of the interpretation of "and you shall take"—that there should be a taking in the hand of each and every individual. In other words, that each person is obligated to take the four species—this is entirely not understood. Why is a verse needed for this? Isn't it true for every mitzvah that each person must perform it individually, like sukkah, matzah, tefillin, and all the mitzvot? And why isn't there an interpretation that the obligation of sukkah, matzah, and tefillin is on each and every individual? For it is obvious that it is so, that every positive commandment is for each person in Israel to perform.

However, it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that in the version of the Rif, it is written "and you shall take"—indicating that the taking should be complete in the hands of each and every individual. Look there. And this is its explanation: that all four species should be complete for each and every individual and not in partnership, because in a partnership, each one does not have a complete taking in their hand. And since partnership is excluded, it follows that "yours" means from your own, to exclude the borrowed and the stolen. That is to say: if not for "and you shall take," I would have included partnership from "yours." But since partnership is excluded by "and you shall take," therefore "yours" comes to exclude the borrowed and the stolen. For even though at the moment it is a complete taking, nevertheless it is not fundamentally yours. And also according to our version in the Gemara, this is also the explanation: "and you shall take"—indicating that the taking should be for each and every individual, meaning a complete taking. And in the Torat Kohanim it is stated "and you shall take for yourselves"—each and every one, look there. And this is also the explanation, that each and every one should have a complete lulav, a complete etrog, and similarly all the species. And this is a complete taking, and it is clear with the help of Heaven.

And know: Regarding the fact that one does not fulfill the obligation with a borrowed [item], the commentators questioned from the previous section, Siman 14: Even though a borrowed tallit is exempt from tzitzit, as it is written "your garment" – and not someone else's, nevertheless, when one borrows a tallit with tzitzit, it was explained there that one can bless on it. This is based on the words of the Rosh, who wrote that since the lender lent it to him, he may bless on it. If it were impossible for him to bless until it is his own, we say that surely the intention is that it should be as a gift on condition of return, see there. Similarly, in Even HaEzer Siman 28 regarding the ring of betrothal, where one betroths with the groom's ring, nevertheless, when it was lent, we say that the intention was that it should be as a gift on condition of return. If so, here too: when he lent him the lulav, why do we not say that his intention was that if it would not be effective, it would be as a gift on condition of return, which is effective for the etrog as will be explained? (Taz there, subsection 5, and Magen Avraham Siman 658 subsection 3, and Keneses HaGedolah, Sukkah chapter 4, note 100.)

Many have struggled with this issue. There are those who want to say that indeed, the same applies to an etrog, and one can recite a blessing over it if it was lent without any specific stipulation (Magen Avraham, this siman, subsection 9). However, this does not seem correct, because according to their view, when the Torah excludes a borrowed item, it refers to when he explicitly says: "I am lending it to you," and not when it is given as a conditional gift to be returned. In such a case, our rabbis would have needed to clarify it (and the Machatzit HaShekel also expresses doubt about this). 

In my humble opinion, this is not a valid comparison at all. While it is true that we use this reasoning, it applies to items that are not diminished by this, such as a tallit or a ring, since it is not an obligation for him, obviously. But an etrog on the first day, where there is a mitzvah and an enhancement of the mitzvah – the lender must have an etrog for the entire day, as it is stated in the Gemara (41b) about the people of Jerusalem, that wherever they went, their lulav was with them. Therefore, it is certainly not agreeable to him to remove it completely from his possession for the entire day. And it is obvious that if his intention was to give it as a conditional gift to be returned, he could keep it for the entire day, and how would he do this and lose the enhancement of the mitzvah for himself? This is akin to the saying: "Do we tell a person to sin so that his fellow may merit?"

Therefore, if he explicitly says he gives it as a conditional gift to be returned, it is agreeable to him, and he fulfills the mitzvah, as I wrote in siman 658. But to say that his intention is automatically assumed to be such – it is clear that this is certainly not his intention. Also, for another reason, it is not comparable, for surely a person does not wish to completely remove his own item from his possession. Only with a tallit and ring do we say that it is as if he said he gives it as a conditional gift to be returned, and not entirely but partially. This is not the case with an etrog, where a partnership does not help, and you would have to say that he completely removed it from his possession – surely we do not say this unless he explicitly stated so himself.

Therefore, regarding all these four species, if one of them was borrowed, stolen, or robbed, whether from a Jew or from a non-Jew, whether before despair (ye'ush) or after despair, one does not fulfill one's obligation on the first day of the festival according to Torah law. For we need "And you shall take for yourselves," and this is not yours. And if one found one of them or all of them, if it is before despair, one does not fulfill the obligation, but if it is after despair, one fulfills the obligation. For regarding found objects, we hold that despair acquires, as I have written in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 259. But in the case of robbery and theft, despair does not acquire, as I have written there in Siman 353. And even if despair did acquire, or there was a change of domain after despair, as I have written there, nevertheless, it is forbidden because of the principle of a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. And it is written, "I am the Lord who hates robbery in burnt offerings."

And this is when the acquisition is through the mitzvah, for then it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression. But if he acquired it before the mitzvah, such as if he acquired it through a change of action, or a change of name, according to the laws regarding this – and if so, it became his before the mitzvah, and he does not owe him the original item, but rather needs to pay him money – he can fulfill the mitzvah with it, for this is not a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, and he can take it and recite a blessing over it. And there are those who say that although he can take it and fulfill his obligation with it, nevertheless, it is forbidden to recite a blessing over it, because one should not mention the name of Heaven over something that was originally stolen or robbed. And concerning this it is said: "And a thief who blesses has blasphemed the Lord." One should be concerned about this opinion, and in cases of doubt regarding blessings, we are lenient. (And how do you find that the acquisition comes through the mitzvah? For example, if at the time when he prepared it for the mitzvah – the change occurred then.)

All of this applies to the thief or robber himself. However, if he sold it or gave it as a complete gift to another person, and the original owners had already despaired of recovering it before the thief sold or gave it away, it is thus acquired by the buyer or recipient through the owner's despair and the change of possession. The buyer or recipient is not obligated to return anything, and it is considered genuinely theirs. They are also permitted to recite a blessing over it, because, for them, the term "blasphemer" does not apply, as they did not commit the sin. But if the original owners have not yet despaired, another person cannot fulfill their obligation with it even during the entire festival, due to the principle of a commandment that comes through a transgression. Meaning, it is still considered the property of the robbed party, and the buyer is using it unlawfully. The buyer must return it to the robbed party since it is before the owner's despair.

And even if it is after despair (ye'ush), no one else is permitted to fulfill their obligation with it unless he has acquired it or received it as a complete gift, as explained. But if the thief or robber lent it to another, or gave it to him as a gift on the condition that it be returned, even though the owners have already despaired, the borrower does not fulfill his obligation with it on the first day of the festival, since it is not acquired by him through a change of domain along with despair, as this is not considered a change of domain, because he is required to return it to the robber. However, on the other days when one may fulfill the obligation with a borrowed item, he may also fulfill it with this, and this is not considered a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, since the owners had already despaired before it was lent to him. There is no sin involved for the borrower, only for the robber himself, for with him it is always considered a mitzvah that comes through a transgression.

A Jew who buys from a non-Jew one of the species of the lulav that grows on the land of the non-Jew should not cut it himself, because there is a concern that the land might be stolen property in the hands of the seller. Land cannot be stolen, meaning it never leaves the possession of the original owner. Therefore, if the Jew cuts it, he essentially steals it from the original owner. Even though the original owner has already despaired of recovering it, it has already been explained that despair alone is not effective. Therefore, the non-Jew should cut it, and when he transfers it to the Jew, the combination of despair and change of possession will apply. Hence, if the Jew is not cutting it for himself but for another, it is also permissible, as the change of possession will occur with the other person, and it is permissible for him to cut it himself.

All of this is ideally. But after the fact, even if one picks a little bit for oneself – he has fulfilled the obligation and may recite a blessing over it, for this is merely a general concern, lest it be stolen by the seller. All the more so in a place where there is a "law of the land" regarding this matter; if the one holding the land holds it by the law of the land – there is no concern at all, and he may pick it for himself and for his own use. And certainly if he holds the land from the king himself, there is no concern. This applies outside of the Land of Israel, but in the Land of Israel, if one picks an etrog for himself, there is another concern due to the obligation of tithes. This is not the place to elaborate on this, but it is explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 331. Consequently, since there is a concern of the obligation of tithes – it is considered untithed produce, and one does not fulfill the obligation with it, as I have written.

This matter needs to be clarified: When it comes to the nobility, they have winter gardens called "enzaviyim," where palm branches and myrtles grow. If the noble himself gives him a palm branch or myrtle, or if the noble's wife gives it to him, he may cut it himself. But if one of the household members, or the gardener known as "agradnik," gives it to him, the Jew should not cut it himself, because perhaps they are giving it without the noble's permission, and it would be considered theft. Rather, they should cut it and give it to him, as I have written.

All four of these species, if one of them belonged to an Asherah tree, meaning it was worshipped as idolatry as was done in ancient times, if a Jew acquired it – it is completely invalid, even on the other days when it does not need to belong to him, because an item belonging to a Jew cannot be annulled and is designated to be burned. Anything designated to be burned is considered as if it is already burned, and its measure is considered diminished. And each one [of the species] requires a specific measure, as will be explained in the following section. However, if it belongs to a non-Jew and the Jew did not intend to acquire it but only to return it to him – ideally, he should not take it because it is repulsive for the mitzvah. Even if it was planted not for the purpose of worship and was later worshipped, and it is permitted for ordinary use – nevertheless, for the mitzvah, it is repulsive. But after the fact, if he already took it – he fulfills his obligation on the other days, since it can be annulled. And even though it has not yet been annulled, since it can be annulled, its measure is not considered diminished. And even though it is forbidden for benefit – we maintain that mitzvot were not given for benefit. On the first day – it is invalid because it is not his. But if it has been annulled – he can acquire it, and it is also valid on the first day.

And this applies specifically when they worship it. However, if they do not worship it, but rather plant it so they can eat its fruits, or for the beautification of the courtyard – it is permitted, just as for a common person, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, siman 143. But if they planted it for the beautification of idol worship – it is forbidden. The laws of Orlah, Tevel, and Terumah were explained in the previous siman. And one who vows not to derive benefit from his own lulav or that of his friend – it is invalid to take it on the first day, as it is not "yours," since it is not suitable for all manners of benefit for him. And even though he can annul his vow – nevertheless, as long as he has not annulled it, it is not "yours." And it seems to me that if he took it and then annulled his vow – he has fulfilled [the obligation], as the sage uproots the vow from its inception. And on the other days there is no concern at all, since it does not need to be his. And if it is because he vowed not to benefit from it – this is not considered benefit, as mitzvot were not given for pleasure.

And know: Among all the invalidations that have been explained in this section and the previous section, there are some that are invalid for all seven days, and there are some that are invalid only on the first day, but not on the other days, as will be explained. Behold, the Rambam in Chapter Eight, Law Nine wrote, and this is his language: All invalidations due to blemishes that we have explained, or due to theft and robbery – are only on the first day of the festival. But on the second day of the festival, along with the other days – everything is valid. And the invalidations that are due to idolatry, or because that etrog is forbidden to be eaten, whether on the first day of the festival or on the other days – are invalid. So far his language. And according to his words, even the invalidations due to "hadar" (beauty), like dryness and blemishes – are also valid on the other days. Likewise, all those that are cut off, and all those that are cracked. Also, it is clear from his words that the second day of the festival is like the other days, even though we observe it due to a doubt about the day, nevertheless since we are knowledgeable about the intercalation of the month – in the end, it is only a rabbinic enactment. And it is also explained in the Yerushalmi that all invalidations are only on the first day.

But the Raavad wrote that stolen and dry [lulavs] are invalid for all the days: stolen because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, dry because it is like a dead [object], see there. That is to say, concerning dry [lulavs], it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud that "the dead do not praise God," and consequently, it is not fitting for the other days as well. And similarly, a stolen [lulav], which is a disgrace to perform a mitzvah through a transgression, also makes no distinction [between the days]. This is also the opinion of the Tosafot and the Rosh at the beginning of Lulav HaGozul, see there, where they wrote that the primary taking [of the lulav] was instituted for the other days as it is for the first day. And similarly, [regarding] beauty due to the enhancement of the mitzvah. And in the case of a stolen [lulav], there is a dispute in the Gemara, that according to Rabbi Yochanan, who invalidates it because it is a mitzvah that comes through a transgression, it is invalid. But a deficient or borrowed [lulav] was not instituted [as invalid]. And so wrote the Rosh. According to this, also a lulav with a growth [blemish] is invalid, and similarly, those that are cut off, whose invalidation is due to beauty, are also invalid for all the days. And there are those who also invalidate a deficient [lulav] if mice have gnawed it, because it is repugnant, as will be explained.

Our master, the Beit Yosef, in paragraph 5, ruled according to the Rambam, and this is his wording: All those we mentioned who are invalid due to the blemishes we explained, or because of theft and robbery – this applies only on the first day of Yom Tov. But on the other days – all are valid. And the invalidation that is due to idolatry, or because the etrog is forbidden to eat, or because they are not of their kind, such as a "wild myrtle" or a poplar, or they lack the required measure – whether on the first day of Yom Tov or on other days, they are invalid. And those who observe two days of Yom Tov – the invalid items on the first day are taken on the second, but no blessing is recited. So far his wording. And although according to the Rambam, the second day of Yom Tov is like the other days, as I wrote, nevertheless, regarding the blessing, he was concerned for those who consider the second day of Yom Tov, since it is doubtful whether it is like the first – it has the same law as the first. Therefore, since blessings are not essential – one should not recite a blessing. And for the halacha, the main point is that there is no difference between the second day of Yom Tov and the other days, unlike those who want to be stringent in this matter. And those that are not of their kind, and those that lack the required measure – it is obvious that even the Rambam agrees, and he did not need to mention them because it is an obvious matter. (See Magen Avraham, subparagraph 20, that specifically an etrog which is fit to eat – does not help when it is forbidden to eat. But other species, even if forbidden for benefit – are valid. Only when it is completely disintegrated is it invalid. And he also wrote that orlah outside of Israel is valid on other days, see there, and it needs further study. And be precise and you will find leniency.)

And our master, the Rema, ruled according to the Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Raavad. And this is his language: "There are those who invalidate a stolen [lulav] for the entire seven days, and this is the custom. But one fulfills the obligation with a borrowed [lulav]... and if it is deficient – it is valid on the other days. And if its tip or stem was removed – its law is like that of a deficient [lulav], and it is valid from the first day onward. However, if mice have gnawed it – one should not take it even on the other days due to repulsiveness, until the gnawing of the mice is removed. But if it was dry or speckled, which invalidates it for all seven days, even if the dryness or speckling was cut away – it remains invalid for all seven days, since it comes from a state of invalidation... And blisters (on the lulav) invalidate it for all seven days." So far his language. And that which he wrote that if its tip or stem was removed it is considered deficient, and valid on the other days – there are those who disagree. And they hold that if its tip was removed – its invalidation is due to lack of beauty (hidur), and therefore, one should not be lenient in this (Magen Avraham, sub-section 17). And there is no concern in this, for even if this is so, the opinion of the Rambam is to be lenient even regarding beauty, as I have written (Eliyahu Rabbah, sub-section 15). And there are those who are lenient even with blisters (there). And I say that we should not deviate from the words of our master, the Rema. And blisters – invalidate, and if its tip was removed – it is valid. And the reason that removing the gnawing of mice helps, but not for dryness and speckling, is because mice do not cause a complete invalidation, only because of repulsiveness (there). And the Kolbo permits even with blisters and dryness.

And this is the language of the Kol Bo: "A [species of the Four Species] that is missing, dry, has blisters, swollen, boiled, whose pitom or stem was removed, whose lulav leaves were split, cracked, shriveled, bent, or a myrtle with black or red berries – are valid during the rest of the days [of Sukkot]. But an 'insane myrtle,' a poplar, an Ethiopian etrog, and one that grew in a mold to resemble a different creature – are invalid forever. Likewise, palm branches that are not lulavs at all. Until here is his language." 

Behold, he was very lenient, for he holds like the opinion of the Rambam that even those invalid due to lack of beauty (hiddur) are valid during the rest of the days [of Sukkot]. However, in any case, we can simply rely on the opinion of our teacher, the Rema. And regarding a cracked lulav, our teacher the Rema agrees that it is valid, for its invalidation is only due to the requirement of a complete taking, and it is obvious that it is valid during the rest of the days. But concerning a myrtle with black or red berries, swollen, boiled, whose leaves were split, shriveled, or bent – it seems that these are due to lack of beauty (hiddur), and they are invalid according to our teacher the Rema.

It is permitted to take another person's lulav without his knowledge on the other days, except for the first day, because since it is not damaged by taking it, a person is pleased to fulfill a mitzvah with his property. However, one should not take it from his house to another place, or to the synagogue, without his permission. For taking it from his house, it is certainly not agreeable to him, as I wrote in Siman 14 regarding a tallit, see there. Nevertheless, on the second day of Yom Tov, one should only take it with his knowledge. And although the Rambam is lenient on the second day of Yom Tov as on the other days, nevertheless, in this matter, one should be concerned. And similarly, for all that we are lenient on the other days, on the second day of Yom Tov, when there is another person with a completely valid lulav and etrog, one should ask him to give it as a gift with the condition to return it, and take it with a blessing. Afterwards, he may take his own whenever he wishes. (This is the intention of the Rema at the end of section 5, and the Magen Avraham in section 23. In any case, I believe that we are completely lenient on the second day of Yom Tov as on the other days, relying on the opinions of the Rambam and the Tur and the Beit Yosef).

Although it is known that an etrog is set aside for its mitzvah for the entire festival, nevertheless, it is permitted by means of a condition. That is: it is initially permitted to make a condition on the etrog that it is designated only for the first day, and that one does not separate from it during the twilight period between the first and second days. In that case, it is permitted to eat it on the night of the second day or on the second day. One can fulfill the mitzvah with the remainder since a damaged etrog is still valid, provided it meets the minimum size requirement, which is the size of an egg. However, we are not proficient in making such conditions, as I have written in section 638 regarding the wood of the sukkah, and therefore, one should not do this. For this day, the condition does not help, although some say it does.

It is stated in the Gemara (31a-31b): A dry lulav is invalid. Rabbi Yehuda deems it valid, and there is a story about the people of the towns who would bequeath their lulavim to their children. The Sages said to him: A time of distress is not a valid proof. Based on this, Maimonides wrote at the beginning of the eighth chapter that in a time of distress or danger, a dry lulav is valid, but not the other species. These are his words. And the Geonim said that a dry [lulav], one whose tip is cut off, and all invalid species can be used in a time of distress (Maggid Mishneh). Maimonides holds that since we only find this practice with a lulav, we should not validate others (there). The Tur disagrees with him and rules like the Geonim, see there. According to Maimonides, even with a lulav, only a dry one can be validated, but not other invalid species.

And the Ra'avad, of blessed memory, completely disagreed with this, and wrote that the statement "a time of exigency is not a proof" is not about fulfilling the obligation and reciting the blessing over it, but rather about taking it merely as a symbolic act, so that the mitzvah of the etrog is not forgotten. See there. However, most of our rabbis agreed with the Geonim. Nevertheless, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 6 regarding a time of exigency, where no kosher one is found, that all invalid ones can be taken, but no blessing is recited. These are his words. Since the blessing is not essential, why should we recite it even though the law follows the majority of the decisors? However, those that are not of their kind, such as grafted ones, stolen ones, and those that do not have the required measure, are invalid even in a time of exigency (see Magen Avraham, subsection 24).

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that some permit a dry lulav, even to recite a blessing over it. And so, the custom is to bless over dry lulavs, even if there are fresh ones available to others. But with other species, one should not act this way. And some are lenient even with a dry myrtle, and one may rely on them in pressing circumstances. This is his language. And the matter is perplexing: how can we bless over dry ones when fresh ones are available? Therefore, some have written that the fresh ones are not completely fresh and are almost similar. But when there are fully fresh ones – it is impossible to bless over dry ones (Magen Avraham, section 26). Therefore, nowadays, when there are many fresh ones – it is forbidden to bless over a dry lulav, for they only permitted it due to pressing circumstances, and now this is not a pressing circumstance. All the more so, one should not bless over dry myrtles. However, if one comes to a place where it is impossible to obtain fresh ones – the authorities and our teacher the Rema are sufficient to rely on to bless over them. But a dry etrog – in any manner, it is invalid, and all the more so dry willows, for fresh ones are easily found. See in the next section.

And know: Even though an etrog (citron) that is lacking is valid on the other days [of Sukkot], this is when a small part has been cut off, and the majority remains intact. But one should not cut an etrog into two or three parts, divide it, and use it [for the mitzvah], even in pressing circumstances, and even if each piece has the size of an egg. For this is not called a lacking etrog, but rather a piece of an etrog. "Lacking" is called when the main part remains, and a small part is missing, and this is how one should rule. (What the Rema wrote: "And all this is regarding the blessing, but without a blessing, one may take all the invalid [species], and not bless on them; thus far his words" – this requires much investigation. For if his intention is also regarding those that are not of their kind, as the Magen Avraham wrote in subparagraph 28 – it's difficult: from where did he take this? And it seems more to me that his intention is also regarding a dry etrog and a dry willow as per the opinion of the Geonim, and not on other matters. And his intention is that even though he disagrees with the Beit Yosef, and rules only on the lulav and hadas, nevertheless without a blessing he agrees with him. Examine and you will find light.)

The measurement of the length of the lulav is not similar to the measurement of the length of the hadas (myrtle) and aravah (willow), for in their case, one measures from the end of the wood to the top. But with the lulav, one measures from its end, not to the top but to the end of the spine, meaning to the place where the leaves are attached to the spine. The leaves from that point onward, which have no spine, are not included in the measurement, as clarified in the Gemara (Sukkah 32b). And one should not be surprised that we measure from the very end: are there no leaves at all there? This is not a wonder, for since the majority of its length has leaves, it does not need more. And the Torah says "a branch of a thick-leaved tree" regarding the hadas, meaning the main part is the wood, and consequently, one measures the entire wood for all of them. For this reason, it appears that one does not measure the lulav from the spine upward, because from that point onward it is not wood, but leaves. Therefore, with the hadas and aravah as well, if the leaves extend above the wood, the measurement is only up to the end of the wood, not including the leaves that extend above the wood.

And the Rambam wrote in Chapter 7, Law 8: What is the minimum length of each type (of the Four Species)? The lulav (palm branch) must be no less than four handbreadths, and its measurement is taken from its spine alone, not from the tips of the leaves. The myrtle and willow must each be no less than three handbreadths. So far his words, and the same is written by the Rif. According to this, the length of the lulav is sixteen thumb-breadths, and the length of the myrtle and willow is twelve thumb-breadths. However, our rabbis have already questioned their words, for it is explicitly stated in the Gemara there that the measurement is with a cubit of five handbreadths, and according to this, the lulav must be thirteen and a third thumb-breadths, and the myrtle and willow ten thumb-breadths. This is the opinion of the Rosh, the Tur, the Raavad, and all our rabbis. And this is the main ruling. Only the opinion of the Ramban, of blessed memory, is: that although the myrtle and willow are according to the measure of a cubit of five handbreadths, and therefore the Mishnah which required three handbreadths for their measure – they are ten thumb-breadths. Nevertheless, the handbreadth that the lulav exceeds them is like a general handbreadth of four thumb-breadths, and according to this, the lulav is fourteen thumb-breadths up to the spine.

And the ruling: Certainly, if it is possible to be stringent according to the words of the Rif and the Rambam, it is good. However, the main ruling follows the majority of the poskim (halachic authorities), as I have written. And know: if the myrtle and willow branches are very large, nevertheless, the spine of the lulav must be a handbreadth taller than them. There is no limit to their length; even if they are very long, they are kosher.

The mitzvah of the four species is that each person should take one lulav, one etrog, three hadassim, and two aravot. For the phrase "fruit of a beautiful tree" (refers to the etrog), the Torah indicates one fruit; "branches of date palm trees" – "branches" is written without the letter vav, which implies one; "boughs of thick-leaved trees" – three: "bough" – one, "tree" – one, "thick-leaved" – one (Rashi 34b); "willows of the brook" implies two. Therefore, "boughs of thick-leaved trees" is not written because it would imply two, like "willows of the brook," and we need three. Also, from the plain meaning of the verse, we understand that there are three hadassim, for it is impossible to say one – that would not be "a bough," and it would suffice to write "a thick-leaved tree," like "a beautiful tree." And it is impossible to say two – it would have to write "trees of thick-leaved," and it would be like "willows of the brook." Rather, the "thick-leaved" refers back to the "bough," meaning three boughs, that is, three branches of myrtle (Bach). And in this way, it resembles a bough. (And surely Rabbi Akiva, who says one myrtle and one willow, holds that it refers to the species. But we, who follow Rabbi Yishmael, must say as I have written. And Ramban rules like Rabbi Akiva, but Rambam rules like Rabbi Yishmael, and so do the Geonim, as Maggid Mishneh writes. And so Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled, and this is the accepted halacha. And perhaps if one only has one myrtle and one willow, they should take them, for in a pressing situation, we can rely on Ramban. Also, Raavan and Raavya ruled like Ramban, as Mordechai writes. And they should be taken without a blessing. This is what seems correct to me in my humble opinion.)

On the myrtle branches and the willows - one may add as many as they wish. For if it were written explicitly "three" and "two," it would not be possible to add. But now that it is not written explicitly, rather it is written in a language of plurality - one may add. And so was the custom of the ancients for the sake of beauty (Maimonides' glosses there). And what is found in the words of Maimonides there in this language: "And if one wishes to add myrtle branches so that it will be a large bundle - he may add, and it is a beautification of the mitzvah." But for the other species - one should not add to their number nor subtract from them, and if one added or subtracted - it is invalid. This is his language, implying that also for willows one should not add - indeed the Ran of blessed memory brought the version "And if one wishes to add myrtle branches and willows - he may add." And besides this, Maimonides wrote in a response that a mistake fell in his books, and it should be said: "And if he added, it is not invalid" (Kesef Mishneh). For thus our Rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote (34b) that "You shall not add" only applies when adding a different species, see there. However, regarding the etrog and the lulav, since the Torah commanded one each - it is obvious that it is forbidden to add. But regarding the myrtle and the willow - it is obvious that one may add as many as they wish. And see in section 28.

The Tur wrote that three myrtle branches—even if all three are cut at their tops—are valid. The Rambam also validated a cut willow, but this is not clear. Thus far his words. The laws of cut branches have already been explained in previous sections (Beit Yosef). Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 1: "In a pressing situation where there is no valid myrtle, one may suffice with one myrtle that is not cut." Thus far his words. The Ramban holds that even one cut myrtle is sufficient, and it is proper to rely on his opinion in a pressing situation (Magen Avraham, small section 1). Nevertheless, it seems to me that since the blessing is not essential, one should not recite the blessing over it. And know that when purchasing one or all of the four species from a non-Jew, do not belittle his price, and even give him slightly more than its value so that he does not belittle them (there, beginning of section 649). This means that one should not say: "How undervalued these mitzvot are by Israel, as they pay so little for them." (But the intention is not like with tefillin in section 39, where one should not discard them. For the four species do not have sanctity when not used for the mitzvah. Also, tefillin are not suitable at all, but these species are used for decoration. Rather, the intention is as written by the Machatzit Hashekel, see there.)

According to Torah law, it is not required to bind all the species of the lulav, hadassim, and aravot together. Whether they are bound or not bound, it is valid (Talmud, Sukkah 33a). For it is not written "bundle" as it is with hyssop, where it says "a bundle of hyssop" (Exodus 12:22). Not only that, but there is not even an obligation to take them together. Rather, even if they are taken one after the other, one fulfills the obligation, as Maimonides writes there, and this is his wording: Once one lifts these four species, whether he lifts them together or one after the other, whether with the right hand or the left hand, he fulfills the obligation, provided that he lifts them in the manner they grow. But if not in the manner they grow, he does not fulfill the obligation. And the proper way to perform the mitzvah is to lift a bundle of the three species in the right hand and the etrog in the left hand. And then one should wave them forward and backward, upward and downward… until here is his wording.

And this is what he wrote, "a mitzvah performed properly," meaning: although according to the law it does not require binding, nevertheless, it is a preferred mitzvah due to "This is my God, and I will glorify Him" to bind it (Gemara there, 33a). And this is the language of the Tur: One should make from the myrtle, willow, and lulav one bundle. Although we maintain that the lulav does not require binding, it is a mitzvah to bind it for the sake of beauty. And since there is no obligation to bind it, even if one binds it with a different species, it is acceptable. And there is also no concern of interposition, even though the binding interrupts between the hand and the lulav, since it is for beautification, it does not interpose. Similarly, the same species does not interpose, therefore, if leaves from the lulav or myrtle fall off and remain within the bundle in a manner that interrupts, there is no concern. And Rashi explained: Although it does not require binding, nevertheless, initially, it is an obligation to bind it due to "This is my God, and I will glorify Him" – to beautify oneself before Him with the commandments. And if one did not bind it from the previous day, or if the binding became untied on Yom Tov, it is impossible to bind it with a complete knot. Rather, one binds it like a bundle of vegetables, wrapping the bundle around and tucking the end of the bundle into it without tying. So far his language. And the same applies that one can do it by making a loop. The difference between Rashi and the previous opinion is that Rashi holds that "This is my God, and I will glorify Him" is an obligation, but it does not invalidate [the mitzvah]. However, it is an obligation initially. And according to the previous opinion, there is no obligation at all, only an enhancement of the mitzvah (see Beit Yosef).

Therefore, ideally, it is a mitzvah to bind them with a complete knot, which means two knots one on top of the other. And one can bind them not with their own kind, as I have written. But one must be careful that within the binding there should not be something that is not of its kind that would create a barrier, for something of its own kind does not create a barrier, but something not of its kind does create a barrier. Therefore, as is customary with the old myrtles, which are wrapped around with a string, one should be careful to remove the string from them, so that the string does not become an interruption in the binding. However, to wrap around them with something for decoration is permitted even if it is not of their kind, for anything for decoration is not a barrier for us, as we do not require binding, as the Tur wrote.

And our master the Rema wrote at the end of section 1: There are those who wrote to make the binding in another way: they wrap these three species around, and insert the wrapped head into the wrapped circle. Up to here is his wording, meaning: even on weekdays, and they do not make a knot upon a knot. And the reason seems to be: because this way is more beautiful. Therefore, now the custom is to make beautiful rings from the lulav leaves themselves, and insert the three species into the rings. And they beautify the work with a nice braid of three spaces, and each species is inserted into its space. And this is an adornment for the mitzvah, and so is the custom.

It is also written that the myrtle should be tied higher than the willow, and the myrtle and willow should be lowered within the binding of the lulav, so that all three species are held in the hand at the time of the blessing. Some have written to make three bindings on the lulav, and this is the custom. This is the end of his language. All of this is not essential but for beautification. Since the myrtle is more important than the willow, as it has a good fragrance, it should therefore be more prominent than the willow. In order to hold them all at the time of the blessing, the myrtle and willow should not be placed slightly within the binding, for if so, when one takes the lulav, these will not come within the palm of the hand. Rather, they should be placed within the binding up to its base, and one will hold them all. The three bindings on the lulav are to prevent the leaves from separating, and this is a beauty for the lulav, as anything held by three is more stable. We also currently follow this, except that two bindings encompass all, and one is for the lulav alone. None of this is essential, but it is for the beautification of the mitzvah. There are also symbolic hints in this. The myrtle, being more important, is on the right, the willow on the left, and the lulav in the middle. This is the custom. (According to the Ari, the myrtles are divided to the right, left, and middle, and the willows, one to the right and one to the left.)

And one should take the bundle in their right hand, with the tops facing upward and the bases downward, so that it is in the manner of their growth. And all mitzvot require the manner of their growth. If not, one has not fulfilled the obligation. We derive this from a verse (Leviticus 23:40). The etrog should be in the left hand. Therefore, the etrog is in the left hand and the three species are in the right hand, because these three are a set, and the etrog is one. Additionally, the blessing is on the lulav, hence it should be in the right hand; just like the blessings over enjoyment, where the object being blessed should be held in the right hand, as I wrote in Siman 206. 

Why not hold them all in the right hand? Because it is written "the fruit of a beautiful tree, palm branches, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook," and it does not say "and palm branches" — we understand from this that the Torah insists the etrog should be separate. However, one should bring the hands close together, so that the etrog is connected to the three species, and God forbid to separate them from each other. This is also the practice during the recitation of Hallel and the Hoshanot. 

When one puts down the species, first put down the etrog and then the three species, because what is taken first is put down last. A mnemonic for this is the tefillin of the hand and the head; when putting them on, the hand comes first, and when removing them, it is last. One should not pass the etrog from hand to hand; rather, one should place it down and the other person should come and take it (Magen Avraham, small section 8, in the name of the Shlah). I do not know the reason for this, and with the lulav, there is no such stringency. 

Our custom is to hold the lulav with the spine facing oneself, and although there are those who say the spine should face outward (ibid.), nevertheless, this is the custom.

Some say that a left-handed person (an "iter yad") holds [the lulav] like everyone else: the lulav in the right hand, which for him is the left, and the etrog in the left hand of everyone else, which for him is the right. This is also the opinion in the Tur. However, others say that this is not the case, and instead, he holds the lulav in his right hand, which is the left for everyone else, and the etrog in his left hand, which is the right for everyone else. This is the custom and the primary ruling, similar to the laws of tefillin, as ruled by the Rosh. There is an error in the Tur, and it should state the opposite (Taz, small section 3), as the Tur himself ruled in his hints. Additionally, how could he not mention the opinion of the Rosh? Rather, it is a printing error, as also written by the Maharshal. However, this is only ideally. After the fact, if he switched [hands], it does not invalidate, because even for everyone else, if one took the lulav in the left hand and the etrog in the right hand, it does not invalidate, and certainly for a left-handed person. If he is ambidextrous, he holds the lulav in his right hand and the etrog in his left hand, like everyone else. (And what the Taz questioned in small section 4 is resolved according to what the Magen Avraham wrote in small section 9. Rabbeinu Chananel explains that everyone has not fulfilled [the mitzvah] if they switched from right to left. The Magen Avraham wrote that it is proper to be concerned and take it afterward without a blessing as the law. According to this, the words of the Rema are clear. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 4: A person who does not have a hand takes the lulav with his forearm, and similarly the etrog. Thus far his language. He compared this to what they said in Sanhedrin (45a) regarding the thumb of the hand, where the blood needs to be sprinkled, that if he does not have it, he sprinkles it on its place. This is perplexing because the law is not like this, see there. However, the truth is that it does not say "and you shall take with your hand," but this is when he does not have two hands. But if he has a left hand, he takes the lulav with his hand, and the etrog with his forearm, for his forearm relative to his left hand is considered like a left hand, obviously. And if he does not have two hands, he takes the lulav with his right forearm, and the etrog with his left forearm. The same law applies if his hands are in pain or bound, and the like. But taking with teeth is not considered taking (see Eliyah Rabbah section 13 and Sha'ar HaTziyun). But to take all of them in one hand - certainly not, because the Torah was particular that the etrog should be by itself, as it did not say "and a palm branch," as I wrote. And it would be understandable if binding were required to say that the intention of the Torah is not to bind them together. But since binding is not required, certainly the Torah's intention is not to take them in one hand (see Magen Avraham section 10).

It is well known that one must recite a blessing for all commandments prior to performing them, and immediately before performing them. It is also known that as soon as one takes the lulav and etrog in his hand, he has fulfilled the commandment. Now: how should he proceed with the blessing? If he recites the blessing after he has taken them in his hand, he is not doing so prior to performing the commandment. If he recites the blessing before he has taken them at all, it is not immediately before performing the commandment, for by the time he takes all of them, which is the commandment, there will be an interruption. Therefore, our Sages taught us that he should take the lulav in his hand, recite the blessing "on taking the lulav," and on the first day also "Shehecheyanu." Immediately thereafter, he should take the etrog and fulfill the commandment. For before he has taken the etrog, it is considered prior to performing the commandment.

There is another suggestion: to also hold the etrog and turn it upside down with its stem facing upward, and one does not fulfill the obligation in this manner, since it must be held in the way it grows. One then recites the blessing, and afterward turns it right side up. This is the practice of the masses. Additionally, there is another suggestion: to intend not to fulfill the obligation, for even according to the opinion that mitzvot do not require intention, if one explicitly intends not to fulfill the obligation, one certainly does not fulfill it. Accordingly, one can hold the lulav properly, intend not to fulfill the obligation, recite the blessing, and then intend to fulfill the obligation. However, it is not appropriate to do this, as it can easily lead to mistakes since the only indication is in one's thoughts. And who can guarantee that one will think correctly (Taz, subsection 5; Magen Avraham, subsection 12)? If one did this, it is done. There is also a suggestion to hold the lulav and etrog in the left hand, recite the blessing, and then transfer the lulav to the right hand (ibid.). This too is not advisable, for it is certainly far-fetched to say that one does not fulfill the Torah obligation in this manner. Even if the Torah is particular about this, as I have written, it is more reasonable to say that one fulfills the Torah obligation. However, one can say that in such a scenario, one certainly intends not to fulfill the obligation. Nevertheless, the proper way is the first method, as I wrote in the previous section. However, if one forgets and holds them all properly without reciting the blessing, one should recite the blessing while they are still in one's hand, for as long as they are in one's hand, it is considered the continuation of the mitzvah. It is similar to one who forgets to recite the blessing "Hamotzi" and recites it in the middle of the meal, as I wrote in Siman 167 (ibid., subsection 11). One should recite the blessing standing. One should also take it and shake it while standing. If one sits, one still fulfills the obligation, as standing is not an absolute requirement after the fact; even initially, it is only for the honor of the mitzvah. (And what I wrote that we derive "for you"-"for you" from the Omer, this is merely a support). Before shaking, one should consider it as if passing before performing the mitzvah (Tur).

One should only recite the blessing once a day. Afterwards, when taking it (the lulav) again, it is done without a blessing. This is not comparable to the sukkah, which is an obligation throughout the day and night. And even though with tefillin, if one lays them for just one hour, he has fulfilled the mitzvah of tefillin, yet he still blesses whenever he lays them; nevertheless, it is not the same. Truly, the mitzvah of tefillin is all day long, and it is just that we are unable to fulfill it due to being occupied and the need for bodily cleanliness. But the mitzvah of lulav is only the act of taking it once, and that suffices. The fact that one takes it several times is merely due to the love of the mitzvah, and one does not bless for this. And do not say: since the Sages instituted shaking it during Hallel, why should one not bless it before Hallel, even if he blessed in the morning? It can be said that the Sages did not institute a blessing for these shakings. Moreover, he already shook it at the time of the blessing. And know: the blessing of "Shehecheyanu" should be recited at the time of taking it, not when making it before the festival. Even though the Talmudic law (Sukkah 46a) indicates this, nevertheless, our custom is not so for the sukkah and all mitzvot. Also, in the Talmud there, it is found that they blessed at the time of performing the mitzvah, not at the time of preparing it.

It is written in Orchos Chaim: An incident occurred with our teacher, Rabbi Meshulam, who took the lulav on the first day of Yom Tov and recited the blessings "al netilat lulav" and "shehecheyanu." Afterwards, he looked at it and did not find the aravah (willow). He then took some aravot (willows) and placed them in the lulav, took it again, and also took the etrog, and recited the blessings "al netilat aravah" and "shehecheyanu" because of the aravah. Although it is sufficient to take only the aravah separately (as one fulfills the mitzvah by taking them one after the other, as I have written), it is preferable to perform the mitzvah by taking all four species together. This is also found in the writings of the Ra’avad, of blessed memory (Beit Yosef). According to this, the same law applies to all the species, that if one forgot or did not take a species in the proper manner, he must take it again correctly and recite the blessing for that species. Therefore, if one took the etrog upside down, recited the blessing, and did not correct it, thinking he fulfilled the mitzvah, and then realized it was upside down – he must take them again and recite "al netilat etrog." In the incident with Rabbi Meshulam, it must also be said that some time elapsed after the blessing; for if it had been immediately, why would he need to recite the blessing again? On the contrary, that would be considered "over la’asiyatan" (performing the mitzvah immediately after the blessing), as one takes the etrog after the blessing. Rather, it is certain that some time elapsed, and he had already performed the waving, or was in the middle of the waving. This will be further clarified in section 28.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: If one made a handle and placed the lulav in it and took it – it is acceptable, since taking with the aid of another object is still considered taking, as long as it is done respectfully. However, if it is not done respectfully, such as placing the lulav in a vessel and then taking it – he has not fulfilled his obligation. And if he wrapped a cloth around it and took it, or wrapped a cloth around his hand and took it – some say he has not fulfilled his obligation. Thus far are his words, and this needs clarification.

And the matter is thus: It has already been explained that an interposition invalidates the lulav. Nevertheless, if one holds it using a handle, in the manner that one holds a tool with tongs, it is not considered an interposition, because this is the usual way of holding it, and taking it with something else is still considered taking. There are those who wish to say that this is only when the entire lulav is outside of his hand, and he holds it with an extended handle made from a cloth; in such a case, it is not considered an interposition since he is not holding the lulav in his hand (Magen Avraham, section 14). This means that an interposition is only called so when the lulav is within his hand and wrapped with something else, in which case the other object interposes between his hand and the lulav. But when the entire lulav is outside his hand, and he holds it using a handle, it is not considered an interposition, and taking it with something else is still considered taking.

But it does not seem correct to say so. On the contrary: would the lulav being within his hand be considered worse? And this is explicitly explained by the words of the Tur, who wrote: even if one made a handle, etc., it is permissible, even if the entire lulav is outside his hand, etc. Thus are his words. He wrote: even if the entire lulav is outside his hand, all the more so when it is within his hand, because through a handle there is no concern of interposition (and so wrote the Perisha, and in the Eliyah Rabbah, section 20). And although there is someone who wrote this (Beit Yosef), this is not the law (according to Rava and Rabba). According to the law, there is no difference whether the entire lulav is outside his hand or within his hand, as using a handle is permitted. (And so it appears from the Bach, and the Taz, section 6. And the Tosafot in Sukkah 37a who wrote in this manner - it is according to Rabba, see there. And this is not exact as proven from their words in Pesachim and Yoma 58a, see there carefully, and this is not the place to elaborate. Be precise and you will find ease.)

And this is on the condition that it is done in a respectful manner. However, using a vessel is not considered respectful, and in any case where one holds the vessel, he does not fulfill the obligation. Some distinguish between holding the vessel from the top, which fulfills the obligation, and from the bottom, which does not fulfill the obligation (see Beit Yosef). This is not the main ruling, as using a vessel is considered disrespectful. The vessel is made for protection, not for use through it. This is not the case with a handle, which is made specifically for use, and therefore it is permissible. All of this applies when the handle is a separate entity, and therefore it does not constitute an interposition. But if one wraps a cloth around the lulav and takes it, or if one wraps a cloth around his hand and takes it, it is considered an interposition and invalid. This is not like a handle, and it is not considered taking through another object, but taking with an interposition. Even though some say that if one wraps it around his hand, the cloth is nullified to the hand and does not interpose, this is not the ruling, and in any case, it interposes (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 16. And what he wrote in subparagraph 15 follows his reasoning in subparagraph 14. But according to what I have written, it is not so, and see Machatzit HaShekel. Be precise and you will find clarity).

And our master, the Rema, wrote that the custom is to be stringent and remove the tefillin and rings from one's hands. But according to the law, there is no need for concern, since the entire hand is not covered by them. Thus far his words. The statement regarding the removal of the tefillin pertains to their custom, where they did not remove the tefillin before Hallel. But we remove them before Hallel. And the statement that as long as the hand is not entirely covered, it does not constitute an interruption, even though in immersion even a small part is considered an interruption – this is because the entire body requires immersion. But here, one does not need to hold the lulav along its entire length. And even if one holds the etrog by its stem, it is still considered holding. Therefore, if only a part of the hand is exposed, it is holding it partially. (Regarding the question raised by the Bach and the Magen Avraham in subsection 18 from the Gemara 37a, concerning the lulav holders of the Exilarch's house, look there – I do not know. Because this was told to them so that they would not bind it entirely, and they would leave a place to hold it. And so it is implied from Rashi, look there. And scrutinize and you will find clarity.)

The Sages instructed to shake [the lulav] at the time of the blessing and during Hallel. The reason for the shaking is explained in the Midrash on the verse "Emor": Since on Rosh Hashanah the entire world comes to judgment, and no one knows who will emerge meritorious and who will be found guilty, the Holy One, blessed be He, gave this commandment to Israel so that they would rejoice with their lulavim. See there. And this is what is written: "Then the trees of the forest will sing for joy before the Lord, for He comes to judge the earth." This means: they will sing with the trees of the forest when they emerge meritorious before the Lord when He comes to judge the earth. And with what will they sing? With "Hodu" and "Hoshea Na" (Beit Yosef). For after this it is written, "Give thanks to the Lord... and say, save us, O God of our salvation" (Tosafot 37b, s.v. "BeHodu"). And why were these four species chosen? Because on the festival [of Sukkot] we are judged regarding water (Rosh Hashanah 16a), and these four species grow by the water. When we perform the commandment with them, the waters are blessed, and therefore we rejoice with them.

Where are the na'anuim (shaking of the lulav) done during Hallel? At the beginning and end of "Hodu LaHashem" — that is, at the first "Hodu" and at the last "Hodu" at the end of Hallel. And at "Ana Hashem Hoshia Na" — one shakes twice, since it is repeated. Thus, one shakes four times during Hallel. Nevertheless, also at the time of the blessing, one should do the na'anuim. Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Tur write that the congregation shakes at every "Hodu" that they respond to, and at the end when it is repeated — they shake twice. Thus, they shake eight times during Hallel: six times at "Hodu" and twice at "Ana." There are those who say that the prayer leader also shakes when he says "Yomar Na Yisrael," since this is like speaking to the congregation; therefore, he shakes with them (Ta”z, subsection 9). And this is the custom of the Ashkenazim. But the Sephardim shake only according to the first opinion. It appears to me that if someone wishes not to shake like the rest of the congregation, he is permitted to do so, and there is no issue of "lo titgodedu" (do not form separate groups). The proof is from a Mishnah there, where Rabbi Akiva said: I observed Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua, and all the people were shaking, but they only shook at "Ana," see there. If "lo titgodedu" applied here, they would not have done so. Rather, since it is not an absolute obligation, one can act as seems appropriate to him. It is obvious that at the time of the blessing in the Sukkah, one shakes all the na'anuim there. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 17 is not understandable at all; perhaps there is a printing error, see there.)

The shakings are directed to six directions: four cardinal points and upward and downward. The matter is: one moves and brings [the lulav] to the One to whom the four directions belong, upward and downward to the One to whom the heavens and the earth belong (Gemara there). To indicate that the Holy One, blessed be He, governs the heavens and the earth and all directions of the world, as in the matter of "To You, O Lord, is the greatness... To You, the heavens and also the earth, for the Lord is the God in the heavens above and on the earth below, there is none else." And in the matter of the intention of "One," in the recitation of Shema as I wrote in Siman 61, see there. And furthermore: to stop harmful winds and evil dews (there). This means: every commandment prevents calamities, and also the remnants of the commandment prevent (there). Especially when done with joy, as it is written in the rebuke: "Because you did not serve the Lord your God with joy." Therefore, now that it is "the time of our rejoicing," and we fulfill the main commandment which is the taking [of the lulav], and the remnants of the commandment which are the shakings, and we show that we dedicate our souls and bodies to God, to serve Him, blessed be He, with joy, and consequently, by this merit, all kinds of troubles referred to as harmful winds and evil dews will be stopped from upon us. This means: all troubles come because of the portion of Satan, who descends and accuses, ascends and prosecutes. And this is done in the manner of "May the Lord rebuke you, Satan" (Kesef Mishneh in the Gemara there, examine and you will find it easy). And this is [the meaning of] "Save us, O God of our salvation" – from these harms. And similarly: "Please, O Lord, save us now."

And how are the shakings performed? The Rambam wrote in Chapter Seven that one should move forward and back, up and down, and shake the lulav three times in each direction. How? One moves forward and shakes the top of the lulav three times, then brings it back and shakes the top of the lulav three times. The same applies to moving it up and down. This is his language. Meaning: one moves forward and shakes, brings it back and shakes, three times consecutively. According to this, there are six shakings in each direction. And when he wrote three times in each direction, he meant three for moving forward and likewise three for bringing it back (as the Lechem Mishneh also wrote). In total, this makes thirty-six times. This is also what the Tur wrote. And he wrote that some say that moving forward and bringing back is a single shaking. Others say that shaking is not necessary at all, and that the moving forward and bringing back is the shaking, see there. But in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is explained that shaking is necessary, only the question is whether one shaking suffices for both moving forward and bringing back, or whether moving forward requires its own shaking and bringing back its own shaking. And since this is an easy matter without much effort, the Rambam wrote to be stringent. It is not appropriate in such a matter to be lenient (as the Kesef Mishneh also wrote).

And our master, the Rema, seems to contradict himself. For he wrote in Section 9: "One shakes the lulav and rustles the leaves with each movement... And the forward and backward motion itself is the shaking, for he moves it forward and backward three times in each direction." This is his language. However, his intention is certainly that shaking is required, but the rustling is not after he has moved it forward and after he has brought it back, but rather at the time of the forward motion, and at the time of the backward motion, one rustles the leaves. And this is our custom (and this is the intention of the Bach and the Magen Avraham in Subsection 20).

It is also written that one tilts the head of the lulav in the direction he is shaking it. When shaking it downward, he turns it downwards, and it is considered as being in its natural growing position since he holds it in his hand in the way it grows. Some are meticulous not to turn the lulav when shaking it downward, but the custom follows the first opinion. And so it seems to me the main practice should be. Thus far his words. This means that one should not move the lulav evenly, but rather diagonally, so that its top is facing that direction. And if one questions: if so, then downward is not in its natural growing position? This does not concern us, for the important point is that he holds them in his hand in their natural growing position. But the fact that he tilts them is of no consequence. And he agrees with this. But we do not do so. (And so the Taz wrote in subsection 12. And according to the Ari, one should not tilt it downward at all, and downward is like upward, only the height differs. Pay attention and you will find it easy.)

One should circle to the right when shaking: east, south, west, north, up, down. In the writings, it is stated: east, south, north, up, down, west (Magen Avraham, subsection 21). Some follow this practice. In this matter, even a left-handed person should do as the rest of the world (ibid.), as the directions do not change for him. One should take care to connect the etrog to the lulav during the shakings and shake them together. There was an incident with a certain great individual who separated the etrog from the lulav, and another great individual was shown in a dream that he did not do well (Taz, subsection 14 and Beit Yosef). Know that all the shakings are not essential. In whatever way one shakes, he has fulfilled his obligation, since the main aspects of the shakings are not essential (see Magen Avraham, subsection 22. It is puzzling since the Rema also says this if we scrutinize his words, see there. Pay attention and you will find it easy.).

These four species are interdependent. If one of them is missing, it is invalid, and one should not recite the blessing on the remaining ones, because they are all part of one mitzvah, just like the four corners of the tzitzit which are interdependent.
