Nevertheless, one should take them as a mere commemoration. One should not wave them, so as not to think that one has fulfilled the mitzvah. Some have ruled that only the prayer leader should take and wave them, and the congregation should not take them at all, so they do not err in making it a fixed practice. There is no difference in this regard between the first day and the other days, for all that the Rabbis instituted, they instituted in a manner similar to the Torah's essence. If one had all four species available and took them one by one, he has fulfilled the obligation, as I wrote in paragraph four, provided that all of them were in front of him and he intended to take them, and there should not be a long interruption between them. He should take the lulav first and recite the blessing "on the taking of the lulav," having in mind also the other three species. If he spoke between them, he needs to recite a blessing on each one individually. Some say that he does not need to recite the blessing again, just as with the shofar when one spoke in the middle of the blasts, as I wrote in section 592 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 25). However, this is not comparable, because in that case, one is compelled to blow one after another, but here, the main requirement is to take them together, and only if taken one after another, it is still valid. Since he spoke between them, it nullifies the initial intention completely. (And also, what Magen Avraham questioned about the law I explained in paragraph 15, that if one did not have the willow and later recited the blessing "on the taking of the willow," from section 672 regarding Chanukah candles, where if one lit three candles on the fourth night, one should not recite the blessing on the fourth when lighting it, see there. I am puzzled: there, one has already fulfilled the main mitzvah and it is only an enhancement, but with the lulav, one did not intend to take the willow, thinking it was in the bundle. There are many reasons why this is not comparable, also to section 206. The law is clear as the Ra”m stated there, and so wrote the Taz, subparagraph 16, and the Eliyahu Rabbah, subparagraph 36).

If one of the species (of the four species) is missing, one should not take another species in its place, for this may lead to the mistake of taking it in future years as well. This is not the case when they are taken as a remembrance, as I have written, for no mistake will arise since everyone knows that four species are required, and this is common knowledge. It is forbidden to add another species to the four species due to the prohibition of "bal tosif" (not to add to the commandments). However, according to the principle that mitzvot require intention, one does not transgress unless one intends to do so. This is what the Tur wrote, that it is specifically if one takes them for the sake of the mitzvah (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 27. The words of the Taz, Siman Katan 17, are difficult). But some say that since we hold that a lulav does not require binding, there is no "bal tosif" unless one intends to add, for how does "bal tosif" apply? Each one stands by itself. Only if one intends to add does "bal tosif" apply, and this is the main halacha. Nevertheless, even without "bal tosif," it is not appropriate to add another species to the four species, for in any case, it appears as adding (Magen Avraham and Taz, ibid.). Similarly, one should not take more than one lulav and one etrog. However, with a hadas (myrtle) and aravah (willow), one may add as many as one wishes, as I wrote in Section 2. Some invalidate placing a "hadas shoteh" (wild myrtle) in the lulav in addition to the three that fulfill the requirement of being braided, as this is considered another species. Others permit it, as it is ultimately a type of myrtle. This seems to be the main halacha. However, those who are meticulous do not add at all to the three myrtles and two willows, and this is the common custom among us. (And certainly one should not add another etrog and lulav, as some say that "bal tosif" applies to this, as I have written. What the Magen Avraham wrote in Siman Katan 28 from the Jerusalem Talmud: if one placed them on the ground, it is forbidden to handle them, this does not apply to us, as it pertains to Shabbat, and to them who used to take them on Shabbat. What relevance does this have to us? And it is obvious that on Shabbat they are muktzeh.)

The mitzvah of lulav is during the day and not at night, as it is written: "And you shall take for yourselves on the first day"—during the day and not at night (Sukkah 43a). Similarly, it is written (there): "And you shall rejoice before Hashem, your God, for seven days"—days and not nights (ibid.). This is not comparable to the mitzvah of sukkah, where it is written, "You shall dwell in sukkot for seven days"—and nights are also included, because it is written "tashvu"—like dwelling in a residence. Additionally, we derive it from the inauguration service, where it is written: "You shall dwell day and night for seven days" (ibid.). Fundamentally, it is not a comparison, because there the mitzvah is continuous, hence the night is included in the day, as it is written: "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." This is not the case with lulav, where the mitzvah is only for the moment one takes it, and one fulfills the obligation. And if it were to be thought that one fulfills the mitzvah also at night, it should have been written "And you shall take for yourselves on the first" and not "on the first day." Rather, we learn from this that it comes to teach that it is during the day and not at night.

Its time is from dawn until the stars appear. However, the optimal mitzvah is to take it from sunrise, as all mitzvot that apply during the day ideally should be performed from sunrise. But if one performed them from dawn, they have fulfilled their obligation, as it is taught at the end of the second chapter of Megillah that from dawn it is considered day. And this is what our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 1: "Its time is from sunrise" – meaning the optimal time, as he concludes: "And if one needs to rise early to go on a journey, he takes it from dawn." Up to here is his language. And even though its time is the whole day, nonetheless, those who are zealous perform mitzvot early and take it immediately at sunrise. However, if one did not take it in the morning, one should take it all day long. And during twilight, it should be taken without a blessing (Magen Avraham), even on the first day.

And know that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that the primary mitzvah is during the time of Hallel. This is surprising, as earlier they said that the diligent perform the mitzvah early and bless immediately at sunrise. And behold, Hallel is much after sunrise! Moreover: we have not heard even from the most meticulous that they would wait to bless until Hallel. Rather, their intention is: if one only has the etrog and lulav for one hour, and if he blesses in the morning he will not have them at the time of Hallel – it is better to wait for Hallel and bless then, in order to wave during "Hodu" and "Ana" as the Sages instituted. But one who will have them also for Hallel – it is obvious that it is more praiseworthy to bless in the sukkah in the morning and wave, and afterward take them to the synagogue for the time of Hallel. And thus the great ones of the world and all of Israel practiced. (Or their intention is that the primary mitzvah is: that also during Hallel he should take them.)

It is mentioned in the Gemara (41b): This is how the people of Jerusalem would act: A person would leave his house with his lulav in hand, go to the synagogue with his lulav in hand... And it is said there that even during the recitation of the Shema and prayer, he would hold it in his hand. And although it is forbidden to hold other items in one's hand during the recitation of the Shema and prayer, however, this mitzvah (commandment), because it is cherished by him, will not lead to distraction (Tur). Based on this, our master the Rema wrote (Section 1) that the meticulous person should hold the lulav in his hand when he leaves his house for the synagogue, even during prayer. And he should also bring it back to his house, in order to cherish the mitzvah. Thus far his words. And they wrote that if one is not always meticulous in his actions, it appears ostentatious if he does this (Taz). It seems to me that this only applies to holding it during prayer, where it appears ostentatious, as if he is confident that the mitzvah will not distract him. But regarding bringing it to the synagogue himself, and bringing it back to his house from the synagogue, certainly in this there is no issue of ostentation, just as one carries his tallit and siddur. This is something every person should do, and this is our obligation, and this is proper for us.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: It is forbidden to eat before taking the lulav. And if one forgot and ate, and remembered at his table on the first day, which is a Torah obligation – he must stop, even if there is enough time in the day to take it after he has eaten. From the first day onward, if there is enough time in the day – he does not need to stop, but if not – he must stop. Thus far is their language. It is explained that even on other days, which are rabbinic, it is forbidden to eat before taking the lulav. Some are uncertain whether tasting is permitted. It seems to me that drinking hot beverages is certainly permitted, even on the first day, just like before prayer. There is one who wants to say that the second day has the same status as the first day due to the doubt of the day (Taz). However, this is not necessary, as it has already been explained in Siman 639 that all the stringencies of the first day do not apply on the second day, see there. And one who does not have an etrog can eat. If he waits for the etrog to arrive, he should wait until midday for a fixed meal, but he can eat a temporary meal (see Magen Avraham). And our teacher the Rema wrote that if one began eating more than half an hour before the obligation time – even on the first day, he does not need to stop, provided there is enough time in the day. Thus far is his language. There is one who disagrees with this (Taz). However, this is uncommon, as how could it be that one would start eating before dawn? And if he was compelled to do so due to illness – it is obvious that he does not need to stop. The Rif and Rambam did not mention any of these laws at all. And the Rosh already wondered about this, see there. (For all of this is in the Gemara 38a. It seems to me that they hold like Rabbi Zeira there: It is a mitzvah to stop, and if he did not stop – he should take the lulav in the afternoon. This is straightforward and does not need to be explained. And what Rabbi Zeira said afterward: here on the second day of Yom Tov, from the fact that it teaches: one who is on the road – he does not hold this. And like the question of Tosafot there in the beginning of "from the fact that it teaches," where we find this language also regarding the shofar, see there. They hold that Rabbi Zeira came to explain the position of Rav Safra, not as a halacha. And this is also implied by Rashi, see there thoroughly. But in truth, this is not an accurate inference. And since the Rif and Rambam completely rejected it – therefore, one should not be overly stringent about this. Be precise and you will find leniency.)

It is well known that the etrog and all the species are designated for their mitzvah for all the days of the festival, unless one stipulated that they would not refrain from them during twilight, as I wrote in Siman 639. And we also wrote there that one should not do so; see there. According to this, the etrog is forbidden to eat until after the festival. But to smell it is permitted. And the hadas (myrtle) is forbidden to smell, for a reason that will be explained.

And so our sages of blessed memory said (Sukkah 37b): A myrtle used for a mitzvah – it is forbidden to smell it. An etrog used for a mitzvah – it is permitted to smell it. What is the reason? The myrtle, which is designated for its fragrance, when it is set aside for the mitzvah, its fragrance is also set aside. The etrog, which is designated for eating, when it is set aside for the mitzvah, it is set aside from eating – but not from smelling. That is to say: the general rule is that when something is designated for a mitzvah, it is set aside from its usual purpose. Therefore, the etrog is set aside from eating, which is its usual purpose. And the myrtle is set aside from smelling, which is its usual purpose. However, if one explicitly set aside the etrog also from smelling – then it is certainly forbidden.

The Tur wrote that one who smells an etrog should not recite the blessing "Who gives pleasant fragrance to fruits," as Rabbi Simcha stated that it is not primarily intended for fragrance. However, the Ra'avyah wrote that one should recite the blessing. Therefore, our master the Beit Yosef wrote that since there is a dispute whether one should recite the blessing or not, it is better to refrain from smelling it. Rabbi Simcha's opinion is not understood: the blessing "Who has given pleasant fragrance to fruits" is for fruits that are meant to be eaten, so why shouldn't one bless on its fragrance? Perhaps he refers specifically to an etrog used for the mitzvah, which requires further investigation. Additionally, on Shabbat, it is forbidden to smell the myrtle, as it is set aside for the entire seven days. (I have seen that the Magen Avraham wrote as I have, that specifically for a mitzvah one should not bless, see there.)

It is well known that designation [for a mitzvah] is not significant. Therefore, as long as the items have not been lifted for the mitzvah, they do not have sanctity and are not set aside for the mitzvah. Nevertheless, if one designated them on the eve of the festival to be for the mitzvah, they automatically become set aside, since he designated them with intention, and they are treated like all items that are set aside. However, they are not prohibited from benefit until they have been lifted for the mitzvah. Yet on the festival, there is no practical difference with this set-aside status, for they are permitted to be handled, since he did not set them aside from handling; on the contrary, he designated them to bless upon and handle them. But on Shabbat, they are prohibited due to their set-aside status (this is what seems to my humble opinion).

It was taught (42a): A woman may receive the lulav from her son or husband and return it to the water on Shabbat, during the time when they would recite the blessing over the lulav on Shabbat, as will be explained in Siman 658. And the lulav stands in water so that it does not wither, and it is permitted to return it to that water on Shabbat. And even though repairing a vessel is prohibited on Shabbat, nevertheless, since it was already standing in this water, it does not appear as if one is repairing a vessel. And even a woman, who is exempt from the mitzvah of lulav, we do not say that the lulav is muktzeh (set aside) for her, and thus forbidden to move. This is not the case, for since it is suitable for a man, a woman is also permitted to handle it (Gemara). However, nowadays, when we do not recite the blessing on Shabbat, it is considered completely muktzeh and is forbidden to move.

It is only permitted on Shabbat to return it to the same water, but not to add other water, and certainly not to completely replace it. On Yom Tov, it is permitted to add water, but completely replacing it with other water is forbidden, as this would be considered fixing a vessel. On Chol HaMoed, it is a mitzvah to completely replace it with other water, so that it remains fresh and beautiful. It seems to me that the addition on Yom Tov should be less than half, because more than that would not be considered an "addition." It is proper to take a new willow each day of Chol HaMoed and bind it with the lulav, as this is an enhancement of the mitzvah. However, care must be taken that if it is inserted into the bundle, it should not be pulled strongly from below, as most of the leaves might straighten out.

A non-Jew who brought a lulav or etrog or hadas or aravah from outside the boundary — the Rashba wrote that it is permissible to take it, for the sages only prohibited something that came from outside the boundary to the one for whom it was brought; and even this is not in handling, but in eating and benefiting. But in handling — it is permitted, and there is no enjoyment here, for the commandments were not given for enjoyment. And so wrote the Tur, see there. And there is also no decree: that one would tell him to bring it, for it is not common for a person to perform a commandment that comes through a transgression (Beit Yosef in the name of the glosses of Asher ben Yechiel). Additionally, in a matter that involves enjoyment, we decree, lest one say to bring it for enjoyment. But since the commandments were not given for enjoyment — we do not decree lest one say (Taz).

And specifically if it only came from outside the boundary. But if it was cut off on Yom Tov, even if it was not cut off for him, it is considered muktzeh and it is forbidden to take it even on the first day [of the festival], even if he has no other lulav and thereby will miss performing the mitzvah. For in cases of "sit and do not act," the Sages upheld their words, as they did even in cases involving karet, such as sprinkling on Pesach at the beginning of the fourth chapter of Pesachim. However, if it was detached on the first day [of Yom Tov], it is permitted on the second day of Yom Tov, even according to those who say in Siman 515 that it is also forbidden on the second day, so that one should not tell another to detach it; here they agree that since he does not derive benefit from it, there is no reason to tell him to do it (Magen Avraham). But on the first day, it is forbidden even to move it, and even if it was detached on the second day of Yom Tov, it is also forbidden to move it.

And know that from the words of the Rashba it is clarified that it is specifically if the non-Jew brings it to him from outside the Shabbat boundary—it is permitted. But to send a non-Jew to bring the etrog from outside the Shabbat boundary is forbidden. However, the custom is not like this, and in settlements they send the etrog from place to place on Yom Tov by a non-Jew. And so wrote the Mordechai in the sixth chapter of Eruvin, and these are his words: Rabbi Yehuda HaLevi permitted telling a non-Jew to bring the etrog even from afar on Yom Tov, in a case where there was a compulsion and they did not have an etrog, because the boundaries are rabbinic. And even outside of twelve mil. These are his words. And for those who hold that twelve mil is from the Torah—it is certainly forbidden outside of twelve mil. And so we ruled earlier in Siman 596 regarding the shofar, that a double rabbinic restriction in a place of a mitzvah is permitted. And so we instruct in practice. But one should not send on Shabbat for the Yom Tov that follows it (Taz). And there are those who say that even if the first day falls on Shabbat—it is forbidden to send on the eve of Shabbat for the second day, because since it is rabbinic—we do not override one rabbinic prohibition for another (Magen Avraham). And there are those who disagree, because since the sages permitted in a place of a mitzvah—it is permitted even for a rabbinic mitzvah (Magen Avraham). And I believe that this is the custom. And a Jew sends to another Jew by way of a non-Jew, and it is not appropriate to say: why should he commit a sin for his friend? Certainly, he should do it, for his friend did not fail in this, and the sages permitted it, and he is obligated to do it for him, and all Israel are responsible for one another (see Magen Avraham). And see above in Siman 307.

Our sages of blessed memory said in Bava Kamma (9b): "Enhancing a mitzvah up to a third of its cost." Rashi explained that if one finds two items to purchase, one more beautiful than the other, he should add a third of the price and buy the more beautiful one. This is the end of his statement. This implies that this is applicable when he has not yet purchased. But if he already purchased, he is not obligated to do so. However, the Rosh wrote that even if he already purchased, he must sell it and add a third to buy the more beautiful one, see there. And perhaps Rashi did not mean it precisely. However, our master the Beit Yosef in his great book wrote that Rashi meant it precisely, see there. And one should not ask: according to this, there is no end to the matter, for if later he finds something more beautiful, will he need to add another third? It can be said that this is only for the first time, and by this, he fulfills the enhancement of the mitzvah.

And this is the opinion of the Tur, who wrote: "An etrog that is fit for the mitzvah, and one finds another more beautiful than it – it is a mitzvah to add up to one-third of the original price in order to replace it with the more beautiful one." So are his words. But our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in these words: "If one finds two etrogim to buy, and one is more beautiful than the other – he should take the more beautiful one, provided that they do not charge more than one-third extra for it compared to its fellow." These are his words, and he wrote like Rashi: when he has not yet bought it. And even though the Rosh and the Tur explain this to mean even when he has already bought it, nevertheless, since it is only a matter of beautification of the mitzvah, he did not worry about being strict in this matter. For this reason, he also wrote "one-third extra." And in truth, in the Gemara it remains unresolved, but he chose to be lenient in this matter, that one-third extra means one-third of the price of the etrog he bought, and "from outside" means half of the price of the etrog he bought. (And regarding what the Magen Avraham raised in subsection 5 in the name of the Yesh Sh, that if so, if he happens to encounter one hundred etrogim, etc., and he answered with difficulty, see there. And according to what I wrote – there is no difficulty at all, for we only say this once, whether according to Rashi's explanation or the Rosh's. And in practice, it seems to me that it is correct to be stringent like the Rosh and the Tur where possible, even when he has already bought it.)

Some of our rabbis explained this in a completely different manner: It does not refer to a regular etrog when one finds a more beautiful one, as these matters are immeasurable. Rather, the explanation is as follows: The measure of an etrog is the size of an egg. When one has an etrog that is precisely the size of an egg, it is certainly not considered beautiful when it is exactly its measure. If afterwards, he finds one larger than it, he is obligated to add up to a third of the previous amount to buy the other (Sefer Mitzvot Gadol in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, and the Rosh in Bava Kamma there). However, regarding other matters of beautification, he is not obligated in this respect. Similarly, with other commandments, this interpretation does not apply (Magen Avraham, small section 2 and small section 3). Even with respect to the measure, it is only to exchange it and add a third from within. But if the other does not wish to accept it, and he would need to buy both, he is not obligated (ibid., small section 4). Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef brought both interpretations.

It is stated in the Gemara there: "Up to one-third — from his own funds; beyond this — from the Holy One, blessed be He." Rashi explains: "Up to one-third from his own funds — he is not reimbursed in his lifetime. Beyond this — from the Holy One, blessed be He — the Holy One, blessed be He, will reimburse him in his lifetime." Thus far his words. This means he enjoys the fruits in this world, and the principal remains for him in the World to Come (Tosafot). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: If someone does not have an etrog or other transient mitzvah, he is not required to spend a great fortune on them. As it is said: "One who spends, should not spend more than one-fifth," even for a transient mitzvah. And this applies specifically to positive commandments, but for prohibitive commandments — he should give all his money before transgressing. Thus far his words. 

There is a question as to whether his intention is that up to one-fifth one is required to spend on a mitzvah. If so, in the Gemara that tells of Rabban Gamliel spending a thousand zuz for an etrog, it illustrates how beloved mitzvot were to them. And according to this, for Rabban Gamliel, a thousand zuz must have been more than one-fifth of his assets, for otherwise, he would have been obligated by law. This is surprising, since he was the leader of Israel and a very wealthy man. Therefore, it seems to me that this is merely an example. And it is not logical to give one-fifth for a mitzvah, thereby being unable to give charity at all (see Beit Yosef and Magen Avraham, subsection 7, which require further study). If one has only five selaim and needs to redeem his son and buy an etrog — he should buy the etrog, for this is a transient mitzvah and the other is not, and he can redeem him at another time.

Know that on the first day of Yom Tov, if in one place there is a lulav but no minyan for prayer, and in another place there is a minyan but no lulav — it is obvious that one should go to the place with the lulav (Magen Avraham, beginning of Siman 655). And even on the second day of Yom Tov and all days of the festival, if one can pray alone — he should go to the place with the lulav. Only if he cannot pray alone — he may go to whichever place he prefers, since both are rabbinic obligations. But if he cannot even say the Shema — he should go to the place where they pray. Not on the first day, for the mitzvah in its time is precious. (Regarding what the Magen Avraham wrote about the incident of Bar Kamtza, that it is permitted to transgress due to fear, see there. His intention was regarding the sacrifice, which Rabbi Zechariah ben Avkulos did not permit — there is no proof, as there it was about saving all of Israel, see there. Examine and you will find clarity.)

If one purchased an etrog at a high price because it was very beautiful, and someone came and stole it or cut it and invalidated it, there is an opinion that says he is not obligated to return such an etrog, but only a kosher etrog. A proof is brought from Bava Kama (78a), where if someone set aside an ox for a burnt offering and another person came and stole it, he can exempt himself with a sheep (Mahari Minz). However, this is not a valid comparison, because in that case the sacrifice is not monetarily valuable, as it cannot be sold, but must be brought to the Temple. Therefore, he may exempt himself with something less valuable. But the etrog has monetary value since it can be sold, and it is obvious that he is obligated to pay him according to its value (Mishneh LaMelech, Chapter 16 from Ma'aseh HaKorbanot). This is clear. (What the Ba'er Hetev wrote in the name of the Shiltei Gibborim, that if someone sold an etrog and it was found to be rotten, the burden of proof is on the one who wants to extract money from another; see there. And it is obvious that if not much time has passed, so that it could not have rotted with the buyer, it must have rotted with the seller, and the sale is reversed. This applies to all similar cases. However, sometimes sellers are vague about such matters of loss to the buyer.)

It is taught at the end of the third chapter of Sukkah (42a): A minor who knows how to wave [the lulav] is obligated in the mitzvah of lulav in order to educate him in the commandments. And it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud: It is not only about waving, but also about taking it forward and backward, up and down, etc. See there. And our youths take the lulav and recite the blessing, but they do not wave it in all directions as in the Jerusalem Talmud, even if they have reached the age of education. It can be said that this is because they are not proficient in this.

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: "A minor who knows how to wave the lulav properly - his father is obligated to buy him a lulav… this is their language." And it is a wonder: where is it explained that he should buy it for them? And it suffices to give them his own lulav (Taz in the name of Rashal). However, the intention is when his hand can afford it (ibid.). And in places where the four species are inexpensive, and certainly in such a manner it is better so that he may have his own for Hallel. Furthermore, it is difficult to transfer ownership of a lulav to a minor on the first day, as will be explained in the next section. However, this is in places where the four species are inexpensive. But with us - it is fortunate if one family can afford to buy the four species for themselves, and even that is not common.

And I have a doubt: regarding the established law that on the first day a person does not fulfill their obligation with the lulav of another, and it must be transferred to them in the manner that will be explained in the following section, does this also apply to a father and his adult sons, and his sons-in-law who are dependent on his table, such that each one also needs, according to the law, a lulav of their own? Or perhaps, since we find in several laws that those who are dependent on his table are considered subordinate to their father, they can all fulfill the obligation with a single lulav, and it is considered "yours" since it is from their own? And this seems to be the main point according to my humble opinion. Nevertheless, this requires further consideration.

From the Torah, the lulav is only taken in the provinces on the first day, as it is written: "And you shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a beautiful tree," etc. And in the Temple, it is taken for seven days, as it is written at the end of the verse: "and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God for seven days." The Sifra expounds: not in the provinces for seven days. And this "rejoicing" refers to the rejoicing of the lulav, as it is not plausible to say it refers to the rejoicing of the peace offerings, as in "Re'eh," where it is written: "and you shall rejoice during your festival." For if so, why is it not written also about Shavuot as in "Re'eh"? Moreover, there it is written in the singular form: "and you shall rejoice," and not "before the Lord your God." Therefore, it certainly refers to the lulav. (And in the Jerusalem Talmud, there is a dispute about this; see there.)

And when the Temple was destroyed, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, along with his great court in Yavneh, decreed that the lulav should be taken in the provinces for seven days, as a remembrance of the Temple. For we are obligated to make a remembrance of the Temple, as it is written (Jeremiah 30:17), "Zion is one that no one seeks out"—implying that it requires seeking out. And we bless every day "Who has sanctified us... concerning the taking of the lulav," for even for a rabbinic commandment we bless "Who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us," as with the Chanukah candle. And where did He command us? From "You shall not turn aside from the matter that they shall tell you" etc. And the Rambam wrote in the seventh chapter that this decree, along with all decrees, will revert to the way it was before when the Temple is rebuilt, see there. And I do not know his source. On the contrary, from what we learn in the fifth chapter of Maaser Sheni regarding the fourth-year vineyard: it was a condition that whenever the Temple would be rebuilt, it would revert to the way it was before. And this was to adorn the marketplaces of Jerusalem with fruits, see there. And it implies that in other matters this is not so, and this requires investigation. (And know that there are those who wish to say that what we say in Sukkah 46a: from here onward, concerning the commandments of the elders, means that this is how one should bless, contrary to Rashi's interpretation. And this is nothing, for even if we interpret it this way—Rab and Shmuel disagree, as with the Chanukah candle. Investigate and you will find it easy.)

It is proven in the Gemara, at the beginning of the chapter "Lulav and Aravah," that even in the Temple, where all seven days [of Sukkot] are from the Torah, nevertheless, on the other days when [Sukkot] falls on Shabbat, they would not take the lulav, as a decree lest one carry it four cubits in the public domain, similar to the shofar. But on the first day, they would take it, even when it falls on Shabbat. And although in the Temple the first day is equal to all the other days, nevertheless, since on the first day there is an obligation also in the provinces, the Rabbis did not decree in the Temple, unlike the other days. And so wrote the Rambam in the seventh chapter. And he further wrote: that in the time of the Temple, the lulav was also taken in the provinces on the first day that fell on Shabbat, since they did not decree in the Temple, they did not decree in the provinces either. However, this was in a place where the messengers of the court would reach, who knew when the Festival day was. But those far away who observed two days out of doubt would not take [the lulav] even on the first day, because perhaps it was not the Festival day. See there.

And since the destruction of the Temple, the sages prohibited taking the lulav on Shabbat on the first day, even for the inhabitants of the Land of Israel who sanctified the month, because of the distant border regions who do not know the established month, so that everyone would be equal in this matter, and some would not take it on Shabbat while others do not. Since the obligation of one day is the same everywhere, and there is no Temple to depend on. In other words: during the time of the Temple, because it was taken in the Temple, it was taken everywhere, as the messengers would come and inform that today is a festival day. But when there is no Temple, the sages equated their measures everywhere (Kesef Mishneh). For the Temple is distinct in many matters from the province, and it is not appropriate to equate them. This is not the case when the Temple is destroyed, and in our time when everyone acts according to the calculation—the matter remains as it was, that the lulav is not taken at all, neither in the Land of Israel nor outside it on Shabbat, even on the first day, even though everyone knows the establishment of the month. However, our custom on the festival is as if we are not proficient, for this reason, we observe two festival days in the Diaspora.

And even though in the observance of the second day of Yom Tov we differ from the residents of the Land of Israel, this is because it is not possible otherwise, for we are compelled to observe the second day of Yom Tov in order not to deviate from the customs of our ancestors. To suggest that the residents of the Land of Israel should also observe a second day of Yom Tov for our sake – it is impossible to institute such a significant change for this reason. However, regarding the "sit and do not act" (passive observance) concerning the lulav, it is possible to align both practices (see Lechem Mishneh). And why did they not establish the practice of lulav similar to that of the shofar, where it is taken wherever there is a court? It can be said that concerning the shofar, which is only for one day, they established it so. But the lulav, since it is taken on other days as well, they did not establish this. Additionally, the shofar, which is meant to bring the remembrance of Israel before their Father in Heaven, they did not want to completely nullify (Tosafot Megillah 3a). And nowadays, everything is equal, for both shofar and lulav are not taken on Shabbat in any place, neither in the Land of Israel nor outside the Land.

It is forbidden to handle the lulav on Shabbat, as it is considered muktzeh (set aside). However, there is an opinion that for its own use or its place, it is permitted, similar to a shofar in Siman 588 (Taz, subparagraph 3). This is a surprising view because the lulav is designated for its mitzvah for all seven days, and it is not comparable to a shofar (and this is also implied by the Magen Avraham at the end of Siman 588, and the Pri Megadim also challenges this view). But it is permitted to handle the etrog because it is fit for smelling, as I wrote in Siman 654, that it is not set aside from its scent. Even according to what I wrote there, that due to the disagreement regarding the blessing, one should not smell it, one can bless on the scent of another fruit and smell it (there). And it is forbidden to put the etrog on clothing even on Yom Tov, because it creates a new scent. There is an opinion that permits this since it is not intentional. And the principle of "inevitable result" does not apply here, as there is no aspect of labor at all. What was explained in Siman 511 that it is forbidden to create a scent – this is by means of coals, because there is extinguishing and kindling, which is not the case with an etrog (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2, in the name of the Shelah). Nevertheless, one should be stringent, as ultimately it does create a new scent (Magen Avraham there. And this is not conclusive, as what is stated that kindling is permitted on Yom Tov – in the case of incense, there is also extinguishing, as Rambam wrote there. Examine it and you will find it simple).

It has already been explained that on the first day of Yom Tov (festival), a person cannot fulfill his obligation with his friend's lulav, as it is stated: "And you shall take for yourselves" — from your own. Therefore, one can only fulfill his obligation if his friend gives him the etrog and all the species as a complete gift. Even if he gives it to him as a gift on the condition that it is returned, it is still considered a gift, for we hold according to Choshen Mishpat, Siman 241, that a gift on the condition to return it is not called a usufructuary acquisition, but rather a complete acquisition of the item itself. However, this is a condition that must be fulfilled to return it, and it is a condition like all conditions, and the condition must be upheld. If he does not return it, he has not fulfilled the obligation, because since the condition was not fulfilled, the gift is nullified. The same applies to other conditions, such as if he says: I am giving you this etrog on the condition that you go to a certain place. If he goes, the gift is upheld, and if not, the gift is nullified. And so it is with all similar cases.

And specifically when he said to him in this language: "I give you these four species as a gift on the condition that you return them to me." But if he said to him: "They shall be yours until you fulfill the obligation with them, and afterwards you will return them to me" – he has not fulfilled his obligation, for this is not the language of a gift, but the language of a loan. And on the first day – one does not fulfill the obligation with a borrowed item. And it seems to me that even if he said: "They shall be yours as a gift until you fulfill the obligation with them" – this also does not help, for it is not a true gift but only temporary, and it then reverts to being like a loan. And what we said about a gift on the condition of return, that it requires it to be returned to him, and if it is not returned he has not fulfilled his obligation – this applies even if it was lost from his hand and he wishes to compensate him – he has not fulfilled his obligation. And not because he is liable for accidents like a borrower, for even if it died due to the work it was performing, which even a borrower is exempt from, here he has not fulfilled his obligation because the condition was not met, and the gift is nullified. Therefore, even though in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 241, Se'if 11, we brought two opinions regarding the obligation to pay when it was lost, nevertheless, regarding fulfilling the obligation – he has not fulfilled it. (See Rosh, Chapter 3, Siman 30.)

In Choshen Mishpat, it is explained that if one said "on condition that you return it to me" without specifying when it should be returned, the borrower can return it whenever he wishes. However, this is not the case with an etrog, as the Tur writes: "Even if one gave it to him without specifying 'on condition that you return it to me,' it is assumed that his intention is that it should be returned, because it is needed to fulfill the mitzvah. If it is not returned, the mitzvah is not fulfilled." This is the end of his words. Certainly, this is the case when he said "on condition that you return it to me." However, from the Tur's language, it implies that this is specifically when the giver has not yet fulfilled the mitzvah with it. But if he has already fulfilled the mitzvah, it is not the same. Therefore, even if it was given "on condition that you return it to me," if the giver has already fulfilled the mitzvah, the borrower can return it whenever he wishes.

Nevertheless, it is impossible to say so, for the source of this law is from the "Itur" (Beit Yosef), and there too it is written in the language of the Tur. He brought proof from Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Yehoshua, Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, and Rabbi Akiva, who were on a ship, and there was only one etrog, which belonged to Rabban Gamliel. He took it and fulfilled his obligation with it, and then gave it to Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yehoshua to Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah to Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Akiva returned it to Rabban Gamliel. And yet Rabban Gamliel had already fulfilled his obligation with it! And the Ran also wrote this law in this language. And some have learned from here: that one who gives a lulav to his friend on the first day of the festival – it is assumed that it is given on the condition that it will be returned, even if not explicitly stated, because a person does not relinquish his mitzvah and give it to others, etc. Thus far his words. Hence, he wrote that a person does not relinquish his mitzvah, meaning: that he should not take his mitzvah and give it to others. And this is also the intention of the Tur, who says: because he needs to fulfill his obligation with it, meaning: that he needs to have the mitzvah all day, and not just to fulfill his obligation with it. And so it must be said regarding the intention of Rabbeinu Beit Yosef in section 5, who wrote in the language of the Tur, refer there. (And it requires investigation as to why the commentators on the Tur and Shulchan Aruch did not comment on this at all.)

According to this, all the more so if he said: "On the condition that you return it to me" — it must be returned to him immediately. And our master, the Beit Yosef, who wrote in paragraph 4: "If he gave it to him on the condition that he returns it — he fulfills the obligation... and returns it... and if he did not return it, he has not fulfilled the obligation... and likewise, if he returned it after the time of the commandment — he has not fulfilled the obligation." Until here is his wording, which implies that he can delay it for many hours, as long as he returns it within the time of the commandment — this is not correct. Our master, the Beit Yosef, took the extreme position that if he returned it after the time of the commandment — he has not fulfilled the obligation, but if within the time of the commandment — he fulfilled the obligation post facto. However, in any case, it is not properly done, for initially, he is obligated to return it immediately. And so it is clarified in Choshen Mishpat there.

And know that there is one who wrote that this applies specifically when he said, "on the condition that you return it to me." But if he said, "on the condition that you return it," and did not say "to me"—even if he returns it after some time, he has fulfilled the commandment (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). And indeed, this is what our Rabbi the Rema wrote in Choshen Mishpat there, and we also explained there in section 13. However, in any case, it is not understood, for is it worse when he said, "on the condition that you return it," than when he said nothing, where he is obligated to return it, and if not, he has not fulfilled it, as explained? And one must say: it seems he holds that indeed this is worse: since he did not say "to me"—it reveals his intention that he is not particular about when it is returned. Nevertheless, this requires further investigation. (And indeed the source of the Rema's ruling is from the responsa of the Rashba, part 1, section 1000, see there. But it is possible that the Rashba does not agree with the ruling of the Tur, that even in a general case, he must return it to him. And this also seems to me somewhat from his language there. But according to the Tur, it appears to me in my humble opinion that even if he said to him "return it," he is obligated to return it to him today.)

And with what has been explained, that when he gave it to him without specification he is also obligated to return it to him, for it is assumed that he gave it with that intention – our teacher the Rema wrote in section 5 that he must return and give it to the owner as a gift, so that it will belong to the owner and he will fulfill his obligation with it. Until here is his language. And similarly, even if he explicitly said "on the condition that you return it to me" – he must return and give it to the owner as a gift (Magen Avraham, subsection 6 in the name of the Rosh). The reason is simple: for he gave it to him as a complete gift, but conditioned that it be returned to him, like any other condition. Consequently, he must also return it to him as a gift, for if not – it would not leave his possession. And they questioned our teacher the Rema regarding his conclusion "so that it will belong to the owner" – for certainly this is not the reason, as if he does not return it as a gift – it would automatically belong to the owner, since the condition was not fulfilled. Rather, on the contrary: this is for the benefit of the recipient, for if not – he would not fulfill his obligation with it, since the condition was not fulfilled (the Gra). And I say that our teacher the Rema intentionally wrote this. For certainly when he said to him, see there, that he should return it to him – it is only for the benefit of the recipient. But when unspecified: although we say that it is assumed he gave it with the intention that it be returned, nonetheless, he did not explicitly say so, and perhaps this was not his intention. Therefore, in this case, it is for the benefit of the owner (and especially according to what I wrote that the Rashba does not agree with this ruling).

In this matter, when he said "on the condition that you return it to me" or without any specification—which is considered as if he made a condition—the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 5, and this is their language: "However, even if it was not returned to his hand but to another, and another to another, and the last one returns it to the owner—he has fulfilled his obligation." This is their language. They learned this from the etrog of Rabban Gamliel, who gave it to Rabbi Yehoshua, and Rabbi Yehoshua to Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah, and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah to Rabbi Akiva, and Rabbi Akiva returned it to Rabban Gamliel. But in truth, there is no proof from there, because they were on the sea in a ship, and all of them were together. And Rabban Gamliel's intention was to benefit them. On the contrary, they spared Rabban Gamliel the trouble, so he would not have to give it to each of them individually. And it seems that according to their opinion, if so, Rabban Gamliel should have said "give it to each one," and since he did not say this, one can infer that it is not necessary. However, in any case, even so, there is no proof except in an unspecified case, but not when he said "on the condition that you return it to me," because the incident with Rabban Gamliel was in an unspecified manner. And it seems to me that the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch also intended this ruling only in an unspecified case, and not in "on the condition that you return it to me." But in the responsa of the Rashba there, it is explained that even in "on the condition that you return it to me"—he is permitted to do so. And it seems that this is only said in retrospect, but initially—it is not proper to do so.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in section 4 that it is permissible to give someone an etrog as a gift on the condition that he does not consecrate it, as it is no less valid than a gift given on the condition that it is returned. This is his wording. Meaning: In the case of a gift on the condition that it is returned, it is impossible to consecrate it, for if he consecrates it, he has nothing to return. And yet, it is still considered a gift, and similarly in this case. And in Choshen Mishpat, section 243, paragraph 9, we explained this matter, see there. And one should not ask: according to what I wrote there, whenever it is evident that he is not giving it completely, it is not a gift. And regarding the etrog, it is certainly evident, for we said that even in a general case, his intention is that it will be returned to him. For in truth, they only said this there when it is evident that he is giving it only so that the recipient will do a favor for the giver, see there. And not in this kind of case where he is enabling him to perform a mitzvah, for it is certainly his intention in any way that it will be effective.

Some say that even if one said to another, "Lend me your etrog," and he gave it to him without specifying anything, he has fulfilled his obligation. For we say that his intention is that if the language of lending does not work, he gives it as a gift, similar to the case of the tallit mentioned above in Siman 14 and the betrothal ring in Even HaEzer Siman 28 (Magen Avraham, subsection 3, and Taz above in Siman 14). However, we have already written above in Siman 649, subsection 5, that this is not analogous, and he has not fulfilled his obligation in this manner; see there. Similarly, there is an opinion that if a man's wife gave the lulav on the first day as a gift on condition to return it or without specifying, and the man is not at home, it is not effective, because perhaps the man's desire is to sell it and receive money for it (there). But it is known among us that the master of the house does not typically do so, and certainly, she can do so, and he has fulfilled his obligation. (See Shaarei Teshuva, subsection 1, in the name of Machaneh Ephraim, that one must be careful that the buyer of an etrog pays before the holiday, because the acquisition of money is by Torah law, and taking possession is rabbinic. And some hold that rabbinic acquisition does not work for Torah law; see there. But we have already explained several times in Choshen Mishpat that there is no doubt that it is effective, and this is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, Chapter 5 of Maaser Sheni.)

It is stated in the Gemara (Sukkah 46b): A person should not acquire a lulav for a minor on the first day. What is the reason? A minor can acquire, but he cannot transfer ownership. Since a minor cannot transfer ownership to others according to Torah law, it follows that if he returns it, it is not legally returned. And if you ask: If so, it is also not legally acquired by the minor, since it was only given to him on the condition that he returns it – this is not the case. For since it is impossible for him to return it, it is as if it were a condition that cannot be fulfilled, and the condition is nullified, while the act remains valid (Ran there). However, some say that this applies only if the minor has not yet reached the age of discernment. But once he reaches six years old, which is the age of discernment as I wrote in Choshen Mishpat, Siman 235 – he can give a gift, as I wrote there (ibid.). From the language of Maimonides and the Tur, it does not seem so, as they wrote simply "a minor" (see Lechem Mishneh, chapter eight, which also questions this). It is best to say to the child: "Take and bless the etrog," and not use the language of acquisition. Certainly, if he holds the etrog and lulav in his hand together with the child – it is permissible, as it has not left his possession.

It is stated in Bava Batra (137b): Brothers who bought an etrog with household funds; one of them took it and fulfilled the mitzvah with it. If he can eat it – he has fulfilled the obligation, and if not – he has not fulfilled the obligation. And this is its explanation: That they inherited an etrog from their father, or they bought an etrog with their father's funds as part of the household assets. As long as they have not divided, and one of the brothers took it without their knowledge and fulfilled the mitzvah with it – we see if the brothers do not mind each other, and he can eat it without their permission. For example: there are many etrogs in the household assets; or many etrogs can be found in the city; or they have already fulfilled the mitzvah and do not need it anymore (Rashbam) – he has fulfilled the obligation, as it is considered "yours," since it is entirely his. And if not – he has not fulfilled the obligation, as it is required that it be entirely his, not partially his (there). And he does not fulfill the obligation until they give him their share as a complete gift. According to this, it only depends between whether they mind or do not mind. And if they do not mind – he has fulfilled the obligation. And so it seems from the words of the Tur, see there.

But the Rambam wrote in Chapter 8, Halacha 11, and this is his language: Brothers who bought etrogim with joint funds, and one of them took an etrog and fulfilled his obligation with it. If he is able to eat it, and the brothers do not object to this – he has fulfilled his obligation. If not – he has not fulfilled his obligation until they give him their share as a gift. And if one bought an etrog and another a pomegranate (a type of fruit), or if they bought together an etrog, a pomegranate, and a citron with joint funds – he has not fulfilled his obligation with the etrog until they give him their share as a gift, even though if he ate it – they would not object to his eating it. Up to here is his language. And this is the way of the Rif according to their version in the Gemara there, that we require two conditions: that they do not object, and that they also have etrogim themselves. For otherwise, their implied waiver is not effective, as perhaps they also specifically want an etrog. But whenever there are other etrogim, even though this one is more beautiful – we are not concerned with it (Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh on the Ran in Chapter 3 of Sukkah, see there). And in the Shulchan Aruch, the first opinion was not brought at all, as they were stringent regarding a Torah obligation.

Similarly, partners who purchased an etrog or lulav in partnership – neither of them fulfills their obligation on the first day until the second gives him his portion as a gift. For partners certainly are particular with each other. And this is specifically when they did not buy it for the purpose of the mitzvah. But if they bought it for the purpose of the mitzvah, they fulfill their obligation with it, since it is assumed that they acquired it with the intention that each one would give his portion as a gift at the time he fulfills his obligation with it. Therefore, in places where an etrog is not readily available, and the entire community buys an etrog in partnership, the reasoning is also the same, that since they purchased it so that everyone would fulfill their obligation with it, it is assumed as though it was explicitly stated that the entire community gives their portion to whoever takes it to fulfill their obligation, on the condition that he returns it to them. The Rashba explained this in a responsum (part 1, siman 62), and this is his wording: “Anything that the community has taken – does not require a gift, nor an explicit condition, and each one fulfills their obligation with it automatically due to retroactive clarification: since it is not suitable for division, it becomes clear when this one takes it that he is taking his own, for each one has given his portion to his fellow at the time of taking, for this is the condition under which they took it.” And this is similar to the partners in Nedarim, chapter 4 (46b) regarding a courtyard that does not have the law of division; see there. In such a manner, everyone agrees that there is retroactive clarification. The details of this law are explained in Yoreh De'ah, siman 266. And since not everyone agrees with this, as explained there, it is therefore good to announce that each one should give his portion to his fellow as a gift (Magen Avraham, section 10). And this is not the custom, because among us, it is rare for one to have an etrog by himself, and many partners in one etrog, and it is generally assumed that the intention is according to the law.

Collection of Etrog Money – It should be collected according to wealth, as the enhancement of a mitzvah (commandment) applies more to the wealthy. There is an opinion that it should be half according to wealth and half according to the number of people (see Sha'arei Teshuvah, subsection 11). In our communities, we purchase from communal funds. However, on Hoshana Rabbah, we place a bowl, and each person gives a small amount as they wish. A woman is exempt from giving Etrog money because she is exempt [from the mitzvah]. However, our women, who make the blessing, are required to give. Anyone who has their own Etrog does not need to give. Every person should strive and be diligent in the mitzvah, to buy their own Etrog and Lulav, in order to fulfill the mitzvah in its enhanced form. (The Magen Avraham in subsection 12 writes: If someone has their own Etrog, and in another city, there is no Etrog at all, it is better for them to benefit the public and send theirs there, and they will make the blessing on the communal one. And the Sha'arei Teshuvah in subsection 12 writes: Even for an individual living in a village without an Etrog, one should do so, see there. We have not heard of anyone who does so, as in our times, everyone can obtain an Etrog, even if it is expensive. Nevertheless, it is available, which was not the case in previous generations.)

In the morning, they enter the synagogue, but they do not come as early as on Shabbat. They pray the Yom Tov prayer and recite a piyyut (liturgical poem), each place according to its custom. If the first day falls on Shabbat, they switch the piyyut of the second day to the first, because on the first day the poet speaks about the Four Species, and on the second about the Sukkah. They complete Hallel, and then say the full Kaddish. They take out two Torah scrolls; in the first, they read five aliyot from the portion "Shor O Kesav," and the maftir reads from the second Torah scroll about the additional offerings in "Pinchas." The Haftarah is from Zechariah: "Behold, a day is coming," because it mentions the matter of Sukkot. They pray Musaf and say in the Kedusha "Adir Adireinu," the priests raise their hands, the Kohanim recite the Priestly Blessing, and the prayer leader concludes with "Sim Shalom."

Regarding the Hoshanot – there are different customs. Rabbi Saadia Gaon wrote to say them after Hallel, and this is the custom of the Sephardim. The reason is simple: since they hold the lulav and etrog in their hands, they should say the Hoshanot with them as well. According to this, the prayer leader does not say the full Kaddish after Hallel, but rather after the Hoshanot. However, the Tur wrote to say the Hoshanot after Musaf, and this is the custom of the Ashkenazim. The reason is that since the circuits (hakafot) are a remembrance of the Temple, where they would circle the altar, and in the Temple, the circuits were after the additional offerings (Musafim) – therefore, we also do so (Beit Yosef). Some say the full Kaddish after Musaf before the Hoshanot, and also say Kaddish after the Hoshanot. But we do not follow this practice; rather, after Musaf we say the Hoshanot, and then the full Kaddish. The matter of the Hoshanot will be explained in the next section with the help of Heaven.

The matter of the Hoshanot is a remembrance of the Temple. For it is taught (Sukkah 45a): Every day they would circle the altar once, and on the seventh day, seven times. And in the Temple, they learned this from Jericho, as it is said in the Jerusalem Talmud there and in Midrash Shocher Tov on the verse "Hear, O Lord, righteousness" (Psalms 17:1). Therefore, we also circle the Bimah with our Lulav and Etrog every day once, and on Hoshanah Rabbah seven times. We place a Torah scroll on the Bimah and cry out "Hoshanah," meaning: "Save, please, Your people, the remnant of Israel, from all the troubles surrounding them – by the merit of the Torah and by the merit of Your great name." For it is as if "I am with him in distress" and "Save, please, for Your sake, our God…"

Therefore, we say: "Ani v'Hu Hoshia Na," which are two names from the seventy-two-letter name, derived from three verses: "Vayisa," "Vayavo," and "Vayet." These two names were chosen for the phrases "And I am in the exile" and "He is bound in chains," indicating, as it were, that the Holy One, blessed be He, is in exile. As our Sages, of blessed memory, said: "They were exiled to Babylon, and the Divine Presence went with them," as it is written: "I am with him in trouble." The term "Ani" (I) always refers to the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written throughout the Torah: "I am the Lord..." – for besides the Holy One, blessed be He, no one can truly say "I," which is a term of power, from the root "on," because there is no power besides Him. Additionally, it is written: "I, I am He who puts to death and brings to life," and this verse speaks of the protection of Israel. Therefore, we say: You who said "I, I am He" – save us now (Rambam in his commentary on the Mishnah there). And "Hu" also refers to the Holy One, blessed be He, as they are the last two letters of the Tetragrammaton. And it is necessary to pronounce "v'Hu" with a shuruk (u) and not with a cholam (o). Also, "Ani v'Hu" in gematria equals "Ana Hashem" (Rashi there).

A single Torah scroll is placed on the bimah, and on Hoshana Rabbah, seven Torah scrolls. Some take out all the Torah scrolls. A candle is placed in the Ark in honor of "a mitzvah is a candle and the Torah is light." There should be no objection that this is a mundane matter, for since it is done in honor of the Torah, there is no concern. The encircling is done to the right, as all turns should be to the right. Therefore, when the people face the Torah scroll on the bimah, the north is to the right. According to this, the prayer leader should first turn their face towards the bimah, otherwise, the south would be to their right. However, the custom is not so, and the prayer leader follows the congregation (see Magen Avraham; according to what I have written, this is clear). On Shabbat, there is no encircling since there is no lulav on Shabbat. Even in the Temple, there was no encircling on Shabbat. A Torah scroll is not placed on the bimah on Shabbat. But the "Hoshanot" are recited on Shabbat, as Rabbi Yosef Karo wrote in section 3: there is an opinion that "Hoshana" is not recited on Shabbat, but this is not the custom. Thus is his wording, and this is the Ashkenazi custom. The Sephardim do not recite it.

It is customary to encircle [the bimah] even for one who does not have a lulav (Beit Yosef). Some say that one who does not have a lulav does not encircle, and this is the prevalent custom. On the seventh day, they take the willow with the lulav to encircle (ibid.). However, we do not practice this, and the Ari Zal commanded not to combine the willow with the lulav. One who has experienced mourning during the festival does not encircle, nor does one who is in the twelve-month mourning period for a father or mother, and this is the custom. Even though there are those who dispute this (see Beit Yosef), nevertheless, this is the custom, because we are asking for mercy, and he is under judgment, unless the mourner is the leader of the community and is compelled to encircle.

For the Mincha prayer, it is recited like the "Yotzer" prayer, and similarly for the Maariv prayer as on the first night. The Tur writes that for the Kiddush on the second night, one says Kiddush, then the Shehechiyanu blessing immediately afterward, and then mentions the Sukkah. The Shehechiyanu blessing only applies to the Kiddush and not to the Sukkah. Even if the first day is a weekday, one fulfills the obligation of the Shehechiyanu blessing concerning the Sukkah. Therefore, one should not interrupt between Kiddush and the Shehechiyanu blessing with mentioning the Sukkah. Rabbi Eliezer of Metz writes that even on the second night, the Shehechiyanu blessing is said last, just as in the order of "Yaknehaz," even though the Shehechiyanu blessing does not apply to Havdalah. My master and father, of blessed memory, agreed with the first opinion. This is his wording: It is not comparable to Havdalah, which requires a cup [of wine], and therefore, one should not interrupt with the Shehechiyanu blessing between "Borei Peri HaGafen" and Havdalah. But with regard to the Sukkah, there is no connection to the cup, and if so, why interrupt with the Sukkah between Kiddush and the Shehechiyanu blessing (Beit Yosef)?

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, ruled in accordance with the Rosh, that on the second night, "Shehechiyanu" is recited first, and so we practice. Nevertheless, there are some great authorities who wrote that the primary opinion follows the Avi HaEzri, that there should be no distinction between the first night and the second night, and one should precede with the blessing for the Sukkah and then the Shehechiyanu, as on the first night. Some great authorities practiced this way (Maharshal and Bach). And it is obvious that one who did not eat in the Sukkah on the first night should bless for the Sukkah first and then the Shehechiyanu on the second night (Magen Avraham).

On the second day, we pray the same way as on the first day. We take the lulav and recite the blessing "on the taking of the lulav," and this continues for all seven days. Even though this practice is rabbinic in nature, we still recite a blessing over it, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 658; see there. Regarding the "Shehechiyanu" blessing on the lulav on the second day of Yom Tov, some say that it is not necessary to recite it because it was already recited yesterday. And even if yesterday was a weekday, we still bless at the time of making the lulav bundle before Yom Tov, according to the Talmudic law. Others say that it is necessary to recite it because the blessing was only instituted either at the time of making the bundle or at the time of taking the lulav. If yesterday was a weekday, it was neither the time of making the bundle nor the time of taking the lulav (both opinions are in the Tur). Nevertheless, our custom follows the first opinion, and this is also the ruling of the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, as it is clear that the "Shehechiyanu" of yesterday is not less significant than the making of the bundle before Yom Tov. Only when the first day falls on Shabbat, we then recite the "Shehechiyanu" on the second day, as we did not recite it on the lulav yet. In such a case, it is similar to the shofar, for which we also recite the blessing on the second day.

And we take out two Torah scrolls. In the first, we read five people from "When an ox or a sheep" (Leviticus 22:26-23:44), and in the second from the offerings of the additional sacrifices in "Pinchas," all as yesterday. Only the haftarah is in Kings: "And all the men of Israel assembled" (I Kings 8:2) until "when I brought them out of the land of Egypt" (I Kings 8:21), where the seven days of the festival are mentioned. And we pray the additional prayer and the Priestly Blessing – all as yesterday.

During Chol Hamoed (the intermediate days of the festival), one prays Ma'ariv (the evening prayer), Shacharit (the morning prayer), and Mincha (the afternoon prayer) as on a regular weekday, and mentions "Ya'aleh Veyavo" in the "Avodah" blessing. If one did not say it, they must repeat the prayer. Each day, one blesses the lulav and completes the Hallel. This is unlike Pesach, where Hallel is not completed, because on Sukkot, each day is considered a separate festival, as evidenced by the differences in their sacrifices. One reads from the Torah portions related to the day, as will be explained, and prays the Musaf prayer of the festival. One says the Hoshanot as printed in the siddurim, and others from what is said on Hoshana Rabbah, such as "I will arrange my supplication" and "God of salvations." However, there are those who follow the order of the Hoshana Rabbah Hoshanot sequentially, and seemingly, why should we change this? But one does not object to a custom in matters where there is no halachic impediment, whether done one way or another.

And since the reading during Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of the festival) can only occur on these six days, from the second day until after the seventh day on each of which it is only possible for one reader to read, and each day there are four readers, for on Chol HaMoed four are called up to the Torah reading – it is thus necessary that the second person reads what the first person read. There are various customs regarding this. Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote that on the first day the Kohen reads "On the second day," and the Levite reads "On the third day," and the third and fourth repeat this, meaning: the third reads "On the second day." However, the fourth reads both: "[On] the second day" and "On the third day," due to the uncertainty of the day, so that one person reads both doubtful portions. And on the second festival day, he does not read "On the second day," so as not to disrespect the second festival day, to avoid showing that there is a concern of it being a weekday. And in this manner, they read on all the days.

But our custom, according to our teacher the Rema, is as follows: The first [person] reads "On the second day," the Levite reads "On the third day," the third [person] reads "On the fourth day." The fourth [person] reads the doubtful days: "On the second day" and "On the third day," and so on each day. Only on Hoshanah Rabbah, the Kohen needs to start from "On the fifth day," the Levite [reads] "On the sixth day," the third [person] reads "On the seventh day," and the fourth [person] reads "On the sixth day" and "On the seventh day," as it cannot be done otherwise, obviously. And this is our simple custom. And all of this pertains to outside the Land [of Israel]. But in the Land of Israel, where there is no doubt regarding the day, each person reads the passage for his respective day. For example, on the second day, everyone reads "On the second day," and on the third day, "On the third day," and so on in this manner.

On Shabbat that falls during Chol HaMoed, for Ma'ariv, Shacharit, and Mincha, one prays the Shabbat prayer. And one says "Ya'aleh V'yavo" in the blessing of "Avodah". If one did not say it, they must repeat the prayer. For Musaf, one prays the festival prayer and includes Shabbat, concluding with "Who sanctifies the Shabbat, Israel, and the seasons". "Adir Adireinu" is said in the Kedushah, and Hoshanot are recited. Kohelet is read after Shacharit. If Shemini Atzeret falls on Shabbat, one recites the Shemini Atzeret prayers without a blessing. Two Torah scrolls are taken out. In one, the portion "Re'eh Atah Omer…" is read, and the Maftir is the portion for the day. The Haftarah is from Ezekiel concerning Gog and Magog, which will occur during the festival of Sukkot. The Haftarah concludes with "Who sanctifies the Shabbat, Israel, and the seasons".

On this day, an additional commandment is added, which is the mitzvah of the willow. The primary observance of this mitzvah was in the Temple, as it is a law given to Moses at Sinai that they would bring another willow in the Temple, separate from the willow that is part of the lulav. And a person does not fulfill their obligation with the willow that is in the lulav. The measurement is even one leaf on one branch. How was this mitzvah performed? Every day of the seven days, they would bring large branches of willow, which were eleven cubits long, which were found in a place near Jerusalem. And they would set them upright around the altar, which was ten cubits high, and their tops would bend over the altar by one cubit. And when they would bring it and arrange it, they would blow a series of trumpet blasts: a long note, a series of short notes, and a long note again. However, if Shabbat occurred during the days of the festival, they would not set up the willow, unless the seventh day fell on Shabbat. Even though nowadays Hoshana Rabbah does not fall on Shabbat, in the time of the Temple, when they would sanctify the month based on sighting the new moon, it could happen. Then they would set it up on Shabbat, to publicize that it is a mitzvah, and since it is not written in the Torah, it requires publicizing. They would bring it to the Temple on the eve of Shabbat and place them in a gold basin filled with water so they would not wilt. And on Shabbat, they would set them up around the altar, and the people would come and take them as they did every day. This is the order of the willow in the Temple.

And in our times, the latter prophets, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, and the Men of the Great Assembly, who were the ones to establish ordinances in Israel (Rashi, Megillah 21a), instituted that since it is not explicitly mentioned in the Torah, they did not establish it every day like the lulav, but only on the seventh day it is taken, as a remembrance of the Temple. How is it done? One takes one branch or many branches, excluding the willow that is part of the lulav, and strikes it on the ground or on a vessel two or three times. And without a blessing, since this act is not a complete mitzvah. It is proper to strike it five times, and there is a reason for this.

And it has already been explained that the minimum requirement for the willow is even one leaf on one stem. However, it is unbecoming to have it this way, so we take a beautiful willow because of "This is my God, and I will glorify Him." The custom is to take five stems and bind them, and there is a reason for this. The required length is the same as the willow used with the lulav. Any disqualifications that apply to the willow of the lulav apply here as well, such as if it is cut off at the top or if it is withered, and the like. Except for the falling of leaves – it is still valid, even if only one leaf remains, as I have written. It does not need to be shaken, only beaten. Some say it should also be shaken. And our master the Rema wrote in Section 4 that the custom is to do both: shake it first, and then beat it. Thus are his words. We are not familiar with this custom.

And it is not taken except by itself, so that nothing else is bound with it. However, one can hold something else in their hand, and this is not considered a separation between the hand and the willow. They were not so strict about this, since it is only a custom. Nevertheless, it is forbidden to hold it in a disrespectful manner, and one should take it in their hand with honor. Some are particular not to bind it with the lulav due to the concern of separation. However, this is not the case, for anything done to beautify it is not considered a separation (as the Magen Avraham writes in subsection 4), as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 651. Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in subsection 3: There is an opinion that even on this day, one should circle with the lulav and not with the willow. However, the custom is not like this, but rather to circle also with the willow. This is his language, but we customarily circle only with the lulav. And the Arizal already warned not to attach the willow to the lulav at all. It is customary for the synagogue attendant to bring the willow to sell, as was the custom in the time of the Temple. With us, it is difficult to be careful about this as well, because the poor bring them to the houses, and it is charity for them to receive something in return. There is no strictness in all these matters, as long as one's intention is for the sake of Heaven.

And it has already been explained that a person does not fulfill his obligation with the willow branch in the lulav, even if he raised it twice: once for the lulav and once for the willow. And even though there are those who say that he fulfills his obligation in this manner, nevertheless, we do not hold this way.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 7: There is an opinion that says one cannot take it (the willow) with the lulav at the time when fulfilling the obligation, until after one has blessed, taken, and shaken (the lulav) initially. If one did take it, one transgresses the prohibition of "Bal Tosif" (not adding to the commandments). But after the first shaking, one can take it with the lulav, and certainly during the encircling (Hoshana Rabba). And even though it was written that if one took it, one transgresses "Bal Tosif," this seems like an error to me. Nonetheless, there is no harm in being cautious regarding his words. He also wrote: Even after taking and shaking, one must hold the willow alone to recognize that it is an obligation. And at the time of beating (the willow), one should take it by itself and fulfill the obligation with it. Thus far his words. And certainly, "Bal Tosif" does not apply here since we hold that the lulav does not require binding. If so, it (the willow) is also included in the willows of the lulav. Furthermore, "Bal Tosif" only applies to a completely different species, as I wrote at the beginning of Siman 651, see there (and it is from Tosafot, Sukkah 34b, s.v. "Arvei").

And our master, the Rema, wrote about this: The common custom is to take the willow with the lulav in the morning, at the time of the waving and during the circling, until the time of the beating, and then take the willow alone. And it is better not to take it with the lulav at all. And even those who take it with the lulav, it seems to me that after they finish circling, they should remove the lulav from their hand and hold the willow, because they make the hoshanot separately all the time while saying supplications for water, and they wave the hoshanot at the time they say hoshanot, and afterwards they beat them. Thus far his words. And we have already explained that we follow the better way he wrote, and we never combine the willow with the lulav, but only the lulav alone. And even at the time of saying the hoshanot, we hold only the lulav alone. However, when we reach the prayer "Answer the faithful," we put down the lulav and take the willow until the beating. Also, we do not customarily wave the willow. And it is proper to consider his words and wave a little.
