(What the Magen Avraham wrote in subsection 8 to take two separate twigs, and some wrote seventeen twigs, and not to bind them together, see there – we do not follow this, but we take five twigs and bind them together).

There is an opinion that the "hoshana" with the lulav, even though it is thrown away, is not considered an article of sanctity but rather an article of mitzvah. Nevertheless, one should not tread on it disrespectfully, as I wrote in Siman 21 regarding the tzitzit. Similarly, the willow branch that is taken today has the same ruling. There is also an opinion that it is forbidden to benefit from the willow branch after it has been taken, for it was designated for its mitzvah for the entire day, unless one stipulated that it would only be designated until after the beating. However, in truth, some say that such a stipulation does not help for this day, as it is automatically designated for the entire day. There are differing opinions on this matter. (See Magen Avraham, Siman 649, subparagraph 19, and this Siman, subparagraph 9. See also what is written there in subparagraph 21.)

Rabbi Moses Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 9: The custom is to store the hoshanot (willow branches used on Hoshana Rabbah) for baking matzot, in order to perform a mitzvah with them. This is his language. Meaning: since one mitzvah was performed with them, let another mitzvah be performed with them. And certainly, this is correct. However, because of the long duration, it is difficult to guard them, and sometimes they are left in disgrace. Therefore, it is better to burn them, just as we burn the sukkah's s'chach (roofing). And this is our custom.

And there is someone who says that one should be careful not to cut willow branches for a Jew from a non-Jew's field, even with his permission. The rationale for this we explained in Siman 649, Section 10. In a situation where it already happened, there is no concern, as I wrote there. If Hoshanah Rabbah falls on a Sunday and the non-Jew cut the willow branches on Shabbat and brought them, they are valid since he did it for his own purposes. However, if the Jew instructed the non-Jew to cut them on Shabbat, it appears to be forbidden. There is an opinion that permits even in such a case, based on the Responsa of the Rashba (Magen Avraham, Section 10). But this is very puzzling, and the Rashba did not address this matter at all. Rather, he was asked if the branches were cut on the second day of Yom Tov, whether it is permissible to place them in the bundle of the lulav on the second day of Yom Tov, and he ruled that it is forbidden. He mentioned nothing further (Responsa of the Rashba, Part 1, Siman 297, and also the Pri Megadim remained in doubt about this). This is what our teacher the Rema wrote in Section 11, and this is his language: "However, if a Jew instructed to cut it, and there is public visibility in the matter, one should be stringent if there is another willow." This is his language, implying it is only a stringency due to public visibility, but by law it is permitted if he instructed before Shabbat to cut it, and did not tell him specifically to cut it on Shabbat. But if he told him to cut it on Shabbat, it appears to be forbidden by law, especially for a mitzvah matter. See what I wrote in Siman 252. There is a need for further investigation by law if there is no other willow.

Since an additional mitzvah has been added today, which is the conclusion of the festival, and on the festival we are judged concerning water, and in water is included sustenance and other matters – therefore, it is the custom of all Israel to have an awakening on this day in two ways. The first, like the days of judgment, meaning: many stay awake most of the night, and they read Deuteronomy because in it is the essence of the love and fear of God, they read Psalms, and say the special "Yehi Ratzon" for Hoshana Rabbah. Before dawn, they go to immerse in the mikvah, and they rise early to go to the synagogue, and the prayer leader wears the kittel. They say "Shir HaYichud" and "Anim Zemirot" as on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and the melody within the prayer is as on the Days of Awe. During the circling of the hakafot and the recitation of the hoshanot, they cry a lot, as on Yom Kippur. They also increase the number of candles somewhat, as on Yom Kippur, because on the festival we are judged concerning water, and today is the final judgment. It is customary to untie the binding of the lulav, and they have written a hint for this. (And the Rama wrote in the name of the early authorities that there is a sign in the shadow of the moon on the night of Hoshana Rabbah, regarding what will happen to him or his relatives in that year. However, one should not be meticulous about this, so that his fortune will not be adversely affected. Also, many do not fully understand this matter. It is better to be simple and not to investigate the future. Thus far his words. And truly, it is forbidden for the people of Israel to look at such matters. In one moment, when one repents, he transforms from bad to good. We have nothing other than to lift our eyes to our Father in heaven.)

The second custom: they treat this day somewhat like a Yom Tov (holiday). This means that they recite the Psalms of Shabbat and Yom Tov in Pesukei Dezimra, but they do not recite "Nishmat". They do recite "Mizmor LeTodah". When taking out the Torah, they say "Shema Yisrael" as on Yom Tov. They recite the Kedushah of "Na'aritzach... Adir Adireinu" and the Kaddishes of Musaf are recited in the Yom Tov melody. It is not customary to perform weekday work until after leaving the synagogue. Our master, the Rema, wrote that one should recite the piyut "Zachor Brit" when there is a brit milah on Hoshana Rabbah, and it is recited before "Ana Ezon Chayin". This is his language. However, among us, it is not customary to recite this piyut at all during the year.

And it is also customary to have a festive meal on Hoshana Rabbah with good food. Certainly, anyone who is able to eat with appetite at night should do so, and it will be enjoyable and satisfying for them. However, I am troubled by the practice of many who eat to the point of being full, so much so that they are disgusted by food at night. It is certainly wrong to do so, for at night it is the Yom Tov of Shemini Atzeret, and one is obligated to eat with appetite. Therefore, one should not have a fixed meal during the day, so that they can eat with appetite at night. This is my practice as well. And the custom is to say “Yom Tov tov” (Good Yom Tov), unlike on weekdays.

An etrog on the seventh day – is forbidden all day, for it has been set aside for all seven days. Its prohibition starts from the first day, even before one has recited the blessing over it, since it was set aside for the mitzvah on the eve of the festival (Taz). Even if it became invalid after the mitzvah was performed with it – nevertheless, it is forbidden for all seven days, since it was set aside for all seven days. However, on the eighth day – it is permitted. And although during the twilight between the seventh and eighth days – it is still set aside due to the doubt of the previous day, nevertheless, we do not say in such a case: since it was set aside during twilight – it is set aside for the entire day. It is not similar to a sukkah, as will be explained in Siman 667, which is forbidden even on the eighth day, for there it was set aside during twilight by a deed, as one was obligated to eat there. This is not the case with an etrog, which is only due to the previous day (Tosafot Sukka 12, beginning with "Ad").

In the Diaspora, where two days of Yom Tov are observed, the etrog is prohibited on the eighth day because of the uncertainty of the day. It is permitted on the ninth day, even if the ninth day falls on a Sunday. We do not say that Shabbat prepares it for permissibility, and that it constitutes preparation from Shabbat to Yom Tov, because this is not considered preparation for something that was already in existence and no action was done to it (Magen Avraham, Small Paragraph 2). Nevertheless, there are those who prohibit it when it falls on a Sunday due to the reason of preparation. And be aware that an etrog that has become invalid is also permitted on the eighth day in the Diaspora (Taz), because it is impossible to prohibit something that has become invalid to such an extent.

One who sets aside seven etrogim (citrons) for seven days—each one fulfills the mitzvah with it and eats it the next day. And even though it was prohibited during twilight, nevertheless, since it was designated only for one day, it is as though he explicitly stipulated that he is designating it solely for the mitzvah (Magen Avraham). And know that the Jerusalem Talmud holds that if an etrog becomes invalid, it ceases to be set aside (muktzeh), but this is not the approach of our Talmud (see Taz).

Even if one finishes their meal on the seventh day in the morning, and in the Land of Israel where there is no need to sit in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret, nevertheless, one should not completely dismantle the sukkah, since it is necessary to sit in it all day until night. Perhaps a meal will come up, and one will need to eat in the sukkah. However, the utensils that are needed for the house can be taken out of the sukkah from mincha (afternoon prayer) onwards. It seems that this refers to mincha ketana (the later mincha), as it is then evident that one is doing so in honor of the festival, preparing the house for the final festival day, and this is not considered disrespectful to the sukkah.

And if he does not have a house and is compelled to sit also on the Eighth day in the sukkah in the Land of Israel, it appears as if he is violating "Bal Tosif" (the prohibition of adding to the commandments). However, this is not a complete violation of "Bal Tosif" because we hold that to transgress "Bal Tosif" not in its proper time, one needs intention to do so for the sake of the commandment (end of the third chapter of Rosh Hashanah). But without such intention, one does not transgress "Bal Tosif." Nevertheless, it is still inappropriate, and the sages have said (Sukkah 48a) that one must invalidate the sukkah, meaning at least by removing an area of four by four handbreadths from the roof. And even though removing three handbreadths of airspace would also invalidate it, there is not as much of a visible indication. It is obvious that if one needs to eat on the seventh day, he must eat in the sukkah. Be aware that the concern of "Bal Tosif" only applies on the Eighth day, and in the Diaspora on the Ninth day, because they are adjacent to the days of Sukkot. But if one wants to eat in the sukkah after the festival, he does not need to do anything, because then it does not appear as "Bal Tosif." He does not need to remove anything or damage it and can sit and eat in it.

And this is all in the Land of Israel. But outside of the Land of Israel, one does not need to do anything on the seventh day, since one must dwell in it on the eighth day of Shemini Atzeret. And on the eighth day, what should one do? After finishing eating, one takes down their utensils from the afternoon onwards to their home, due to the honor of the last festival day. And even though it is burdensome to oneself from the first day to the second, in any case, it is impossible in another manner, for at night it is impossible to take them down. And there is no burden in this, for one does not arrange them properly in the house until the night, and merely taking them down we have no concern.

And what should one do outside of the Land of Israel when they do not have a house and are compelled to eat in the sukkah even on the ninth day, so as not to appear as if they are adding to the mitzvah? And it is impossible to diminish [the sanctity of the sukkah], for on a festival it is forbidden to diminish. The Sages said (in that same place) that this is how one should act to make it recognizable: If it is a small sukkah in which it is forbidden to place a candle on other days, as I wrote in Siman 639 – place a candle in it. And if it is large, where it is permissible to place a candle in it – bring in pots and dishes and similar items, which are forbidden to bring into the sukkah, as explained there, in order to make it recognizable that it is disqualified and that its mitzvah has already been completed. And it does not appear as "bal tosif" (adding to the mitzvah).

And know that the Rosh, of blessed memory, towards the end of Sukkah, inferred from Rashi's commentary there that even outside the Land [of Israel], one must make some distinction on the seventh day in the sukkah to indicate that what is eaten there on the eighth day should not be considered as "adding to the mitzvot." However, he rejected this, see there. And indeed, there is not such a strong proof from Rashi, see there. Nevertheless, it seems to me that the essence of this matter depends on the manner in which we sit on Shemini Atzeret, which will be explained in Siman 668. (The Rosh interpreted what Rashi wrote on Sukkah 48b, in the commentary beginning with "Ha Lan" – for the people of Babylonia who light the candle, that it refers to the seventh day. It is possible to say that it refers to the eighth day. See Beit Yosef and Knesset HaGedolah there.)

Even though it is explained in Siman 668 that an etrog (citron) on the eighth day is permitted in the Land of Israel, nevertheless, a sukkah and its decorations are prohibited on the eighth day, because since they were set aside (muktzeh) during the twilight period between the seventh and eighth days, they remain set aside for the entire day. This is not similar to an etrog, as its being set aside is not due to an action but because of the previous day. This is not the case with a sukkah, where one must sit there during the twilight period, and if a meal were to coincide with this time, one would eat in the sukkah, thus making its setting aside a matter of action, as I wrote there. Consequently, in the Diaspora, where people sit in the sukkah on the eighth day as well, it is also prohibited on the ninth day for this reason; for the ninth day in the Diaspora is like the eighth day in the Land of Israel. 

And know that what we have said regarding the prohibition of using the sukkah pertains to when it has fallen down, for if it is still standing, it is anyway prohibited due to dismantling a structure. And if Simchat Torah falls on the eve of Shabbat, there are those who customarily prohibit the sukkah and its decorations also on Shabbat, because if you permit them on Shabbat, it would appear that Yom Tov prepares for Shabbat. However, we have already explained in Siman 668 that regarding something that is already in existence, preparation is not applicable. Nevertheless, there are those who are stringent, as I wrote there; see there.

Some have the custom that when they leave the sukkah, they say: "May it be Your will... just as we have merited to sit in this sukkah, so may we merit to sit in the sukkah made from the skin of the Leviathan." It is well known that it is forbidden to prepare from one festival day to the next. Therefore, on Shemini Atzeret, when bringing down the utensils from the sukkah, it is forbidden to set up the tables and benches in the house for the night, as this constitutes preparation. It is sufficient that we permit bringing them down from the sukkah during the day, because it is not possible to do so at night. But to set them up and arrange them is forbidden until night. This is the case when the bringing down is a separate action and the arranging is a separate action. However, if when bringing them down one sets them in their place, there is no issue, as this does not involve a unique action and exertion. (This resolves the difficulty the Magen Avraham has in subparagraph 3 with the words of the Maharil. The Maharil forbids searching for the Torah scroll from Shabbat for Yom Tov because of preparation. It seems to me that if one recites some verses from the Torah there, it is considered learning for that time and not preparation.)

On the night of Shemini Atzeret, we pray the first three blessings and the last three blessings, with the sanctification of the day in the middle. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote to say "And You gave us... this eighth day, the festival of assembly." Our master, the Rema, wrote that we customarily do not say "festival" on the eighth day because we do not find it referred to as a "festival" anywhere. Rather, we say "this eighth day of assembly," thus is his wording. And there are those who say that one should say "this eighth day of the festival of assembly" (Rashal and Taz), and this is the custom of the world, and so it is printed in the prayer books. The reason: the term "festival" refers to Sukkot, for Shemini Atzeret is the assembly of the festival of Sukkot. However, many of the great ones of Israel agreed with the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch to say "this eighth day, the festival of assembly." There are many proofs that it is called "festival," and in the Torah, it is subordinate to the festival of Sukkot, but it is a festival in its own right, and it is called a "festival." Thus it is in the Siddur of Rav Amram Gaon. (And it seems to me a proof from the Tractate Soferim, chapter 19, which says there about the seventh day of Pesach that one says "on this seventh day of assembly," and does not mention "festival" because it is not a festival in its own right. Thus is its wording. Consequently, Shemini Atzeret, which is a festival in its own right, is called a festival. And although we do not practice on the seventh day of Pesach as per the Tractate Soferim, it is still a great proof. Furthermore, an a fortiori argument: the seventh day of Pesach, which is not called a "festival" and is not a festival in its own right, we say "this festival of matzot"—all the more so on Shemini Atzeret, which is a festival in its own right, we should say "festival." And if one said "festival of Sukkot"—it seems to me in my humble opinion that he does not need to repeat the prayer; see Sotah 39, and in Taz, Yoreh De’ah, Siman 240.)

In the Diaspora, one eats in the Sukkah on Shemini Atzeret, both at night and during the day, because it is a doubt whether it is the seventh day. However, one does not recite the blessing on sitting in the Sukkah. One makes Kiddush and recites the Shehecheyanu blessing, as it is a festival in its own right. The halacha is thus decided in the Gemara (Sukkah 47a): on the eighth day, we sit [in the Sukkah], but we do not recite a blessing. 

Nevertheless, we see different customs among the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) regarding this: The Mordechai, in the name of the Ra’avyah, wrote that it is forbidden to sleep in the Sukkah on the eighth day because of "bal tosif" (the prohibition against adding to the commandments). For while in eating, there is a distinction since one does not recite the blessing, in sleeping, there is no such distinction (Magen Avraham). 

And even though it is not a complete "bal tosif," as I wrote in Siman 668, regarding "bal tosif" not in its time, it requires intention. Nevertheless, it appears as "bal tosif." Additionally, in reality, one is sitting for the sake of the mitzvah due to the doubt. Nevertheless, a distinction is required since we are knowledgeable in the fixing of the month. This will be further explained in Section 5 with the help of Heaven.

And for this reason, it is customary to leave the sukkah immediately after the morning meal (there). There are those who do not sit in the sukkah at night but do sit during the day (there), but this is not a proper custom (Tur). Some make Kiddush and taste something in the sukkah, then go home to eat. However, many prominent authorities have already protested against these practices, stating that since the halacha is concluded in the Gemara that one should sit in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret, one must therefore sit in the sukkah all night and all day. Additionally, one must sleep in the sukkah, without any distinction from the rest of the festival.

In my humble opinion, there is substantial basis for the customary practice of the Jewish people, and all the words are true, though they require explanation. For indeed, it is true that the halacha is decided in the Gemara that we sit [in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret], but our rabbis, the Tosafists, wrote there, and this is their language: "We sit – but they did not want to institute taking the lulav because of the doubt, since it is a festival and [the lulav] is muktzeh (set aside) for carrying, and it would be noticeable that one is acting in a weekday manner. But the sukkah – sometimes one's sukkah is pleasant to him, and he eats in it even on a festival." Thus far is their language. And similarly, the Tur wrote, and this is his language: "It is not relevant in his sitting there to say: how can it be considered weekday behavior? Because it is common sometimes to sit in the shade of a sukkah, even not for the sake of the mitzvah of sukkah." Thus far is his language. It is explicitly stated that the main reason for the permission is because it is not noticeable that he sits there for the sake of the mitzvah. But if it were noticeable that he does so only for the sake of the mitzvah – it would not be proper to sit there.

And according to this, everything is clear. For certainly, in warm countries like Babylonia, and in the western and southern countries, where during Sukkot the weather is pleasant and good, they are certainly obligated to eat and sleep in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret, just like in the entire holiday. But in northern countries like ours, where most of the time the weather is cold, if we exempt ourselves throughout the entire Sukkot due to the cold, we would nullify the mitzvah of sukkah from ourselves. Therefore, we are forced to sit and sleep in the sukkah throughout the entire Sukkot. In truth, most people exempt themselves from sleeping in the sukkah due to this reason, as I wrote in Siman 639. However, on Shemini Atzeret, when the Sages commanded us to sit in the sukkah in a way that it would not be evident that it is for the sake of the mitzvah, this is something almost impossible in our countries. Therefore, God forbid we should nullify the decree of the Sages, but nonetheless, we must make some sign that it is not for the sake of the mitzvah. And that is: if someone sleeps in the sukkah all the days of the holiday, he should not sleep in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret. And if someone does not sleep in the sukkah, then this is not a sign, so he must make another sign, which is: either not to eat in the sukkah at night or to eat a small meal outside the sukkah during the day. However, these two ways are flawed. Therefore, the best sign is to leave the sukkah immediately after the morning meal, to show that we are not doing this for the sake of the mitzvah. And this is the essence of the established customs (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And one should not eat the evening meal on Shemini Atzeret until it is nighttime. For if one eats it before nightfall and after the evening prayer, one cannot recite the blessing "to dwell in the sukkah" because he has accepted upon himself the holiday of Shemini Atzeret, and yet it is still day. Nevertheless, if this occurs, one should not recite the blessing "to dwell in the sukkah" (Magen Avraham, subsection 3). There is an opinion that even initially one may do so (Taz). However, this is not the custom, for in any case, on every holiday, we do not eat before nightfall.

On the Torah reading on Shemini Atzeret in the Land of Israel, which is only one day, they do the Hakafot and read from "Vezot HaBeracha" to complete the Torah. Afterwards, they read from Bereshit until "Asher Bara Elokim La'asot." The reason for this is so that the Satan does not have an opening to say that they finished the Torah and do not want to study it anymore (Tur in the next section). The Haftarah is "On the eighth day of the assembly," and the Haftarah reading is "And it came to pass after the death of Moses." Outside of the Land of Israel, they read "Kol HaBechor." If it falls on Shabbat, they begin with "Aser Te'aser." There are places where even on a weekday they begin with "Aser Te'aser" because it is the time for tithes, and this is our custom. The Haftarah is "On the eighth day of the assembly," and the Haftarah reading in Kings is "And it came to pass when Solomon finished," because Shemini Atzeret is mentioned there. They return the Torah scrolls, say Kaddish, and the sexton announces "He who causes the wind to blow and the rain to fall," and the laws for this are explained in Siman 114, see there. (Those who follow the Sephardic custom also do the Hakafot on Shemini Atzeret after the evening prayer.)

In the Diaspora, where they observe two days of Yom Tov, on the night of the ninth day they recite Kiddush and the Shehecheyanu blessing. The next day, they take out three Torah scrolls. From the first scroll, they read "V'zot HaBerachah" until the end of the Torah. From the second scroll, they read from "Bereshit" until "asher bara Elokim la'asot," as explained in the previous section. From the third scroll, the Maftir reads as on the previous day. The Haftarah is "Vayehi Acharei Mot Moshe." 

In places where they have only two Torah scrolls, they read "V'zot HaBerachah" from the first scroll, and "Bereshit" from the second scroll, and then they return to the first scroll for the Maftir. However, they should not read two portions consecutively from the same Torah scroll. This applies in all cases where three Torah scrolls are needed, but only two are available.

And they call this day "Simchat Torah" because they rejoice and make a feast for the completion of the Torah. In Ashkenaz, it is customary that the one who completes [the reading] and the one who begins [the new cycle] make donations, and they invite others to a feast. It is customary to increase the number of people called up to the Torah, and they read the same portion multiple times. There is no concern about this on this day since it is the custom for everyone to be called up to the Torah on this day. Even children are called up to the Torah, and with them they read "The angel who redeems me." And our teacher, the Rema, wrote that it is customary to conclude even with a minor who is called up, even though some say that only a Torah scholar should conclude. Nowadays, since the chazzan reads, there is no concern. This is his language. Nowadays, they do not allow a minor to conclude, and they sell this [honor] for money to the highest bidder. It is also customary for two people to be called up together and to recite the blessings, and although this is not proper, nevertheless, because of the joy of the conclusion they do so. And it is also customary to read at night due to vows and donations, but there is no basis for this. Therefore, in many places, it is customary only to call up three people, and this is our practice.

Additionally, it is customary to recite verses during the evening and morning prayers: "You have been shown" etc. All the Torah scrolls in the ark are taken out, and they circle the bimah seven times, reciting hymns, songs, and praises, and they dance in honor of the Torah. And although dancing is not permitted on Yom Tov, as I wrote in Siman 341, it is allowed in honor of the Torah. The priests do not ascend to the platform to bless the people because they are accustomed to drink wine or strong wine after the Torah reading. They should be careful not to burn incense or make noise to express joy. Some do not fall on their faces (in supplication) until after Rosh Chodesh Mar-Cheshvan. With Heaven's help, the laws of lulav have concluded.

In the Second Temple period, when the wicked Antiochians ruled, they decreed harsh decrees upon Israel and nullified their holy religion. They did not allow them to engage in Torah study and mitzvot, and they seized their wealth and their daughters. They entered the Temple, breached its walls, and defiled the pure items, causing great distress to Israel and oppressing them greatly. Until the God of their ancestors had mercy on them and delivered them from their hands, saving them through the holy and pure Hasmonean priests, Mattathias and his sons, who fought against Antiochus and vanquished him. The victory was not by natural means, as the Hasmoneans and their group of pious men were very few, while Antiochus came against them with a large army, many elephants, chariots, and horsemen. But God, who desires His people Israel, delivered the mighty into the hands of the weak, the many into the hands of the few, the impure into the hands of the pure, and the wicked into the hands of the righteous. The traitors from Israel who had joined Antiochus were also killed and delivered into the hands of the Torah scholars. Then the name of Heaven was magnified and sanctified in the world, the light of the Torah shone in its purest form, and the name of Israel was exalted among the nations.

The final miracle occurred on the twenty-fifth of Kislev. Another miracle was shown to them from the heavens through "a mitzvah candle and the light of Torah." As we learn in the Talmud, Tractate Shabbat (21b): What is Chanukah? The Rabbis taught: On the twenty-fifth of Kislev, the days of Chanukah are eight, during which eulogies and fasting are not permitted. When the Greeks entered the Temple, they defiled all the oils in the Temple, and when the Hasmonean dynasty overcame them and emerged victorious, they searched and found only one flask of oil with the seal of the High Priest, and it contained enough oil to burn for only one day. A miracle occurred, and they lit from it for eight days. The following year, they established and made these days as a holiday with Hallel (praise) and thanksgiving.

Explanation of the matter: When they purified the Temple, all of them were ritually impure from contact with the dead due to the war, and someone impure from contact with the dead can only be purified after seven days with the sprinkling on the third and seventh days, and one day is required for preparing pure oil (Beit Yosef). Additionally, there was pure oil at a distance of four days' journey, and by the time they would go and return, eight days would have passed (Ran there). They had nothing to light the Menorah with. All the sacrifices for the daily offerings were brought, as a communal sacrifice overrides impurity. Therefore, they could also light the Menorah candles for this reason, as the lighting of the Menorah also overrides impurity, as it is taught in the Torat Kohanim, Parashat Emor (end of chapter 13): "He shall arrange the lamps before the Lord continually"—"continually" even on Shabbat, "continually" even in a state of impurity. However, the oil had to be pure, as only impurity due to contact with the dead is permitted for the community, not other types of impurities, as explained in Pesachim (67a). The oils had been defiled by other impurities, through contact and carrying. All the olives were impure until they could obtain olives connected to the ground, which do not contract impurity, and eight days would pass. Therefore, when they found this flask sealed with the seal of the High Priest, and it was placed in such a way that it had not been moved, for otherwise, it would have become impure through movement (Tosafot Shabbat there). Additionally, if they had seen it, they would certainly have taken it, thinking there were precious stones inside (Ran there). The Holy One, Blessed Be He, performed a miracle for them, for even though there was only enough oil for one day, they lit from it for eight days until they could make pure oil. Therefore, they established eight days for praise and thanksgiving. (See Bach, and according to what I have written, it is easily understood straightforwardly.)

And even though the miracle was only for seven days, since there was enough oil for one day, however, since only an eighth part was lit each day—it turns out that the miracle was also on the first day (Beit Yosef). And some wrote: because they were prevented from performing the mitzvah of circumcision, which is on the eighth day (Shiltei Giborim on the Hagahot Maimoniot there). And some wrote: because at that time they rededicated the Temple from the defilement that Antiochus the wicked had caused (there).

The truth is thus: In the Midrash it is stated that the construction of the Mishkan (Tabernacle) was completed on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, but it was not dedicated until the first of Nissan, the month in which the Patriarchs were born. And the Holy One, blessed be He, compensated for this in the days of Mattathias (this Midrash is cited in the Maharsha there). Therefore, they made it like the dedication of the Mishkan, which had seven days of inauguration, and on the eighth day, the beginning of the service in the Mishkan was completed by Aaron and his sons, as explained in the Torah. Similarly, King Solomon, when he dedicated the Temple, it is written in Chronicles (II 7): "And Solomon observed the festival for seven days, and on the eighth day, they held a solemn assembly," see there. Therefore, in commemoration, they also called this festival "Chanukah," from the term "dedication of the altar" and "dedication of the house." And there is also a hint to the twenty-fifth day: Chanu-Kaf-Hey (rested on the twenty-fifth). Additionally, another reason is explained in the Book of Maccabees: because due to the decrees, they were prevented from offering sacrifices during the past Sukkot and Shemini Atzeret. Therefore, in memory of this, they made Chanukah eight days. Consequently, when Heaven showed them the miracle of the oil, they demonstrated their agreement to make it eight days. (And this is what they said in Shabbat there: the following year, they established it, etc., meaning: after they saw that Heaven agreed with them to make it eight days, through the oil that burned for eight days. And in commemoration of this miracle, they established the lighting of candles on Chanukah, as written by the Tur.)

And on Chanukah, it is forbidden to fast, except for a fast due to a dream, which one may fast even on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And one must make up the fast for the fast due to a dream, just as on Shabbat and Yom Tov. And know that there are those who prohibit fasting even on the eve of Chanukah (Bach in Siman 682) on the basis of what is explained in Siman 573: that even though the Megillat Taanit was nullified, nevertheless, for Chanukah and Purim, it was not nullified, see there. And in Megillat Taanit, it is also forbidden to fast before or after these days, but for after, there are those who say in the Gemara that it is permitted, and therefore, one should not be stringent. However, for before, it is forbidden. And there are those who prohibit even after (Shach). But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch ruled earlier in Siman 573 and later in Siman 682 that it is permitted to fast both before and after. The matter that the Megillat Taanit was not nullified regarding Chanukah and Purim pertains to the days themselves, but not to before or after, for regarding this, even for Chanukah and Purim, it was nullified. And some fast on the eve of Chanukah instead of the eve of Rosh Chodesh Tevet that falls on Chanukah (Magen Avraham there). And one who has this custom should not change it, but ideally, one should not do so. All the more so, one should not decree a public fast, neither before nor after (there). Nevertheless, one who wishes to rely on the Tur and Shulchan Aruch and fast—who can protest against him? All hearts seek the Lord, provided his intention is for the sake of Heaven.

Eulogizing is also forbidden on Chanukah, except for a sage in his presence, for even on a festival we eulogize him, and certainly on Chanukah. Some say that for a sage in his presence, we also recite the "Tziduk HaDin" (justification of the divine decree), although others disagree with this, and it is only permitted to deliver a discourse about him (Levush). One does not fast on a yahrzeit (anniversary of death), nor on the day of a wedding, except for a fast of a dream, as I have written.

Chanukah permits the performance of labor. The Gemara there states "and they made them holidays with praise and thanksgiving" – it does not mean actual holidays, but rather days of joy. Even Purim was not accepted as a full holiday, as it is stated in Megillah, and certainly Chanukah is not. However, women customarily do not perform labor while the candles are burning, and one should not be lenient with them (Tur). Some of the Chanukah miracle was performed through a woman, when it was decreed that every married woman be first taken by the commander, as Rashi explains in Shabbat (23a). Additionally, another miracle occurred later through Judith, who fed the enemy milk. Because of this, some are meticulous to eat cheese on Chanukah, even though this did not happen during the time of the Chanukah miracle. However, if they have the custom not to perform labor all day – some say to abolish their custom, some say not to abolish it, and some say not to abolish it on the first and last days (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). We have not heard of these customs, and our women only refrain from labor during the lighting.

The increase in meals that we have – these are optional meals. They were not established as feasts and celebrations like Purim because Haman's decree was against our bodies: "to destroy, kill, and annihilate" – therefore we need to bring joy to the body. However, the decrees of Antiochus were to abolish the Torah and commandments. And even though this is worse than bodily decrees, at the end of the day, they are decrees against the soul. Therefore, we need to bring joy to the soul with Hallel, thanks, hymns, songs, and praises, and the body has no part in this (and this resolves the question of the Taz in subsection 3). Nevertheless, some say there is a small mitzvah to increase in meals. Firstly: the joy of the soul is somewhat dependent on the joy of the body, as is perceptible. Additionally: to commemorate the dedication of the Tabernacle, which was established with feasting and joy. And also, one can sing hymns and praises during the meals, and then it certainly becomes a mitzvah meal. But those who play cards – their punishment is great, and unfortunately, this plague has spread within the house of Israel. Woe to us that this has happened in our times, and there are many types of sins associated with this! May He, the Merciful One, forgive sin. And whoever can abolish it – his reward is very great.

And since the miracle happened with candles, they established to light candles every night to commemorate the miracle (Tur). And every person needs to be very meticulous with them. Even a poor person who is supported by charity should ask or sell his garment and buy oil to light. For anything that is publicizing the miracle, the obligation is even upon the poor, just like the four cups (Magid Mishneh and Beit Yosef). And one who is careful with this will have children who are Torah scholars (Gemara there 23b), as it is written: "For a commandment is a candle, and the Torah is light." Meaning: by the merit of the mitzvah candle of Shabbat and Chanukah, one will merit the light of Torah.

It appears that for the Hanukkah candle and the four cups (of wine) – there is no limit to their expenditure. For although in all other commandments there is a limit up to a third (of one's resources) for a commandment, as I wrote in Siman 656 regarding the etrog, or a fifth as I wrote there, nevertheless, for these mitzvot which are publicizing the miracle, and it was required for a poor person to sell his clothing – there is no limit to the matter. And there is one who says that even here one should not spend more than a fifth (Pri Megadim). But this does not seem correct (and so wrote the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger). However, in truth, this is not common, and the expenditure in this case is small. But according to the law, it appears as I have written.

How many candles should be lit? Thus we learned in Shabbat (21b): The mitzvah of Chanukah is one candle per household. Those who are meticulous (mehadrin) light one candle for each member of the household. The most meticulous of the meticulous (mehadrin min hamehadrin), on the first day, light one candle, and from then on, add one more each day. Our Rabbis, the Tosafists, explained that the most meticulous of the meticulous do not follow the practice of the meticulous in lighting one candle for each person. For if they did, since their reasoning is that the onlooker should be able to tell how many days of Chanukah there are by the number of candles, lighting according to the number of people in the house would not make it clear how many days it is. For example, if one sees four candles, it could be that there is one person and it is the fourth day of Chanukah, or there are two people and it is the second day, or four people and it is the first day. Therefore, they would only light one candle for the entire household, two on the second night, and so on.

But the Rambam, of blessed memory, at the beginning of the fourth chapter wrote: How many candles...? Each and every house lights one candle... and those who are meticulous light candles according to the number of people in the house... and those who are even more meticulous... light one candle for each person on the first night, and add one more candle each subsequent night... How so? If there were ten people in the household, they light ten candles on the first night, and twenty candles on the second night... And the simple custom in all our cities in Spain is that all the people in the household light one candle on the first night, and add one more candle each night, until on the eighth night they light eight candles, whether there are many people in the household or just one person. Until here is his language. And the custom of the people of Spain is like the Tosafot.

In the Gemara, two reasons are given for this. The first: corresponding to the days that have passed. That is, so that people will know how many days have passed since Hanukkah began, and the day on which one lights is also counted among the days that have passed. According to this reason, it certainly seems that the words of Tosafot are more appropriate, because if we light according to the number of people in the house, we still would not know [how many days have passed], as I have written. But there is another reason: because we ascend in holiness. And it appears that this reason is according to the conclusion (from the elders who are alongside, see there). According to this reason, we do not worry about knowing the days, and according to this, it is clear that the words of Rambam seem more appropriate, that we can fulfill the mitzvah even as those who are meticulous (Gra). According to this, the primary ruling is according to Rambam. It is perplexing that when Rambam brought the custom of Spain, he did so in the opposite manner: why did he not write that it is not according to the law, and why did he not protest against them, since it is not according to the sugya of the Talmud? (See Lechem Mishneh, who also raised a similar question.)

It seems more likely that the reasons given in the Gemara do not contradict each other, and multiple reasons can exist for one mitzvah. In the Gemara, it does not say they argue about the reason for the matter, but rather about the matter of the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. Beit Shammai holds: on the first day, eight [lights], on the second day, seven, decreasing each day. And Beit Hillel holds: on the first day, one [light], on the second day, two, increasing each day. And in this, it says there that they argue about what Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree on. One says that Beit Shammai holds that the recognition should be for the incoming days, and Beit Hillel for the outgoing days. And another says that Beit Shammai holds like the bulls of the festival that decrease, and Beit Hillel holds: we ascend in holiness and do not descend. But Beit Hillel themselves can hold both reasons together. (And so it is in Massechet Sofrim, Chapter 1, Halacha 5, see there.)

However, even without this, the words of the Tosafot are not understood regarding what they said, that if we light according to the number of people in the household, there will be no distinction. For we can light according to the number of people in the household and there will be a distinction, meaning: each person in the household lights in a separate place, as we do. And then the observer will have a distinction of how many days have passed in Hanukkah. However, this is also appropriate, for according to the strict law, we light at the entrance adjacent to the public domain, on the left side, and within the handbreadth adjacent to the entrance, as will be explained. And if so, necessarily all would be in one place, and there would be no distinction. Now, not in all places do they light at the entrance adjacent to the public domain, as will be explained. And as with us, who do not know of this and light inside the house. And in such a case, even the Tosafot agree to follow the Rambam, and each one lights in a separate place, and there will also be a distinction. And see in section 15.

And according to this, everything aligns well. For the Tosafot wrote this according to the Talmudic law, where they would light at the entrance to the public domain, and thus the Sephardim would do. And the Rambam: either he refers to lighting in one's home, or even according to Talmudic law, one can choose as they desire since each has its advantages and disadvantages. Therefore, the Rambam did not rebuke the Sephardim. Behold, our teacher the Beit Yosef in section 2 ruled like the Tosafot, that this is the custom of the Sephardim, and the Maggid Mishneh also wrote that this was their custom. And our teacher the Rema wrote like the Rambam, and this is his wording: "And some say that each member of the household should light, and this is the prevalent custom. And they should be careful to place their candles each in a distinct location, so that it is recognizable how many candles are being lit." This is his wording, and it is like the Rambam. And he made it clear that each one should place in a distinct location, as we light in the house, and in such a manner, even the Tosafot agree. Thus, it turns out that they do not fundamentally disagree, but it varies according to the situation of the place of lighting. (And with this, the wonderment of the Taz in subsection 1 is resolved, that we do not find that the Ashkenazim follow the Rambam and the Sephardim like the Tosafot. All of this is explained in Knesset Yechezkel, section 17. And also the Gra in subsection 5 hints to this, and this is the main point. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And behold, nowadays our custom has reverted to the opinion of the Tosafot. For Rambam wrote to light according to the custom of the household, whether men or women, etc. Thus are his words. And certainly, it is so, for women are obligated in the Chanukah candle just like men. And we have never heard otherwise, and even when there are several grown sons, they fulfill their obligation with their father's lighting, even if there are other people. Occasionally, someone might bless and light by themselves. It seems to me that there is also a reason for this, as we are accustomed to light at the entrance of the large room, where most people come and go. Therefore, it is like the times of the Talmud, where everyone needed to be in one place, and there was no distinction. However, it seems more likely that since they fulfill the obligation regardless, they are not concerned about this, and can do as they wish. It is sufficient for us to be among those who beautify the mitzvah, even if we are not among the most scrupulous – nevertheless, we have fulfilled the mitzvah (so it seems in my humble opinion).

And one who does not have much oil, such that he cannot provide each candle with the required amount—he should give a lot to one candle, so that it will have the required amount generously, and with the remaining oil, he should provide a little to each of the others. For if he distributes it equally among all, none will have the required amount, and his blessing will be in vain, and he will not fulfill the mitzvah. And if he has enough for the required amount for all the candles, but his neighbor has none at all—it is better that he gives a little to his neighbor, and he only lights one candle (Magen Avraham, subsection 1). For it is better that he is not meticulous and his neighbor also fulfills the mitzvah, than for him to be meticulous and his neighbor does not fulfill the mitzvah at all. And in this case, it does not apply to the principle of "sinning so that your neighbor may merit," for he too fulfills the mitzvah. However, one must be careful in this matter: for example, if today is the fourth day, and he is compelled to give to his neighbor as I have described, and he only has enough for four candles. When he gives one candle’s worth to his neighbor, he should not light three himself, but only one, for three on the fourth day has no relevance at all. Similarly, in such a situation, one who does not have enough oil for all the candles of the day—should only light one, and it should be according to the basic law.

A candle that has two wicks counts for two people, for those who make a candle for each one. But for those who add an additional candle every night, two people should not light one candle, because then it will not be recognizable how many candles are being lit today (see there, subsection 2). However, when the candle is large and has many wicks, and one lights at one end and the other at the other end, in such a way that there is a significant separation between them, it is recognizable that they belong to two people, and they can light in this manner (it seems to me).

If one fills a bowl with oil and surrounds it with wicks, if he places a cover over it such that the flame diminishes and the distinction between each wick is noticeable, then each wick counts as a separate candle. But if he does not cover it and the flames intermingle, it is considered a bonfire, and it does not even count as one candle. Even if he does cover it, it must be done before lighting. If he lights it first and then covers it, it is of no benefit since the initial lighting was invalid, and the critical moment is at the time of lighting (Be'er Heitev, subsection 5, in the name of Rabbi Eliezer HaLevi). Therefore, one should be careful to place the candles in a row and not in a circle, as that would resemble a bonfire. Additionally, they should be placed evenly, not with one protruding and one recessed, so that it is clear that each one is a distinct entity.

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 4: "It is permissible to light in candelabras called 'lampas,' since each candle is very much separated from its neighbor." Until here are his words, meaning: Even though we have said that one should not light in a circle, as I have written, nevertheless, in a circular 'lampas' it is permitted, because they are far from each other and are well distinguished. Nevertheless, it is written that those who are meticulous do not light in round candelabras, as this is not considered an enhancement for the Chanukah candle (Taz and Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 4 in the name of the Rashal). Meaning: the Chanukah candles are not considered enhanced when in a circle. However, our candelabras, which are linear, are indeed considered enhanced. And so is our custom, only that each candle should be a finger-width apart from its neighbor (Eliyahu Rabbah). And some require two finger-widths (Pri Megadim). There is no fixed rule for this, as it depends on how they are made. The main thing is that each candle should be recognizable on its own (see Tur).

When making candles from wax, one should not attach two candles together, and certainly not more. This is akin to a torch, which is a mitzvah only for Havdalah, but not for Chanukah candles, nor for Shabbat and Yom Tov candles, as it does not appear as candles but rather as a bonfire. Likewise, one should take care to keep a distance of at least a finger's width between each candle, because otherwise the flames may merge, appearing like a bonfire. This applies in all matters, as it is essential that each candle appears separate from the other. (The Maharshal wrote that when lighting in round candlesticks, one should hang them a handbreadth near the entrance, starting with the middle candle closest to the entrance, and then proceed clockwise. However, it has already been clarified that this is not considered an enhancement, and one should light them evenly.)

And know that I saw one of the great ones who thundered against our master, the Rama, and against the custom, and wrote that it constitutes blessings in vain. This is regarding what our master, the Rama, wrote: "And there are those who say that each member of the household lights, and this is the custom." Until here is his language, and this is according to the Rambam's system, as I have written. And it is an error, for the Rambam did not say that each member of the household lights, but rather the head of the household lights according to the number of people in his house. And even the Gemara that said: "And the scrupulous [light] a candle for each and every one" did not say "a candle each and every one," but "a candle for each and every one." Meaning, that the head of the household lights a candle for each member of his household. And this is what the Rambam explained: that if he has ten people, he lights ten candles on the first night, and on the second – twenty, and so forth until the end. And this is all on the head of the household. But for two people to light in one house – this constitutes a blessing in vain, and it is forbidden to do so (Galia Massekta, Siman 6). And according to this, it makes sense what we struggled with in paragraph 7 in the words of the Tosafot, who wrote that if we light according to the number of household members – there would be no recognition. And after all, each one can light in a separate place? But if we say that the obligation is only on the head of the household – it makes sense, for he lights in one place.

In truth, the words of our teacher, the Rema, are correct. The inference from the phrase "a candle for each one" referring to the head of the household is indeed accurate. However, does this mean that if each person lights a candle for themselves, it is worse? There is proof for this from the end of the seventh chapter of Eruvin (82b) concerning the merging of courtyards and alleyways, where it is taught: What is the measure? ... A fig's worth for each and every one. This means that one person can acquire for everyone a fig's worth for each individual. Now, if each person contributes a fig's worth, is it not effective? Indeed, the main form of merging is that each person gives their portion. Similarly, at the beginning of the eighth chapter of Eruvin concerning the merging of domains, it is taught: What is the measure? Two meals for each and every one. Shall we then say that if each person gives, it is not effective? On the contrary, this is the main form of merging, and the Rabbis leniently allowed one person to give on behalf of everyone. Here too, with the Chanukah candle, the main principle is that each person should light a candle for themselves, and the Rabbis leniently allowed the head of the household to light on behalf of everyone. You must necessarily say so, as will be explained with Heaven's help. (It seems to me that this is the intention of Rashi in 41b in the explanation beginning with "and those who are meticulous," see there. Otherwise, what did he add to the language of the Talmud? See there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

For one of the great authorities has already asked: What distinguishes the commandment of the Chanukah lights from all other commandments? For all other commandments, every individual Israelite is required to perform the commandment, but for the Chanukah lights, it is only the head of the household who is obligated (Pnei Yehoshua there, and it remains unresolved). However, in truth, it is well explained. For we find that with the etrog (citron), each individual is required to take the four species in hand, and with the shofar (ram's horn), one person blows, and everyone else listens. This is because with the etrog, the commandment is the taking, and with the shofar, the commandment is the hearing. However, it is impossible to hear without blowing, and therefore, one person blows and everyone hears. Similarly, with the reading of the megillah (scroll of Esther), one reads and everyone listens. And here, regarding Chanukah, the commandment is the seeing: to see the candles when they are lit, and this is the publicizing of the miracle. Therefore, a blessing was instituted for the one who sees, as it is stated in the Gemara there. However, it is impossible to see without lighting, and therefore, it was instituted that the head of the household lights, and all the members of the household see. Nevertheless, it is not entirely similar to the shofar and megillah. For with the shofar, the commandment is only the hearing, as we bless "to hear the sound of the shofar." And with the megillah, the listener is considered as if they have recited it themselves. But with the Chanukah lights, the essence of the commandment is the lighting, as we bless "to light the Chanukah lights." However, seeing is also a commandment, and therefore, one who sees blesses "Who performed miracles," as I wrote in Siman 676.

Therefore, our sages of blessed memory did not impose an obligation on each individual to light [the Chanukah candles], since there is also a mitzvah in the mere sight [of the candles]. And this is what they said: "The mitzvah of Chanukah is a candle for each person and their household." That is to say, the head of the household lights the candles, and the members of the household fulfill the mitzvah by seeing them. Those who are meticulous in the performance of mitzvot [mehadrin] ensure that each individual also has a part in the lighting, by having a candle for each person. Meaning, if it is possible for each person to light their own candle, similar to other mitzvot where each person performs the mitzvah in its entirety - it is obvious that there is nothing greater than this. However, even if the head of the household lights a candle on behalf of each member of the household, they all have a part in the lighting, and this too is considered mehadrin. It is only in the case of the most meticulous [mehadrin min hamehadrin], who also make a distinction for the days, because each day was a miracle in itself - the oil lasting for all the days - that our sages disagree whether this nullifies the mehadrin. This is the opinion of Tosafot. Or, that even in this, the ordinance of the mehadrin is fulfilled, according to the Rambam. And the words of our Rabbi, the Rema, are firm and established, and Moses is the truth and his Torah is the truth.

And since the primary purpose of the mitzvah is to publicize the miracle, therefore our Sages of blessed memory decreed that one should not light them inside his house. Thus, the Sages said: The Chanukah lamp - it is a mitzvah to place it at the entrance of his house on the outside. If he lived in an upper story, he should place it in the window that is adjacent to the public domain. And during a time of danger, he places it on his table, and that suffices. Rashi explained: "At the entrance of his house on the outside" - because of publicizing the miracle, and not in the public domain but rather in his courtyard, as their houses opened into the courtyard. Thus far his words. Meaning: if you thought it was in the public domain, it would have said: "at the entrance of his courtyard on the outside." And because it says: "at the entrance of his house on the outside," and the house opens into the courtyard, one understands that it is referring to the courtyard. And Tosafot questioned this from what it says later: a courtyard that has two entrances requires two lamps. But the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol and the Hagahot Maimoniot (Fourth Chapter, letter 30) have already written in the name of the Ri: that it is not specifically referring to the courtyard, as we do not find that we need lamps in the courtyard, but rather in the house that is in the courtyard. Thus far their words. And it is also explained from the words of the Rambam there, who wrote: "at the entrance of his house on the outside, within the handbreadth adjacent to the entrance, on the left of the one entering the house." Thus far his words. (And what Tosafot questioned in the beginning "mitzvah," from what they said about a lamp that has two mouths being sufficient for two people - it implies for two houses. And if it were at the entrance of the courtyard - it would be for this one on the right and for that one on the left. Thus far their words. And I wonder: do we not find it in two houses, one within the other, and they exit through one entrance to the courtyard? This requires further investigation.)

However, the Tosafot wrote: "At the entrance to his house from the outside" — and it refers to a case where there is no courtyard, but rather the house stands adjacent to the public domain. But if there is a courtyard in front of the house, it is a mitzvah to place it at the entrance of the courtyard, etc. Thus are their words. Similarly, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch, in section 5, wrote the following: "The Chanukah lamp — it is a mitzvah to place it at the entrance adjacent to the public domain from the outside. If the house opens to the public domain, place it at its entrance. And if there is a courtyard in front of the house, place it at the entrance of the courtyard. And if one lives in an upper story and does not have an entrance that opens to the public domain, place it in a window adjacent to the public domain. And in a time of danger, when it is not permitted to fulfill the mitzvah, place it on one's table, and that suffices." Thus are their words. And I am astonished: since Rashi, the Ran, the Rambam, the Ri, the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol (SeMaG), and the Hagahot Maimoniot — who are many — explained differently than the Tosafot, how is it that they did not bring their opinion at all? This requires investigation. (However, in Masechet Sofrim, chapter twenty, halacha five, it is written: "The Chanukah lamp — it is a mitzvah to place it at the entrance adjacent to the public domain." See there.)

It is established that it is forbidden to use the light of the Chanukah candles, as will be explained in Siman 673. Therefore, when one lights in their home on their table, they need another candle in order to use its light. We do not say: since one is compelled in any case to light on their table, they are thereby using its light against their will, for even if they light another candle, its light also aids in their use. Nevertheless, one is obligated to light another candle so that the usage is also from a non-holy candle, and also for recognition, so it will be known that it is forbidden to use its light. If there is a bonfire there, another candle is not necessary, as one can use the light of the bonfire. However, if the person is distinguished and it is not their custom to use a bonfire, they need to light another candle. From this derives the custom that the “shamash” (attendant candle) with which the Chanukah candles are lit should also be lit not far from the Chanukah candles, so that if one does use it, they use the light of the shamash and not the Chanukah candles.

It is a mitzvah to place the Chanukah menorah below ten handbreadths (tefachim) near the ground, as this makes it evident that it is for the mitzvah. A regular lamp used for mundane purposes is not placed so low (Rosh). Nevertheless, one should not place it less than three handbreadths from the ground, as in such a case it would not be evident that it is for the mitzvah at all. However, if it is placed above ten handbreadths, one has fulfilled the obligation, provided it is placed below twenty cubits (amot). If it is placed above twenty cubits, it is invalid, as above twenty cubits it is not within the field of vision. Even if it is later lowered, it remains invalid, as the lighting must occur in a valid location. One must extinguish it, place it below twenty cubits, and relight it. Some say that nowadays, when lighting indoors, it is valid even above twenty cubits, since the house has a roof and walls, making it visible even above twenty cubits, similar to a sukkah with walls reaching the s'chach (roofing). The Tur disagrees, stating that this applies only to a sukkah where the eye can see the entire roof. But here, with the candles placed below the ceiling, there is no difference. This seems to be the opinion of most poskim (halachic authorities), who do not differentiate in this matter. When lighting in a window, it seems there is no difference, and one can place it anywhere one wishes, whether below three handbreadths from the base of the window or above ten handbreadths, as in a window it is noticeable in any location (as implied in Magen Avraham, Section 6). When lighting at the entrance, if there is a threshold, it seems to me that we measure from the threshold, not from the ground. One should ideally place it within ten handbreadths from the threshold and above three handbreadths from the threshold. It is obvious that if the candelabrum is tall, we measure from the location of the candles, not from the top of the candelabrum. The Rambam does not mention the requirement of being within ten handbreadths at all, because there is a refutation of this in the Gemara. However, most poskim rule according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, as this refutation is not substantial, and the halacha is established as such. This is the primary ruling, and this is our practice.

It is a mitzvah to place the Chanukah candle within a handbreadth adjacent to the entrance. Otherwise, since it is lit outside, it will not be apparent that it is a Chanukah candle, as there is no indication at all that the homeowner placed it there (Rashi 22a, s.v. "mitzvah"). One should place it on the left side, so that it is surrounded by mitzvot: the mezuzah on the right and the Chanukah candle on the left. Therefore, if there is no doorway suitable for a mezuzah, it should be placed on the right, as in all cases the right side is preferable. If it is placed within the doorway, on the side post, and it is very wide, one should place it from the middle of the entrance towards the house on the left side, and not from the middle of the exit. (The Beit Yosef, the Bach, and the Taz in subsection 6 elaborated on this. But the simple explanation is as I have written. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Here is the translation of the given halachic passage from the Aruch Hashulchan:

Now, we do not light [the Chanukah candles] outside. And even though there is no danger among us, in any case, it is almost impossible because in all our countries, the days of Chanukah are stormy days, with rain, snow, and strong winds. And it is impossible to place them outside unless they are enclosed in glass. And the Rabbis did not trouble us so much. Moreover, by doing this, the mitzvah would not be so recognizable. And also, not in all places will they allow this. Therefore, we all light inside the house. And since the recognition is only for the members of the household, and there is no recognition for the public at all, it is not so critical if we do not light in the handbreadth next to the entrance. Nevertheless, the custom is to light in the handbreadth next to the entrance, as in their days, and this should not be changed. Or they light inside the entrance on the left doorpost. However, if there are many members of the household, and each one wants to fulfill the mitzvah individually, it is impossible to light in the handbreadth next to the entrance, as the candles will mix, and it will not be recognizable at all how many days of Chanukah it is. Therefore, it is better for each person to bless in a designated place, such as by the windows, and the like. However, they should not light in a place where candles are lit all year round, like on the table and the like, because then it will not be recognizable at all. And even though the recognition is only for the members of the household, there still needs to be some recognition. And so, the custom is to light the Chanukah candle not in a place where candles are placed all year round. And it is better than everything if he has a window that opens to the public domain, to place them by the window so that the public can also see through the window, and there will be publicizing of the miracle (Magen Avraham, Small Section 8). And this is my practice.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that in the synagogue, the menorah is placed on the southern side, in memory of the menorah that was in the south. However, the arrangement depends on a dispute in Menachot (98b) whether the menorah was placed east-west or north-south. Seemingly, since Rabbi holds there that it was placed east-west, the law follows Rabbi when he is in disagreement with another. However, the Rambam and Sefer Mitzvot Gadol wrote in the laws of the Temple that it was placed north-south. Nevertheless, our custom is to arrange it east-west, as Rabbi Rema wrote. In any case, those who arrange it north-south should retain their custom (Magen Avraham, subsection 9), as they can rely on the opinions of the Rambam and the Sefer Mitzvot Gadol.

It is obvious that one does not fulfill their obligation with the candles lit in the synagogue, and each person must go back and light at home, even if they have recited the blessing in the synagogue. This is because the obligation is upon each household, and the lighting in the synagogue is solely for the sake of publicizing the miracle. And if you ask: How can one recite a blessing over the synagogue candles? The answer is that it is due to publicizing the miracle, similar to the blessing recited over the Hallel on Rosh Chodesh. Nevertheless, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote in section 7 that one recites a blessing over the synagogue candles, even though he holds that one does not recite a blessing over the Hallel on Rosh Chodesh (see Shaarei Teshuva, section 10, where the Chacham Tzvi raises this question). However, this is also acceptable. Firstly, because usually there are guests or single people who do not have a home and fulfill their obligation with the synagogue lighting. And even if this is not the case, since the primary purpose of the lighting is to publicize the miracle, and at home, we cannot achieve the same level of publicizing the miracle as in the times of the Talmud when they would light outside, therefore, the synagogue serves as the main place for publicizing the miracle, and it is appropriate to recite the blessing there. Nevertheless, one does not fulfill their obligation with this, as I have written. In the synagogue, it is customary to light between Mincha and Maariv, as there is more publicity at that time. On the eve of Shabbat, some have the custom to light before Mincha in the synagogue. This is also our custom, for even the Shabbat candles are lit before Mincha. If the one lighting is the prayer leader and he hastens to pray, he can recite the blessing and light one candle, and the rest can be lit by the sexton or another person. Also, in his own home, there is no prohibition if the head of the household begins the lighting and another person completes it. Nevertheless, it is preferable that the head of the household completes the lighting himself and lights all the candles personally.

It is stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 23a): A courtyard that has two entrances from two different sides requires two candles. And Rashi explained: that the house has two entrances, see there. And he follows his opinion, that the lighting is at the entrance of the house near the courtyard. But according to Tosafot, it is as it sounds, and the reason is: because of suspicion, that perhaps the townspeople who will walk on this side and not see candles will say: just as he did not light on this side, he also did not light on the other side. But when they are on the same side, they will see that there are candles at the other entrance. And it is obvious that when lighting in two places, one should only recite one blessing at the first lighting, and not bless at the second lighting since it is only because of suspicion. And this was all in their time, when they would bless and light at the entrance of the courtyard or the entrance of the house. But nowadays, when everyone lights inside the house, and the recognition is only for the household members and not for the public, even if a courtyard or house has many entrances on many sides, one lights only in one place. For the household members know that it all belongs to one homeowner. And this is the simple custom.

And know: Our teacher, the Rema, in Section 8, regarding the law that when there are two doorways on one side, one does not need to light in both doorways, wrote: This is when they are in one house. Thus are his words. This implies that if they are in two houses, one must light in both, even if they are on one side. And so he explicitly wrote in his book Darkei Moshe at the end of this section in the name of the Kol Bo, see there. This is not understood at all, for in the Gemara there it is explicitly explained that the suspicion is due to the townspeople, who know that they belong to one person. Rather, if they are on two sides, they will say that he also did not light on the other side, as I wrote, and not on one side. If so, what difference does it make whether it is one house or two houses, since they know that they belong to one person? And if we say that in two houses they would not know that they belong to one person, how do we know to say this? This requires study. (It is possible to say, if we are particular about the suspicion, that they will say since he did not light at this entrance, etc., why would they suspect him of this? It is not similar to Pe'ah, where the custom is to leave it only at the end of the harvest, see there. But certainly, even the townspeople are not so knowledgeable that there is only one homeowner here, but they will more likely assume that there is only one homeowner when they are on one side and in one house, and in one of the houses it was lit. But if one of these is missing, they will think that there are two homeowners. Examine and you will find it clear.)

It is taught (Shabbat 21b): Its mitzvah is from the time the sun sets until people cease [to pass by] in the marketplace. And this is half an hour after sunset (Rif and Rosh). And Maimonides wrote in the fourth chapter, law 5: One does not light the Chanukah candles before the sun sets but at its setting, neither delaying nor advancing. If one forgot or intentionally did not light at sunset, one may still light until people cease [to pass by] in the marketplace. And how long is this time? About half an hour or more. If this time has passed, one does not light. And one must put enough oil in the lamp so that it burns until people cease [to pass by] in the marketplace. Thus far are his words.

And it is explained from his words that if one lights after sunset, he does not need to put enough oil for half an hour, but only until the point when people are no longer in the marketplace. And it is similarly explained from the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef in section 2, who wrote: If one forgot or intentionally did not light at sunset, he should keep lighting until people are no longer in the marketplace, which is about half an hour, as that is when people are still passing by, and there is publicizing of the miracle. Therefore, one needs to put in enough oil for that amount of time. This is the end of his words, and this is in accordance with the words of the Rambam (and so also wrote the Magen Avraham in subsection 2).

And this is all according to the Rambam, that after the time when people have ceased to walk in the marketplace, one does not light. But the Tur ruled that if one did not light, the time extends the whole night, contrary to the Rambam, etc., until here is his language. And if so, one must always provide this measure. Therefore, the Tur wrote the measure at the beginning of this section, see there, to indicate that this measure always applies. According to this, even nowadays when we light in the house, this measure is also required. And it is possible that in this the Rambam also agrees, that specifically in their time, when the recognition was for those in the public domain, after the time when people have ceased to walk in the marketplace, there is no longer any recognition for them. If so, why should one put oil for thereafter? But nowadays, when the recognition is for the household members, it is indeed necessary to have recognition for half an hour. And this is the simple custom, and one should not change it. (And it requires investigation why this was not discussed in the Shulchan Aruch, and perhaps because it was obvious to them.)

And know: That even regarding the primary time, there is a dispute between the Rambam and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch. For the Rambam wrote: "with its setting," which means: at the beginning of the setting. But the Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: "at the end of the setting," which means: at the emergence of the stars, as I wrote in Siman 692. And this matter depends on the dispute regarding the primary time of the setting of the sun: whether it is the beginning of the setting or the end of the setting. As explained earlier in Siman 261, the Rambam holds that it is the beginning of the setting, and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch follow the view of Rabbeinu Tam that it is the end of the setting, as I wrote there. And the world practices according to the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, and bless "Ner Chanukah" after the evening prayer. But there are those who follow the Rambam, and bless after the Mincha prayer at the beginning of twilight. And even though nowadays the lighting is done at home, nonetheless, whatever can be done according to the enactment of the Sages is done. And furthermore: even nowadays, when lighting by the window, there is recognition by the public domain. And in Masechet Sofrim Chapter 20, it implies like the Rambam, who says the mitzvah of lighting is from the setting of the sun. And if they lit during the day – one does not benefit from it, and does not bless over it, for they said: one does not bless over the candle until benefiting from its light. Thus far his words. And after the beginning of the setting – indeed, one benefits from the candle, but this is not a conclusive proof, obviously.

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in Section 1 that there is an opinion which says that if one is occupied, he may light [the Chanukah candles] from "Plag HaMincha" and onwards, provided he puts enough oil so that it will burn until people have finished leaving the marketplace. This is his language. And the proof for this is: for on the eve of Shabbat, we light the Chanukah candle before sunset.
