And indeed, one must be careful on the eve of Shabbat to place a lot of oil, more than the usual amount every day, at least in one candle, so that it will burn until people have finished leaving the marketplace. However, in truth, Shabbat is not a proof, because it is impossible otherwise. For according to the Rambam, after people have finished leaving the marketplace, one cannot light [the Chanukah candles], as I have written – one cannot light the Chanukah candle on Saturday night. But in a situation where it is not possible otherwise, it is different, and here too on the eve of Shabbat it is the same.

The Tur writes in the name of the Tosafot that for us, it is not necessary to be meticulous about the time set by our Sages, of blessed memory, as this was only for them who would light outside, and after the foot traffic ceases, there are no passersby. But for us, who light indoors, and the recognition is only for the household members, there is no need to be particular about the time, except to light while the household members are still awake and not asleep, because otherwise, there is no recognition for them either. The Tur wrote, and this is his wording: “It appears that even for us, it is necessary to be meticulous about the measure (time), because even though we light indoors, since we light at the entrance of the house and it is open, there is recognition for passersby.” End of his wording. This was in the time of the Tur, but now that we light entirely in the inner rooms, it is not necessary to be meticulous about the time, but only to light while the household members are awake (Beit Yosef). And this is what our Rabbi the Rema wrote: “Some say that nowadays, when we light indoors, it is not necessary to be careful to light before the foot traffic ceases in the marketplace. Nevertheless, it is good to be careful even nowadays.” End of his wording, in order to fulfill the ordinance of the Sages. And most Jews are still careful now to light at the time set by the Sages. And there are those who say that even to study is forbidden when the time arrives. And if one has not yet prayed Maariv, he should light first and then pray Maariv (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). This applies to those who always light after Maariv. But there are those who initially light before Maariv, after the beginning of sunset, according to the words of the Rambam that we have brought.

And it has already been explained that even during the time of the Gemara, according to the Tur, if one did not light at the proper time, one may light throughout the entire night. All the more so now, everyone agrees with this. There are those who wish to say that after midnight one should light without a blessing (there, subsection 6 in the name of the Rashal), but it does not seem correct to say this, for as long as the members of the household are awake, one should light with a blessing. However, when they are asleep, one should light without a blessing (there), for there is no recognition by any person. And we require that there be recognition by others, besides the one lighting. However, if there is even one person, or one woman, or a boy or girl with some understanding, one should recite the blessing, for there is recognition by them. And even if they have already lit by themselves, nonetheless, in the end, there is recognition by them. However, ideally, one should light at the beginning of the night, when the members of the household are gathered together, and before eating (there), for then the recognition is greater and there is publicizing of the miracle.

However, if the night has passed and he did not light [the Hanukkah candles] – the mitzvah is lost. And he should not light during the day, for "what benefit is a candle in daylight?" And even if he wants to light in a dark room – it does not help, because there is no lighting during the day, and this has no compensation. However, on the other nights – he lights as usual like other people, even though he missed one night. And not like the one who wants to say that he lost all the nights, and compares it to the counting [of the Omer] (see Beit Yosef), for this is not a valid comparison. For with the counting, the count is the main point, and since he missed the count – they are no longer "complete." But with the Hanukkah candle – one candle is sufficient according to the law, and the number does not prevent [the fulfillment of the mitzvah]. And how could he lose the other nights because of this?

If one put a lot of oil in the lamp, more than the required amount – he can extinguish it after it has burned for half an hour. And afterwards, it is also permissible to use its light, since it was set aside for the mitzvah only for the required period. There is an opinion that says it is permitted to extinguish it, but using its light is forbidden (Shulchan Aruch, small section 4 in the name of the Rema), because there is no distinction in use between before and after the required time. Some have written that the custom is also not to extinguish it (ibid. in the name of the Bach). Certainly, if that is the custom, one should not change it, but in our community, the custom is to extinguish it. One should make nice wicks, but not long ones. Wax candles should be made long, as it is an enhancement of the mitzvah. Also, the candle holder should be nice and adorned.

It is a preferred mitzvah to light Chanukah candles with olive oil, because it draws well into the wick, and its light is very clear (Shabbat 23a). Additionally, the miracle occurred with olive oil. If olive oil is not available, it is a mitzvah to use other oils whose light is clear and clean. In these countries, the custom is to light with wax candles, because their light is as clear as oil (Rema). Nowadays, there are candles made from hardened fat, called "stearin," whose light is even clearer than wax, and many people use these for lighting. Now, someone who is at home should certainly fulfill the mitzvah in the most beautiful way with olive oil. However, when traveling, and it is not possible to carry a candlestick and oil, one should light either with wax or with hardened fat.

It is stated in the Gemara (Shabbat 21b): Wicks and oils that the Sages said not to light with on Shabbat may be used for Chanukah. This means: on Shabbat, there are wicks that should not be lit because the flame flickers on them, and oils that do not draw well into the wick. However, for Chanukah, there is no concern with this. The reason for the prohibition on Shabbat is that since they do not burn well and it is difficult to use such a light, we are concerned that one might tilt the lamp to improve it so that it burns well. But for the Chanukah lamp, since it is forbidden to use its light, why would one tilt it? What difference does it make if it burns well or not? Even on Shabbat of Chanukah, it is permitted to light the Chanukah candles with these. Although on Shabbat there is another concern that since it does not burn well, it might go out and one might come to rekindle it, there is no concern with this either because we hold that if the Chanukah light goes out within its required time, one is not obligated to relight it. Therefore, even on Shabbat, there is no concern with this according to the law. However, on Shabbat, one must be careful not to put in more oil than the required amount. If one puts in more than the required amount, it is forbidden because after the required time, it is permitted to use its light. Then there is a concern that one might tilt it. It is also obvious that the "shamash" (the auxiliary candle used to light the Chanukah candles) that is placed near the Chanukah candles must not be made of those materials, because it is permissible to use its light, and we are concerned that one might tilt it. (This is the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 1. He is referring to Shabbat, but the language is somewhat unclear, see there.)

It seems to me that although the Gemara generally states that wicks and oils which may not be used for lighting on Shabbat may be used for lighting on Chanukah, this is not an absolute rule. For surely there are items that cannot be used for lighting on Shabbat and also cannot be used for lighting on Chanukah, even on weekdays. Specifically, one may not light on Shabbat with something that has a bad smell, as we are concerned that one might leave it and go out, as I wrote earlier in Siman 264. It is obvious that the same applies to Chanukah, for the main aspect of publicizing the miracle is the visibility of the candles. Additionally, there are items that we do not light with because their smell spreads, as we are concerned that one might benefit from them, as explained there. It is also obvious that this same concern applies to Chanukah candles, as it is forbidden to benefit from them. Even if we say that the concern of benefiting applies only on Shabbat, since it could lead to a capital offense, whereas on Chanukah it is merely a prohibition – nonetheless, on Shabbat it is certainly forbidden, and the Gemara states the rule applies both on weekdays and on Shabbat. Therefore, it is certain that this rule only applies to the main disqualifications of wicks and oils stated in the chapter "With What May One Light," due to the reason that the flame is not good. This is not the case with other concerns.

It further appears to me that it is permissible to light the Chanukah candle in a lantern, for it is still considered visible. As I wrote earlier in Siman 75, that if nakedness is behind a lantern, it is forbidden to recite the Shema opposite it, because of "and let not see in you any nakedness"—see there. Thus, it is clear that visibility through a lantern is considered visibility, and consequently, the same applies to the Chanukah candle.

To light the Hanukkah candle with items that are forbidden to derive benefit from, such as oil from orlah (fruits of the first three years) or butter that has been cooked with meat fat, and the like – is permitted. Since it is forbidden to use them and it is only for the mitzvah [commandment] – we hold that mitzvot were not given for enjoyment. And so ruled one of the great authorities (Be’er Heitev, subsection 1 in the name of Sha'arei Ephraim). However, there is someone who disagrees with this, arguing that since these items require burning or burial – they are considered as if their measure is pulverized. And the Hanukkah candle requires a measure (Sha’arei Teshuvah, subsection 1). But this is not so, for the Tosafot have already written in Eruvin (2b s.v. "aval") that the concept of pulverization only applies to something that needs to be in one solid mass. But something that is valid through joining together, like a side post – the concept of pulverization does not apply. And certainly with oil, where there is no joining of masses. I am astonished at the one who says otherwise.

It has already been explained that the primary mitzvah is with olive oil. Therefore, if someone comes home and does not find olive oil, and he takes wax candles for the Chanukah lights, attaches them to the wall, and begins to recite the blessing, and in the meantime, they bring him olive oil—even if he has only said "Blessed are You"—he should complete the blessing over the wax candles. He should not discard them to take the olive oil, because this would be a disgrace to the wax candles, as they too have been sanctified by the beginning of the blessing. Therefore, one should not shame them for the sake of enhancing the mitzvah. However, if before he began the blessing they brought him olive oil, he should set aside the wax candles and light with olive oil, for through preparation alone they have not been sanctified (as stated there in the name of the Chacham Tzvi). Some say that even if he attached them to the wall but did not begin the blessing, he should not set them aside for olive oil (as stated there in the name of the Shevut Yaakov), but this is not the primary view. And it is obvious that one should not light half with wax candles and half with olive oil on one night, as this appears like two separate things (as stated there). I have seen it written that a wax candle resembles a torch, and one does not recite the blessing over a Chanukah light (see Taz in the name of the Maharal of Prague). I do not know what kind of torch this refers to unless it is when two are intertwined together, as I have written in Siman 671.

It has already been explained that it is forbidden to use the light of the Chanukah candles, whether it is the main candle which is the primary obligation or the additional candles. The reason is due to the disrespect of the mitzvah, as it appears that it is not important when one uses its light. Therefore, even a minor use is forbidden. For example, to examine coins by its light or to count money in front of it is forbidden. Some say that only a use that needs to be done close to the candle, such as examining or counting money, is forbidden. But a minor use done from a distance is permitted (Beit Yosef, Darkei Moshe). However, some forbid even this, as it is still considered a disrespect of the mitzvah (Bach and Taz, subsection 3, and Magen Avraham in the name of Rashal). And the custom is to be stringent, and even to eat from a distance is forbidden. And even though one might benefit by sitting in one’s house from them, as there is light in the house and one will not stumble while walking, this is an incidental benefit and is indirect. This is not comparable to directly using their light for any kind of use. And when there is a "shamash" (an additional candle used to light the others) it is permitted, as will be explained.

Some say that it is permissible to use the light of Chanukah candles for a mitzvah-related purpose, such as studying by their light. Since the reason for the prohibition is due to disrespecting the mitzvah, this (i.e., studying) is not considered disrespect but rather an honor (Atur in the Tur). 

One should not ask: If so, why is it permitted to light with oils that do not burn well on Shabbat of Chanukah, due to the prohibition of using their light, as there is a concern that one might study and tilt the lamp? This is not a question, for in any case, it is forbidden to study by the light of a lamp alone; one must study with another person who will remind them (as I wrote in Siman 275). 

There is an opinion that permits only temporary use but does not allow regular studying (Taz, subsection 4). These matters are puzzling to one who examines the Tur (and the Taz's question there requires further investigation; examine it carefully and you will find it easy).

Nevertheless, some say that there is no difference between secular and sacred usage, as any use in front of the Chanukah candles diminishes their recognition as being for Chanukah. This is the opinion of most of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law), and such is the widespread custom.

The Tur wrote that because it is forbidden to use the light [of the Chanukah candles], they add one more candle so that if one uses its light, they will use that candle, etc. And the last one will not be designated as a Chanukah candle, etc. It is not called a "shamash" because the shamash is used to light the other candles. Thus far is his wording. Our master, the Beit Yosef, added in section 1 to say that it should be placed somewhat distant from the other mitzvah candles. Thus far is his wording. For if not, it would spoil the enhancement of those who are meticulous in their observance, as they would think that this many days have passed since Chanukah. However, from the words of the Tur, it does not imply this, as he wrote that they asked his brother, Rabbeinu Yechiel: When they light one more candle in general, without specifying which one, can they later choose whichever one they want to be the shamash, the first, the middle, or the last? And he replied that one should not separate the Chanukah candles, therefore it should be the last one. Thus far is his wording. And if you think that it needs to be placed far away, what kind of question is this? For he has already designated the one that was placed far. Rather, it is certain that it stands equal with the other candles. And if you ask: If so, does it not spoil the enhancement? One can say: Since this was the custom, everyone knows that there is one extra beyond the count of the days, and therefore the count of the days is also known. (And I am astonished that the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch did not point this out, see there. Be precise and you will find it simple.)

However, our teacher the Rema wrote about this, and this is his language: "In these countries, the custom is not to add another candle, but rather to place the 'shamash' (the attendant candle) next to them, which is preferable. And it is advisable to make it longer than the other candles, so that if one needs to use its light, one will use that candle." Until here is his language. 

And truly, I do not understand the opinion of the Tur and the custom in his days, and why they needed an additional candle. Is the shamash not sufficient? And one cannot say that they did not have a shamash, since the Tur concludes: "And there is no 'shamash' among them, because the shamash is the one with which the candles are lit." Until here is his language. If so, they did have a shamash, so what more is needed? Especially since the shamash is preferable, as our teacher the Rema wrote. His reasoning: This clearly proves that it is not counted among the number of candles (Magen Avraham, Siman 6). Additionally, it is longer or placed higher than the other candles (ibid.).

It seems to me that their reasoning is because it is difficult for them regarding what Rava said in the Gemara, that another candle is needed to use its light. The difficulty is: What is he informing us? It is obvious, since it is forbidden to use its light. And indeed the Ran explains that this refers to a time of danger, when one places it on the table and is compelled to use its light, as I wrote in Siman 671, section 21. But the Tur holds that this is its explanation: that an additional candle is needed in the arrangement of the candles, and it is not sufficient to have a shamash standing at a distance, or another candle in the house, because we are concerned that one might use the light of the Chanukah candles. Therefore, another candle is needed in the arrangement of the candles themselves, as I wrote in section 9. But those poskim who wrote that another candle is needed, and to place it separately (as written in the Beit Yosef and Bach, see there), do not hold like the Tur, but rather like our custom as written by the Rema. (And the Beit Yosef and Bach, as well as the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch, wrote that they are all of one opinion, and also that the Tur's intention was to place it separately. And we have already proven that this is not so, and that they are two different opinions. Examine and you will find the truth.)

And it appears to me that our custom, as written by Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema), is to satisfy both opinions: also the opinion of the Tur that the additional candle should specifically be placed among the candles for the reason we mentioned; and the opinions of the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that require a separate candle to be placed by itself. This means that we place the shamash (the attendant candle) among the candles, and it is taller or higher than all of them. In this way, we fulfill the opinion of the Tur that it should be together with the candles, and the opinion of the poskim to place it by itself so that it is clear that it is not part of the count of the candles. And here it is clear that it is not part of the count, since it is distinct from them, as I have written.

And know that there are those who have written that even though there is another candle, it is forbidden to use their light, because the onlooker might say that all of them were lit for his own benefit, as sometimes a person lights several candles (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, in the name of the Ramban; see there). However, these words are perplexing: it is clearly implied from the Gemara and the poskim (decisors of Jewish law) that when there is another candle, it is permissible to use their light. And even though the light is increased by the Chanukah candles, we are not concerned about it, for there is no degradation of the mitzvah, and it is evident that it was lit for the sake of the mitzvah of Chanukah (Taz, subsection 5). This matter is not mentioned in the Tur and the poskim. 

(The Ramban who wrote this reasoning did so when placing it on his table, as the Machatzis HaShekel wrote. This reasoning, that an onlooker says it was lit for his own benefit, was only stated in the Gemara when lit in an unusual place; see there. But in its proper place, it is only a matter of degrading the mitzvah. And when there is another candle, there is no degradation of the mitzvah, as the Taz wrote. The intention of the Maor is also this, when it is placed on his table, as the Ran wrote. And in the Maor, it is not found at all when there is a shamash (attendant candle) among the candles, as the Magen Avraham wrote. And he himself brought this in the name of the Riv, and this is the intention of the Riv. The words of the Magen Avraham require further investigation. Also, what he wrote in subsection 5, that if many are lighting, each one needs a shamash; see there. The custom is not so. Also, the Rashal disagrees with this, as he wrote there.)

Rabbi Moses Isserles wrote at the end of paragraph 1: If a Chanukah candle, which is forbidden to derive benefit from, gets mixed with other candles, even one in a thousand—it is not nullified, because it is considered an item of significance. Therefore, one should light from the mixture enough so that it is certain that a permitted candle is burning along with the forbidden candle, and then one is allowed to derive benefit from them. This is his language, meaning: if it was lit and then immediately extinguished, it is forbidden to derive benefit from it. For if it had not yet been lit—it is not forbidden to derive benefit from it, as designation alone does not constitute a matter. But once it is lit—it becomes forbidden to derive benefit from it. And even though he himself ruled in Yoreh De'ah, at the beginning of section 110, that only an item which is always counted is not nullified, but if sometimes it is also sold by weight—it is nullified. And if so, it is clear that candles are sometimes sold by weight. However, Chanukah candles are always sold by count, due to the importance of the mitzvah, and therefore they are not nullified. Therefore, there is no permission other than if a permitted candle is burning together with the forbidden candle. That is, if one Chanukah candle got mixed up—light two candles; if two got mixed up—light three, and so on. And just as with the Chanukah candle itself, if there is another candle—it is permissible to use its light, as explained, so too in mixtures, if there is another permitted candle, it is permissible to use its light. And even though the light is increased also by the forbidden candle, nevertheless we are not concerned about it, as I have written regarding the Chanukah candle itself.

And there are those who disagree with the fundamental rule, arguing that it is not considered an item that is counted (davar shebeminyan) because after it becomes mixed, its significance is nullified, and it is no longer considered an item that is counted, and thus it is nullified one in two. And all the more so, since it has been extinguished, its significance is nullified even when it stands alone (Taz, small section 6 and small section 7), and it is nullified one in two, as in the case of a dry item mixed with another dry item (and so the Magen Avraham wrote in small section 9 in the name of the Rashal). And since the fundamental prohibition of an item that is counted is only rabbinic, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah there – one can rely on the lenient opinions. And there are those who want to prohibit here because of the principle of kavua (fixed). But it is not so, for there is no biblical kavua here, since the prohibition is not discernible by itself. And rabbinic kavua is only because of an item that is counted. And since we have clarified that this is not an item that is counted – consequently, the kavua is removed. These matters are explained in Yoreh De'ah there. (See Sha'arei Teshuva, small section 9, which wrote about this. And the main opinion is as I have written, scrutinize and you will find it lenient.)

In the Gemara, it is established that if the candle goes out, one is not required to rekindle it. This means that once it has been lit and there was enough oil for the required amount of time, the primary mitzvah (commandment) is the lighting itself. Thus, he has fulfilled his obligation and does not need to light it again. Even on Erev Shabbat (the eve of the Sabbath), when one lights while it is still daylight and it goes out before the acceptance of Shabbat, which is still during the day, nevertheless, he is not required to rekindle it. The same law applies if, after lighting, he tries to adjust it and accidentally extinguishes it—he is not required to light it again.

There are those who say that on Erev Shabbat, one is obligated to relight it without a blessing, as he already recited the blessing properly (Magen Avraham, section 12 in the name of Rashal, and Taz, section 9). Certainly, during the week, if someone wishes to be stringent upon himself and relight it, he should not recite a blessing over it. It is proper to be stringent and relight it without a blessing. Even though, according to the law, it is not necessary, it is no less than enhancing a mitzvah.

All of this applies when he placed enough oil and did not place the lamp in a windy location. If he did not put enough oil or placed it where the wind blows, which initially caused it to extinguish, he is required by law to relight it with a blessing, as the initial blessing was in vain. Some say that if it was due to the wind, he should not recite a blessing again (ibid.), as maybe the wind was not strong enough to definitely extinguish it. But if it was definitely strong enough to extinguish it, it is clear that he must recite the blessing again.

An earthenware lamp that was lit for one night becomes old and repulsive, and one should not light with it on another night. Rather, one should take a new one each night. If one only has an old one, he should heat it with fire each night, so that it becomes like new. A metal lamp does not need to be new, and a glass or coated earthenware lamp has the same status as metal. However, the wicks certainly do not need to be replaced until they are completely consumed, because a wick does not become repulsive. On the contrary, an old wick is better for lighting than a new one, as it is taught: "A wick that has been singed" (Shabbat 28b: a wick that has been folded but not singed, and Rashi explains that 'singed' means it has been charred so that it lights well).

One may light a Chanukah candle from another Chanukah candle, and there is no disrespect to the mitzvah in this, for he is lighting sacred from sacred. Even though one might say that it diminishes the mitzvah somewhat, as some oil is taken from the candle when lighting another – this is nothing, for nothing is actually taken from it, and we do not worry about this at all. However, this is specifically when lighting directly from one to another without any intermediary. But to light from one to another through a non-sacred candle, meaning to light a non-sacred candle from a Chanukah candle, this is certainly forbidden as it constitutes disrespect to the mitzvah, as the sacred is serving the non-sacred. Even if his intention is to light another Chanukah candle from the non-sacred one, it is still forbidden, for at the moment when the non-sacred candle is lit, there is disrespect. There are those who permit this as well, and they do not see any disrespect to the mitzvah since the intention is to light another Chanukah candle from it. (This depends on the Talmudic discussion in Shabbat 22b, where we follow Shmuel who permits lighting from candle to candle. There is a dispute among the authorities regarding using an intermediary. Those who forbid it believe it diminishes the mitzvah. Even though the opinion of Rav who forbids it due to diminishing the mitzvah was refuted, it was not a complete refutation, as explained by Tosafot in the discussion on "What was the conclusion?" and in the Rosh there. See Beit Yosef.)

Even according to the opinion that permits it, if there is concern that the weekday candle will extinguish before using it to light the Chanukah candle, it is prohibited because then it would be used only for a mundane purpose, which constitutes a disgrace to the mitzvah. There is an opinion that permits even in such a case, questioning why we should be concerned about this. Even if it might happen, what disgrace is there? After all, it was initially lit for a sacred purpose (Taz, Section 2). However, our teacher, the Rema, wrote that the custom is to be stringent with Chanukah candles, not to light even from one candle to another, as the primary mitzvah is only one candle, and the rest are not as much for the mitzvah. Therefore, one should not light one from another. Thus far his words. Certainly, if one of the candles goes out, it should not be relit from another Chanukah candle, since there is no mitzvah in relighting it, as we hold: if it goes out, it does not need to be rekindled, as I wrote in the previous section (Magen Avraham). In truth, all these reasons are weak, for since the primary prohibition is due to the disgrace of the mitzvah, there is no disgrace here at all, since it is still a mitzvah candle. However, since this is the custom, it should not be changed. Certainly, it is forbidden to light the shamash from a Chanukah candle, as there is no mitzvah in it at all, and this is forbidden by law. Know that all of this applies within the time of its required duration. But after the required time has passed, its sanctity ceases, and it is permitted to light even a weekday candle from it, as it is permitted to extinguish it, as I wrote in Section 672. It is also permitted to benefit from it, and certainly, it is permitted to light from it.

A mitzvah candle – it is permissible to light from a Chanukah candle according to the fundamental law, for example: to study in its presence or to pray. Therefore, in a synagogue – all the candles burning there are considered for a mitzvah, and it is permissible to light one from another. Hence, in a synagogue, one can light one candle from another, whether they are synagogue candles, Shabbat candles, or Chanukah candles. They can be lit from one another, as they are all for a mitzvah. However, it is forbidden to light an ordinary candle from the synagogue candles, as explained in Siman 154, see there.

(The Gra in his commentary on section 5 wrote that this, which permits lighting one from another with synagogue candles, refers to lighting from one candle to another through a kindling stick. But according to those who prohibit it due to the disrespect of the mitzvah, it is forbidden, as mitzvot do not cancel each other out, and it is considered disrespect to the mitzvah, see there. And I do not understand how this relates to mitzvot canceling each other out, for in any case, it is not disrespectful as is evident. And although the Ran wrote this rationale regarding using a Chanukah candle for a mitzvah purpose, the main reason he wrote was that they made it analogous to the Menorah, see there. Furthermore, using it is different, and it requires further examination. Also, what the Magen Avraham wrote, that in our Mordechai, it is prohibited in all mitzvah candles to light one from another, see there, it must be said that his intention is through a kindling stick, as the Pri Megadim wrote. See there, and in Mordechai, and in the glosses of Rabbi Moses Tikten. And Mordechai speaks there of a kindling stick, but if so, the words of the Magen Avraham need examination, as there is no contradiction at all. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

Even though the mitzvah of lighting the Chanukah candle cannot be fulfilled without placing the candle in its proper place, just as it cannot be fulfilled without lighting it, and we hold that if one holds the candle in his hand for the entire duration of the lighting, even in a place where it is required to be lit – he has not fulfilled the obligation. Similarly, we hold that one must light it in the place where it is to be set, meaning at the entrance of his house on the outside according to the Talmudic law. But if one lights it inside and then brings it outside – he has not fulfilled the obligation. From all this, it seems that placing the candle is also part of the mitzvah, and one who is disqualified from lighting, such as a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor – is also disqualified from placing it in its proper place. Nevertheless, this is not the case, and the halacha as decided in the Talmud there is that the lighting constitutes the mitzvah, not the placing. If a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor places it in its proper place, and an adult lights it – it is valid. There are further practical differences for several matters, as will be explained (and if he held it for a short time in his hand – he has fulfilled the obligation).

And if you ask: If so, why indeed does one not fulfill the obligation when holding the candle in one's hand? The reason is that in this manner, there is no indication that it is for the mitzvah of Chanukah, and an observer would say: He is holding it for his own need, and not for a mitzvah, and thus there is no publicizing of the miracle. And for this same reason, if one lit it inside and then brought it outside, one has not fulfilled the obligation, because an observer would say: He lit it for his own need. Furthermore, since the lighting is the mitzvah, it must be lit in the place where it is to be placed. However, this reason only applies to them, who had a specific place for lighting outside the entrance of their house, and not for us, as we light in any place.

And since the mitzvah is fulfilled by lighting and not by placing, therefore there is no requirement for placement for the sake of the mitzvah. If it was already placed in its location, one lights it for the mitzvah and does not need to lift it and replace it for the sake of the mitzvah. But this is not the case with lighting. If it was already lit beforehand, it must be extinguished and relit for the sake of the mitzvah of the Hanukkah light. Moreover, even if it was lit for the mitzvah of the Hanukkah light and it continues to burn from day to day, it must be extinguished and relit anew. And thus our sages of blessed memory said: A lantern that was burning all day, which was lit before Shabbat for the sake of the mitzvah of the Hanukkah light and continues to burn until after Shabbat, must be extinguished and relit for the sake of the mitzvah.

And know that even though we said that in this time there is no fixed place for lighting, in any case it is forbidden to light it in this place with the intention of placing it in another place. One must leave it in its place for its duration, which is half an hour. However, if it happened that one lit it and it remained here, and afterward, due to some reason, it was moved from its place – one has fulfilled the obligation in this time. In the synagogue, some say that it is permissible to initially light it in this place with the intention of placing it in another place (Beit Yosef), since the lighting in the synagogue is merely a custom. Nevertheless, one should be careful not to do this initially (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 2). And we have already written in Siman 671 that one is obligated to place oil in the lamp before lighting it according to the required measure. And if one blessed over a small amount of oil and lit, and afterward added oil – one has not fulfilled their obligation, since we require the measure at the time of lighting, because the lighting constitutes the mitzvah. And this is simple. (And that which the Beit Yosef in paragraph 2 wrote this law in the name of "there are those who say" – this is his way in the Shulchan Aruch when he only mentioned this law from one authority. And it is also simple that if one added oil after the blessing and before the lighting – one has fulfilled the obligation.)

A woman lights the Chanukah candle and can fulfill the obligation for men as well, for she is obligated in the Chanukah candle just like a man, as they too were part of the miracle, and the miracle was also done through them, as I wrote in Siman 670. A deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor do not light, even if the placement was done by an adult, for it has already been clarified that the main mitzvah is the lighting and not the placement. Some of the great early authorities said that a minor who has reached the age of education can light on behalf of adults (Ran in the name of the Itur). This is based on the Jerusalem Talmud in Megillah, which states that they instituted for a minor to read the Megillah. However, none of the early authorities wrote this, and we do not practice this even regarding the Megillah. Nevertheless, if each member of the household lights individually, certainly this minor who has reached the age of education can light on their own. 

One who has already lit can still recite the blessing for another person or for a woman if they are unable to light and bless. They should stand next to him, and he should intend to fulfill their obligation, as with all blessings on commandments, for one who has already fulfilled their obligation can still fulfill it for others. A blind person – some say that he is obligated in the Chanukah candle even though he cannot see, as he does not need to benefit from the light. Nonetheless, if he can participate with a small amount of money, he should do so. If he has a wife, she blesses on his behalf. If he does not have a wife, he blesses himself, and others assist him if he is unable to light by himself (Magen Avraham, Siman 4). There are those who hesitate and say that a blind person should not bless, and it is correct to do so since the main aspect of publicizing the miracle is the seeing, and he does not see. Therefore, it is proper whenever possible for the blind person to refrain from blessing.

On the first night of lighting the Chanukah candle, one recites three blessings: "to light the Chanukah candle," and some say "the candle of Chanukah," and in the Tur the version is "of Chanukah" in two words, and so it is in Maimonides, chapter three, see there, similar to the Shabbat candle where we bless in this manner. However, in the Shulchan Aruch it is written: "Chanukah candle," and so it is according to the Arizal. And some have written "ofChanukah" as one word (Shelah). They have written that the Shabbat candle, which is made for use, is appropriate with the phrase "of Shabbat." But the Chanukah candle, which is forbidden for use and is solely for Chanukah itself, does not fit with the phrase "of Chanukah," as it is not "of Chanukah" but Chanukah itself. In any case, there is no strict requirement. And we have the custom to say "Chanukah candle."

And know that there is a great question regarding this blessing: How can we bless "to light" (l'hadlik) with a lamed, when in Pesachim (8b) it is clarified that any mitzvah that a person is not obligated to do personally and can delegate to a messenger – we do not bless with a lamed, but rather with "al" (on). If so, we should bless "on lighting the Chanukah candle." Indeed, it explicitly states in the Jerusalem Talmud Sukkah (Chapter Three, Halachah 4): How do we bless on the Chanukah candle? Rav said: "Blessed... who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us on the mitzvah of lighting the Chanukah candle," see there. So why did the Gemara in Shabbat say "to light the Chanukah candle" (23a)?

One of the great Rishonim answered: Since everyone must contribute with coins, it is as if he is doing it himself (Ran on Pesachim there). Indeed, there are great Rishonim who said that we should read in the Gemara: "on lighting the Chanukah candle" (Beit Yosef in the name of Shibolei HaLeket, see there, and in Shiltei HaGibborim in the name of Riaz, and in Tanya, see there Rabbi Yosef). Some of our Rabbis explained that since everyone lights in their own home due to the cherishing of the mitzvah – it is as if it is incumbent upon him to do it (Rosh there).

And with further explanation, it seems to me: Since there is no house that does not light the Chanukah candle, and everyone is obligated at the very least to see them because of publicizing the miracle – it is as if it is incumbent upon each one to do it. (And in my humble opinion, it appears because the term "lighting" implies even if it is already lit. And we hold that this does not suffice. Therefore, the term "on lighting" implies only that it should be lit, but "to light" implies that it is not sufficient if it is not lit, as stated in the Gemara there: it does not suffice if he does not light it himself. See there.)

Second blessing: "Who performed miracles for our forefathers, in those days at this time." At first glance, this seems to be a redundant expression. It appears to me that the correct wording is "at this time" and not "and at this time" (as stated by the Magen Avraham), and it seems that in some versions it was written "and at this time." In my humble opinion, the main point is this: the primary miracle of the Hasmoneans defeating Antiochus did not occur on this particular day of the 25th of Kislev, but rather over many days during which they conquered them. It was only at this time that there was an additional miracle of the oil flask they found. Similarly, in the blessing of the Megillah: the main miracle of turning the heart of Ahasuerus occurred many days earlier, as Esther's banquet was on the second day of Passover, and from then he began to pursue Haman. But on the 13th of Adar, there was a separate miracle, as the Jews killed their enemies on that day, as it is written: "On the day when the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, the situation was reversed..." Therefore, there are two miracles: one "in those days," and the second "at this time" literally. One must say "at this time" with a chiriq vowel. The third blessing is "Shehecheyanu," and one must also say "to this time" with a chiriq vowel under the lamed (there).

From the first night onward, one recites two blessings: "to kindle" and "who performed miracles." However, "Shehecheyanu" is only recited on the first occasion, similar to the festivals where "Shehecheyanu" is only recited once. But "who performed miracles" is recited every night, since each day was a miracle in itself with the oil flask. One should begin lighting after completing all the blessings, as the blessings must precede the act ("over la'asiyatan"). Even though this specifically applies to the blessing "to kindle," it does not apply to "who performed miracles" and "Shehecheyanu." Proof of this is that even an observer recites them, as will be explained, and the observer recites them after the lighting. Refer to paragraph 14.

And indeed, this is how it is in Massechet Sofrim (Chapter 20, Halacha 6), and this is its language: The one who lights the candles blesses "to light the candle," and says "these candles we light... and for Your salvation," "Blessed are You, Hashem, who has kept us alive," and says "who performed miracles" etc., thus far its language. And in the gloss of Maimonides, Chapter 3 (Section 2), it is written that this is how Maharam acted, see there. However, our teacher the Rema wrote that all the blessings should be recited together before lighting. And his reasoning is clear, for how is it possible to interrupt between the blessings? Consequently, since "to light the candle" is blessed first, it follows that these too should be blessed first, so as not to interrupt. And it appears clear to me that even in Massechet Sofrim the intention is not to say the two blessings after "these candles." And the proof: for the Tur wrote to make the three blessings together, and afterward wrote in the name of Massechet Sofrim to say "these candles," and that this was the custom of Maharam and the Rosh, of blessed memory, see there. Thus, it is explicit that this is the interpretation, or there is an error in Massechet Sofrim and one must say the two blessings first, for many errors have fallen into it as is known. And this is the main ruling, and so did Maharam act, and so it is in the responsa of Mahari"l, and so we practice.

The statement "one who sees [the Chanukah lights] must recite a blessing"—Rashi explained that this applies to someone who has not yet lit in their home, or someone who is on a ship, see there. And from his wording, it appears that anyone who has not yet recited the blessing in their home, even though they will still light in their home, must nevertheless recite the blessing upon seeing [the lights]. And it is possible that afterward, when they light in their home, they will only recite the blessing for lighting. However, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in Section 3 wrote: Whoever has not lit and does not intend to light that night, and no one is lighting for them in their home, should recite the blessing "Who performed miracles," and on the first night, they also recite "Shehecheyanu." If afterward, on the second or third night, they come to light, they do not recite "Shehecheyanu" again. This is their language. And they hold that one who intends to light that night does not recite the blessing upon seeing [the lights]. Likewise, this is written by the Rosh, the Ran, and the Mordechai. The Ran added, saying that we do not find that one who has fulfilled the mitzvah is obligated to return and recite the blessing upon seeing [the lights], see there. (And from Tosafot Sukkah 46a, s.v. "one who sees," it appears that even if one has already fulfilled [the mitzvah], they must recite the blessing, because Chanukah is different and is not comparable to all other mitzvot, see there. And in practice, we follow the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch.)

And know: Regarding what they wrote, that if they light for him in his home, he does not need to recite the blessing upon seeing [the Chanukah lights], there are those who disagree. Even though he is exempt from lighting himself, nevertheless, the blessings of "Who performed miracles" and "Who has kept us alive," which are expressions of gratitude and are obligatory upon his person—how can he be exempt, since he did not hear the blessings nor respond "Amen" (Bach)? There is also proof from Rashi and the Rosh, who wrote that one traveling on a ship recites the blessings. And can it be that one traveling on a ship does not have someone lighting for him at home?

Rabbeinu Yerucham wrote that there is a dispute on this matter, and this is his wording: Some of the great authorities wrote that if they lit for him in his home, he does not need to recite the blessing when he sees another’s candle. And some of them wrote that even if they lit for him in his home, he still needs to recite the blessing when he sees [another’s candle]. This is the end of his wording (there). And it seems that the main ruling is that the Rif and the Rambam wrote simply: The one who sees [the lights] must recite the blessing. Similarly, the Maharshal ruled that only one who participates with money and hears the blessings and responds "Amen" does not need to recite the blessing. But if they light for him in his home, he must recite the blessing.

(And the Magen Avraham in section 1 wrote: From Tosafot in Sukkah 46a, it does not seem so, as the Machatzit Hashekel explained his intention there. And I wonder: On the contrary, from their words, it is clear that even one who has already recited the blessing must recite it again, as I wrote, and they debated this matter there. And in my humble opinion, the main ruling is like the Bach and the Maharshal, and so ruled the Eliyah Rabbah in section 4, who brought many authorities who wrote similarly. And what the Magen Avraham wrote in section 2, that if so, why did Rabbi Zeira not participate with money? I wonder: Rabbi Zeira was referring to the blessing "to kindle," but "Who has kept us alive" and "Who performed miracles"—he recited on others' [candles] upon seeing them. And the Bach, who wrote that his person is not exempt, was referring to "Who has kept us alive" and "Who performed miracles." And certainly, this is so, just as one who did not recite "Who has kept us alive" on the first night certainly recites it on the second night. And similarly on the festival, and here too it is the same. And also, the Taz in section 4, who wrote that the Mordechai is unique in this, if he had seen that many held this view, he would not have said so, as the Eliyah Rabbah wrote there. And in my humble opinion, this is the main ruling. Be precise, and you will find it easy.)

After lighting the first candle, one should say: "These lights we kindle for the salvations, for the miracles, and for the wonders that You performed for our forefathers through Your holy priests. And all eight days of Chanukah, these lights are sacred, and we do not have permission to use them, but only to look at them, in order to give thanks to Your name for Your wonders, for Your miracles, and for Your salvations." This is the version in the Tur. And while saying this, one should complete the lighting. This is for the sake of publicizing the miracle. However, if one did not say this, it does not invalidate [the lighting]. The Rambam does not mention this at all, although it is found in Massechet Sofrim. (And regarding what is written that there are thirty-six words here, corresponding to the number of Chanukah lights – I cannot account for the count.)

If one forgot and lit one less candle than required, they should light it without a blessing, because the blessing made initially covers all the candles (Magen Avraham). Additionally, since the primary mitzvah is fulfilled with one candle, one does not recite a blessing for the enhancement. Therefore, even if one forgot two or more candles, they should light them without a blessing. It seems to me that this is specifically if one remembers within the lighting time. But after the lighting time has passed, one should not light the forgotten candles at all, because if they light them, they will not be fulfilling the mitzvah in the best possible way ("mehadrin min hamehadrin"), as the first candles have already gone out. If so, why light them without purpose? The recognition of the mitzvah is only when all the candles are burning together.

We have already written that even someone who has already fulfilled the obligation can light on behalf of another and recite the blessings, such as a woman who does not know how to light and recite the blessings. However, this is on the condition that she stands next to him and answers "Amen." But if she is not present, he should not recite the blessings. Similarly, it is permitted for her to light while he recites the blessings (Magen Avraham, end of sub-section 4). There is an opinion that when another person recites the blessing, he should say "for the lighting of the Chanukah candle" (Magen Avraham in the name of the Bach), since the mitzvah is not currently incumbent upon him. Another opinion states that the wording should not be changed, and he should bless "to light" (Magen Avraham in the name of the Ran). This is also the custom. After all, he should have blessed this way himself, as I have written in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud. Nevertheless, according to our Talmud, we do not bless in this manner, for reasons that have been explained. Therefore, there is no difference whether one lights himself or through an agent.

Our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in section 5: One should begin lighting on the first day with the rightmost candle. On the second night, when adding one candle next to it, one should start and recite the blessing on the additional candle, which is more to the left, in order to turn to the right. Similarly, on the third night, when adding another candle next to the first two candles, one should start with the additional candle and begin the blessing with it, and then turn to the right. This is the procedure for every night. Thus, one always recites the blessing on the additional candle, which represents the miracle, as each additional day signifies an increase in the miracle. Until here are his words.

And I have seen someone who wrote that this has no reason, as this is only for those who are extremely meticulous, and should one set aside the main mitzvah and recite the blessing on the optional? Rather, the main principle etc. is that one should recite the blessing on the main mitzvah, on the candle closest to the entrance (the Gra, subsection 6). But I do not understand these words. This would be relevant if one were lighting one candle and did not bless, and then lit the second and blessed – there would indeed be a question: how can one bless on the additional and not on the main? But according to our teacher, the Beit Yosef, one always blesses on the first candle, which is the main one, and the rest are additional. And what he calls "additional" – this is regarding the order of placing the candles concerning the previous day, as each day one blesses on the new candle. But it is indeed the first, and it is the main mitzvah, so what is the issue? Therefore, we follow the words of our teacher, the Beit Yosef (and being next to the entrance is not essential).

And the Levush disagrees with our master the Beit Yosef for another reason: that which he said that the additional candle should be on the left, and one should light from left to right, and this is the corner towards the right. But the opposite is true: that the corner towards the right is from right to left, as one always starts from what is more to the right and goes from right to left. Like the sprinklings in "Which is their place": south-eastern, north-eastern, north-western, south-western. And so it is in human nature to turn from right to left, like in dances. And so it is in our writing: from right to left. Therefore, the main principle is always to start from the right and to go from right to left, see there. And there are those who added to this that we can always bless in this way on the additional candle, meaning: that the candle where the lights are kindled should be in the handbreadth close to the entrance, on the left side of the entrance, and one should start with the candle closest to the entrance. And on the second night, one should start with the second candle and go from right to left (Taz, end of subsection 6). And in Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 106) it is written: that the people of Rhinus acted according to our master the Beit Yosef, and the people of Austria according to the Levush, see there. And our master the Beit Yosef decided according to the people of Rhinus. And the great ones wrote that it is always good to place the menorah within the entranceway on the doorpost, for then they will all be within the handbreadth close to the entrance. For if one places them by the wall next to the entrance, not all will be within the handbreadth close to the entrance. And so it is proper to act.

And behold, even regarding turning to the right, where the Levush disagrees with Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef, the primary opinion also follows the words of Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef. And so it is explicitly stated in Rashi and Tosafot on Yoma (17a, beginning of "Mideraminan"), and this is the language of Rashi of blessed memory: he counts and proceeds to the right, from the north to the west, and from the west to the south, and from the south to the east. Thus far his language, and so wrote the Tosafot. Hence, from left to right is called the way to the right (Pri Chadash in Siman 128). And indeed, it is explicitly stated in the Sea that Solomon made in Kings (7): three face north, and three west, and three south, and three east. And from this our sages of blessed memory derived (there, 58b): that all turns you turn should be to the right, see there (and this is hinted at by the Magen Avraham in subsection 5). And what the Levush brought regarding the sprinklings on the altar – this is also so, as he would stand outside and face inward. And in every matter that a person does, it should be from left to right, which is the way to the right. (And what he brought as proof from our writing, it is also the opposite in writing each letter itself in Ashurit script, which goes from left to right. There is a great secret in writing from right to left in general, and from left to right in particular: to include the left in the right, and the right in the left, as known to the sages of Kabbalah. And what he wrote about the custom of dances – this is the way of nature, not the way of intellect. Be precise and you will find ease.)

It is straightforward that someone who did not recite the blessing upon lighting the first candle may still recite it as long as the candles are still being lit. However, after the lighting, one should not recite the blessing, because we require the blessing to be recited "before performing the mitzvah." This is according to the Rambam in the eleventh chapter of Blessings. According to those who disagree, one may still recite the blessing, as we explained in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 19, Section 4; see there. However, in my humble opinion, it seems that regarding the Chanukah candles, since there is a mitzvah in seeing them, and the main aspect of publicizing the miracle is through seeing them, one may still recite the blessing afterwards. We wrote a similar reasoning in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 28, Section 30 regarding the covering of the blood. (And in Sha'arei Teshuvah, Section 5, it is not written so; see there. But to me, it appears as I wrote.) And there are those who say that "Who performed miracles" and "Who has kept us alive" may be recited afterwards, but "to light" should not be recited after lighting the first candle, because the rest are only for beautification, and it is not appropriate to bless on them (The Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger). I do not understand this: are the other candles less significant than drying one's hands after washing, which is also not essential, and yet the drying is considered "before performing the mitzvah," as I wrote in Siman 158? This requires further study.

The Gemara (23a) states: A guest is obligated in the Chanukah candle, but he can participate with a small coin together with the host. This means: Someone who does not have a wife and home, but rather he alone resides permanently in another's house – the obligation is upon him to light the Chanukah candle. And if he does not want to light it himself – he participates with the host, and one of them recites the blessing, and the other responds "Amen." However, when he is a guest and he has a wife and home in another place – they light in his home, and he is also exempt. But there are those who say that the blessings of "Who performed miracles" and "Who has kept us alive" – he is obligated to see the Chanukah candles and to recite these two blessings on the first night, and on all other nights only the blessing of "Who performed miracles." And we have already written about this in the previous section, paragraph 7, and our opinion leans this way, even though there are those who disagree. See there.

The Rif and the Rambam wrote at the end of the fourth chapter: A guest who has his own entrance, even though they light for him in his host’s house or he participates with money – still, he needs to light on his own because of suspicion, see there. And it seems that this applies only according to the Talmudic law, where they would light at the entrances of courtyards or houses. But for us, who light inside the house – there is no suspicion. And there are those who wrote that nowadays, when we light inside, if the guest has a room to himself – he should light (Magen Avraham, small section 3). And I do not understand why: for in the house there is no suspicion, as the members of the household know that he participated with money, or that he has a wife and house elsewhere?

And it seems to me that certainly when he participates with money – he does not need to light on his own. Rather, when he does not participate, and the members of the household think that he does not have a wife and house – in this case, perhaps there is suspicion, and it requires further investigation. And there are those who add further and say: that even if he does not have a room to himself, since it is customary for every guest to light – he is also obligated to light because of suspicion, for who knows if he is single or married (Eliyahu Rabba, small section 1)? And if this is the custom – certainly one follows the custom. But what he wrote "who knows etc." – is not understood: for this only applies to a young bachelor. But someone who is older – it is obvious that he has a wife. Therefore, this requires further investigation.

And know that there are those who wrote that when lighting because of suspicion – one does not need to make a blessing (Kenesset HaGedolah). This is not correct, for since he is lighting on his own, if so, he does not wish to fulfill his obligation with the household’s lighting, so why not bless (and this is also implied by Magen Avraham, small section 4)?

And know that in the time of the Talmud, one had to light because of suspicion when he had an entrance open to himself, as I wrote – this applies even if both entrances are on the same side, one needs to bless. And this is not similar to Siman 677, where the suspicion is on the homeowner, and the townspeople know that both belong to one person. But in the case of suspicion regarding a guest – certainly, there is suspicion even on the same side, for he does not belong to this homeowner (ibid, small section 2).

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote: The statement that if one has an entrance open to himself, he needs to light at his entrance — this is true even if that house is designated only for sleeping, and he eats at the table of the house owner. The same applies to a son who eats at his father's house. Thus far their words. And even if he regularly eats at his father's house, since he has a room for sleeping by himself — he needs to light because of suspicion. And even though the main consideration is the place where he eats, as Rabbi Rema wrote, that some say that nowadays, when we light indoors, one should light where he eats, and that is the custom. Thus far his words. Nevertheless, according to the Talmudic law, if he has an entrance open to himself, the suspicion is because of those who pass by there and do not know that he does not eat there — therefore, he needs to light. But nowadays, when the lighting is indoors, it depends only on the place where he eats. Therefore, a guest who eats with the house owner, and certainly a son who eats at his father's house — does not need to light separately in his room, since the household members know that he eats together with them, and he is considered part of the household. The mitzvah of Chanukah lights is "a man and his household," meaning: for all the household members. (This is what it seems to me in my humble opinion. And it seems to me that this is also the intention of the Magen Avraham in subsection 6, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.) And it is obvious that one who eats at his friend's house occasionally — needs to light separately for himself, or his wife lights for him at his house, where he resides. (There in subsection 7. And what he wrote that nevertheless it is better for him to do it personally than through his agent, see there — I do not understand his intention. If so, why did Rabbi Zeira in the Gemara not do so? It requires investigation.)

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote in section 2: A minor who has reached the age of education must light [the Hanukkah candles]. Until here is his language. This law should have been written at the end of Siman 673, and our teacher the Rema wrote it there. However, here it is a different issue, as there it discusses when the custom is that each member of the household lights separately. And here it does not discuss this, rather the intention is: A minor who has his own household is obligated to light because of suspicion, like an adult (and this is implied from Magen Avraham, subsection 8, see there). And there are those who exempt minors (there), and their reason: Since it is only because of suspicion, one is not obligated to educate the minor in this as well (Machatzit Hashekel).

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 3: Some say that even though they light for him in his home, if he is in a place where there are no Jews, he should light with blessings. Thus are their words. The reason: because he is obligated to see [the candles], due to publicizing the miracle. And here – he will not see the candles burning. They also wrote: that even if he is with Jews and sees the candles, if he wants to be stringent upon himself and light on his own – he lights and blesses over them. And so is the custom. Thus are their words. Meaning: even though he has a wife and home, and she will certainly light for him, nevertheless he can say: I do not wish to fulfill [the obligation] with this, and I will light on my own. And indeed, this is our custom, that anyone who is traveling – lights where he is, even though they light for him at home. And this is considered an enhancement (there, subsection 9, in the name of Terumat HaDeshen). And the Mahari”l wrote that it is a common custom for guests and young men to light (there). It seems to me, in my humble opinion, that since most travels are by rail, and it is difficult to light there as is known – one can simply rely on his home, where they light for him. However, he will not see the Chanukah lights, and therefore it is good that he lights one candle in the carriage where he sits, and blesses over it, as with one candle he can manage without the travelers being particular. And it is better not to be among those who beautify the mitzvah and to fulfill the main mitzvah, than not to see the Chanukah light at all. Certainly, someone who has no home is obligated by law to light there, if he will not arrive at any place that night.

The Tur wrote: The remaining oil and wicks from the first night – one adds to it and lights on the second night. If it remains on the second night – one adds to it and lights on the third night, and so on for all the nights. If any remains on the eighth night – one makes a separate bonfire and burns it, since it was designated for its mitzvah. Thus far is his language. And this is from the Pesikta, as I have written, the Rosh in the name of the Sheiltot. 

And the commentators have questioned: for above in Siman 672 it is explained that the remaining oil after the required amount – it is permissible to extinguish it and use it. And they answered: there it refers to when one put more than the required amount, and it was designated for its mitzvah only according to the required amount. And here it refers to when one put the required amount, and from this it remains, which is certainly forbidden (Beit Yosef and Bach). 

And based on this, Rabbi Yosef Caro wrote in section 4: The remainder on the eighth day of the oil required for the lighting measure – one makes a bonfire and burns it separately, since it was designated for its mitzvah. Thus far is his language. But if one put more than the required amount – the surplus is permitted. And the commentators of the Shulchan Aruch agreed to this, see there. 

And there are those who answered: here it refers to when one put it without specifying, therefore it is holy even more than the required amount, for it is presumed to have designated all of it. And above it refers to when one did not explicitly designate only the required amount (there in the name of R. Yitzchak Abuhav). And there are those who rejected this answer, that even without specifying – it is not holy except according to the required amount (Beit Yosef, and Magen Avraham small section 10, and Taz there). 

And there are those who answered that here it does not mean that it is forbidden to benefit from it, but the intention is to remove it from the world. And also above the intention is so, that the Rabbis made it like an item of holiness that requires burial (see Taz). That is to say: it should not be disposed of disrespectfully. And this does not seem to be the meaning from the language of the Tur.

And I am astonished at our rabbis: According to the language of the Tur, there is no contradiction at all, for certainly, no more than the required amount was designated. But here it is a different matter, and that is: when some oil remains from the first day, and it is left until the second night, it means that the surplus was designated for the second night, and so from the second to the third, etc., and what remains from the seventh night was designated for the eighth night, and this is certainly forbidden. And the next day, on the eighth night, when more oil is added, only the required amount is forbidden. But who can say that what remained from the seventh night was burned and what was added on the eighth night remained? Perhaps what was added was burned, and what remained was designated from the previous day? And this is why they precisely said: what remains from the first night, add, etc., and they should have said: what remains from the Chanukah lamp, make a bonfire and burn it. Rather, certainly only in such a case should it be burned, for the reason we have written. But when one adds oil to the Chanukah lamp, the surplus is not sanctified.

Oil designated for the Chanukah lamp that got mixed with other oil, and the remaining oil is not sixty times the amount to nullify it, the Tur and Shulchan Aruch write that one should not add oil to reach sixty times to nullify it, for one does not nullify a prohibition ab initio, even a rabbinic prohibition. And even though in Yoreh De’ah, Siman 99, it is explained that some say that for a rabbinic prohibition, if it got mixed and there isn't sixty, one can add until it reaches sixty, here it is considered as something that has a permitted use, since it can be saved for the next year's Chanukah lamp. And even though the Tur wrote not to save it, to avoid coming to a stumbling block, and even placing it in a repulsive vessel does not help, because for lighting it does not become repulsive, nevertheless, since by the basic law it is permitted to save it, it is considered as something that has a permitted use (and this is the intention of the Magen Avraham, Siman 12). And even though with wood that fell from a palm tree on Yom Tov, we permitted in Siman 507 to add prepared wood to them and burn them, this is because one does not benefit from it until after it is consumed (Tur), as it is stated at the beginning of Beitzah. This is not the case here, where one benefits at the time of lighting when adding to nullify until sixty. (And it requires examination why the Shulchan Aruch did not write the words of the Tur, that it is forbidden to save it for the next year due to a stumbling block. And perhaps he holds that, in any case: if you rule it as something that has a permitted use, we permit him to save it, as it would be a contradiction. Delve into it and you will find it easy.)

In Siman 263, it is explained that between the Shabbat candle and the Kiddush of the day, the Shabbat candle takes precedence if one cannot afford both, because household peace is more important than anything else. The Shabbat candle represents household peace, preventing people from sitting in darkness and stumbling as they walk. Certainly, the Shabbat candle takes precedence over the Chanukah candle, even though Kiddush is a Torah obligation. Though one can make Kiddush over bread, if even bread is lacking, the Shabbat candle is still preferable. This is even more so against the Chanukah candle, which is a rabbinic enactment. Even though many authorities hold that Kiddush itself is only rabbinic and one fulfills the Torah obligation through prayer, nonetheless, its essence is from the Torah. Despite the fact that the Chanukah candle publicizes the miracle, household peace is greater than all. However, one candle suffices for household peace, and with the remainder, one should buy a Chanukah candle (Magen Avraham).

If one has a Shabbat candle but does not have wine for Kiddush, if he purchases a Chanukah candle, the Chanukah candle takes precedence because of the publicizing of the miracle (pirsumei nisa). This is specifically when he has bread. But if he does not have bread, bread takes precedence even according to the opinion that it (lechem mishneh) is a rabbinic commandment, for lechem mishneh is a Torah obligation (Taz). There is an opinion that even against bread, a Chanukah candle takes precedence (Bach). It seems that the first opinion is correct: even if we say that it is not a Torah obligation, nevertheless, bread certainly contributes to domestic peace, as is evident. Similarly, a Chanukah candle takes precedence over Havdalah. However, for a Chanukah candle, when he has one candle, that is sufficient, and with the remainder, he should buy wine for Kiddush and Havdalah, since according to the law, one fulfills the obligation with one candle.

Some say that in our times, when we light the Chanukah candle at home, we should not say that the Shabbat candle takes precedence. It is preferable to light the Chanukah candle, and thus there will be light in the house. Although it is forbidden to eat by its light, it is still better to eat in its presence than to completely nullify the Chanukah candle, since it cannot be done otherwise (Magen Avraham). However, there are those who disagree with this (Eliyah Rabbah). Nevertheless, one may rely on this in a pressing situation, for regarding the primary purpose, some say that it is permitted for the purpose of a mitzvah, as I wrote in Siman 673, and the Shabbat meal is certainly a mitzvah meal.

On Friday afternoon, one must light the Chanukah candle before the Shabbat candle. This is not only necessary if one accepts the Shabbat through the lighting of the Shabbat candle, in which case it would be forbidden to light any further candles, but even if one does not accept Shabbat through this lighting, it is still impossible to light the Shabbat candle before the Chanukah candle. This is because it is not proper to perform mundane tasks after lighting the Shabbat candle. Additionally, from the time of the Talmud, it is understood that lighting the candle was the final act (as the Ran elaborates in the second chapter). This is also implied by the language of the Tur, that the Behag rules that the Chanukah candle precedes the Shabbat candle because the lighting signifies the acceptance of Shabbat. He wrote that Tosafot stated that this acceptance is not dependent on the lighting, and one can light the Shabbat candle first, etc., up to this point. This means that according to the law, one can technically light the Shabbat candle first, but it is nevertheless better to light the Chanukah candle first (as the Bach also wrote, see there).

However, the Rashba of blessed memory in his responsa (Part 1, Siman 1000) ruled to light the Shabbat candle first, because when one practice is frequent and the other is infrequent, the frequent one comes first, see there. And I am puzzled: for it explicitly states in the Gemara (23b) that if one has only enough for either Kiddush or the Chanukah candle, the Chanukah candle takes precedence because of the publicizing of the miracle, which is more important than the frequent practice of Kiddush. And one must say that he holds this ruling applies when one would completely forgo one of the practices, but not in terms of which to perform first. And this reasoning is written by Tosafot there. And here it can be explained further: that on Erev Shabbat when one lights while it is still day, the publicizing of the miracle is not yet applicable.

Nevertheless, the widespread custom in all Jewish communities is to light the Chanukah candle before the Shabbat candle, because our women accept Shabbat with their lighting. Even if a man lights and explicitly does not accept Shabbat, which in such a case is permissible even according to the Behag (Ba'al Halachot Gedolot) – nevertheless, we prioritize the Chanukah candle. However, if it happens that one lit the Shabbat candle first, they should recite the blessing for the Chanukah candle afterward, provided they have not accepted Shabbat with the lighting. If Shabbat was accepted, or if a woman lit, who generally accepts Shabbat with her lighting – someone else should light the Chanukah candle for her, and she should listen and respond "Amen."

One recites the blessing for the Chanukah candle: "to light the Chanukah candle" on the eve of Shabbat, even though one lights it while it is still daylight. Since it is impossible to do otherwise, the obligation necessarily applies at that time. At the very least, it is no less significant than a preparatory mitzvah, for which we also recite a blessing, such as when constructing a sukkah before the festival. According to the Talmudic law, one recites "Shehecheyanu" (Sukkah 46a), and according to the Jerusalem Talmud (Berakhot, Chapter 9, Halacha 3), one also recites "to make a sukkah". All the more so for the Chanukah candle on the eve of Shabbat. However, one must be careful to use a lot of oil so that it will burn through the night for the required duration, which is half an hour. (It is obvious that in any case, one should not light it before Plag HaMincha.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote: On Friday night, one must place something outside between the candles and the door, to prevent the wind from extinguishing the candles when the door is opened. This is his language. And this applies to their situation, where they would light at the entrance of the house facing the courtyard, where there is wind. But for us, who light in inner rooms – this does not apply. And one should not ask: If there is a concern that the wind will extinguish the candles, then during the week as well, it should not fulfill the obligation, since it is not fit to burn for the required duration? One can say: Indeed, it is not certain that it will be extinguished. Furthermore, when the door is closed – it is obvious that it will not be extinguished. However, because of the severe prohibition of Shabbat, one must be cautious even in such a case. The detailed laws of this matter are explained in Siman 277; see there.

He also wrote: On the eve of Shabbat, it is forbidden to fix the candles on the door itself, behind the door. And there are those who permit it. Thus far his words. This also depends on the details explained there. There is no difference whether it is behind the door or on the side in front, as it is all one reason: whether this is considered extinguishing or not. And there the reasons for the disagreement on this matter are explained, see there.
