One should not perform the Havdalah ceremony over Chanukah candles because they are forbidden for personal benefit, and the blessing "Creator of the lights of fire" is not recited until one benefits from their light. However, one can first perform Havdalah with it, then extinguish it and light a Chanukah candle with it (Bach). This is preferable because, since one mitzvah has already been performed with it, another mitzvah should also be performed with it (see Taz). But this depends on the clarification of whether Havdalah takes precedence or Chanukah candles take precedence?

Rabbeinu Beit Yosef wrote: One lights the Chanukah candles in the synagogue before Havdalah. Thus is his language, and the reason he explains in his great book: because we delay ending the day. See there. However, if so, why specifically in the synagogue? And Rabbeinu Ramah wrote about this: Certainly in one's home, one lights and then performs Havdalah, for he already performed Havdalah in the synagogue. Thus is his language, and it implies: because he already performed Havdalah in the synagogue, otherwise, Havdalah would precede. And so it seems, for certainly it is difficult to bless "Borei Meorei Ha'esh" after already using the Chanukah light. And this reasoning was written by the Kolbo in the name of the Raavad of blessed memory. And even though one does not benefit from the Chanukah candle, nonetheless one uses its light. And furthermore: one benefits from the shamash (helper candle), therefore in one's home, one should perform Havdalah first. And only in the synagogue, where the publicizing of the miracle is very great, it is appropriate to light the Chanukah candle first. Also in one's home, if one already heard Havdalah in the synagogue. But otherwise – Havdalah precedes. And this is our custom. Also: the main reason for delaying the end of the day – there is no reasoning in this, for this is relevant if we were behaving with the customs of Shabbat. But since we light the Chanukah candle – necessarily the day has already ended. Furthermore: Havdalah is frequent, and it pertains to ending Shabbat. But the Chanukah candle – necessarily pertains to the following day. Therefore, it is certain that only in the synagogue is this done, for the reason we wrote. (The Magen Avraham wrote that one who forgot "Ata Chonantanu" – should perform Havdalah first, see there. And it implies that he holds that each person should light first. And so wrote the Eliyah Rabbah, and so it appears from the Gra. But the Taz and the Maharal of Prague ruled to perform Havdalah first. And so it seems to me, in my humble opinion, to be the main approach, for the reasons we wrote. And although they rejected the words of the Taz, nonetheless according to what I wrote it fits well. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

During all eight days of Chanukah, one says "Al HaNissim" in the Grace After Meals in the blessing of the land. That is to say: one begins with "We thank You" and says until "and at all times," and then says "Al HaNissim" until "to Your great name." After that, one says "And for all these, Lord our God, we thank You..." Similarly, in the prayer (Amidah), after "We give thanks" until "we hope in You": "Al HaNissim" until its end, and then says "And for all..." and "All the living shall thank You, Selah..." Since these blessings are not requests but rather expressions of thanks, and "Al HaNissim" is also an expression of thanks, therefore it was established in the context of giving thanks. Unlike "Ya'aleh Veyavo" which is a request, it was established in the blessing of prayer in "R'tzei." It seems to me that one should say "Ve'al HaNissim" since there are already expressions of thanks before, and this is an addition. In the prayer books, it is written "Al HaNissim," but it seems it should be said with a vav ("Ve'al HaNissim").

One must say "when the evil [kingdom] stood" – the "reish" with a sheva, and the "shin" and "ayin" with a kamatz. And one must say "to make them forget Your Torah, and to cause them to transgress the statutes of Your will" without a "mem" (Magen Avraham). Some say "from the statutes" (Pri Chadash), and so we say, for this language is more straightforward. And we say "when [the evil kingdom] stood against Your people Israel," and there is no need to say "when it stood against them," for this is redundant since we already say "against Your people Israel." And one must say at the end "and they established these eight days of Chanukah," not as some say "these eight days" without mentioning Chanukah, for this is incorrect, as everything must be explicitly mentioned (there). And we say "for the salvations and for the battles." Some say "for the wonders." It seems to me that on Chanukah one should say "for the battles" since the Hasmoneans fought against Antiochus. But on Purim, there was no war, so one should say "for the wonders." And we say "just as You performed miracles for our forefathers…" However, our teacher the Beit Yosef wrote that we do not say "just as You performed…" but rather conclude with "and You performed miracles and mighty deeds for them in those days…" Some say that it is said. This is his language up to here. The reason for the first opinion is that "just as" implies a prayer, that just as You performed miracles for our forefathers, so too do for us, and one does not say prayers in the last three blessings. But some say that it is said, and this is our custom. The congregation is different, as we say during the Ten Days of Repentance "and inscribe…" and "in the Book of Life."

If one forgets "Al HaNissim" (the prayer for miracles), whether in the Amidah prayer or in the Grace After Meals, one does not need to repeat it. This is not similar to "Ya'aleh Veyavo" of Rosh Chodesh (the new month) and Chol HaMoed (the intermediate days of a festival), which are days that have an additional offering. This is not the case with Chanukah, where the obligation is merely one of thanksgiving. However, if one remembers during that blessing, as long as one has not yet said God's name, even if one has said "Blessed are You" and then remembers, one goes back. And even though one is not obligated to go back, in the Grace After Meals, one should say in the "Harachaman" section at the end: "May the Merciful One perform miracles and wonders for us, as You did... in the days of Mattathias" until the end. Similarly, in the Amidah, one can say "Al HaNissim" after "Yihyu L'ratzon" (the concluding prayer). And know that on Shabbat, one must say "Al HaNissim" also in the Mussaf (additional) prayer, and similarly in the Mussaf of Rosh Chodesh Tevet. And even though there is no Mussaf on Chanukah, nevertheless it is a day that requires four prayers, and one must mention Chanukah in all of them.

On Chanukah, we complete the Hallel because a miracle with the oil jug occurred each day. Additionally, each day is distinct in terms of its candles, according to those who are meticulous in their observance, and it is similar to Sukkot, where the sacrifices differ each day, and we complete the Hallel. Furthermore, we read about the princes (Nesi'im), and each day's prince is different from the others. Hence, each prince should complete the Hallel for his sacrifices (Beit Yosef). Additionally, as I wrote in Siman 670, they established the eight days of Chanukah in place of the days of Sukkot that were not observed then. Consequently, we complete the Hallel during Chanukah just like during the festival of Sukkot.

All eight days of Chanukah, we do not say Tachanun, "Tzidkatcha Tzedek," "Ya'ancha," or Tziduk HaDin. Similarly, at Mincha on the eve of Chanukah, we do not say Tachanun, as I wrote in Siman 131. It is forbidden to fast on these days, as I wrote in Siman 670, and we slightly increase the festive meals and recite songs and praises, as I wrote there.

And we read from the Torah on Chanukah each day from "Naso" in the section of the offerings of the princes. The reason is stated in the Pesikta: because the work of the Tabernacle was completed on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, as I have written in Siman 670. And we begin with "And it was on the day that Moses completed," which is the start of the matter. There are places that begin with the Priestly Blessing, because the miracle happened through the Kohanim (priests) of the Hasmoneans, and it is a beautiful custom (Tur). However, this is not the common practice, because it is not related to the offerings.

And how is the reading conducted? On the first day, we begin with "And it was on the day that Moses had finished," which contains many verses, and we divide it between the Kohen (priest) and the Levi (Levite). The third person reads from the portion regarding the prince of Judah. Some say that the Kohen reads the entire section of "And it was on the day that Moses had finished," and the Levi and the Israelite read from the portion regarding the prince. The reason is that since the main reading concerns the princes, most of the readers should read from the portion about the princes. This is also the customary practice.

On the second day, the Kohen reads "On the second day" until "one young bull." The Levi reads from "one young bull" until "on the third day." The Israelite repeats and reads "On the second day." Some say that the Israelite should read "On the third day," as it is better to read the portion of the following day rather than repeat what the previous readers have already read, if possible. This is our custom, and similarly for each day.

On the eighth day, the Kohen and the Levi read "On the eighth day," as this is the obligation of the day. The Israelite reads from "On the ninth day" until the end of the princes' portions, including the section "This was the dedication of the altar," and also from "When you light the lamps" until "Thus was the menorah made," as this all constitutes a single topic, and it is necessary to complete it in its entirety.

On Shabbat of Chanukah, we take out two Torah scrolls. In one, we read the weekly portion, which mostly falls on the portion "Miketz." In the second, we read the section for Chanukah as the Maftir, corresponding to the day of Chanukah it is. The Haftarah is from the prophecy of Zechariah about the menorah: "Sing and rejoice." If the first day of Chanukah falls on Shabbat, resulting in two Shabbatot of Chanukah, the Haftarah on the second Shabbat is from the prophecy of Solomon in Kings: "And Hiram made." Rabbi Moshe Isserles (the Rema) wrote that if a wedding falls on this Shabbat – we read the section for Chanukah. This is his exact wording. Meaning: and not "I will greatly rejoice." This is according to their custom, but in our practice, we never read a special portion for the groom.

If Rosh Chodesh Tevet falls on Shabbat, three Torah scrolls are brought out. In the first scroll, six men are called to read from the weekly Torah portion. It is forbidden to call more than six men because the seventh reader must read from the second Torah scroll, as he is part of the required number of readers. In the second Torah scroll, the seventh reader reads from the section for Rosh Chodesh, as the more frequent (Rosh Chodesh) takes precedence. Even though Hanukkah involves publicizing the miracle (pirsumei nisa), the one who reads the Haftarah will read from the Hanukkah section, and by doing so, the Haftarah will be related to Hanukkah. He begins with "On the Shabbat day," since it is Shabbat. The one reading the Haftarah reads from the third Torah scroll about Hanukkah and recites the Haftarah for Hanukkah: "Sing and rejoice." If Rosh Chodesh falls on a weekday, two Torah scrolls are brought out. Three men read from the first scroll for Rosh Chodesh, and the fourth reads from the Hanukkah section according to the day's order (see Siman 684, paragraph 4).

If the reader made an error and read the fourth aliyah for Rosh Chodesh, if they have not yet taken out the second Torah scroll, there is no need to read more. This is because we do not give precedence to Chanukah, as it does not have a Musaf sacrifice. However, if they have taken out the second Torah scroll to avoid its disgrace, it is necessary to read a fifth aliyah for Chanukah and recite Kaddish afterward. If Kaddish was said after the fourth aliyah, it should not be repeated (Magen Avraham). Even if the mistake is realized during the reading of the fourth aliyah, it should not be interrupted, and it should be completed for Rosh Chodesh, and the reading for Chanukah is forfeited (ibid). Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote: If one made a mistake and started reading for Chanukah, they must stop and read for Rosh Chodesh. His exact words are: "This is similar to putting on the head tefillin before the hand tefillin" (ibid). Some disagree and hold that the Kohen should complete the Chanukah reading, and afterward read for Rosh Chodesh (Taz and Rabbi Naftali Katz). If three verses have already been read for Chanukah, even according to Rabbi Moshe Isserles, it is obvious that it counts towards the number of readers, and afterward, read the third aliyah for Rosh Chodesh (Eliyah Rabbah). In practice, one should follow the view of those who disagree, to avoid the disgrace of the Torah scroll. The same law applies on Shabbat Chanukah when it coincides with Rosh Chodesh. (And this is stated regarding weekdays to highlight that even on weekdays one adds a reader, all the more so on Shabbat. Rabbi Akiva Eiger).

Our sages of blessed memory instituted the reading of four special Torah portions in the month of Adar, which is adjacent to Nisan. This means that if it is a leap year, they are read in the second Adar. The first is Parashat Shekalim, in memory of the mitzvah of the half-shekel, which every Jew was required to give each year for the offerings of the Temple treasury, to purchase the daily offerings and all communal sacrifices. The second is Parashat Zachor, to juxtapose the commandment to obliterate Amalek with the downfall of Haman, who was a descendant of Amalek. It is read before Purim. The third is Parashat Parah Adumah (the Red Heifer), whose burning was close to Nisan, in order to prepare for the Passover with purity. The fourth is Parashat HaChodesh, in which the mitzvah of preparing for Passover is mentioned. 

In the Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah, it is stated: It would have been logical for the portion of Passover to precede the portion of the Red Heifer, for on the first of Nisan the Tabernacle was erected, and on the second day the Red Heifer was burnt. Why did they place it earlier? Because it concerns the purification of Israel (Rashi on Megillah 29b).

The portion of Shekalim is read on the Shabbat that is adjacent to Rosh Chodesh Adar, either before it or on the Shabbat that falls on Rosh Chodesh Adar. This is because in Adar, they would announce regarding the shekalim, as it is taught in the beginning of Shekalim. And the reason is: because Rosh Chodesh Nisan is the beginning of the year for this matter, to bring communal offerings from the new donation, as it is written: "This is the burnt-offering of the month in its month for the months of the year." The word "for the months" is extra; the Torah said: bring the offering from the new donation. And from where do we know that it is Nisan? We learn from "This month shall be for you," as it is written: "It is the first for you of the months of the year." Just as here, it is Nisan – so too for the months of the year, as it is written in "Pinchas," it is also Nisan. Therefore, they would announce in Adar to bring their shekalim, so that they would be ready for Rosh Chodesh Nisan, and they would announce thirty days in advance. And we fulfill this by reciting verses with our lips in memory of this.

Therefore, on the Shabbat before Rosh Chodesh Adar, after reading the weekly Torah portion, we read for the Maftir the beginning of the portion "Ki Tisa" until "to atone for your souls." The Haftarah is from Kings: "Jehoash was seven years old when he began to reign," which speaks about the matter of the Shekalim, until "they will belong to the priests." Some begin earlier, from "Jehoiada made a covenant," and this is the custom of the Sephardim. Their reasoning seems to me to be based on the principle stated earlier at the beginning of Siman 284, that it is preferable for the Haftarah to contain twenty-one verses, unless the matter is completed (with fewer verses), see there. From "Jehoash was seven years old" until "they will belong to the priests," there are only seventeen verses. Therefore, they begin four verses earlier, which is also related to the matter of Jehoiada and Jehoash. However, the Ashkenazi custom is not so. It appears that their reasoning is that while it is true that this is related to Jehoiada and Jehoash, nevertheless, it is not related to the matter of the Shekalim. Therefore, it is considered as if the matter is completed.

If Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, three Torah scrolls are taken out. In the first scroll, six men are called up to read from the weekly portion. Specifically, it must be six and no more, in order to read the seventh portion from the second scroll, which is an obligation of the readers, as I wrote in the previous section regarding Rosh Chodesh Tevet that falls on Shabbat. Refer there to Section 4. In the second scroll, the seventh man reads from the portion of Rosh Chodesh, beginning with "U’v’yom HaShabbat" ("And on the Sabbath"). In the third scroll, the Maftir is read from the portion of Shekalim. The reading of Rosh Chodesh takes precedence over Shekalim because it is more frequent. Consequently, the Maftir reads the Haftorah related to Shekalim, not related to Rosh Chodesh, since the Maftir read from Shekalim in the Torah, and therefore the Haftorah in the Prophets must be related to the Torah reading of the Maftir. (The Levush wrote that at least six men are called up where it is not customary to call up more than seven, see there. This implies somewhat that it is permissible to call more than six in the first scroll where it is customary to add more. I find this puzzling: how can it be that the second scroll would not include the obligations of the seven readers? This is also evident from the language of the Tur, and there is also proof from the Gemara in Megillah 29b, see there. Analyze and you will find the reasoning easy to understand.)

On the second Shabbat before Purim, we read the portion of "Zachor." Many legal authorities hold that the portion of Zachor is from the Torah, meaning that there is a Torah obligation to read the section about the obliteration of Amalek once a year. However, in the days of Mordechai and Esther, they established the obligation on the Shabbat before Purim to juxtapose the obliteration of Amalek with the downfall of Haman, as I have written. It is written: "And these days are remembered and observed" – one must precede the remembrance of Amalek to the observance of the mitzvah of Purim. Some say that one also fulfills the Torah obligation by reading the portion of "Vayavo Amalek" on Purim (Magen Avraham at the end of this section). In my humble opinion, this is not so, for the Rambam in the Sefer HaMitzvot in positive commandment 188 wrote that we were commanded to eradicate the seed of Amalek, etc., and in commandment 189 wrote that we were commanded to remember what Amalek did to us, see there. This is mentioned only in the portion of "Zachor": "Remember what Amalek did to you… when you have rest… you shall blot out…" But in "Vayavo Amalek" it does not mention the mitzvah of remembering for all of Israel, nor the mitzvah of obliteration. There it is written: "For I will utterly blot out…" but it does not say "You shall blot out," which implies that we are obligated to do so. Additionally, in the Megillah (18a), it is explicitly implied that the primary obligation is in the portion of "Zachor," as it says: "Zachor" – can it mean in the heart? The Torah says: "Do not forget" – thus the forgetting of the heart is already stated. So how do I fulfill "Zachor"? By words. See there. Thus, the obligation is only in the portion of "Zachor." However, this is certainly true when one reads it in the Torah in the portion of "Ki Teitzei," that one fulfills the Torah obligation. But from the rabbinic decree – it is specifically before Purim. The Haftarah for the portion of "Zachor" is in Samuel (I 15): "Thus said the Lord of Hosts: I remember what Amalek did…" until "Givat Shaul." Some begin one verse earlier: "And Samuel said to Saul" because it is the beginning of the section.

On the third Shabbat, we read the portion of Parah, from the beginning of "Chukat" until "it shall be unclean until the evening," where all the laws of the Red Heifer are explained. The haftarah is from Ezekiel (36), from "And the word of the Lord came to me… Son of man…" until "I have spoken and will act." Some add another two verses until "and they shall know that I am the Lord," because that is the end of the matter. See there. Since the prophet rebukes them there for their impurity, it was therefore established for Parashat Parah, which purifies the impure.

On the fourth Shabbat, we read the portion of "This month shall be for you" until "you shall eat unleavened bread." The haftarah is in Ezekiel (45). The Sephardim begin from "Thus said the Lord God: In the first [month], on the first of the month…" until "the continual burnt offering," as this pertains to the matter of the first of the month of Nissan. The Ashkenazim begin two verses earlier, from "all the people of the land," and continue three verses beyond "the continual burnt offering" until "a man from his inheritance." Their reasoning seems to be: although these verses are not specifically about the first of the month of Nissan, since the entire chapter concerns the prince in the future, and these verses also pertain to the prince and are in the same chapter, they are therefore included.

Know that even in these portions, this is only for the maftir. But all seven aliyot, or more where additions are made, are read from the weekly portion, as I wrote regarding Parashat Shekalim.

When the first of Nissan falls on Shabbat, three Torah scrolls are taken out. Six aliyot are read from the first scroll, the section for Rosh Chodesh is read from the second scroll, and the "month" portion is read from the third scroll, similar to when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Shabbat, as previously explained.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 7: There are those who say that the portion of "Zachor" and the portion of the Red Heifer must be read from the Torah. Therefore, those who live in places without a quorum must come to a place with a quorum on these Sabbaths to hear these portions, as they are from the Torah. And if it is impossible for them to come, they should still be careful to read them with their cantillation and intonation. Thus far his words. And it is preferable to travel to a quorum for this reading than for the reading of the Megillah. And even though the reading of the Megillah overrides all other matters, as I will write in section 687, nevertheless, it can be read individually, unlike the Torah portions, which can only be read with ten people (Taz, section 2, in the name of the Terumat HaDeshen).

However, the great latter authorities wondered: From where do we say that even the portion of the Red Heifer is from the Torah? There is no hint of this in the Gemara, and therefore, they ruled that it is not from the Torah (Magen Avraham). In my humble opinion, it seems that there is a hint to this in the Torah, as in the portion of the Red Heifer it is written in the middle of the portion: "It shall be a statute forever for the children of Israel," and in the Sifri, it is interpreted to mean that it applies for generations, see there. For the ashes of the Red Heifer are not dependent on the Temple, for even in the time of the Amoraim they had the ashes of the Red Heifer, as it is said: "The companions would purify in the Galilee" (Chagigah 25a, see also Niddah 6b in Rashi). And at the end of the portion, it is again written: "It shall be for them a statute forever," which is redundant, but it comes to teach regarding the reading of the portion, even at a time when there are no ashes of the Red Heifer. As it is said in Zevachim (101a): "The scripture advanced it for its reading," and Rashi explains there in Niddah: "That they should read about it," see there. And all the more so in our time, when the actual commandment is not in effect, but would have been if we had the ashes of the Red Heifer, it is certainly possible to say that there is an obligation to read the portion.

It is understood implicitly that these four special Torah readings cannot be consecutive. Since we advance the reading of "Shekalim" to the Shabbat before Rosh Chodesh Adar, and "Zachor" needs to be close to Purim, there is naturally a break of one Shabbat. The general rules are as follows: If Rosh Chodesh Adar falls during the week, even if it falls on Friday, we advance the reading of "Shekalim" to the previous Shabbat. Consequently, the next Shabbat is a break, since it is not the Shabbat closest to Purim. On the third Shabbat, we read "Zachor." Sometimes, there is also a break between "Zachor" and "Parah." How is this? Rosh Chodesh Adar only falls on one of the days of Zayin, Bet, Daled, and Vav (Saturday, Monday, Wednesday, Friday). 

When it falls on Saturday, we read "Shekalim" on that day, and on the second Shabbat, we read "Zachor," since Purim will be that week on Friday. There is no break between "Shekalim" and "Zachor," but the break will be between "Zachor" and "Parah." That is, on the fifteenth day, which is the Shabbat after Purim, we do not read "Parah," because there will still be two more Shabbatot before Rosh Chodesh Nisan. It is better to combine "Parah" with the month, as it pertains to the purification for Pesach. If Rosh Chodesh falls on Monday, the break is on the sixth day of the month between "Shekalim" and "Zachor," to keep "Zachor" close to Purim. Otherwise, there is no break. Similarly, when Rosh Chodesh falls on Wednesday, the break is on the fourth day of the month, just like when it falls on Monday. However, when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on Friday, there are two breaks: one on the second day of the month between "Shekalim" and "Zachor," to keep "Zachor" close to Purim, and the second between "Zachor" and "Parah," on the sixteenth day of the month, to keep "Parah" close to the month.

And they have established a mnemonic for this: ZTV, BV, DD, and BVYV. This means: when Rosh Chodesh Adar falls on the seventh day, the interruption occurs on the fifteenth of the month, which is: ZTV. When it falls on the second day, the interruption is on the sixth of the month, which is: BV. When it falls on the fourth day, the interruption is on the fourth of the month, which is: DD. And when it falls on the sixth day, there are two interruptions: on the second and the sixteenth, which is: BVYV. 

The Rambam writes in Chapter Thirteen of the Laws of Prayer, Law 21, and these are his words: "You find that sometimes there will be an interruption between the first and second Shabbat, or between the second and third. And sometimes there will be two interruptions: between the first and second, and between the second and third. But between the third and fourth, there should be no interruption." These are his words. 

The reason is: that [the readings of] "Shekalim" and "Zachor," as well as "Zachor" and "Parah," have no connection to each other, and therefore an interruption can be made between them. But "Parah" and "Chodesh" are connected to each other, and therefore no interruption should be made between them. (The Magen Avraham writes: that in all four parshiyot, we do not mention the souls of the deceased, and we say "Tzidkatcha Tzedek." These are his words. And "Av Harachamim" – there are those who customarily say it. In my humble opinion, it seems that it should not be said, because we do not mention the souls of the deceased, and they are Shabbatot of joy, and they are not worse than the Shabbat on which we bless the new month.) 

With the help of Heaven, this concludes the laws of Chanukah.

The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote that on Chanukah and Purim, it is permitted to fast before and after them. This is their language. Meaning, even though we hold that regarding Chanukah and Purim, the Megillat Taanit was not nullified, as I wrote in Siman 686, and it is written in the Megillat Taanit that everything written in it - it is also forbidden to fast before and after them; nevertheless, it is permitted to fast because regarding before and after, even Chanukah and Purim were nullified. And even though there are those who disagree regarding Chanukah, as I wrote in Siman 670, nevertheless, the Fast of Esther was accepted by all of Israel. And at the beginning of Megillah (2a), it says the thirteenth is a time for gathering for all. And Rabbeinu Tam explained: that everyone gathers for the Fast of Esther, and the villagers come to the towns to say Selichot and supplications, because on this day they gathered to defend themselves, and they needed mercy (Rosh and Ran at the beginning of Megillah). But Rashi of blessed memory explained this for another matter, which is: that they gathered to take revenge on their enemies, see there. And in the She'iltot of Rav Achai, it is explained and gathered explicitly according to Rabbeinu Tam, and this is his language: What is "gathering"? A day of fasting. And what is "a day of assembly"? That they assemble on it, fast, and request mercy. This is his language. And Rambam in the fifth chapter of Taanit, law 5, wrote that this fast is a remembrance of the fast they fasted in the days of Haman, as it is said: "the words of the fasts and their cry". This is his language. And the Tur wrote according to Rabbeinu Tam, see there.

And one should not ask: Isn’t this fast explicitly mentioned in the scripture, as it is written “to confirm these days of Purim...” and as they confirmed upon themselves “the matters of the fasts and their cry”? However, in truth, the phrase “the matters of the fasts” does not refer to “to confirm...” Rather, this is the explanation: to confirm the days of Purim for feasting and joy, as Mordechai the Jew and Queen Esther confirmed upon them, and as they confirmed upon themselves and their descendants the matters of the fasts and their cry. Meaning: Just as all of Israel accepted upon themselves the four fasts in remembrance of the destruction of the Holy Temple, so too they accepted upon themselves these days for feasting and joy (Ran, Chapter Two of Taanit). And one must necessarily say so, for the fast of Mordechai and Esther was in Nissan, as explicitly stated in the beginning of Chapter Twenty-One of Masechet Sofrim, and this is its wording: "The custom of our Rabbis in the West is to fast the three days of the fast of Mordechai and Esther separately, after Purim, on Monday, Thursday, and Monday." And why do they not fast them in the month of Nissan? Because on the first of Nissan the Tabernacle was erected. Thus far his wording. Thus, the fast of Esther before Purim is not mentioned at all. And from the words of the Rambam, it is also proven so, as he wrote: A remembrance of the fast they fasted in the days of Haman. And if you would think that they accepted it upon themselves – this is not a remembrance, but an obligatory fast of words of acceptance, which is much stricter. And indeed, we are very lenient with the fast of Esther, as will be explained. Therefore, one must necessarily say as I wrote. (And the Bach wrote: The opinion of the Rambam is that this fast is a fast of words of acceptance, and it is very strict, see there. In my humble opinion, this is not the case. And indeed, in the name of the Raavad, the Ran wrote there that “the matters of the fasts and their cry” refers to the fast of Esther, see there. However, even the Raavad only said this as a mere support, as explained there. Examine it and you will find it light.)

Therefore, all healthy Jews have the custom to fast on the thirteenth of Adar, and they recite Selichot, the Confession, and "Avinu Malkeinu," and they read "Vayechal" as on any public fast day, in memory of the fasts that were observed during the days of Haman. And why do we not commemorate the three days of fasting? Because we do not impose a decree on the community that is difficult to fulfill (Beit Yosef). And when Purim falls on a Sunday, the fast is advanced to the preceding Thursday. And why do we not fast on Friday? Because it is not appropriate to initially establish a fast on Friday, to increase in Selichot and supplications, and they would not be able to prepare for Shabbat (Tur). Also, it is not honorable for Shabbat to enter it while being afflicted. (And there are those who fast both night and day, and there are those who fast for three dispersed days after Purim, as explained in Masechet Sofrim. But in our times, we have not heard of this at all. And the Magen Avraham wrote that the Mahari"l would not teach halacha on the Fast of Esther, because people are preoccupied with purchasing necessities for Purim, see there. And he brought the opposite: that even on Purim itself they would study before their teacher, see there.)

And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: This fast is not obligatory. Therefore, one may be lenient in times of need, such as for pregnant women, nursing women, or for someone who is ill but not in danger. Even those who have eye pain, if they suffer greatly, should not fast and may make it up later. But other healthy people should not separate themselves from the community. These are his words. Even one who is traveling and finds fasting difficult (Magen Avraham), as long as the fast does not harm them. We must scrutinize his words, as he considers pregnant women, nursing women, and someone who is ill but not in danger. These individuals are not required to fast even on the four fasts, as I wrote in Siman 550!? However, for pregnant and nursing women, we can explain: there I wrote that it applies only when they suffer greatly, see there, but here they are not required to fast even ordinarily. But what he wrote about someone who is ill but not in danger is very surprising, as even on Tisha B'Av it is permitted, as I wrote in Siman 554, that the Rabbis did not decree in cases of illness, see there. And this is without danger, for in cases of danger, even on Yom Kippur, one is obligated to feed them, as I wrote there. And these matters only make sense for one who holds that this fast is from the words of the Prophets and is very stringent, as I wrote, and not according to what we hold that it is merely a custom. Further investigation is needed. (And the Eliyah Rabbah wrote: that it seems from the Gemara that they are obligated to fast – I do not know any such implication. And what he wrote from Beit Yosef in the name of the Ra'avad at the beginning of Siman 627 – the Ra'avad follows his own reasoning, as I wrote.)

Furthermore, it is written: if Purim falls on a Sunday, the fast is observed on the preceding Thursday, and if a circumcision takes place on that day, it is permissible to eat at the circumcision meal, and those who eat will fast on the following day, Friday. These are his words. Meaning, certainly, during any fast we would not permit eating at a circumcision meal, even on the Fast of Esther which is lenient. However, when it is postponed to the preceding Thursday, we allow anyone who wishes to eat at the circumcision meal, since there is another day to fast, as by strict law it would have been more appropriate to establish the fast on Friday, but out of respect for the Sabbath, we did not do so. Therefore, anyone who wishes to eat today and fast tomorrow is not prevented from doing so. But the father of the child, the sandek, and those similar to them are permitted to eat at the circumcision meal, without any obligation to make up the fast, even if it is not postponed. And so it is with the three fasts, except for the Ninth of Av, because it is considered their festive day (Kesef Mishneh in the name of the Gra, see there). However, there is an opinion that even when postponed, one should not eat at the circumcision meal unless they are directly related to the celebration, and even then, they should not fast the next day, because it is forbidden to establish a fast on the eve of the Sabbath (Taz). This seems to be the primary opinion.

And it has already been explained that some people fast for three days, in commemoration of the three days of fasting during the time of Haman. This is done after Purim, spaced out on Monday, Thursday, and Monday, as explained in Tractate Soferim. In our times, we do not observe this due to the weakness of the generations. When the month of Adar begins, we increase in joy. And one who has a legal dispute with a non-Jew should take it up in Adar, as it is a successful and good month (Taanit 29b), and its constellation is strong.

The residents of a city can establish a special day in commemoration of a miracle that happened to them (Magen Avraham). They can observe it similar to Purim. However, there are those who question this, arguing that since the Megillat Taanit was nullified, how can new holidays be added? This is also questioned in the Talmud in Rosh Hashanah (18b): If you think that the Megillat Taanit was nullified, how can we add new holidays? See there (Chatam Sofer). If a miracle occurred to someone in Adar and they vowed to commemorate it, some say it should be observed in a leap year during the first Adar, unless the miracle occurred during the second Adar in a leap year. Others say it should be observed in the second Adar (Magen Avraham). The primary opinion appears to be the first one, as in all matters, the first is considered primary for yahrzeit and bar mitzvah (see there in Magen Avraham and Eliyah Rabbah).

A person is obligated to read the Megillah at night and to repeat it by reading it again during the day, as it is stated: "So that my glory may sing praise to You and not be silent, O Lord my God, I will give thanks to You forever" (Psalms 30:13). This means that the verse is initially expounded as "O my God, I cry by day but You do not answer, and by night but I find no rest" (Psalms 22:3). This verse is in the Psalm "Ayelet Hashachar," which is interpreted concerning Esther in Yoma (29a). And since they cried out day and night, we commemorate the miracle by reading it both during the day and at night (Rashi). However, it seems difficult to understand how one mitzvah can be observed both during the day and at night, as most mitzvot are either observed only during the day, like tzitzit, tefillin, shofar, and lulav, or only at night, like the eating of matzah and counting of the Omer. Therefore, the verse "So that my glory may sing praise to You and not be silent" written in the Psalm "I will exalt You, O Lord, for You have lifted me up," which is expounded in the Pesikta regarding Mordechai, Esther, Haman, and Ahasuerus (there), says, "So that my glory may sing praise to You, O Lord my God, I will give thanks to You forever"—both by day and by night. This means that since the reading of the Megillah is akin to a blessing of gratitude, where we thank and praise Him for the miracle He performed for us, this applies both day and night without interruption, as it says: "O Lord my God, I will give thanks to You forever"—and it is like the recitation of the Shema and prayer, which are observed both day and night.

And our Rabbis, the Tosafot, the Rosh, and the Ran wrote that the primary mitzvah of the reading and the publicizing of the miracle is during the day and not at night, as it is written: "I will call out by day..." This means: Even though I read during the day, which is the main time, nonetheless, the night is also not to be silent for me. The main Purim feast is during the day, as well as the sending of portions (Mishloach Manot). And it is written: "And these days are remembered and performed" – Remembrance is likened to performance. Just as performance is during the day, so too remembrance is during the day (Tosafot). Therefore, in the Mishnah at the end of the second chapter of Megillah, it is taught: The entire day is valid for the reading of the Megillah. And at night – it does not teach that the entire night is valid, because the main reading is during the day (Rosh). According to this, even though one blesses "Shehecheyanu" on the reading at night, he must bless again for the reading during the day, because the main reading is during the day (ibid). However, the Rambam, in truth, ruled in the first chapter of Megillah that one does not bless "Shehecheyanu" again during the day, and this will be explained in Siman 692.

Seemingly, there is a practical difference in the law: If one can only hear the reading of the Megillah once, either by day or by night, according to these Rabbis, it is better to choose the daytime because it is the primary time for the reading. According to the Rambam, one should choose the nighttime, as it comes first, and one should not pass over the commandments. However, in truth, there is no proof, for it is possible to say that even according to the Rambam, the daytime reading is the primary one. It is just with regard to the "Shehecheyanu" blessing that he holds it is impossible to bless "Shehecheyanu" twice on one mitzvah. Similarly, according to these Rabbis, even though the daytime reading is the primary one, nevertheless, one should not pass over the mitzvah and should read it at night since it comes first, and one should not pass over the commandments. This seems to me to be the main practical ruling.

The time for reading the Megillah at night is the entire night until dawn. And even though the ideal time for reciting the Shema is only until midnight, this is because we are concerned that one might procrastinate and not read it at all. But the Megillah is cherished, and we are not concerned about this. Nevertheless, it is obvious that those who are diligent perform mitzvot early, and one should read it at the beginning of the night. And specifically after the appearance of the stars. If one read it during twilight, it seems to me that he has fulfilled his obligation after the fact, because a rabbinic doubt is ruled leniently, and he does not need to read it again. After dawn, one should not read it, because even though for the Shema it is considered night, as I wrote in Siman 58, this is because it is still called "when you lie down." However, for all other matters, it is considered day (as the Magen Avraham states). And the time for reading the Megillah during the day is ideally from sunrise until sunset. After the fact, if one read it after dawn, he has fulfilled his obligation, just as is the case with all mitzvot that are performed during the day; ideally, they should be done from sunrise, but after the fact, they are fulfilled from dawn, as is taught at the end of the second chapter of Megillah. (What the Magen Avraham wrote regarding one who converted before sunrise is straightforward: he is exempt from the night reading and obligated in the day reading. However, in Yoreh De'ah Siman 267 there are opinions that a conversion at night is not effective, see there. And see Machatzit HaShekel, and in the Yerushalmi, chapter 2, halacha 3, it is explicitly stated that he is obligated in the day reading. See there.)

Reading the Megillah, even though one can fulfill the obligation individually, as I wrote at the end of Siman 690, nevertheless, its primary mitzvah is in public, as "In the multitude of the people is the King's glory," and there is publicizing of the miracle. The larger the community, the greater the publicizing of the miracle. Therefore, our sages of blessed memory said (Megillah 3a): Priests during their service, Levites on their platform, and Israelites standing in their places – all interrupt their work and come to hear the reading of the Megillah in public. Similarly, one interrupts Torah study and comes to hear the reading of the Megillah in public. Even public Torah study is interrupted, as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud (Megillah, Chapter 2, end of Halacha 4), that the study hall is interrupted to hear the reading of the Megillah. The study hall is a place for public Torah study, as explained at the end of Sotah. Although certainly Megillah reading is also Torah study, nevertheless, the time taken to gather all the people and begin reading the Megillah is considered a disruption of Torah study. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 3, who brings from Knesset Hagedolah that the Gemara implies that public Torah study is not interrupted. This is based on what it says there: "It is not difficult – one refers to many, the other to an individual." Magen Avraham, as well as the Bach, explained that this refers to all of Israel, as in the case of Joshua, see there, and it could be so. But to me, it is not difficult at all, as the Gemara says that for many, there is no logical inference, but nevertheless, one must interrupt Torah study to hear the Megillah. Furthermore, regarding public Torah study, this ruling does not apply at all, for even if they read the Megillah themselves, they are still a public. And if the reason is due to "In the multitude of the people is the King's glory" – there is no proof that because of this one interrupts Torah study. One must examine this in the case of the study hall, and perhaps at that time there were not ten people. Also, Lechem Mishneh wrote that public Torah study is interrupted as well, see there.)

And since we set aside the study of Torah for the sake of the Megillah, all the more so we set aside other commandments for it. There is nothing that takes precedence over the reading of the Megillah, except for a "met mitzvah" (a corpse with no one to bury it), which, if one encounters it, one must first bury it and then read the Megillah. And know that our teacher, the Rema, wrote: when there are not enough people to bury the corpse, it is considered a "met mitzvah," and the reading of the Megillah is set aside for it. This is a surprising matter, for in every place mentioned in the Talmud where a "met mitzvah" is referred to, it means that the corpse is lying in disgrace and has no one at all to bury it. But if it is not lying in disgrace, and certainly if there are people to bury it, it is not considered a "met mitzvah," and one should first read the Megillah and then bury the dead (Magen Avraham, subsection 4, and Eliyah Rabbah, subsection 3). This is indeed very surprising. However, it seems to me that our teacher, the Rema, also holds this view, but his intention is as follows: for example, if they had already begun to deal with the burial before the time for the Megillah arrived, then even though the time has arrived, they do not interrupt for the honor of the dead. They complete the burial and then read the Megillah. And in this case, certainly the obligation lies on those sufficient to bury it. He was brief in his words, but this must be his intention. It is simple that saving a life overrides the Megillah, even if there will not be enough time left to read it, for nothing stands in the way of saving a life. The decisors did not need to mention this, as it is obvious and known. Therefore, one who attends to a dangerously ill person, and there is no one else to take their place, is forbidden to leave for the reading of the Megillah.

And our master, the Rema, wrote: All this applies only when there is enough time to do both. But if it is impossible to do both, no Torah commandment is postponed for the reading of the Megillah. And the reason a deceased person takes precedence is only if it is possible to read the Megillah afterwards. This is his language. But if it is close to nightfall, the Megillah should be read, as it is possible to bury him even at night. And it is obvious that if it is impossible to bury him at night due to robbers, the reading of the Megillah is postponed. (There, subsection 6).

However, the commentators on the Shulchan Aruch disagree fundamentally with his words. For certainly, whenever they said that one thing is overridden by another, the intention is that it is completely overridden. Even if there is still time to bury the dead afterward, the reading of the Megillah is overridden by a met mitzvah (an unattended corpse) (see there and Taz, subsection 2). And there are those who also disagree with what he wrote, that no Torah commandment is overridden by the Megillah, as Torah study is completely overridden (Taz, there). But this is not difficult at all: for Torah study cannot be said to be completely overridden, as Torah study is both day and night. And when one needs to perform a commandment, there is no time for Torah study then, for if not, how could one ever perform commandments? And regarding that of a met mitzvah, it seems to me that his intention is not in the case of a corpse lying in disgrace, for certainly, in such a case, the reading of the Megillah is completely nullified. Rather, it is in the case of a corpse not lying in disgrace, as I have written in subsection 6.

Circumcision and reading the Megillah: If there is enough time for both, reading the Megillah takes precedence because of the publicizing of the miracle. However, if there is not enough time for both, circumcision, which is a biblical commandment, takes precedence over the Megillah, which is rabbinic (Pri Chadash). But the author of Terumat HaDeshen (Siman 266) wrote the opposite: if there is enough time, circumcision takes precedence, and if there is not enough time, the Megillah takes precedence because circumcision can be performed the next day (Kenesset HaGedolah). The primary opinion follows the first view, and even Terumat HaDeshen concludes this way, see there. (On the contrary, he critiques someone who wanted to say that circumcision takes precedence, and when there is not enough time, he did not write at all, only in a case of doubt if there is enough time. And in this case, it is certainly so, that we do not postpone a doubtful circumcision because of a certain reading of the Megillah, since circumcision can also be done the next day, which is not the case with the Megillah. But when there is certainly no time, circumcision takes precedence because its primary mitzvah is on the eighth day, see there. Examine and you will find it easy.)

What is the time for its reading? As it is taught at the beginning of the Megillah: The Megillah is read on the eleventh, on the twelfth, on the thirteenth, on the fourteenth, on the fifteenth, no less and no more. And we derive it from what is written: "To confirm these days of Purim in their times" – the sages established many times for them. And these are the times for its reading: Any city that was surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua son of Nun, whether in the Land of Israel or outside the Land, even if it does not have a wall now – they read the Megillah there on the fifteenth of Adar. And this is called a "walled city." And any city that was not surrounded by a wall from the days of Joshua, even if it is surrounded now – they read it on the fourteenth, and this is called a "city." And Shushan the capital, even though it was not surrounded by a wall in the days of Joshua – they read it on the fifteenth, because the main miracle happened there on the fifteenth, as it is written: "And the Jews who were in Shushan gathered... and rested on the fifteenth of it."

The reason for the distinction in this mitzvah between unwalled cities and walled cities is because the primary miracle did not occur equally in both. As it is written: "And the rest of the Jews who were in the king's provinces gathered... on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar, and rested on the fourteenth, and made it a day of feasting and rejoicing. And the Jews who were in Shushan... rested on the fifteenth, and made it a day of feasting and rejoicing." Therefore, the unwalled cities, who dwell in unwalled cities, celebrate the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of joy and feasting and a festival, and sending portions... This is what is written afterwards: "And he sent letters to all the Jews... to establish for them the fourteenth day of the month of Adar, and the fifteenth day of the same, every year, as the days on which the Jews rested from their enemies..." This means that they established these two days, the fourteenth for the unwalled cities and the fifteenth for the walled cities. The reason is explained: "As the days on which they rested," meaning that the miracle for the unwalled cities occurred on the fourteenth, when they rested from their enemies, and for the walled cities, the miracle occurred on the fifteenth, like Shushan, where they did not rest until the fifteenth, and on the fifteenth, they rested.

And perhaps you will say: Why indeed is the rest not equal? However, this matter is clarified from the Megillah itself, as it is written: "In the twelfth month... on the thirteenth day of it, on the day that they were to destroy... it was turned to the opposite... the Jews gathered... and no one could stand before them." Consequently, they rested after this day and made the fourteenth day a day of feasting and joy. However, it is later written: "And Esther said... let it be granted to the Jews who are in Shushan to do tomorrow according to today's decree... and the Jews who were in Shushan gathered also on the fourteenth day of the month of Adar... Therefore, since they were occupied with war on the fourteenth day as well, it follows that their rest was not until the fifteenth day. Hence, all walled cities learned from Shushan, which was also a walled city, to observe Purim on the fifteenth day, and the unwalled cities on the fourteenth day. And even though we attribute the surrounding of a wall to the days of Joshua son of Nun – this is for another reason, as will be explained. Nevertheless, the main reason is: since Shushan was a walled city, all other walled cities compared themselves to Shushan, and all unwalled cities to the fourteenth day. (And this is the intention of the Ran at the beginning of Megillah. And this resolves the difficulty of the Beit Yosef, see there. Be precise and you will find the truth.)

And why did they attribute the walled cities from the days of Joshua? We should have attributed them from the days of Ahasuerus, like Shushan. The Jerusalem Talmud states: To honor the Land of Israel, meaning that the Land of Israel was desolate in those days. Since they needed to establish a distinction between walled and unwalled cities, if they had established the walled cities from the days of Ahasuerus, the entire Land of Israel would have been considered unwalled, without even one fortified city, which would be the greatest dishonor. Therefore, they established it from the days of Joshua. (And the Ramban, of blessed memory, wrote that at that time, most of Israel was in the Land of Israel from the time of Cyrus, and the walled cities thought they were not in danger because they were fortified like strongholds. Therefore, it is written only, "Therefore the unwalled Jews..." And the walled cities were not mentioned at all until God enlightened their eyes, and they found support from the Torah. Mordechai, Esther, and the Men of the Great Assembly stood and established for these on the fourteenth and for those on the fifteenth. And the Ran, of blessed memory, rejected this, see there. And it seems to me, on the contrary, that the walled cities were in greater danger, and therefore they did not rest until the fifteenth.)

And it is expounded in the Gemara there: Besides the fourteenth and fifteenth, there are three additional times: the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth. This is for the villagers who do not have a permanent synagogue. They only gather in the city on Mondays and Thursdays because of the Torah reading, and also to judge, because the court sits on Mondays and Thursdays as instituted by Ezra in Bava Kamma (82a). The villagers are not proficient in reading the Megillah and need someone from the city to read it for them. The sages did not trouble them to stay and come on the fourteenth day. Sometimes the day of assembly is on the eleventh, sometimes on the twelfth, and sometimes on the thirteenth, as will be explained (Rashi, beginning of Megillah).

How so? If the fourteenth day falls on a Monday or Thursday, it is read on that day like all of Israel. However, if it falls on another day, they advance it and read it on the nearest market day to the fourteenth. How so? If the fourteenth falls on a Sunday, they advance it and read it on Thursday, which is the eleventh day. If it falls on a Tuesday, they read it on the preceding market day, which is the thirteenth day. If it falls on a Wednesday, they advance it and read it on Monday, which is the twelfth day. Similarly, if it falls on a Friday, they read it on Thursday, which is also the thirteenth day. And beyond this, it is not found, as is obvious. And know: all those who advance it are not permitted to read it with fewer than ten men, unlike in its proper time, as I will write in Siman 692.

And since the reason is because of the day of assembly, therefore when the villagers do not customarily go into the city on Mondays and Thursdays, they only read it in its proper time, on the fourteenth. And what defines a "city" and what defines a "village"? We learned in the Mishnah (5:1): What is considered a large city? Any place that has ten idle men. Less than this – it is considered a village. And "idle men" are those who sit day and night in the synagogue and are sustained by the community, so that there will always be ten present for prayer in the synagogue. And even a metropolis, which is a marketplace and many people come to it from outside, if it does not have ten idle men – it is considered a village (3:1). And the Rambam omitted this, and his reason will be explained in section 10. And likewise, we say in the Gemara there: A metropolis that was settled and then fortified – is considered a village. And this too the Rambam did not bring, because he holds like the explanation of Rashi, that this does not refer to the matter of the Megillah but to the matter of walled cities. But the Tosafot there wrote that this is regarding the Megillah, see there.

Maimonides wrote that if there are not ten people present, their solution becomes their problem, and they are considered like the residents of a large city, and therefore they only read on the 14th [of Adar]. So are his words. And the Raavad expressed strong objection to this; see there. However, this is explicitly stated in the Jerusalem Talmud (First Chapter, Halacha 4), and the matter is as follows: The Jerusalem Talmud and Maimonides do not agree with the view of Rashi and Tosafot, which is that the "day of assembly" for the villages is when they enter the city, as we have explained. Rather, they have their own synagogue, but they only gather there on Mondays and Thursdays. Therefore, there must be ten Jews in the village, for if not, they would not gather even on Mondays and Thursdays. Consequently, their status is like that of a city, and they only read on the 14th [of Adar]. This is what is meant by "their solution becomes their problem." That is to say, although when there are not ten, it is a remedy to consider them like a village, as I have written regarding a city without ten idle men, here it is problematic because there are not ten at all. And although from our Talmud it appears to follow Rashi and Tosafot, Maimonides did not concern himself with this, and he holds that our Talmud also interprets like the Jerusalem Talmud.

And this was all in a time when Israel was dwelling on their land, the years were in their proper order, and the court's messengers would go out to inform the people when Purim is and when Passover is, so that they would not come to the stumbling block of chametz on Passover. But in this time, when Israel is scattered and spread out, and our eyes are turned to the reading of the Megillah, and everyone knows that the time of reading the Megillah is on the fourteenth of Adar, and from there thirty days until the eve of Passover – we do not read it even in the villages except in its appointed time. And the practice of reading it before the time on the day of assembly has been nullified. Rather, most of the world reads on the fourteenth and those in walled cities on the fifteenth.

It has already been explained that walled cities from the time of Joshua bin Nun, even if they are not currently walled, read [the Megillah] on the fifteenth [of Adar], even if they are outside of the Land [of Israel]. The Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 1: even if there are not ten idle men [who engage in Torah study and prayer], look there. And despite the fact that in the Gemara (3b) it states that it is judged like a village – this is only if it was not walled from the time of Joshua bin Nun, for then its law is to read on the fourteenth like a city. Therefore, when there are not ten idle men – it is considered like a village. But in a walled city, whose law is to read on the fifteenth – it is never considered like a village. So wrote the Tosafot and the Rosh there. And this is also the opinion of the Rambam, who omitted this law, as I wrote in section 7. But the Ramban and the Rashba hold that this law applies even to a walled city from the time of Joshua bin Nun (see there in the Magid Mishneh and Beit Yosef). And the Ran agreed with the Tosafot, see there. And there is proof for this from the fact that in the Land of Israel, they read in several places on the fifteenth, even though there are not ten idle men. However, one could say that since there are ten men who regularly go to pray every day, morning and evening – it is considered as if there are ten idle men.

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote: specifically, if it was surrounded [by a wall] first and then settled, or if it was settled initially with the intention of surrounding it later. This excludes a case where it was initially settled with the intention not to surround it, but generally, it is surrounded first and then settled. This is their language, as is the custom in most places: they first surround with a wall and then settle them (Ran). They raised a difficulty on this: that earlier in section 406 it was explained the opposite, that first, they build houses and afterward surround with a wall (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). However, this is not a contradiction, for indeed, at first, they build some houses, and afterward, they surround with a wall, and then the main settlement increases. Therefore, earlier, where we only require an enclosure for dwelling, it is called "settled and then surrounded." Since there were some houses, the enclosure is considered for dwelling. But here, regarding a walled city, we require it to be surrounded first and then settled, meaning the main increase in settlement comes after the enclosure (Taz, subsection 2). And this is the truth, which is why in Eruvin, the language used is "enclosed for dwelling" and "not enclosed for dwelling." And in Megillah, the language used is: "settled and then surrounded," "surrounded and then settled," because this refers to the main settlement, not just for dwelling purposes. (Similarly, in Eruvin 24a it says: opened first and then surrounded, surrounded and then opened. And it does not use the term "settled" but "opened" for a few houses. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

It is stated in the Gemara there: A city and everything adjacent to it, and everything visible with it, is considered as part of the city. "Adjacent" even if it is not visible, such as when the village is situated in a valley. "Visible" even if it is not adjacent, such as when it is situated on a mountain. Provided that they are not more than a mil (a certain distance) apart; this applies to "adjacent but not visible." However, "visible but not adjacent" can be even more than a mil. And some say that in both cases the limit is a mil, but on a mountain, the incline is not measured (Taz, subsection 3).

A city that is in doubt whether it was surrounded by a wall during the days of Joshua or not – we read on the fourteenth and fifteenth [of Adar]. And at night, but one should only recite the blessing on the fourteenth, which is the time of reading for the majority of the world, and we follow the majority. In this case, the principle of "fixed" does not apply, as "fixed" only applies when all doubts pertain to a single location, like the case of nine stores (Eliyah Rabbah). Furthermore, even a "fixed" situation is considered as half and half, and how can one recite a blessing out of doubt? This is not similar to the second day of Yom Tov, which is an ordinance of the Sages for the entire world. Here, the Sages did not establish a rule because this is an uncommon situation, and for a distant occurrence, it is not appropriate to make an ordinance (and this resolves the question of the Rashal, brought by the Taz and Magen Avraham in subparagraph 6). Outside of Israel, this doubt does not exist, especially in all our countries which certainly did not exist in the days of Joshua. As for Tiberias, the Gemara (Megillah 5b) says there is a doubt whether the sea adjacent to it is considered as a wall or not, and therefore we read on both days. And similarly, one should only recite the blessing on the fourteenth, like the majority of the world. (And it is possible that in Tiberias, being a doubt of law – one should not bless neither on the fourteenth nor on the fifteenth, according to the opinion of the Rosh in the Tur also regarding other doubts, see there.)

A resident of a city who went to a walled city, and a resident of a walled city who went to a city: If, when he went, he intended to return home on the night of the 14th before dawn, he reads [the Megillah] according to the custom of his place, even if he was delayed there. But if he does not intend to return until after dawn on the 14th, he reads according to the custom of the place he went to. How so? A resident of a walled city who went to a city, if he intended to return home on the night of the 14th, he reads according to the custom of his place, even if he was later delayed in the city. But if he intended to stay there for part of the 14th, since his intention is to stay there for part of the time of the day's reading, the obligation of that time's reading applies to him, and he reads with them. Similarly, a resident of a city who went to a walled city: if he intended to return home on the night of the 14th before dawn, he reads according to the custom of his place. But if he intended to stay there for part of the 14th, since he did not intend to return to his place at the time of his place's obligation, the obligation of his place's reading is lifted from him, and he is considered as the residents of the place he is staying, to be obligated at the time of their reading (Tur). This depends on part of the day of the 14th, and not the night, because the main obligation of the reading is during the day, as I wrote in Siman 687. Furthermore, in all matters, when one leaves his place for another city, it depends only on his intention to return, and not on the actual return, even if it is much later. So why here does the return depend only on part of the day of the 14th? Rather, our Sages of blessed memory derived this from a verse in the Megillah (Megillah 19a) where it is written: "Therefore the Jews of the open cities, who live in the unwalled towns, make the 14th day..." The phrase "who live in the unwalled towns" is superfluous, because since it is written "the Jews of the open cities," it is understood that they live there. Rather, it comes to teach that an unwalled city's resident for a day is considered an unwalled city's resident, meaning that even if he resides in the unwalled city only for the 14th day, he is considered as an unwalled city's resident. And part of the day is considered as the whole day. Consequently, an enclosed city's resident for a day, or part of a day, is considered an enclosed city's resident, and therefore part of the day is necessary.

However, according to this, it would seem that a resident of a city who went to a walled city, who would be considered as the inhabitants of the walled city, would need to have intended to be there for part of the fifteenth day. Then the obligation of the walled city would apply to him, and not just if he intended to be there for part of the fourteenth day. Indeed, Rashi of blessed memory explained it this way, that a resident of a walled city who went to a city depends on part of the fourteenth day, and a resident of a city who went to a walled city depends on part of the fifteenth day, see there. However, the Rosh of blessed memory disagrees with him and holds that also for a resident of a city who went to a walled city, it depends on part of the fourteenth day. For if he intended to be there for part of the fourteenth day in the walled city, the obligation of the city resident leaves him, and the obligation of the walled city resident applies to him; even if he left there and was in his city on the fifteenth day, he reads in his city on the fifteenth as if he were in the walled city. And this is the path that the Tur followed, see there.

From the words of the Rambam in the first chapter, halacha 10, it becomes clear according to Rashi, who wrote: A city resident who went to a walled city, and a walled city resident who went to a city: if it was his intention to return to his place at the time of reading, but he was delayed and did not return – he reads as per his place. And if it was not his intention to return until after the time of reading – he reads with the people of the place where he is. Until here are his words, and "time of reading" clearly means the reading time of the place. And this is according to Rashi and not according to the Rosh, for according to the Rosh, he would need to say "at the time of the reading of the fourteenth." And so wrote the Maggid Mishneh and the Kesef Mishneh, see there. And this is also the intent of our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 5. (And the words of the Taz in subsection 6 are not clear to me, see there). And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: that if he is in the desert or on a ship – he reads on the fourteenth day like most of the world. Until here are his words. Meaning: that a walled city resident who was in the desert or on a ship – does not read on the fifteenth, for he is not better off than if he were in the city on the fourteenth day. And in this matter, the desert and the ship are considered like a city and not like a walled city, because most of the world is like this. Nevertheless, it appears to me: that if he is destined to come on the fifteenth to his home – he should not read on the fourteenth. For while it is understandable that when he is in the city on the fourteenth, the obligation of the people of that place applies to him. But at sea and in the desert – there is no obligation there, except that if he is there also on the fifteenth, then naturally his obligation is like most of the world. And this is the intent of our teacher, the Rema.

According to our calendar, it is impossible for the fourteenth day [of Adar] to fall on Shabbat. However, the fifteenth can fall on Shabbat, and the Sages forbade those in walled cities from reading the Megillah on Shabbat, as a decree lest one might carry it four cubits in the public domain, similar to the suspensions of the shofar and lulav when they fall on Shabbat. So what should the residents of walled cities do? They read the Megillah on the fourteenth, which is Friday, and also give gifts to the poor on that day, because it is impossible to give money on Shabbat since it is muktzeh (set aside and not to be handled). On the previous Shabbat, they read the portion "Zachor" along with the haftarah "Pakad Pakadeti." In places where it is customary to collect and distribute money to the poor, they collect and distribute it on the fourteenth, which is Friday. On Shabbat, they take out two Torah scrolls, reading the regular portion from one and "Vayavo Amalek" from the other, and the haftarah is "Pakad Pakadeti." They recite "Al HaNissim" and the festive meal is held after Shabbat. This is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud, and accordingly, the sending of food portions is also the next day. There are some who disagree, but one should not deviate from the words of the Jerusalem Talmud. Although the Megillah is not read on Shabbat, inquiries and discussions about the day’s significance are allowed. Some say the Megillah is muktzeh and forbidden to handle (Pri Chadash). This is puzzling: is it not fit for study, and do we not inquire and discuss its significance on this day? Similarly, on all Shabbatot, it is considered like the rest of the Prophets and the Writings (as also stated by the author of Machatzit HaShekel).

The one who travels by sea or goes out in a caravan and will not have a Megillah on Purim – should read it on the thirteenth, or the twelfth, or the eleventh, which are the times for the villages as explained. And he should read without a blessing, as this is only to remember in general. And there are those who say that ten people are required, as for reading not at its proper time, ten are required (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 13). But I do not understand: since it is without a blessing, it is only like regular study, and it is not an enactment of the sages at all. Therefore, some say that if it is impossible for him to wait until these days – he can read even from the beginning of the month, just as a general remembrance. However, if he later comes across a Megillah on the fourteenth day – he should read it again with a blessing, as the previous reading was meaningless, as I have written. And even if he read it on the thirteenth day – it is meaningless, as it was not in its proper time. Similarly, a city dweller who was on the road on the fourteenth and did not have a Megillah, and later came across one on the fifteenth – he should read it on the fifteenth, since it is the time for walled cities. It appears to me that he should read without a blessing, and therefore does not need ten people. And some say he should read with a blessing (Taz, subparagraph 9), but in my humble opinion, this does not seem correct.

It is taught in the Tosefta of Megillah (Chapter Two): Everyone is obligated in the reading of the Megillah: Kohanim, Levites, Israelites, freed slaves, chalalim, Nethinim, and mamzerim, a man-made eunuch and a naturally-born eunuch, one with crushed testicles and one with a severed member – all are obligated and can fulfill the obligation on behalf of the many… Women, slaves, and minors are exempt and cannot fulfill the obligation on behalf of the many. So far its language. However, we hold that women are also obligated, even though it is a time-bound commandment, because they too were part of that miracle. And the language of the Tosefta is also imprecise, for since they are exempt – it is obvious that they cannot fulfill the obligation on behalf of the many. Therefore, it seems that it should be stated: they are obligated, but cannot fulfill the obligation on behalf of the many. And so wrote the Tur in the name of the Behag, and similarly wrote the Shulchan Aruch in the name of some opinions. And the reason is: because it is not an honor for the congregation, just as with a Torah scroll – a woman does not read in public because of the honor of the congregation (see Magen Avraham, subsection 5). Another reason will be explained in section 5.

And all of these: chalalim (those with a blemish making them unfit for priestly service), saris (eunuchs), petzu'a daka (those with crushed testicles) – it is not understood what the novelty (chiddush) is here, and what reasoning there is that would exempt them from reading the Megillah, as it teaches us that they are obligated. And perhaps because it is written in the Megillah: "The Jews confirmed and accepted upon themselves and their descendants," and I might say that the obligation is only on those who have descendants, and therefore a saris, petzu'a daka, and k'rut shofcha (those with severed genitals), who are not fit to produce offspring – are exempt. And similarly, I might say that we require legitimate offspring, excluding chalalim, nethinim (Gibeonites who were servants in the Temple), and mamzerim (those born from certain prohibited relationships), who are illegitimate offspring. It teaches us that this is not a requirement. The obligation of freed slaves is because it is written: "And all who joined them." Therefore, converts (in ancient times) are also obligated in the Megillah. And slaves who are not freed – their status is like that of women in all of Torah law. And the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch wrote "freed" slaves, implying that if they are not freed – they are exempt. However, it can be said that these are included in the category of women. (In Magen Avraham, Section 2, and in Machatzit Hashekel, it is written: according to the explanation that they were also part of the miracle, which was performed through them – slaves are not obligated. And if it is because they were also in danger – they are obligated. See there, and see Bach.)

And since women are obligated, therefore, young girls who have reached twelve years and one day are obligated to hear the reading of the Megillah. Every person should read at home before the women and young girls, or they should go to a women's synagogue. And in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is mentioned that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi would gather his household and read before them. From here, some places have the custom to bring young boys and girls to the reading of the Megillah (Tur). And our Rabbi, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 6 that it is a good custom, see there. However, they should be careful not to bring very young children, as they distract the listeners, and also to warn them to stay in their place, listen, and be silent. And a minor who has reached the age of education – the father is obligated by law to educate him. And the Rambam and the Shulchan Aruch wrote: And we educate the minors to read it, see there. And it is obvious that it is not literal, and the intention is that they hear the reading of the Megillah. (And it is possible that the intention is actual reading, so that they become proficient in it.)

Both the one who reads and the one who listens to the reader fulfill their obligation, provided they hear the entire reading from beginning to end. This is specifically when they hear from a reader who is obligated to read it, for in such a case, even if the reader has already read and fulfilled his own obligation, he can read for others; this follows the rule for all blessings on commandments, that even if one has already fulfilled his own obligation, he can still fulfill it for others. However, if one listens from someone who is not obligated in the matter, such as a deaf person, an imbecile, or a minor, the listener does not fulfill his obligation, for anyone who is not obligated in a matter cannot fulfill the obligation for someone who is obligated. There is an opinion that validates a deaf person (Beit Yosef), but this is not the main opinion. Rather, even after the fact, it is invalid (Taz, subparagraph 1; and from the Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3, it seems to agree with the Beit Yosef, but it is proper to be stringent).
