This specifically applies to someone who is completely deaf. However, someone who is hard of hearing and can only hear with a loud voice or with a hearing tube can fulfill the obligation with his reading, and he himself fulfills his obligation even though he does not hear it with his own ear (Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Shevut Yaakov and Pri Chadash, see there).

It would seem that a woman, since she is obligated, can also fulfill the obligation for men by her reading. Nevertheless, there are those who say that women cannot fulfill the obligation for men. The reason is due to the honor of the congregation, as I wrote in section A. Therefore, even for an individual, she cannot fulfill the obligation, because we do not differentiate (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). There is another reason for this: our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section B that there are those who say that if a woman reads for herself, she should bless "to hear the Megillah," because she is not obligated in its reading. These are his words. The explanation is: the Mordechai at the beginning of Megillah brought that the Bahag holds: women are obligated in hearing the Megillah, but not in its reading. According to this, the Tosefta we brought in section A, that women are exempt from reading the Megillah, is understood, because their obligation is only in hearing. According to this, it is also understood why they cannot fulfill the obligation for men, because they are not obligated in reading. However, the main point is not understood: why are they obligated in hearing, but not in reading? It seems to me that the Bahag holds that it is impossible to say that the reason they were also involved in the miracle is a complete obligation like men. If so, why do we need the comparison of "do not eat chametz" for the obligation of matzah for women in Pesachim (43b)? Let us say it is because they were also involved in the miracle (Tosafot Megillah 4a). Therefore, it certainly is not a complete obligation like men for reading, but hearing suffices. Also, for Chanukah, we can say their obligation is not in lighting but in seeing the Chanukah candle, unless she has a husband, in which case she lights for her husband. Therefore, they do not fulfill the obligation for men by their reading. However, women can fulfill the obligation for other women, since their obligation is the same. (See Magen Avraham, subsection 6, in the name of Midrash HaNe'elam: that even for herself, a woman should not read, but should hear from a man. We must say that he holds that reading was not instituted for them, and this requires further study. The opinion of Rashi and Tosafot at the beginning of Arakhin is that women can indeed fulfill the obligation for men, and so is the opinion of many poskim and the Rambam.)

The Tur and Shulchan Aruch wrote in Section 3: An androgynous person can fulfill the obligation for others of their kind, but not for those who are not of their kind. A tumtum, and one who is half-slave – even for their own kind they cannot fulfill the obligation. This is their wording. The reason is because an androgynous person – everyone is equal. This is not the case with a tumtum, as one could be male and the other female. Similarly, one who is half-slave cannot fulfill the obligation for someone who is completely free, because the slave part cannot fulfill the obligation for the free part. This law is found in the Tosefta at the beginning of Megillah. It appears that this is only according to the opinion of Behag, who holds that women cannot fulfill the obligation for men. Otherwise, why wouldn't an androgynous person fulfill the obligation for those not of their kind, and why wouldn't a tumtum fulfill the obligation for another tumtum?

There are those who say that this is worse than a definite female, because it must be distinguishable whether one is male or female (Beit Yosef). And the reason an androgynous person can fulfill the obligation for their kind is because it is clear to everyone that they are a distinct entity (there). Therefore, also, one who is half-slave and half-free cannot fulfill the obligation for a free person, even though they are obligated from both sides. Nevertheless, since the slave part is not distinguishable by itself, and the free part by itself – they cannot fulfill the obligation for a completely free person. But for themselves – they can fulfill the obligation. For those who hold that a woman cannot fulfill the obligation for others – also for themselves they cannot fulfill the obligation, as the slave part cannot fulfill the obligation for the free part. This is what Rabbeinu the Rema wrote, that there are those who say that even for themselves they cannot fulfill the obligation, and they need to hear it from others. This is his wording, as this is according to Behag who holds that a woman cannot fulfill the obligation for a man. But the fact that they cannot fulfill the obligation for another free person, and similarly that a tumtum cannot fulfill the obligation for another tumtum, and an androgynous person cannot fulfill the obligation for those not of their kind – this is even according to those who hold that a woman can fulfill the obligation for a man (Magen Avraham Section 8 and Section 9). But in truth, this is very difficult, and it appears more correct that according to Rashi and Tosafot, these laws do not apply. And the Tosefta is not the law according to our Talmud (Bach). A clear proof of this is that Rambam did not mention these laws at all, see there, because he holds like Rashi and Tosafot that women are equal to men. Therefore, also a tumtum and an androgynous person can fulfill the obligation for definite males, and similarly, one who is half-slave, as their law is like a woman (so it appears in my humble opinion).

One who hears the Megillah from someone from whom he is forbidden to derive benefit has nonetheless fulfilled his obligation, for mitzvot were not given for benefit. Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in paragraph 5: In a place where there is no quorum, if one person knows and the others do not, one person can fulfill the obligation for all. But if everyone knows, each one should read for himself. This is his language, as he holds that the fact that everyone fulfills their obligation by hearing, even when they are knowledgeable, applies when there is a quorum of ten. But without ten, one does not fulfill the obligation for another, unless the other does not know how to read, which is like a scribe blessing and an unlearned person fulfilling the obligation. But he does not fulfill the obligation for someone knowledgeable. He compares this to prayer, not to the other blessings of mitzvot. However, there are those who disagree, holding that in any case, one person can fulfill the obligation for another, as it is a mitzvah like all other mitzvot, and it is not something of sanctity that requires ten. On the contrary, in such a situation, it is preferable that one read for all, due to "In the multitude of people is the King's glory." Nevertheless, if they wish, each person can read for himself when there are not ten, but it is not necessarily so (Magen Avraham, small paragraph 10). And this is the custom.

The Sages taught in the Mishnah (21a): One who reads the Megillah may do so standing or sitting. Rashi explained: If he wishes, he may stand; if he wishes, he may sit. This implies that even ideally, one may read it while sitting. However, the Jerusalem Talmud questions: Is this only valid after the fact, but not ideally? And it answers that even ideally it is permitted, see there, because the version in the Jerusalem Talmud is: "Standing or sitting – he has fulfilled his obligation," and so wrote the Ran. This is also the version of the Tur who wrote: One who reads the Megillah, whether standing or sitting – he has fulfilled his obligation, implying after the fact, etc., and in the Jerusalem Talmud, it is said that even ideally, etc. Thus far his words.

Maimonides wrote in Chapter 2, Law 7: If one reads [the Megillah] standing or sitting, he has fulfilled his obligation, even in public. However, one should not read sitting in public initially, out of respect for the congregation. Thus is his language. According to this, it is understandable why our holy teacher in the Mishnah used the terms "initially" and "after the fact," meaning that in private, it's permissible even initially, but in public, only after the fact. Additionally, it is permissible for Reuven to read [the Megillah] and Shimon to recite the blessing. This is also mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud, where Rabbi Meir did so. See there. 

One should not start reading the Megillah until he is told "read." However, if there is a designated reader for this purpose, he does not need to wait for the congregation's instruction since he is appointed for this. Moreover, two or more people can read together. Although two voices are generally not discernible, in the case of the Megillah, which is precious, people pay attention, incline their ears, and listen. Nevertheless, this is not the custom. People should be careful to be silent and not assist the reader, as they might listen by heart or from a non-kosher Megillah, which we are concerned might cause them to hear from someone other than the reader and not fulfill their obligation, as I will write in section 9.

The Rashba wrote in a responsum (Siman 467): The listener must hear every single word from the reader. And anyone who holds in his hand a scroll that is not kosher for reading – is much worse off than two people who read together, because he focuses on his reading in that scroll. Thus far his words. That is to say: it is better to listen orally from the reader, or to hold in his hand a kosher scroll. For when he holds a scroll that is not kosher, and he also says the words from his invalid scroll – he will not listen attentively to the reader. And it is not similar to two people reading together, where the listener hears from both – because he himself is not reading. However, when he reads himself – he does not intend to listen to the other reader, and thus he reads from an invalid scroll. Therefore, it is better when he holds a Chumash in his hand to remain silent and only listen to the reader. And thus one of the early authorities wrote: that when the chazzan reads the Megillah – the congregation must be silent and focus their attention on the reader (Beit Yosef). And one should warn the people about this, and see Section 9.

In the Mishnah (19a), there is a disagreement regarding the obligation of reading the Megillah: Rabbi Meir says [one must read] the entire thing, and Rabbi Yehuda says [one must read] "from 'Ish Yehudi' (a Jewish man)." And it is said in the Gemara: the halacha follows the one who says the entire thing. And even according to the one who says "from 'Ish Yehudi'"—it must be written in its entirety. And we learn from this that the entire Megillah must be written completely. Prior to this, it was stated: the Sages taught: if the scribe omitted letters or verses and the reader recited them...—he has fulfilled his obligation. And it raises a difficulty from that which was taught: if there were blurred or torn letters, if their form is recognizable—it is kosher. If not—it is invalid. And it resolves: this refers to the whole thing, this refers to part of it. Meaning: if the whole thing does not have recognizable form—it is invalid, but if part of it— it is kosher. Based on this, the Rashba posed a difficulty: here it is said that if part of it is missing—it is kosher, and afterward it is said that it must be written in its entirety. And up to "Ish Yehudi" would be a minority, and nevertheless it is invalid? And he answered: there is a distinction between its beginning and end and its middle. At the beginning and end—even with a minority missing—it is kosher, and in the middle—it is kosher up to the majority.

Seemingly, his difficulty is not understood: What does one matter have to do with the other? Certainly, if an entire section is missing, it is invalid even if it is a minority, and in this case, it is said that it needs to be written in its entirety. And what they said, that in the case of a minority it is valid, refers to the omission of words or verses, or blurring or tearing. The term "omission" does not apply to an entire section, like many consecutive verses, for this is referred to as a deficiency, and in this case, it needs to be written in its entirety. However, for one verse here and one verse there, the term "omission" applies, and certainly for missing letters and blurring. And it is also explained from the words of the Rambam in the second chapter, see there. And it seems that the intention of the Rashba is similar to this, that the term "omission" does not apply to the beginning and end, only in the middle does the term "omission" apply. And at the beginning and end, the term "deficiency" applies. However, I say that even in the middle, if it is an entire section, it is a deficiency, not an omission. And at the beginning and end, even one verse is a deficiency and invalidates. And perhaps missing a word at the beginning or end is called an omission and not a deficiency, and this requires further study. One should deliberate on this matter.

And the Tur has another approach regarding this matter, as he wrote and this is his language: One must read it entirely and from a written text. If he reads it by heart, he does not fulfill his obligation. Therefore, it must be entirely written before him. This is specifically at the outset, but post facto, if the scribe omitted words, even up to half of it, and the reader recited them by heart, he has fulfilled his obligation. However, if more than half is omitted, even if they are written but blurred and their markings are not recognizable, it is invalid. Thus far is his language. The Tur holds that when it is said that it must be entirely written, that is the ideal. And when it is said that if the scribe omitted words or verses up to the majority it is valid, that is post facto. This is also the opinion of the Rosh there. (And what they questioned the Rosh from what is challenged against Rabbi Chelbo is no question at all. See Taz, subsection 3.)

And our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, in Section 3 combined all the opinions together, writing: "It is necessary that the entire text be written before him initially. However, after the fact, if the scribe omitted words in the middle, even up to half, and the reader recited them by heart – it is valid. But if he omitted the beginning or the end, even a small part – it is not valid. And even in the middle – specifically if he did not omit a complete section. But if more than half, even if they are written but are blurred and their form is not recognizable – it is invalid." Thus are their words.

And now, according to whom do they hold? If according to the opinion of the Rashba, who differentiates between the beginning and end and the middle – he does not differentiate between initially and after the fact, and between a complete section and an incomplete section. And if according to the Rosh – he does not differentiate between the beginning and end and the middle, and also not between a complete section and an incomplete section. And if according to the Rambam, who differentiates between a complete section and an incomplete section, as I wrote in section 5 – he does not differentiate between initially and after the fact, and between the beginning and end and the middle. It seems to me that they fundamentally hold like the Rashba. However, it is certain that even the Rashba agrees that initially the entire Megillah must be properly corrected. They do not need proof for this, as it is obvious that the embellishment of the Megillah requires it to be entirely written beautifully and properly corrected. Even in the matter of a complete section, which is invalid even in the middle – they believe that the Rashba would agree, as I wrote at the end of section 5, because this cannot be called an omission, see there. (See Magen Avraham, small section 5, and this is its explanation: The Kenesset HaGedolah posed the same question as the Taz, asking how the Rashba wrote that it is impossible to differentiate between initially and after the fact, from Rabbi Chelbo's objection regarding writing verse by verse, see there. His words are perplexing: for here the majority is invalid even after the fact. To this, the Magen Avraham answers: Who says there is a difference between majority and minority? In Rabbi Chelbo's case, this is not explained, and what is the objection: let it be said that one is initially and one is after the fact? And if because of the earlier Baraita, which the Talmud differentiates between the whole and part of it – here the Baraita is not brought. Therefore, it is certain that there is no differentiation between initially and after the fact. Nevertheless, it still requires investigation, as it is obvious that the Talmud relies on what was said earlier adjacent to this. However, in truth, the Rashba did not mention initially and after the fact at all, only the Ran explained so. And it seems to me that the Ran interprets the Mishnah: "was writing it, studying it, and correcting it" not like Rashi, who wrote: "or studying it," but rather "writing it, studying it, or correcting it," see there in his interpretation. According to this, it is explained that it was already written, but now he is going over it because it was not yet properly written. According to this, it fits well, see there. Be precise and you will find it easy.)

And we have already written that one who holds in his hand a Megillah that is not kosher should not read along with the reader, but should listen and remain silent, because we are concerned that another person might hear from him and not from the reader, and even he himself might not incline his ears to hear from the reader. There is one who says that he himself can listen (Magen Avraham, section 6). But this is astonishing: Can it be that another person cannot hear from the Shaliach Tzibur (the public reader), but rather it is possible that he might not hear from the Shaliach Tzibur? Here, too, it applies to him himself. And this is what the Poskim said regarding the reason: because of others. The interpretation is that even if he himself says that he is sure he will hear from the reader, in any case, he should not do so because of others. But certainly, he himself should not do so, even if there is no other person, such as when the reader is reading only for him—he should remain silent and listen. And similarly, no person should assist the reader orally. Therefore, those verses that the congregation reads, such as "Ish Yehudi" and "Mordechai Yatza," the reader needs to read them after the congregation has finished, because orally they do not fulfill the obligation, and they need to hear from the reader from a kosher Megillah. (And as I have written—so it is in the responsa of the Rashba that we brought in section 3.)

If one read the Megillah intermittently, meaning with pauses, where he read a bit and then paused, and read and paused, and read from the place he stopped, even if the pause was as long as several hours, he has fulfilled his obligation, even if he conversed in the meantime. However, he is rebuked for his conversation, as I will write in Siman 692. Nonetheless, regarding the reading of the Megillah, he has fulfilled his obligation. This is specifically for the reader. But for the listener, if he conversed in the meantime and consequently did not hear some words from the reader, he certainly has not fulfilled his obligation. He must read it again from the place he stopped until the end. If it was necessary for him to pause, some hold that in the reading of the Shema, if one paused long enough to finish the entire reading, he must start again from the beginning, as I wrote above in Siman 65. It seems that the same rule applies to the Megillah. Or it may be that with the Megillah, since it is called a letter, even in such a case, he does not need to start again from the beginning, just as leniencies are applied for this reason when it is not written according to its proper form. This requires further investigation. Regarding the main ruling, we explained there with the help of Heaven that according to the Rif and the Rambam, even if it was because of an unavoidable circumstance, he does not return to the beginning. See there.

But one who reads out of order in the Megillah has not fulfilled his obligation. This means that if he reads the first verse, then skips the second and reads the third, and afterward reads the second and the fourth – he has not fulfilled his obligation, even if he reads it all. It is as if he did not read it at all, and he must go back and read from the third verse until the end, as it is written: "according to their writing and their appointed times" – just as their appointed times cannot be out of order, for the fifteenth can never come before the fourteenth, so too their writing should not be out of order. And it is also written, "and these days are remembered and celebrated": just as the celebration cannot be out of order, for if one makes the Purim feast, sends portions of food, and gifts to the poor before the fourteenth – it is nothing; so too the remembrance of the Megillah out of order is nothing (17:1). Therefore, if one missed one verse, for example, the second verse, and started with the third – he must go back to the second and read from there in order, the third and fourth until the end. And it has already been explained that it must be read entirely from the written text, and if one reads it by heart – he has not fulfilled his obligation. Therefore, if he read the second verse by heart, and afterward read the third from the Megillah – he has not fulfilled his obligation, and he must go back and read from the Megillah from the second verse in order until the end. (And this is the intention of the Beit Yosef in paragraph 7 who wrote this law again. The Magen Avraham was puzzled in subparagraph 8, and his explanation is perplexing. But his intention is as I wrote, and it refers to the previous paragraph. Examine and you will find it simple.)

The Megillah can be read in any language, provided that the reader understands that language and it is written in that language. For if it is written in Hebrew and read in a foreign language, it is considered as reading by heart. However, with regard to the script, it is not necessary to be particular about in which script it is written. Therefore, if it was written in translation or in another language of the nations, one does not fulfill their obligation by reading it, except for someone who understands that language. And if it was written in Hebrew script and read in Aramaic for those who understand Aramaic, one does not fulfill their obligation, for it is like reading by heart. And since the reader does not fulfill their obligation, it follows that the listener does not fulfill their obligation either. There is a doubt: if the reader has already fulfilled their obligation and reads to fulfill another's obligation from a Megillah written in a foreign language, and the listener understands that language but the reader does not, does the listener fulfill their obligation or not? It seems to me that the listener does fulfill their obligation, for in this case, it cannot be said: since it does not benefit the reader themselves, how can it benefit others through their reading? Certainly, it would also benefit the reader if they understood the language. The lack of knowledge is not an intrinsic deficiency in the reader that would render them unfit, for they could learn the language if they studied it.

And specifically in a foreign language, they need to understand the language. But an uneducated person who hears the Megillah written in Hebrew, even though he does not understand Hebrew at all, fulfills his obligation by hearing it word for word, provided that the Megillah was written according to the rules of sacred writings, as will be explained in the next section. And in the Gemara (18a) they brought a proof for this: for if you do not say so, do we know the meaning of "the royal scribes, the sons of the stallions"? Rather, the commandment is the reading and the publicizing of the miracle, and therefore even someone who does not understand it at all also fulfills his obligation. And one should not say: if so, how can one fulfill the obligation with a Megillah written in a foreign language for someone who understands that language? For it is impossible to translate "the royal scribes, the sons of the stallions" into a foreign language since we do not know what it means. And it must be said: these exact words should be written without translation (see Beit Yosef). And even though according to this, the writing is in two languages – we do not find this to be invalid. And know that Rambam permits a Megillah written in Greek as in Hebrew. And many disagree with him. But even Rambam himself wrote in the first chapter of Tefillin that the clear Greek language has already been lost and forgotten, see there. And it is obvious that a Megillah in a foreign language must be written according to the grammar of that language, on parchment, with proper ink, and all the details that will be explained in the next section.

It is explained in the Jerusalem Talmud that one who fulfills his obligation in a foreign language does so only if he understands that language and does not understand Hebrew. But if he understands Hebrew, he does not fulfill his obligation with a foreign language. For it says there: "One who reads [the Torah] and knows Hebrew as well as a foreign language, can he fulfill the obligation for others who know only the foreign language?" And it concludes there that anyone who is not obligated in a matter cannot fulfill the obligation for the public. Since he himself would not fulfill his obligation in such a manner, he cannot fulfill it for others either. This is also the ruling of the Ramban and the Rashba, of blessed memory. However, from the words of Rashi and the Rambam, it appears that he does fulfill his obligation. The Ran elaborated in challenging the opinions of the Ramban and the Rashba. In the responsa of the Rivash (Siman 370), the Ran, of blessed memory, elaborated to reconcile the words of the Jerusalem Talmud with those of Rashi and the Rambam. Indeed, there are variant texts in the Jerusalem Talmud at the beginning of the second chapter of Megillah and the seventh chapter of Sotah regarding this matter, see there. If it was written in two foreign languages, one who understands both languages fulfills his obligation. But if he understands only one, he does not fulfill his obligation, for what is written in the second language is considered missing for him.

All of this is based on the fundamental ruling. However, in practice, it is entirely impossible to fulfill the obligation with a Megillah written in a foreign language. We have never heard of such a thing in our times, and it is almost an impossibility. Not only according to the opinion that one who understands Hebrew does not fulfill the obligation with a foreign language, but even otherwise, it is difficult. For it must be written according to the precise rules of that language, and if not, it is invalid. Furthermore, what will be done with the phrase "האחשתרנים בני הרמכים"? To translate it is impossible, as I have written, and to write it as it appears in the Megillah – it is certainly not correct to write in two languages initially. And even though the Megillah contains some phrases of Targum (Aramaic translation) – that is not considered two languages, as Targum is close to Hebrew. Moreover, how is it possible to write in another language initially? It is certain that initially, it should be read with the cantillation notes, and this is only possible in Hebrew.

And this is what Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in section 11: One should protest against those who read the Megillah to women in a foreign language, even though it is written in a foreign language. Until here is his wording. And [the term] "women" is not specific, but rather because this was the custom in some place, as the Rivash wrote there. And the reasons are as I have written. And it is good that the Ran wrote on this, and this is his wording: Surely every intelligent person, even in worldly matters, would choose the safer path, and how could we not do so with the commandments of the Holy One, blessed be He? And we should only follow the ways of our holy forefathers. And regarding such matters it is said: "Do not forsake the teaching of your mother."

If one recited [the Shema] while dozing, since he did not fully fall asleep, he has fulfilled his obligation. What is the definition of dozing? It is being in a state of neither fully awake nor fully asleep; if called, he responds, but he cannot give a coherent answer. Even though it is possible that due to the dozing he does not fully comprehend, he nevertheless has fulfilled his obligation, as I have written, even if he does not understand the meaning. However, if one hears [the Shema] while dozing, he has not fulfilled his obligation, because he will certainly miss several words in his listening. And it has already been explained that even if he misses one word, he has not fulfilled his obligation. There is no difference in dozing whether at the beginning of sleep or at the end of sleep (Taz, Section 8), unlike some who make this distinction.

If someone is writing a Megillah, meaning he has before him a kosher Megillah and reads from it one verse and transcribes it into the Megillah he is writing, and does so with each verse until the end; if he intended to fulfill his obligation – he has fulfilled it. And even though he pauses in writing between each verse – it does not matter, as we have already written that he fulfills his obligation even with interruptions. This is specifically when the Megillah from which he is transcribing is entirely written according to halacha. But if he did not intend to fulfill his obligation – he has not fulfilled it, for even if mitzvot do not require intention, the reading of the Megillah does require intention, for otherwise it is as if he did not read at all. Similarly, if he had before him a Megillah that is not corrected, and he reads it to correct it – he has fulfilled his obligation if he intended to fulfill it. For even though there are errors in it – it does not invalidate the Megillah, as I have written, for even if it is missing letters or words – it is kosher if less than half is missing. This is why it is called an "epistle," and it is not similar to a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzot, where even one letter being missing invalidates them. Similarly, if someone is reading the Megillah and reads a verse and interprets or explains it – he has fulfilled his obligation if he intended to fulfill it, for the same reason explained. However, he should not interrupt with other matters while interpreting it, for it is prohibited to initially interrupt with other matters.

The one who reads the Megillah must have the intention to fulfill the obligation on behalf of the listener, and the listener must have the intention to fulfill their obligation through the reader's recitation. One must ensure to hear the entire reading. If even one word is missed, the obligation is not fulfilled. It is sufficient to have the intention to fulfill the obligation at the beginning; it is not necessary to have this intention for every word. And if one did not understand the meaning, it is not a concern, as I have written.

When the reader needs to intend to fulfill the obligation for the listeners, this is when reading at home in front of some people or women. In such a case, the reader must intend to fulfill the obligation for all those listening. However, a public reader in a synagogue, even without specific intention, is considered to intend for all listeners, including those standing outside behind the synagogue, because he has been designated as the public reader to fulfill the obligation for all listeners. As we have learned in Rosh Hashanah (27b): "Similarly, if one was passing behind a synagogue or if his house was adjacent to the synagogue, and he heard the sound of the shofar or the sound of the Megillah, if he intended in his heart, he fulfills his obligation, etc." But the public reader's intention to fulfill the obligation for the listener is not needed.

And what we have said, that the reader must intend to fulfill the obligation for them, is because we hold that mitzvot require intention, as I have written in Siman 589 regarding the shofar (Beit Yosef). One might ask, according to those who hold that for Rabbinic mitzvot everyone agrees that they do not require intention (Magen Avraham Siman 60, subsection 3), and the Megillah is a Rabbinic mitzvah? We must say that since it is from the Writings, statements of acceptance are considered like Torah law in this regard. However, according to what I have written above in Siman 60, subsection 6, that some of the early authorities said that for a mitzvah involving speech, all agree that intention is required, see there – it fits straightforwardly.

It is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud in the second chapter: We do not scrutinize mistakes. Rabbi Yitzchak and Rav Chananel were sitting before Rav. One read "Yehudim" and the other read "Yehudiyim." And he did not correct them, even though one was certainly mistaken, because it suffices that it is called a "letter." And some say this applies specifically to mistakes where the meaning does not change, like "Yehudim" and "Yehudiyim." But where the meaning changes, such as from "yoshev" (sitting) to "yashav" (sat) and from "nofel" (falling) to "nafal" (fell), where one is in the past and one in the present—he should be corrected. According to this, I say that, although it is obvious, if he erred in the cantillation marks, he should not be corrected, and similarly, if he mistook a stress (mel’eil) for a different stress (mel’ra); however, in cases where the meaning changes, such as "she came to bring Vashti... but she did not come" which is stressed in the past (mel’eil), but "and this maiden comes to the king" and "in the evening she comes" which are stressed in the present (mel’ra), if he changed it, it is like changing the meaning, and he should be corrected. However, if after the fact he was not corrected—it seems that in all cases he has fulfilled his obligation, and also in "yoshev" and "yashav" and "nofel" and "nafal," since he said the essential words.

It is stated in the Gemara (16b): The ten sons of Haman and the word "ten" must be recited in one breath. What is the reason? Because all their souls departed together. This means that although they were hanged one after another, nevertheless, by Divine providence, their spirits all departed at the same moment, in the manner of "Let sinners cease out of the earth, and let the wicked be no more. Bless the Lord, O my soul, Hallelujah." And it is clear that this is only ideally; however, if one interrupted between them after the fact, he has fulfilled his obligation. Ideally, one should say in one breath from "five hundred men and Parshandatha" until "ten." And "ten" is included, because the ten sons of Haman were leaders of fifty over these "five hundred men" (Mahari"l). Ideally, one should not pause even between verses except for the time it takes to breathe. And between sections, one should pause for a few moments, as it must be read like a letter (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 17). When saying "On that night the king could not sleep," one should raise their voice, as that was the main part of the miracle (there). And when saying "this letter," one should shake the Megillah (there). And in all these matters, there is no element of essential requirement, as understood.

Since it is called a "letter," therefore the custom among all Jews is that the reader unrolls it before reading it like a letter, to show the miracle. However, the listener, even if he holds a kosher Megillah for himself, does not need to unroll it like a letter and can hold it rolled up. And so did the Mahari"l (there, small section 18). And the reader, after finishing the reading, rolls it back up completely and recites the blessing "Who takes up our grievance," and this is not considered an interruption. Moreover, the blessing "Who takes up our grievance" is not directly related to the Megillah; rather, it is a blessing of thanksgiving to the Holy One, blessed be He (there, small section 19, and see Magen Avraham). Afterwards, "Shoshanat Yaakov" is recited. According to the Jerusalem Talmud, one should say there, "Cursed is Haman, blessed is Mordechai; cursed is Zeresh, blessed is Esther; cursed are all the wicked, blessed are all the righteous." And one must say, "And also Charvonah, may he be remembered for good." And even though according to the Midrash, Elijah appeared in his form, nevertheless, since he appeared in the form of Charvonah, we mention him for good. (And the reason "Cursed is Haman" precedes "Blessed is Mordechai" is because his wickedness came first, and the matter is like "The memory of the righteous is for a blessing, and the name of the wicked shall rot" when mentioning "shall rot." And I am astonished that in the prayer books, they did not print "Cursed are all the wicked, blessed...")

The custom is that the congregation recites four verses of redemption aloud, and afterwards the reader goes back and reads them from the Megillah. For what was said by heart, they have not fulfilled their obligation. And these are the verses: "A Jewish man," "And Mordechai went out," "The Jews had light," "For Mordechai the Jew." Also, "five hundred men" until "the ten" (and "the ten" included) are said by the congregation, because in this lies the main salvation. The custom that children strike at "Haman" is an ancient custom. However, they should be careful not to strike loudly with large pieces of wood, which disrupts the reading of the Megillah, and they open their mouths with laughter and noise, and the listeners cannot hear properly. If it is impossible to stop them, it is better to read at home with a quorum, even though in the synagogue there is a large congregation and the glory of the king. But since the disruption is great, it is impossible to hear properly, especially for the women.

And this is the language of our teacher, the Rema, in paragraph 17: It is also written that children customarily draw the image of Haman on wood and stones, or write the name "Haman" on them, and strike them against each other, so that his name is obliterated in the manner of "you shall blot out the memory of Amalek" and "the name of the wicked shall rot." From this, the custom developed to strike Haman when the Megillah is read in the synagogue. No custom should be abolished or ridiculed, for they were not established without reason. This is the end of his words. The custom is to strike when "Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite" is mentioned, in the manner of "from the wicked comes forth wickedness," "and from the root of a snake comes forth a viper." Any custom established by the great ones of the generation is a custom, and not a practice that people adopted on their own. Refer to what I wrote above in Siman 668. And when they strike "Haman," they should not read but remain silent. (In the end of chapter fourteen of Masechet Sofrim it states: A custom that has no basis in Torah is considered an error in judgment.)

The halachic ruling follows Rav (Megillah 5a) that the Megillah, when read at its proper time, can be read even by an individual. This is contrary to Rav Assi there, who holds that ten people are required, except for the Ba'al Halachot Gedolot who rules like him, and his opinion is considered singular. From Rashi, Rabbeinu Tam as quoted by the Tur, and the Ba'al HaMaor, it is clear that even initially, ten people are not required. Since on this day everyone reads, there is publicizing of the miracle even with an individual. However, from the Rif, the Rambam, the Rosh, and the Ramban, it is understood that certainly for the enhancement of the mitzvah and publicizing the miracle, even Rav agrees that ten people are preferable. Only when ten are not available is it permissible to read individually, and to bless on the Megillah before and after. This is also the custom of the world. The larger the congregation, the greater the enhancement, as "in the multitude of the people is the king's glory." However, if in the synagogue it is not possible to hear well due to the confusion from the beating of "Haman" and the like, it is better to read with ten people at home. There is a doubt whether women join to make up the ten, and it appears that they do not. If it was read in public and an individual did not hear it, he can read it even initially by himself, since it is read in that city with ten, and we do not trouble him to gather ten people, which is difficult, since everyone heard it in the synagogue. We have already written that when an individual reads it at its proper time, he must bless on it at the beginning and the end. It has also been clarified that he must read at home for the women and girls if they did not go to the synagogue, for their obligation in reading the Megillah is equal to that of men.

A megillah is called a "book," as it is written: "and it was written in a book." Therefore, its writing is like that of a Torah scroll. This is what we have learned in the Mishnah (Megillah 17a): If it was written with sam, sikra, komos, or kankantom; on paper or on diftera - it is not valid until it is written in Assyrian script, on a book, and with ink. Therefore, one may only write the megillah with ink, on gevil or klaf, like a Torah scroll. And so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud, the first chapter of Megillah: And if it was written with gall water or kankantom water - it is valid. However, for gall water, it needs gum (Taz). And if it was written with other types of dyes - it is invalid, for we require ink, like for a Torah scroll. It also needs scoring like a Torah scroll itself, which means to score each and every line, not like those who say it is enough to score only the top line (Levush and Magen Avraham, and they were refuted by the Gra and the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger. And so it is written in the Darkei Moshe).

Maimonides ruled that it does not require tanning for its sake. However, Rabbeinu Tam ruled that it does require tanning for its sake, and this is also the ruling of the Rosh, the Tur, and the majority of the decisors. The rationale of Maimonides appears to follow his own reasoning, as he ruled in the first chapter of Sefer Torah that a mezuzah does not require tanning for its sake, as only a Sefer Torah and tefillin require tanning for their sake. Consequently, a Megillah is not more stringent than a mezuzah, as it is obvious that its sanctity is not greater than that of a mezuzah, even though it is called a "Sefer." All the decisors disagree with him regarding a mezuzah, and therefore, a Megillah also requires tanning for its sake, and this is the primary ruling in practice (according to the Gra).

If it was written on paper, or on unprocessed leather, or, according to most authorities, if it was not processed for its specific purpose, or if it was written not with ink – it is invalid. Similarly, if it was written by a Samaritan or a heretic – it is invalid. It appears that a woman is also invalid for writing the Megillah, even though she is obligated in its reading, just as she is invalid for writing a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzot; even though she is obligated in mezuzah, and similarly in Megillah (as per the opinion of Rabbi Akiva Eiger). However, there is an opinion that permits it (Baruch Yosef, as cited in Shaarei Teshuva). 

And it seems to me: for a Torah scroll, tefillin, and mezuzot, we derive from the verse “you shall bind them... and you shall write them” – anyone who is included in binding is included in writing, and anyone who is not included in binding is not included in writing. Consequently, a woman, since she is not included in the binding of tefillin, is also not included in the writing of mezuzah, even though she is obligated, because it is one paragraph with tefillin. However, this does not apply to the Megillah. On the contrary: since she is obligated, she is certainly valid for writing it. And indeed, she is permitted to make tzitzit, sukkah, and shofar, even though she is exempt from them, all the more so she can write the Megillah in which she is obligated. This is also implied by the Tur, the Shulchan Aruch, the Rambam, and all the decisors who did not mention a woman as invalid for the Megillah. A minor is certainly invalid, since he is exempt from Megillah, and besides, he does not have the intellectual capacity to write it properly. If it was written with the left hand – it is valid post facto (Pri Chadash).

And other invalidations that apply to a Torah scroll also apply to a Megillah. These include: "Chak Tochot" (engraving the letters by removing surrounding ink), "Hekef Gvil" (letters must be surrounded by parchment), the protrusions of the letters "chet" and "hei" (their unique shapes), the suspension of the letters "hei" and "kuf" (their unique forms), all the structures of the letters in their correct forms, "Keri and Ketiv" (differences between the written and read text), missing or extra letters, and the adornments of the letters "Shatnez Gatz" (certain letters that have crowns). The Ba'al Halachot Gedolot wrote that the Megillah does not require crowns. His reasoning seems to be that since it is also called a "letter" (Igeret), crowns are not appropriate for a letter. However, the custom is to add crowns, and if one did not, it is still permissible to read from it. Similarly, the lines should be even, and the width of the column should be equivalent to three times the word "Lemishpechotechem" (as in a Torah scroll), as well as all other laws of the Torah scroll. Nevertheless, if there are letters and words not surrounded by parchment or other invalidations, it is allowed to read from it, since even if letters and words are missing up to the majority, it is valid, as I wrote in the previous section. All the more so in this case, provided that the majority is not like that.

And there is a doubt: If one wrote many letters, words, and verses in color, in such a way that if they were blurred or missing, it would be valid, for instance, if it was in the minority as I wrote in the previous section, is it also valid if written in color? Similarly, if they were made by engraving (חק תוכות) or something similar, it is not worse than blurring and missing. Or perhaps: It is certainly not comparable to blurring, where they were valid and became defective. And even to missing it is not comparable, as a change is worse than a lack, as we find regarding a get (divorce document), where a change is invalid and a lack is valid. And similarly with a Megillah (Scroll of Esther): perhaps this is considered to have been written invalidly? This requires further investigation.

And it is also necessary to write it from a written text, and to pronounce each word with one's mouth before writing it. And even though above, in Siman 32, regarding tefillin, it was explained that this is not required, see there – this applies only to tefillin, because the passages are familiar to him by heart, which is not the case with a Megillah (the Gra, Siman 16, and this resolves the question of the Magen Avraham, Siman 4). And it is explicitly stated in the Yerushalmi, and we also rule this way in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 274 regarding a Sefer Torah, see there. And all its sections are made closed, and if they were made open – it is invalid. Thus ruled our teacher, the Rema, in Siman 2 in the name of the Hagahot Maimoniyot, Chapter Two. And I do not know the reason. And I saw a wondrous thing in the Or Zarua HaGadol at the end of the first chapter of Megillah, where it initially lists several open and closed sections. And he wrote "on the seventh day" – open, "in the language of his people" – open, and several other sections. And at the end of the matter, he wrote, and these are his words: Regarding the sections, I did not hear if they should be open or closed, and it seems reasonable to make them closed, similar to tefillin and mezuzot, etc. End of quote. And this is contradictory! Besides, his words are puzzling, for in tefillin, they are open, as I wrote in Siman 32. And also in mezuzah, we hold in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 288 that if they were made open – it is valid, see there. Therefore, it appears that also in a Megillah, if they were made open – it is valid, only ideally, they should be made closed, since it emerged from the mouth of the Hagahot Maimoniyot, and the Raaviah, whom the Or Zarua quoted at the end, see there. (And so wrote the Magen Avraham, Siman 5. And the one who cited the Rema referred to the Piskei Maharai, who is the author of Terumat HaDeshen, and I did not find anything in it.)

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 2 that a column is needed at the end [of the Megillah], and a blank space at the beginning, so it can be rolled around it. This is his language. And our master, the Rema, wrote that the custom is not to make a column at the end at all. This is his language, and this is the simple custom. The Tur wrote the opposite, that a column is needed at the beginning, and a blank space at the end, so it can be rolled around it like a Torah scroll. This is his language. However, it is not exactly like a Torah scroll, as a Torah scroll requires two columns because it is read frequently. But for the Prophets and Writings, one column is sufficient, as stated in the first chapter of Bava Batra (13b). It is obvious that a Megillah is not more important than the Prophets and Writings, and one column suffices. In the Gemara there, the version is like the Tur, that the column is at the beginning. However, Tosafot and the Rosh raised many difficulties with this and have the version the opposite way, that the column is at the end. And this is the main opinion, for it is rolled from its beginning, so how could the column be at its head? And so it is in the Jerusalem Talmud in the first chapter of Megillah, that a column is made for the book at its end, and it is rolled on the column from its end to its beginning. This is the language of the Jerusalem Talmud there at the end of Halacha 9: "And a column is made for the book at its end, for the Torah on both sides. Therefore, the book is rolled to its beginning, and the Torah to its middle." This is his language. (The words of Tosafot are in Bava Batra there, and the words of the Rosh are in the third chapter of Yadayim, and so wrote the Rash. Therefore, the Rosh at the end of the first chapter of Bava Batra wrote the version that the column is at its end, but the Rif has the version like Rashi, that it is rolled from its beginning and not to its beginning. So according to the Rif and Rashi, the column is at its beginning. And this is the reason why the world does not make a column at all for the Megillah, because we do not know how to make the column. And it further seems to me, in my humble opinion, that the reason for the world is that in truth, in the Gemara and the Jerusalem Talmud, a column is not mentioned regarding the Megillah, only regarding other books. And they hold that just as other books are less significant than the Torah scroll because their reading is not frequent, and thus they require fewer columns, so too the Megillah, which is read only once a year, does not require any column at all. And in the days of the early authorities, they made a column for the Megillah because they studied it periodically, when there was no printing in the world. But in our case, where it is read only once a year, it does not require a column at all. Be precise and you will find it easy. And it seems to me that it does not require a sheet of three columns, as it is called an "epistle." And in the third chapter of Masechet Sofrim, it states: "One does not reduce the Torah to less than three columns," which implies only for the Torah.

The ten sons of Haman must be written in the form of a song. However, unlike other songs which have a space under the writing and writing under the space, here one leaves a space between each word, so that their downfall will have no recovery (end of first chapter of Megillah). This means: like a building that is partially built at the top of the wall, partially at the bottom, and with a space in the middle, which will naturally cause it to collapse. And in the Jerusalem Talmud there it says that if it is not done this way, it is invalid. This is why we write a word at the beginning of the line and a word at the end of the line with a space in the middle. It also says there that one should write "Ish" at the beginning of the line and "Ve'et" at the end. Then "Parshandata" at the beginning of the line and "Ve'et" at the end, and so on for all of them until "Vaizata." "Vaizata" is written at the beginning and "Aseret" at the end. The "Vav" of "Vaizata" should be extended, both in its writing and also to be extended slightly in its reading. This is also the custom to continue it with a melody. According to this, there are eleven sections in these lines, as they were ten, and "Ish" and "Aseret" were added, as explained in the Jerusalem Talmud there.

And know that regarding the manner of writing them, there is much controversy. For the Levush wrote that "Ish" (the first word of the Megillah) should be at the top of the page, and "Aseret" (the last word of the Megillah) should be at the bottom of the page. This means not only at the beginning of the line and the end of the line, but also the top of the page and the bottom of the page, meaning it should spread across the entire column, and not to write anything else on that page, not even a single word. And this is what they said in the Jerusalem Talmud: "Ish" at the top of the page, "Ve'et" at its end, meaning at the actual end of the page. There are those who wrote that if it was not done this way, it is invalid (Eliyah Rabbah in the name of Knesset HaGedolah). And in this, they have exaggerated. And proof of this is in the Jerusalem Talmud, third chapter of Megillah (Halacha 7), where it first states the law of its writing: "written on top of writing, and in between them blank space," and it says there that if not done so, it is invalid. And afterwards, it states this law of "Ish" at the top of the page, "Ve'et" at its end, and it does not say that if not done so, it is invalid. And so it is in the thirteenth chapter of Massechet Sofrim, see there. From this, it is understood that this is not a requirement.

However, there are those who say that the main issue is a mistake, as the intention is not the end of the page, but the end of the line. Otherwise, there would necessarily be many large letters, and these are not considered 'large letters' in the Masorah (the Gra, Section 25). In truth, the Jerusalem Talmud there only mentions "Ish" at the beginning of the page, "Ve'et" at its end, and does not mention "Aseret" at all. If so, this fits straightforwardly: "Ish" at the beginning of the page – really at the beginning of the page and the beginning of the line, "Ve'et" at the end of the line, and so on for all of them. However, in the Tractate Sofrim, it is mentioned that "Aseret" is at the end of the page; see there. The intention is the end of the line, or this itself is called "the end of the page" in relation to the width of the page (and this resolves the difficulty of the Chayei Adam, and be precise and you will find it easy). This is also explicitly implied in the Or Zarua HaGadol and in the glosses of the Rosh at the end of the first chapter, where they wrote: "Ish" at the beginning of the line, "Ve'et" at the end of the line, and "Sham" on "Sham", "Ve'et" on "Ve'et". Thus far their language, and they did not mention "Aseret" at the end of the page at all. According to this, these eleven sections are written in eleven consecutive lines. The letters are like all other letters, except for the Vav of "Vizata" which is a large Vav. After that, the rest of the Megillah is written on the same page (there). However, in the Masorah of the Book of Esther, it says "Ish" at the beginning of the page, and "Aseret" at the end of the page and the end of the column. Thus far its language, it is clear that "Aseret" is at the end of the column. Therefore, there are those who say that it is not necessary to start "Ish" at the beginning of the page, but rather first write on this page the verses before this. At its end, when only eleven lines are left, write "Ish" at the beginning of the line and "Aseret" at the end of the page (Chayei Adam in the name of the Gra).

However, the custom follows the Levush, as it clearly appears from Massekhet Soferim. The reason it is not listed in the Masorah with large letters seems to be because it is not similar to other large letters mentioned in the Masorah, where the size of the letter has a mystical significance. This is not the case here, where their size is not due to the essence of the letter but because of the lines, as it is not possible in any other way. Consequently, since it was transmitted that "Ish" is at the top of the page, and "Aseret" at the bottom of the page, it is considered like a tradition regarding large letters, as it is impossible otherwise. The truth is that nothing can be proven from the Jerusalem Talmud since it does not mention "Aseret." Nevertheless, since it says "Ish" at the top of the page, it implies the very top of the page. And since in Massekhet Soferim and the Masorah of Esther it is stated that "Aseret" is at the bottom of the page, it follows that this is so. Some also have the version in the Jerusalem Talmud that "Aseret" is at the bottom of the page (see Beit Yosef). Therefore, it seems to me that ideally, one should write only the ten sons of Haman on the whole page, with "Ish" at the top and "Aseret" at the bottom. This is also written by one of the great authorities (Chayei Adam, and it also seems implied in the glosses of the Maimonides, see there).

The Gemara (19a) states: A Megillah is called a "book" and is called a "letter." It is called a "book" because if it is sewn with linen threads, it is invalid. It is called a "letter" because if one inserts three sinew threads, it is valid, provided they are positioned triangularly. Rashi and Tosafot explain that this means from the beginning of the stitching to the place of the first sinew should be the same distance as from there to the second sinew, and from the second sinew to the third should be the same distance as from the third to the end of the stitching. This is their language. Others interpret that the sinew should be placed at the beginning of the sheet, in the middle, and at the end (Tosafot there). Rambam explains: three stitches at the top of the sheet, three in the middle, and three at the bottom. The Rif explains: two at the two ends of the sheet and one in the middle, and the one in the middle should be exactly in the center. To satisfy all opinions, one should make three stitches at the beginning, three at the end, three in the middle, one stitch in the fourth part on one side, and one stitch in the fourth part on the other side. If he does not have more sinews, it is better to sew the remainder with linen threads than to leave it unsewn. But if he has sinews, he should sew the entire thing with sinews. The stitching should be on the outside, not on the inside. One needs to leave a remnant at the beginning and at the end of the sheet when stitching them together, and a small amount suffices, just as with a Torah scroll, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 288, see there. The reason is so that it does not tear. If he did not leave a remnant, it does not invalidate even a Torah scroll, and certainly not a Megillah.

One does not read the Megillah in a congregation of ten if it is written among the other Writings (Ketuvim). For in such a case, there is no publicizing of the miracle, as it is merely like reading from the Writings since it is written among them. If one did read it in this manner, they have not fulfilled their obligation unless it is distinguishable from the other Writings, such as if it is longer or shorter than the other parchments, in which case it is distinguishable. However, an individual may read it and fulfill their obligation even if it is not longer or shorter, for an individual does not require the publicizing of the miracle to the same extent. This is specifically when it is written on a scroll like a Torah scroll in all its details. But if it is not so, it is inherently invalid, even if it stands alone.

And it appears to me: although we do not find a requirement for the Megillah to end in the middle of a page, nevertheless, if on that same page there is writing from other Writings, it is invalid. For a Megillah is only considered valid if no other matter is written on it, besides the Megillah itself.

If dots are placed in the Megillah, or if the cantillation marks are written, or if the blessings of the Megillah and the poem of the Megillah are written on the first page, it does not invalidate it. This is not similar to having a Ketubah among the Scriptures, which is not acceptable for public reading, or to what we have written that other writings invalidate it, because these are related to the Megillah. Nevertheless, it is forbidden initially (Magen Avraham, section 9). According to the Mordechai, even post facto, it is invalid. Our master the Beit Yosef wrote in section 10: If there is no valid Megillah, one reads it from a Chumash without a blessing. So are his words. And specifically a Chumash that is made in a scroll format, and not our printed Chumashim (ibid., section 10). In my humble opinion, it appears that his intention is not to fulfill the obligation of Megillah reading, but rather he means that one should read from a Chumash to remember the miracle, and if so, even our printed Chumashim are acceptable. Some permit writing the cantillation marks in the Megillah if the reader is not proficient in reading it with its cantillation. In my humble opinion, it is better to read it without cantillation than to write the cantillation in the Megillah (see Bach and Magen Avraham there). If one read from a stolen Megillah, he has fulfilled his obligation, as theft does not pertain to sound. Whether it is permissible to recite a blessing over it was discussed earlier in section 649 regarding the lulav, and the same applies here. Refer there. And the main point is: not to recite a blessing, and the blessings are not essential (see Sha'arei Teshuvah at the end of this section).

The one who reads the Megillah recites three blessings beforehand: "concerning the reading of the Megillah," "who performed miracles," and "who has kept us alive." And why do we not bless "to listen to the reading of the Megillah"? Because the reader is only one person, and all the people are listeners, similar to how we bless "to listen to the sound of the shofar." This is not comparable: there, the listening is the main mitzvah, for if one blows the shofar but does not hear it, he has not fulfilled his obligation. But with the Megillah, if one reads it and does not hear it himself, he has fulfilled his obligation, just like with the reading of the Shema. Therefore, the reading is the main aspect, and the listeners are also considered as readers, for "one who hears is as if he responded" (as written in the Or Zarua and Levush). The congregation answers "Amen" to each blessing, but they do not say "Blessed is He and blessed is His name," as this would be an interruption.

And also in the reading of the Megillah during the day, we recite these three blessings. Rambam ruled that during the day there is no need to recite "Shehecheyanu" since it was already recited at night. However, Rabeinu Tam ruled that "Shehecheyanu" must also be recited during the day because the primary mitzvah is during the day, as I wrote in Siman 687. Even though on Sukkot, one fulfills "Shehecheyanu" if it was recited before the festival at the time of constructing the sukkah, as explained in the Gemara, and if so, the "Shehecheyanu" of the night should not be less significant than that recited before the festival. But Megillah is different because the primary miracle occurred during the day. Therefore, they did not establish the mitzvot of Purim, such as sending portions and the feast, except during the day. Furthermore, ideally, one should recite "Shehecheyanu" on the mitzvot of Purim, such as joy, the feast, and sending portions. However, to establish a specific blessing for them, the sages did not see fit, because all festive days are days of feasting and joy. Nevertheless, it is appropriate to recite "Shehecheyanu" on the Megillah and intend to include the sending of portions and the Purim feast, as the great authorities (Magen Avraham and Shlah) have written. And so, the simple custom in these lands is to recite "Shehecheyanu" also during the daytime reading of the Megillah, and it should not be changed.

The blessing that follows [the reading of the Megillah]—its essence is not related to the Megillah (Ran, beginning of the chapter "HaKoreh Omed"). Therefore, it begins with "Baruch" (Blessed), and it is considered to be adjacent to the blessing that precedes it. It is not similar to the blessing over the Torah, which was primarily instituted for completing the Torah portion, but later it was decreed because of those who enter and exit that each person should bless before and after, and the original enactment remained to begin the final blessing with "Baruch." However, regarding the Megillah, if it had been instituted specifically for the Megillah, it would not begin with "Baruch." Rather, it is a blessing of thanksgiving (Ran), and it was attached after the Megillah. Therefore, it begins with "Baruch," because it is a matter in itself. Hence, we learned in the Mishnah at the beginning of the third chapter: In a place where they are accustomed to bless—they should bless, etc. And it depends on custom, because it is not inherently related to the Megillah. Therefore, we ruled in Siman 692 that even if one interrupted in between, it does not invalidate [the blessing], see there in paragraph 10, because it is not considered an interruption between the reading and the blessing, since the blessing is not directly related to it.

The wording of the blessing in the Tur: "The God who contends our contention, who judges our judgment, who avenges our vengeance, who exacts retribution for us from our oppressors, and who repays all the enemies of our souls. Blessed are You, Hashem, who exacts retribution for His people Israel from all their oppressors, the God who saves." See there. It opens with "Blessed" and concludes with "Blessed" because it is a long blessing containing many matters. And the reason it concludes with two matters: "who exacts retribution..." and "the God who saves," even though we do not usually conclude with two themes – here it is considered one matter, as salvation is not complete without retribution from our enemies (Beit Yosef). And the phrase at the opening "The God who contends..." – in the Rif it begins with "contends," since "Our God" was already mentioned at the start. However, because in the psalm "Ayelet Hashachar," which refers to Esther, she cried out: "My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?!" and since this holy name is associated with kindness, as it is written: "The kindness of God all day" – therefore we say this, because this name helped us (Bach). That is why it concludes with "the God who saves." In the Rambam, it also concludes with "the God who exacts retribution..." See there. (And the main point is that during the time of the destruction – the name of Hashem is not revealed until the future, if Hashem wills. But the name "El" is forever, and this was her cry. Delve and you will find it easy.)

After this blessing, it is customary to say the piyut "Asher Heni'a" and "Shoshanat Yaakov… Arur Haman… Baruch Mordechai…". During Shacharit, however, "Asher Heni'a" is not recited because piyutim have already been said. But "Shoshanat Yaakov" is recited because it is necessary to say "Arur Haman," as it is stated in the Jerusalem Talmud which we brought in Siman 690, see there. If one did not recite the blessings, neither before nor after, he has fulfilled his obligation, as the blessings are not essential. Therefore, one person can recite the blessings and another can read the Megillah. Our Rabbi the Rema wrote that the blessing after the Megillah is only recited in a public setting. This is his language. And the reason can be said to be that since it is not directly related to the Megillah itself, but is a blessing of gratitude due to the publicizing of the miracle, it was only ordained for a public setting where there is publicity, and not for an individual. Note that this is brought in the name of the Jerusalem Talmud (Beit Yosef in the name of the Or Zarua). I have not found this in the Jerusalem Talmud, and none of the early authorities mentioned it. In Shibolei HaLeket, it is brought that the custom of two yeshivot was to recite the blessing after the Megillah even as an individual, and it seems that this is indeed the custom of the world.

There is an opinion that if the reader becomes mute in the middle of reading the Megillah, the second reader must start from the beginning. However, the blessing is fulfilled by the first reader, who recited it on behalf of the entire congregation (Magen Avraham, subsection 2). Many disagree with this and hold that the second reader only needs to start from where the first one stopped (Eliyah Rabbah, Shevut Yaakov, the Gaon Rabbi Akiva Eiger, and Chayei Adam). And this is the main ruling. This is unlike the Torah reading in Siman 284, where each person reads for himself. But the Megillah is read for the entire congregation, and it is similar to the shofar, where the second person starts from where the first one stopped, as I have written in Siman 585.

Megillah: Even though one has already fulfilled their obligation, they may still recite the blessing and read to fulfill the obligation for others. When reading for women, one should recite the blessing "to hear the reading of the Megillah," because there are those who say that they are only commanded to hear it, not to read it, as I have written in Siman 689 (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 5). And there are those who say that it is better to read for women after he has already heard it in the synagogue, because "with the multitude of people is the glory of the King" (ibid.). In my humble opinion, it seems that since the Megillah, when read at its proper time, can be read individually, as I have written in Siman 690, it is preferable that he reads and fulfills his obligation as well, and recites the blessing "on the reading of the Megillah," rather than having already fulfilled his obligation and then reading it again not for his own need. 

Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef wrote in paragraph 2 that one should not converse while it is being read. Thus far his words. There are those who interpret this as referring to the blessing, and this is also implied by the Tur, who wrote that the Eitur said: Since this blessing is dependent on custom, one should not reprimand someone who converses during its reading. The Tur objected to this, arguing that since, ultimately, a blessing is recited, it is forbidden to interrupt. Rabbeinu the Beit Yosef ruled according to the Tur (Taz, subparagraph 2). There are those who interpret this as referring to the Megillah itself (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 4). There is no practical difference, for in both cases, interruptions are forbidden. 

If the listener interrupted during the Megillah reading, they have not fulfilled their obligation, as I have written in Siman 690, because in any case, they did not hear some words from the reader. If the reader interrupted, they have fulfilled their obligation, as I have written there. (And the words of the Magen Avraham in subparagraph 4, who permits the reader to initially interrupt, require great scrutiny. See there and in Machatzit Hashekel.)

Our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 4: If someone is somewhat compelled and cannot go to the synagogue and must wait until after the congregation has read [the Megillah], and it is difficult for him to fast for so long – he can hear its reading during the day, from Plag HaMincha and onwards. But it is forbidden to eat before hearing the reading of the Megillah, even if fasting is difficult for him. So far their words. And they compared this to the evening prayer, which we consider night from Plag HaMincha. But this is perplexing, for what is the connection between the two? There it depends on sacrifices, but here, where the night reading is learned from "and night, and not silence for me" – it is obvious that until the stars come out, it is not night (Pri Chadash). And certainly, this is perplexing aside from that, for it is still not the fourteenth day (and also the Gra in section 10 agreed with the Pri Chadash). And we have never heard of anyone doing so. And what they wrote that it is forbidden to eat before the Megillah – but tasting [a small amount] is permitted if necessary (Magen Avraham section 7). And before its reading, it is forbidden to eat even half an hour before the time, even if one has already prayed the evening prayer (ibid.), but tasting is permitted. And learning is permitted, and we do not worry that he might forget and not read [the Megillah] like with the search for chametz, because since it is dear to him – he will not forget (ibid.). And the daytime reading is after sunrise. If he is compelled, he can read it after dawn (ibid.).

After the reading of the Megillah at night, we recite "Ve'ata Kadosh". It would be appropriate to begin with "Uva LeTzion Goel" because it is a time of redemption. Indeed, in the Siddur of Rav Amram it is written this way, as the Tur mentions. However, the Tur writes that we do not follow this practice because the primary redemption does not occur at night, see there. Regarding the recitation of "Ve'ata Kadosh": it seems to me that since we recounted the miracles that the Holy One, blessed be He, performed for us, we say "Ve'ata Kadosh Yoshev Tehilot Yisrael" (And You are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel), meaning that, so to speak, the essence of His blessed nature is the praises of Israel. Therefore, He rejoices in our well-being and, conversely, feels distress, Heaven forbid, in our time of trouble. This is why we recite "Ve'ata Kadosh" both on Tisha B'Av and on Purim.

If Purim falls on Saturday night, "Vayehi Noam" is also recited, and afterwards a full Kaddish with "Tiskabel" is said. However, after the Shemoneh Esrei and before the reading of the Megillah, "Tiskabel" should not be recited, for it is inappropriate to say "Tiskabel" twice in one prayer service. Some authorities have written to say the Half Kaddish before the Megillah (Levush and Taz). Nonetheless, in customs, it is written to say the full Kaddish, yet certainly without "Tiskabel." The common practice is to say "Tiskabel" after the Shemoneh Esrei and also after "V'ata Kadosh." This is perplexing, and it has already been questioned (there). In any case: if "Tiskabel" is said after the Shemoneh Esrei, it should not be said after "V'ata Kadosh" (Magen Avraham). The most correct practice is that the primary "Tiskabel Tzelotahon" is for the Shemoneh Esrei, and hence it should not be said afterwards. This is the appropriate practice to establish. Also, see what I wrote above, at the beginning of Siman 599, section 3.

When Purim falls on Saturday night, it would be appropriate to recite the Havdalah before the reading of the Megillah. How can we benefit from the light without having first recited the blessing "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh"? At the very least, we should recite the blessing "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh" before reading the Megillah. However, this is not the custom. The reason for this is that everyone needs to recite Havdalah at home and must also recite "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh" for their household. Why should one recite it twice? Therefore, in the synagogue, we also do not recite Havdalah before the Megillah. Additionally, it is our principle to delay Havdalah as much as possible to not completely remove the sanctity of Shabbat from upon us. 

As for benefiting from the light during the reading of the Megillah before reciting "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh," there is no concern in this, as we do not find any prohibition against benefiting from the light before this blessing. After all, we have already recited in the morning the blessing "Yotzer Ha'Me'orot," and there is no issue of benefiting from this world without a blessing. The blessing "Borei Me'orei Ha'esh" is because of its creation on Saturday night, as explained in the Talmud. Thus, our custom is proper.

Know that "Vayiten Lecha" is recited after "Ve'ata Kadosh" or after Havdalah, according to the custom on all Saturday nights. When Purim falls on Saturday night, care should be taken not to bring the Megillah to the synagogue on Shabbat, as it is prohibited to prepare from Shabbat to a weekday. Even through a minor, it is not appropriate. Instead, one should prepare it before Shabbat or bring it after Maariv. However, if one wants to study and expound upon it on Shabbat itself, it might be permissible to bring it, as this is for the sake of Shabbat, since it is permitted to study it on Shabbat. Nevertheless, we are cautious to avoid this situation (see Sha'arei Teshuvah).

One recites "Al HaNisim" on the night and day of the fourteenth, but not on the fifteenth. It is recited both in the prayer and in the Grace After Meals. If one did not say it, they are not required to repeat it, just as on Hanukkah, because there is no additional offering on these days. Even on the night of the fourteenth, although the Megillah has not yet been read, "Al HaNisim" is recited. However, on the night of the fifteenth and during the day of the fifteenth, it is not recited; nonetheless, if one did recite it, it is not considered an interruption, and they are not required to repeat it, since for those in walled cities, the main day of Purim is the fifteenth. Hallel was not instituted for Purim because the reading of the Megillah stands in place of Hallel. Additionally, on the festivals and on Hanukkah, we say "Praise the servants of the Lord..." and not the servants of Pharaoh or Antiochus. But on Purim, we are still the servants of Ahasuerus (as stated in the Gemara 14b). One does not fall on their face (for Tachanun) on Purim. "Lamnatzeach" and "El Erech Apayim" are not recited. It is appropriate to say the Psalm "Ayelet HaShachar" on Purim, as it is expounded to refer to Esther, as is well known. "Mizmor LeTodah" is recited.

They take out a Torah scroll and read "Vayavo Amalek" with three people. It contains only nine verses, even though normally one does not read less than ten verses. For this reason, some repeat the last verse.
