However, our custom is not like this, as it is explicitly stated in the Gemara (Megillah 23b) regarding the haftarah: where the topic concludes, it is different. Here too, in the Purim portion. This is also written by Tosafot and the Rosh (Megillah 21b, s.v. "Ein," see there). After that, they read the Megillah. Afterward, "Ashrei" and "U'va LeTzion." It is proper not to remove the tefillin until after the reading of the Megillah, as it is written in it "gladness and honor," and it is expounded: "gladness" – this is circumcision, "honor" – this is tefillin. Therefore, when there is a circumcision on Purim, they circumcise the infant before the reading of the Megillah, so that we can read "gladness." However, if it is not possible to perform the circumcision in the synagogue, and if they go before the Megillah reading they will not hear the Megillah – they circumcise afterward (see what I wrote above in Siman 137, Se'if 1).

It is a positive commandment of the Megillah of Esther to give gifts to the poor, as it is written: "and sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor." The rule of sending portions will be explained in the following section. And since it is written "and gifts to the poor" in the plural form – therefore, one is obligated to distribute to the poor on the day of Purim, and one should not give less than to two poor people. And one gives to each one a gift: either money, or types of cooked dishes, or types of food (Rambam). And we are not scrupulous about Purim money, saying "this one is honest" and "this one is deceitful and does not need to be given to." Rather, whoever extends their hand to take – we give to them, and we do not need to scrutinize them (ibid.).

It is preferable for a person to increase gifts to the poor rather than to increase his feast and send many portions. For there is no greater and more glorious joy than to gladden the hearts of the poor, orphans, and widows. The one who gladdens the hearts of these unfortunate ones is likened to the Divine Presence, as it is said: "To revive the spirit of the lowly and to revive the heart of the contrite" (Isaiah 57:15). One fulfills the obligation whether giving to men or women, and even to boys and girls, for they too need sustenance. It seems to me that if one gives to a man and his wife, or to a man and his son or daughter who are under his care, he does not fulfill the obligation of giving to two poor people, for they are considered one. One must give specifically on Purim itself. But before Purim, even if one gives explicitly for Purim, it does not suffice, for this is an obligation of the day itself. It is obvious that one does not need to give personally; he may give through an agent. He may appoint an agent before Purim to give gifts to the poor on his behalf on Purim. Women are also obligated in this mitzvah, for in all the mitzvot of Purim, women are obligated as men. It seems to me that a man and his wife fulfill the obligation with two gifts, for they are considered as one body. But his son and daughter who depend on his table must give separately. One may not give gifts to the poor from tithe money or from charity funds that have already been designated. Even a poor person who goes door to door must give two gifts to two other poor people, just as with the Hanukkah lights and the four cups.

It appears to me that although in the Torah "ani" (poor) and "evyon" (destitute) are two different things, as it is written in Deuteronomy: "You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and destitute," and they are two different things as it states in Bava Metzia (111b) that an "evyon" is more afflicted than a "ani". The term "evyon" refers to someone who longs for something and cannot attain it (Rashi there), and in this regard, an "evyon" has no shame in asking, whereas an "ani" does have shame. And we say there regarding a hired worker, that an "ani" takes precedence over an "evyon" (see there). Nevertheless, in any case, they are two different things, and since in the Megillah it is written "gifts to the evyonim" – should we say that it is specifically an "evyon" and not an "ani"? 

However, this is not so. And the proof is that in the portion of "Re'eh" it is written, "If there is a destitute person among you... because there will never cease to be destitute in the land... you shall surely open your hand to your brother, to your poor and to your destitute in your land" – behold, he began with "evyon" and concluded with both, implying that they are the same. And that which is written "gifts to the evyonim" – it is a greater novelty: not only an "ani" who has shame, and in the payment of a hired worker he takes precedence, but even to an "evyon" – you fulfill your obligation, even though he himself asks from you, and certainly to an "ani" who is ashamed to ask, and you preempt and give him – there is a greater mitzvah.

It seems to me that the custom is to give Purim money to all those involved in sacred work: the rabbis, the cantors, the sextons, and the like. And this is proper, as these individuals look forward to receiving Purim money. Nevertheless, one does not fulfill the obligation of gifts to the poor with this. It is not only if they are not poor, but even if they are poor, one does not fulfill the obligation, because for them, it is considered as something fixed and obligatory, and it does not relate to the gifts to the poor that are a Purim obligation. Some make a mistake in this, but to me, it seems clear as I have written.

It is taught in the Tosefta of Megillah (Chapter One): The collection for Purim is for Purim, and the collection for the city is for that city. We are not meticulous with the collection for Purim; rather, we buy calves, slaughter them, and eat them, and the remainder falls into the charity fund. Rabbi Eliezer says: One should not make straps for his sandals from the collection for Purim. This is the end of his statement, and this is its explanation: In their time, they would make a collection before Purim from the householders to feed meat to the poor on Purim. He says that the collector and the townspeople are forbidden to divert it for another purpose, even if it seems to them that less would suffice for the poor. Similarly, the collection of this city should not be given to another. And although they are permitted to make changes sometimes, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 259, nevertheless here there was an ordinance not to change it at all. They buy meat with all the money, and the poor eat as much as they want, and if there is any leftover, it falls to charity. According to Rabbi Eliezer, even the poor person himself is forbidden to change it. This is not the case according to the Tanna Kamma, and the law does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. The Tur ruled according to Rabbi Eliezer, and they were astonished at him, and wrote that his version was "Rabbi Akiva," and the law follows Rabbi Akiva. However, the Tosefta is brought in Bava Metzia (78b), and it is proven there that the law does not follow Rabbi Eliezer. In our times, there is no collection for Purim at all.

And this is what our rabbis, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, wrote in section 2: "One should not divert Purim funds to other charities. This applies specifically to the collectors, but the poor person may use it for whatever he desires." Thus far is their wording. There is an opinion that this applies specifically to the collectors, but the townspeople can divert it like other charity funds (Mordechai). However, the Tur wrote that even the townspeople cannot divert it, as per the simple language of the Tosefta (Magen Avraham, subsection 5). There is also an opinion that money intended in one's heart to be distributed on Purim cannot be diverted (ibid., subsection 4). This is according to those who hold in Yoreh De'ah, section 258, that charity is considered a vow even if intended only in thought. See there, and in Choshen Mishpat, the end of section 252.

We have already written that one is not particular about Purim money, and whoever extends their hand to take – we give them. And in a place where it is customary to give even to a non-Jew – we give, for the sake of peaceful relations. For all types of charity we certainly give to them, as I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 251. However, since Purim money is specifically for the joy of Purim, it is proper to give it only to Jews. Nevertheless, wherever it is customary to give – that is the custom. And our teacher, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Siman 4: In a place where there are no poor people, one may keep his Purim money for himself and give it wherever he wishes. This is his language, meaning: even in another city, since there are no poor people in his city.

Rabbi Moshe Isserles (Rema) wrote in Section 1: Some say that one should give before Purim a half of the coin that is established in that place and at that time, as a remembrance of the half-shekel that they used to give in Adar. And since "Terumah" (donation) is written three times in the portion, one should give three. And it should be given on the night of Purim, before praying Mincha. And this is the custom in all these countries. And in these countries, one should give three large halves, because there is no coin that only has "half" written on it. And in the country of Austria, they should give three half-Weiner, which are also called "half." And so in every country. And only one who is twenty years old and above is obligated to give it. And some say that one should give a half-shekel to charity, besides these three halves, but this is not the custom. Thus far his words. According to this, in our country of Russia, we should give three half-Kopecks, which is the smallest coin. And with a larger coin, three half-Rubles. Besides these two, there is no half. And what he wrote: from twenty years old - this is not the opinion of Rambam in the first chapter of Shekalim and most of the poskim. They hold that anyone from thirteen years old and above is obligated to give the half-shekel. And a minor whose father began to give on his behalf should not stop. And also, the Kohanim and Levites are obligated in the half-shekel, but not women and minors (see Magen Avraham, subparagraph 3). And one can give the half-shekel money to any place they want. It is not necessarily for the repair of the synagogue, which is like the maintenance of the House, as it is only for remembrance. The main half-shekel was for sacrifices, which does not apply now. And some give the half-shekel money to the cantor, and there is no concern in this (ibid.). And it is also customary to give Megillah money to the reader, and there is no prohibition or obligation in this matter.

It is a mitzvah to increase in the Purim feast, as it is written: "joy and feasting." And what is the obligation of this feast? That one should eat meat and prepare a fine meal according to what one can afford. This is what the Rambam wrote, and it implies that meat is certainly required, for without it, the feast has no significance. However, other foods should be prepared as on a festival. By having one meal during the day, one fulfills their obligation, and at night, there is no need to increase the feast. A Purim feast eaten at night, whether on the night of the 14th or the night of the 15th, does not fulfill one's obligation, as it is written: "days of feasting" – days and not nights. Nevertheless, one should also rejoice at night and slightly increase the meal after the Megillah reading. And even if Purim falls on the night after Shabbat, when one is already satisfied from Shabbat, it is still appropriate to rejoice with a small meal.

In the Gemara (Megillah 7b) it is stated: A person is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim until he does not know the difference between "Cursed is Haman" and "Blessed is Mordechai." This is perplexing because if so, one would need to be as drunk as Lot! The Rambam did not write in this manner; rather, he wrote that one drinks wine until becoming intoxicated and falls asleep in his intoxication. This is his language. Perhaps he interpreted "until he does not know..." to mean because he falls asleep. This is similar to what our teacher, the Rema, wrote, and this is his language: "And some say that one does not need to become so intoxicated, but rather should drink more than what one is accustomed to and sleep, and from sleeping, one would not know the difference between 'Cursed is Haman' and 'Blessed is Mordechai.'" Whether one does more or less, the main thing is to direct one's heart towards Heaven. This is his language, and it aligns with the words of the Rambam.

However, it is not understood: according to this, why did the Talmud use the unusual phrase "until he does not know…" – it should have said: "he is obligated to become intoxicated until he falls asleep"? Therefore, it seems more likely that Rambam did not intend to interpret the Talmud this way, but rather he rejected this statement from the law, as the Ran wrote in the name of Rabbeinu Ephraim. Since it is explained in the Talmud that an incident occurred because of this, see there, it was rejected from the law. But the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote exactly in the language of the Talmud: "until he does not know etc.," and this is puzzling. Some have written that they had a song that ended with "Cursed is Haman" and "Blessed is Mordechai," and it was a long song, and when one is slightly intoxicated – he cannot say it all. Others have written in regard to the numbers, that in terms of numbers they are equal, and when one is slightly intoxicated – he cannot calculate. And the Tosafot wrote that the intention is according to the Jerusalem Talmud: "Cursed… Cursed is Zeresh… Cursed are all the wicked, Blessed are all the righteous," see there, and their intention is that in this there is some length. And when one is intoxicated – it is difficult to say it all (Beit Yosef).

And there is an interpretation that "until one does not know…" means: until one cannot decide which was a greater good for us, whether the downfall of Haman or the elevation of Mordechai (see Taz). And in the Hagahot Maimoniot in the name of the Ra’avyah, it is written that this is a mitzvah but not an absolute requirement, see there. And it is not understood, for it uses obligatory language: "A person is obligated to become intoxicated…". And it can be explained that the meaning is: "A person is obligated to become intoxicated" – meaning this is an obligation on everyone "until one does not know…", that is to say: the drinker has the permission to drink "until one does not know…". For certainly, not all people are the same in this, and it says that the obligation is on everyone – each according to his level, and the permission is "until one does not know…": even if one drinks until he does not know – we do not rebuke him.

However, our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in his great book wrote in the name of the Orchot Chaim, and this is his language: A person is obligated to become intoxicated on Purim. Not to become drunk, as drunkenness is a complete prohibition. There is no greater sin than this, as it leads to sexual immorality, bloodshed, and many other sins. Rather, one should drink a bit more than his usual amount. Until here is his language, and it is difficult: if so, what does "until one does not know..." mean? And if it is explained according to any of the interpretations that have been clarified, how did our teacher, the Beit Yosef, leave his words in the Shulchan Aruch, where it clearly implies complete drunkenness? This requires investigation. (And perhaps they will explain: "up to but not including." Practically, one should avoid drunkenness, especially the drinking of hard liquor, as in his drunkenness he will be filled with vomit and excrement, and only drink a bit more than his usual amount and sleep a little.)

It is forbidden to fast on Purim, except for a fast due to a disturbing dream. Even in this case, some forbid it, as I have written in Siman 684 regarding the eve of Yom Kippur. Therefore, one should fast only until after Mincha and then eat (Magen Avraham, subsection 4). Regarding one who has taken an oath to fast on Purim, there is a dispute whether the oath takes effect, as I have written at the beginning of Siman 571; see there. Therefore, one should seek to annul the oath (see Magen Avraham, subsection 4, and examine carefully, and you will find it easy). If the oath is not annulled, it is difficult to permit him to eat; see what I have written in Siman 571.

The Maharil would wear Shabbat clothes on Purim. The meal should be held during the day and not, as is the common custom, beginning close to evening. Our custom is to fulfill the obligation of the meal with a daytime meal, using high-quality bread and preparing significant dishes. One meal is sufficient; more is not necessary, as I have written. Nevertheless, we should justify the custom of the world, for indeed, in the morning, people also eat a Yom Tov meal: meat, fish, and latkes, which are important foods, and also pickled vegetables, called "tzimmes," which are Shabbat and Yom Tov foods. However, the important bread used for the meal, called "kitka," is reserved for the evening. Yet, it is still an important meal, and one can fulfill the obligation of the meal with it. It is good to also use the important bread for the morning meal, and this is our custom. I have seen someone who is uncertain if one fulfills the obligation of the meal with good foods without bread (see Shaarei Teshuvah). To me, it seems that one does not fulfill the obligation, similar to Shabbat and Yom Tov. Additionally, there is no festive meal without bread, as it is written regarding Lot: "He made them a feast, and baked unleavened bread, and they ate"; and concerning Daniel, it is written: "He ate bread and drank wine at their feast." (The Magen Avraham in sub-section 9 did not write this, but in my humble opinion, it seems as I have written.)

And our master, the Rema, wrote in paragraph 2: "It is customary to have the Purim feast after Mincha. Ma'ariv is prayed at night, and Mincha is prayed first while it is still broad daylight. Most of the feast should be during the day, and not as is the custom to begin close to evening. The main part of the feast is on the night of the fifteenth. And when Purim falls on a Friday, the feast should be held in the morning, in honor of Shabbat. And whoever wishes to always hold it in the morning has the permission to do so." Thus is his language. And the reason it is not always the custom to hold it in the morning is because people are busy with the sending of portions (mishloach manot), giving charity, and other matters. And it is a mitzvah to increase the lighting of candles towards the evening, as it is written: "The Jews had light." (There are those who wrote that some have the custom not to eat meat on the night of the fourteenth, so that it should not be said that they fulfill the obligation of the feast at night. This is an astonishing matter, and this is not the custom. See also Taz.)

There is also a writing: Some say that one should eat legumes on Purim, in remembrance of the legumes that Daniel and his companions ate in Babylon. Thus far his words, and I am puzzled: Why mention that Daniel ate, as this is not related to Purim? Indeed, Esther herself ate legumes, as it is stated in Megillah (13a) on the verse: "and she and her maidens were pleased with the best things" – Rabbi Yochanan said that she ate legumes, see there. And there are those who wrote that legumes are for the first night (Magen Avraham, Siman Katan 7). I do not know why it is for the night, and the custom is to eat them during the day. He also wrote that it is good to engage a bit in Torah study before starting the meal, and the support for this is from the verse "The Jews had light and joy," and we interpret "light" as Torah. And one is obliged in feasting and joy a bit on both days, the fourteenth and fifteenth, and so is the custom. Thus far his words.

Furthermore, it is written: "There are those who say that if one person caused damage to another during the joy of Purim, he is exempt from paying." This is his language. Meaning: he did not intend to cause damage, but intended to rejoice, and as a result of the joy, damage was caused. And we have already written this in Choshen Mishpat at the end of Siman 378. However, nowadays, due to our many sins, all joy is mixed, and we do not customarily rejoice to such an extent that it leads to damage. Therefore, now if damage is caused, he is liable to pay. And even in ancient times, he was liable for bodily harm (Magen Avraham, subparagraph 7).

One recites "Al Hanisim" in the Grace After Meals in the blessing of the land, after "Nodeh Lecha" and before "Ve'al Hakol." If one began their meal during the day and it extended into the night, one still recites "Al Hanisim," as we follow the beginning of the meal. Some say not to recite it, but the custom follows the first opinion, which is the primary ruling. However, if one prayed the evening service in the middle of the meal, it appears that one should not mention "Al Hanisim" in the Grace After Meals (and this is also implied by the Magen Avraham at the end of subparagraph 9, in the name of Mateh Moshe, see there). Some say that even if one prayed in the middle of the meal, one should still say "Al Hanisim" in the Grace After Meals. There are those who acted accordingly (Sha'arei Teshuvah in the name of Ya'avetz). In my humble opinion, this is not the case. (And what the Magen Avraham wrote there in the name of Mordechai about parchment - this refers to Shabbat, and when they ate before nightfall according to their custom, as written in Terumat Hadeshen, siman 1, that after the Shabbat meal, sunset occurred, see there.)

It has already been explained that if one did not say "Al HaNissim" in the prayer, he is not required to repeat it. Some say that if one did not say "Al HaNissim" in the Grace After Meals during the meal, he is required to repeat it, because this meal is obligatory (Magen Avraham, subsection 9, in the name of the Rashal and the Shlah). This is surprising: for prayer is certainly obligatory, and yet it does not prevent fulfillment (i.e., one does not need to repeat the prayer). And if it is because this meal is the main expression of joy for the miracle, and therefore it is essential – I do not understand what one has to do with the other. For giving thanks for the miracle – we read the Megillah, and the blessing after the Megillah. But that it should be an essential part of the Grace After Meals – this is surprising. And this is not mentioned in the Talmud or the early authorities. (And the Magen Avraham there dismisses it, because there is no obligation to eat bread. And this is not necessary, for even when there is an obligation to eat bread, as I wrote in Siman 695, subsection 7, nevertheless, that it should be essential in the Grace After Meals is surprising. Furthermore, he can say in "Harachaman": "The Merciful One will perform for us miracles and wonders, as You have done...," as I wrote regarding Chanukah. And even according to their words, if he ate once and mentioned "Al HaNissim" – it is obvious that he does not need to repeat it during the meal. For by law, it is sufficient to say it once, as the Magen Avraham wrote there.)

It is a positive commandment of the Megillah to send portions of food to one another. We require two portions, as it is written "portions" in the plural form. And one fulfills this obligation by sending to one person, as it is written "to his friend" – in the singular form. And even by sending to a wealthy person, one fulfills the obligation. And although in Nehemiah it is written "send portions to those who have nothing prepared," which implies to someone who does not have, or who did not set up an Eruv Tavshilin as our Sages expounded in the second chapter of Beitzah – this was because it was on Rosh Hashanah, when this obligation does not apply. And he only mentioned sending to those who do not have, so that they would have something to eat. However, on Purim – it is a commandment. And the reason is due to the joy, and not because the recipient does not have something to eat. Therefore, even to a wealthy person – one fulfills the obligation. Additionally, it cannot be said that it is only for the poor, because the commandment of gifts to the poor is a separate mitzvah.

It is clear that one must send two types of food, or two types of drinks, or one type of food and one type of drink. This is explicitly stated in the Gemara (7a) where one person sent to his friend meat and wine, see there. But two pieces of one type do not suffice. Just because they are cut into two pieces, does that make them two? And Rambam wrote: One must also send two portions of meat, or two types of food, or two types of cooked dishes, see there. Thus, he wrote "two types," and necessarily one must say that "two portions of meat" means from two types of meat. Or it is possible that this is a printing error, and it should say: "two types of meat like two types of food…"

It further appears to me that in this case, it is not sufficient to send just an olive's bulk or a quarter-log; rather, a respectable portion is required. This is implied by the term "portions," akin to a piece worthy of honor, which should be something significant. Those who send small pieces have not fulfilled their obligation. And whoever increases the sending of portions is praiseworthy, for this increases joy. If one cannot afford to send significant items and still have enough for themselves for the joy of Purim, they can send their meal to their friend, and their friend sends their meal to them, and thereby both fulfill the mitzvah. (From Rashi's commentary, it seems that both fulfill their obligation through a single sending when they eat together, as this is also considered a joyous sending of portions for the other, as explained by the Bach. However, the Rambam and other poskim do not hold this view. It is obvious that one must send something ready for immediate eating and drinking, like roasted or cooked food. But if one sends raw food, they have not fulfilled their obligation.)

Sending portions is to be done during the day and not at night, similar to gifts to the poor. If one sent at night, he has not fulfilled the obligation. If one sent portions to his friend and the friend does not want to accept them, or forgives him, he has fulfilled the obligation. However, if the messenger lost them before they reached the intended recipient, he has not fulfilled the obligation. If he appointed a messenger before Purim to send portions on his behalf on Purim day, he has fulfilled the obligation, as a person's messenger is like himself. If one sent portions to Shimon, and Shimon is not at home but is in the city and will return home during the day, he has fulfilled the obligation. But if Shimon is not in the city and will not return home during the day, he has not fulfilled the obligation, even if Shimon's wife or household members accepted it on his behalf. For it is written "sending portions one to another," and it requires that it reach his friend, who should at least be aware of it.

There is a doubt regarding someone who sent portions to his friend who is far away before Purim, and they will arrive to him on Purim, whether he has fulfilled the obligation of sending portions. There are those who say that he has fulfilled it (Be'er Heitev, subsection 8, in the name of some authorities). However, it seems to me that he has not fulfilled it, because we require the sending of portions to be on Purim itself. Furthermore, the main reason for sending portions is for joy, and what joy does he have now from something that was sent earlier? And if he sent types of meat, and they were later found to be non-kosher – certainly he has not fulfilled it. Similarly, if he sent money, or an object, or even types of food that are not fit for consumption as they are, such as raw meat – he has not fulfilled it. I have seen someone who is uncertain about a fish with an egg on it, whether this is considered two portions, like in the laws of Eruv Tavshilin (there)? It seems to me that as I wrote in section 15 that we require something of significance – consequently, the egg on the fish does not count as one portion, and similarly in all similar cases.

Women are obligated in the sending of portions (mishloach manot), and even though it is written "a man to his friend," since all the commandments of Purim obligate women as they do men. And the term "man" is not meant to exclude a woman, just as it says in "Mishpatim": "And if a man opens a pit," "And if a man’s ox gores," for the entire Torah is written in the masculine form. And a woman should send to a woman, and a man to a man, for it is not proper to foster closeness between a man and a woman. And sometimes this could even raise concerns of betrothal if she is single. But regarding gifts to the poor, there is no concern, since this is a form of charity – there is no fostering of closeness, nor concern of betrothal. All women are obligated in the sending of portions and in gifts to the poor, and even if she has a husband – she is not exempt through her husband, for this is a commandment that is incumbent upon her (see Magen Avraham, subsection 14, and our women are careful and send portions). There is uncertainty if one fulfills the obligation if they send to a minor. In my humble opinion, it seems that one does fulfill the obligation, as it is written "to his friend," and a minor is also included, as is proven from the verse "if a man’s ox gores his friend’s ox," and one is liable for goring a minor’s ox.

Purim is permissible for performing work. And even though it is written "feasting and joy and a holiday," and on a holiday work is forbidden, in truth, they did not accept it upon themselves as a holiday. And the proof is that it is written: "to establish for them... to make them days of feasting and joy...", and it does not say a holiday. Nevertheless, in a place where the custom is not to perform work, it is forbidden to work (Orach Chaim 686:5). And one who performs work on Purim will never see a sign of blessing from that work (ibid.).

The early authorities wrote: Even though labor was not initially accepted upon them, afterward it was accepted as a custom. And they curse anyone who performs labor on it, since its prohibition spread throughout all of Israel. However, joyous construction, such as building a wedding hall for his son, or a pavilion for dignitaries, is permitted. Likewise, labor for a mitzvah is permitted, such as writing for a mitzvah. It is permissible to write legal rulings and biblical interpretations, which bring a person joy, as it is written: "The precepts of the Lord are right, rejoicing the heart." Writing a letter of greeting or reminding someone of their debts, and anything that does not require great focus, seems to be permitted (Beit Yosef). For the needs of the day itself, it is permissible to do even complete labors, even though it could have been done earlier. Additionally, there is no custom to prohibit commerce, because this brings joy (Taz, subsection 1), and therefore it is customary to sit in shops. Nonetheless, one who sets his ways should minimize sitting in the shop on Purim. There are those who fear God who do not open their shops on Purim. And it is permissible to have labor done by a non-Jew.

It appears to me that setting out on a journey from one’s home on Purim is not proper, for the primary rejoicing is with his household, as it is written: "And you shall rejoice, you and your household" regarding the second tithe; and regarding the festivals it is written: "And you shall rejoice, you and your son and your daughter"; unless the journey is necessary for him. And it is a mitzvah to be at home on Purim with his wife and children. And even if he is traveling on the road and is compelled to stop somewhere for the reading of the Megillah – he should also stay for a few hours to fulfill the Purim feast, the sending of portions, and gifts to the poor. It does not suffice that his household gives on his behalf; it is possible that for gifts to the poor he fulfills the obligation, but for sending portions not in his presence – it is certainly not valid at all.

And our teacher, Rabbi Yosef Caro, wrote in section 2: Even in a place where there is a custom, it is only customary on the day of the Megillah reading. But to prohibit one day’s observance for the other is not a custom. Thus are his words, and there is a doubt regarding his intention: Whether he means that there is no custom anywhere to prohibit the fifteenth (of Adar) in unwalled cities and the fourteenth in walled cities, and if so, if a place is found that has such a custom, it is forbidden. Or his intention is: Even if such a custom exists, it is not a valid custom, and we do not pay attention to such a deficient custom. For there are customs that one should not rely upon, as it is stated at the end of chapter fourteen of Tractate Soferim, that any custom which does not have support from the Torah is like an error in judgment, see there. And women have the custom not to work also on the fifteenth, which we call "Shushan Purim" (Darkei Moshe in the name of Abudraham). And it is not clear to me how the custom is with us.

The fourteenth and fifteenth days [of Adar] are prohibited for eulogies and fasting, in every place and for every person, whether in walled cities from the days of Joshua bin Nun who read [the Megillah] on the fifteenth, or for the majority of the world who read on the fourteenth. This is from the Scroll of Fasting, which was not nullified regarding Chanukah and Purim. And the women who lament do so in a manner where they all lament together and clap their hands. But they do not lament where one speaks and the others respond after her. And when the deceased is buried, they do not lament or mourn, except for Torah scholars in their presence, which is permitted, as I wrote in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 340. Similarly, the prayer of Tziduk HaDin and Kaddish are not recited at graves. However, for Torah scholars in their presence, when eulogizing them, Kaddish is recited (Levush).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, ruled in section 4 that all mourning practices apply during Chanukah and Purim, as Rambam ruled in the eleventh chapter of the laws of mourning—see there. Similarly, Rabbeinu Gershom Me’or HaGolah and the Rokeach ruled (in Hagahot Maimoniyot there). And although these are days of feasting and joy, it is taught (Megillah 5b): "Joy" teaches that eulogies are forbidden, "Feasting" teaches that fasting is forbidden—see there, but not mourning (there).

And he wrote in section 5: if Purim falls on a Saturday night, and the mourner is sitting in the synagogue for Mincha on Shabbat—he should not leave until he has prayed Ma'ariv and heard the reading of the Megillah. And the next day—he should not leave his house. End of his words, meaning: Since the Megillah is read in its proper time, it is preferable that the mourner reads it at home rather than go to the synagogue. However, when he is sitting in the synagogue for Mincha on Shabbat, and has already eaten the third meal—it is better for him to wait in the synagogue for the night reading, and the next day he will read it himself at home. The same applies if he needs to go to eat the third meal—he should also read it at night individually at home. But it is obvious that if he does not have a valid Megillah, or does not know how to read it, even on a weekday he goes to the synagogue to hear the Megillah at night and during the day. And if he can gather a minyan at his home to read the Megillah—it is preferable.

(This is the intent of the Beit Yosef and the Rema. See Magen Avraham section 6 and section 10, where he wonders about them. According to what I have written—it fits well. Study and you will find it easy.)

However, the Sheiltot, and Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg, the Rosh, the Tur, and the Mordechai ruled that there is no mourning on Purim. Similarly, our teacher, the Rema, ruled in Section 4 as follows: "And there are those who say that mourning does not apply on Purim, neither on the fourteenth nor on the fifteenth. Even the first day of mourning is postponed because of Purim. But private matters of mourning do apply. And although mourning does not apply on Purim, nevertheless, the days count towards the seven days of mourning, similar to Shabbat." These are his words. It is surprising that our teacher, the Beit Yosef, at the end of Yoreh De'ah, Chapter 401, also ruled that mourning does not apply on Purim and did not bring another opinion, while here he ruled the opposite. (And therefore, some have written that here it is a printing error, and it should state: private matters of mourning apply on Purim.)

There are those who say that a mourner is obligated to send portions, meaning: although sending portions is a form of joy, and a mourner is prohibited from joy, nevertheless, it is ultimately a rabbinic positive commandment. Therefore, he is obligated to send portions even during the seven days of mourning. However, he should not send an item that brings joy. But to the mourner, portions should not be sent throughout the days of mourning, which means all thirty days, and for a father or mother, all twelve months, since they can send to others. Therefore, in a place where there is only the mourner and one other person, it is necessary to send to the mourner to fulfill the commandment, only not to send him an item that brings joy. But if the mourner is poor, it is permissible to give him anything, like any act of charity. (The Rema in paragraph 6 wrote that when there is no one else to send to except the mourner, he should send to him, unless the mourner waives his portion. This is his language. And the intention is not that he must do so and waive, but if he waives, he fulfills the obligation, as I wrote above.)

And know: In Yoreh De'ah, at the end of Siman 384, our Rabbi the Rema wrote that it is forbidden to send portions to a mourner for his father or mother for all twelve months, even on Shabbat in a place where they do not customarily inquire after his welfare on Shabbat. However, in a place where they do customarily inquire after his welfare on Shabbat, it is permitted to send him portions. Thus are his words. And according to this, there is one who says that also here, since the custom is not to observe mourning on Purim, it is permitted to send him portions (Magen Avraham, Subsection 12), and this is the intention of our Rabbi the Rema here, who wrote: "As I have written in Yoreh De'ah, Siman 384 (there)." In my humble opinion, it seems on the contrary, that his intention is: Even though regarding Shabbat it was clarified there that it is permissible, nevertheless Purim is not similar to Shabbat, as there are many opinions that mourning is observed on Purim (and also the Taz, Subsection 3, did not agree with this leniency).

Our master, the Beit Yosef, wrote in Section 7: There is an opinion that an onen (a mourner prior to the burial of a close relative) is permitted to consume meat and wine, because the individual obligation of mourning does not override the communal obligation that is based on Torah law. For rejoicing on Purim is derived from the words of the prophets, which has the status of Torah law. Thus far his words. And if you ask: Surely one can fulfill the rejoicing of Purim after the burial? The answer is that indeed this is true, but the intention is if he cannot bury the deceased on that day. And behold, our master the Rema wrote on this, and these are his words: All the more so, one is obligated in the reading of the Megillah, prayer, and recitation of the Shema. It appears to me that this applies specifically at night, even though the deceased lies before him. But during the day when he wishes to bury the deceased, the burial takes precedence, as I wrote above in Section 687. Therefore, he reads and prays afterward as explained... for it is not more stringent than Yom Tov and Shabbat... Thus far his words, and his words are puzzling (as the Magen Avraham wrote).

And it appears to me, in my humble opinion, that this is its explanation: Certainly, the words of our master, the Beit Yosef, are referring to a situation where he will not be buried today, as I have written. Therefore, although he is technically an onen (a mourner before the burial), nonetheless, the positive commandment of an individual does not override (the communal obligation of Purim). And we say: since he will not be buried today – he is permitted to eat meat and drink wine. And since we nullify his state of mourning due to the joy of Purim, all the more so he is obligated in the reading of the Megillah, prayer, and the recitation of the Shema, because since he will not be buried today – he is not a clear onen. And since it is necessary to nullify his state of mourning because of the joy of Purim – we nullify it completely. Then he states another ruling: since it has become clear to us that when he is not burying him today, we nullify his mourning, therefore, when someone dies at the beginning of the night, and it is not customary to bury at night – we nullify his mourning with respect to the reading of the Megillah, which is a communal obligation, and consequently also regarding the recitation of the Shema and prayer. But regarding meat and wine – it does not apply at night, and we do not permit it. However, during the day, when he wishes to bury him – he buries him, and afterwards fulfills all the mitzvot of Purim. And our master, the Beit Yosef, is referring to a situation where he is not burying him on that day, as I have written. (And with this, all the difficulties of the Magen Avraham are resolved, see there. Analyze and you will find it easy.)

It is permitted to marry a woman on Purim, whether on the fourteenth or the fifteenth [of Adar]. All the more so, it is permitted to perform a Pidyon HaBen [redemption of the firstborn son]. Although it is prohibited on a festival day, as we derive from the verse "And you shall rejoice in your festival" – but not with your wife, on Purim there is no such verse. Nevertheless, according to the reason that one should not mix one joy with another, it is also prohibited on Purim, and this is the agreement of the major later authorities (Magen Avraham at the end of subsection 18 and Pri Chadash). The wedding canopy should be made on the thirteenth, and certainly on the fifteenth it is permitted (this is also written by the Mordechai, cited by the Elya Zuta, that marrying on Purim is not allowed). As for the custom in ancient times of wearing costumes made of shaatnez [a forbidden mixture of wool and linen], and men dressing as women – this is no longer practiced. Additionally, if someone causes damage, they are obligated to pay. Nowadays, due to our many sins, all joy has diminished, and we are not on that level. (What the Rema wrote in section 8 was to uphold the custom of his time, but not for now.)

The first Adar is like Shevat. If the four special Torah readings were read during it, it is of no consequence, and they must be read again in the second Adar. For even according to the opinion in the Gemara (6b) that if they were read in the first Adar post facto, they have fulfilled their obligation, see there, this applies only when it was unknown that the year would be intercalated, which was relevant in the time of the Temple. But now that the calendar is set by calculation and the intercalation is known in advance, they have not fulfilled their obligation. Only regarding eulogies and fasting, the fourteenth and fifteenth of the first Adar are forbidden. And there are those who say that eulogies and fasting are also permitted, arguing that what is stated in the Gemara that it is forbidden also applies when the intercalation was unknown. But the primary halacha follows the first opinion.

Therefore, eulogizing and fasting are forbidden on "Purim Katan," which is the 14th and 15th of the first Adar. We do not fall on our faces, nor do we recite the Psalm "May the Lord answer you on the day of distress." However, other customs are not observed, and work is permitted. Some say that one should increase in feasting and joy on the 14th of the first Adar, but this is not the custom, as it is clearly implied in the Gemara there that there is no obligation in the first [Adar]. And our teacher, the Rema, wrote: However, one should still have a somewhat larger meal to satisfy those who are stringent. "And a good-hearted person is always celebrating." Up to this point are his words, meaning: the main service of God is with joy, and therefore when one's intention is for the sake of a mitzvah, it is a feast and joy of a mitzvah. And may the Lord make us rejoice with the building of the Temple and the coming of the righteous redeemer, Amen. With the help of Heaven, the laws of the Megillah and all the laws of the Shulchan Aruch Orach Chaim are concluded.
